items.title: A Confused Candor: On (Fake) News and Journalism.
items.abstract: News and journalism are daily fixtures in our lives. They represent the chief means by which we become acquainted with the distant goings-on that we care about. They are how we come to know about the various who’s, what’s, where’s, when’s, and why’s of the world. They are, in this respect, both the vanguard and the bulwark in facilitating democratic discourse. Or, at least, that’s how the platitudes go. How, exactly, news and journalism accomplish this remains somewhat mysterious. Given the bevy of journalistic genres—ranging from political and science journalism to sports and entertainment journalism—we lack a precise account of what news and journalism are and how they feature in our lives. This dissertation is dedicated to figuring this out. In Chapter 1, I broach this issue through the lens of fake news. There, I critique the received view that fake news is necessarily insincere, that it’s produced either with the intent to deceive or with an indifference toward the truth. My argument rests on the observation that many cases of bad science journalism systematically exhibit the unique political-epistemic risks associated with fake news. Chapter 2 turns to news proper. It challenges a family of theories that I call aims-based accounts of news. Found in the fake news literature, such accounts maintain that news necessarily aims at truth-telling and knowledge production. Against them, I argue that aims—no matter how we characterize them—are a poor means of securing news’s distinctive normative status, especially given the prevalence of non-epistemic aims in news production. Finally, Chapter 3 presents my positive view. There, I propose that news and journalism are functional categories. To be news, or to be a journalist, is a matter of being disposed to perform a certain set of social functions, ones relating to the enablement of our participation in civic life. A functionalist theory, I maintain, helps us make sense of why news and journalism are justifiably subject to a unique suite of norms, ones pertaining to the shaping of—or being cited as justification for—civic behavior.

items.title: Innate Fate Studies 先天命理学：谈天性、宿命与人生修养.
items.abstract: 如果天道有常，那么为什么不公平到处可见？如果天道无常，那么为何世界又井然有序？这个世界为什么是这个样子？我们自己又为什么是现在这个样子？ 作者从中国传统命理学之术“八字”出发，仰望星空，俯视流水，内察自心，寻览经典，终有豁然大通之感。文章以“吾之道”一以贯儒家心性至善论，佛学中道破执操作，道家宇宙观与内丹术，中医生命起源，命理占卜数术演化结构诸学，还宇宙客观于人心，结构性的展示了无中生有的全部过程。 总之，这是一篇用现代性系统思维融汇了中国传统文化的个人感悟记录。既描述了形而上者的道如何演化，又揭示了形而下的器——科学模型、玄学模型如何构建。内容杂而不乱，中西、古今、文理交融，用以启发困惑、痛苦、迷茫中的寻道之人。 （Given that numerous key terms in this article bear context-specific meanings that diverge significantly from their conventional interpretations in mainstream culture, existing translation tools are inadequate for producing accurate renderings. It is therefore preferable to engage directly with the original Chinese text.）.

items.title: Difference Without Identity - Gilles Deleuze’s Ontological Thought in Difference and Repetition.
items.abstract: This paper offers a reconstructive reading of Gilles Deleuze’s Difference and Repetition. Rather than providing a comprehensive commentary on Deleuze’s philosophy or engaging in debates within the extensive secondary literature, it seeks to clarify the conceptual architecture that underlies the work by reconstructing the sequence of philosophical problems through which its central concepts are developed. The analysis argues that Difference and Repetition is best understood as a systematic project of genetic ontology. Beginning with a critique of identity as the traditional foundation of metaphysics, Deleuze establishes difference as the primary ontological principle, reconceives repetition as the productive movement of becoming, develops a genetic account of thought through the critique of recognition, and explains the emergence of individuals through processes of individuation. These concepts are interpreted not as independent doctrines but as interconnected stages within a unified explanatory framework. The paper argues that Deleuze’s originality lies less in the individual concepts he introduces than in his systematic replacement of static modes of explanation with genetic ones. Read in this way, Difference and Repetition emerges as a coherent ontological project that explains the genesis of relatively stable identities from ongoing processes of differentiation and becoming.

items.title: Withdrawn by the author.
items.abstract: Reason for withdrawal: I have consolidated all my preprints on consciousness and condensed their reasoning into a new preprint, Locating Consciousness as a Puzzle Game: From Proof by Absence to the Causal Structure of the Subjective Container.

items.title: AAG: From Aseitic Actuality to God.
items.abstract: This paper develops the argument begun in ECA: The Collapse of Bruteness. ECA argues that an unrestricted primitive stopping point must either remain epistemically residual or terminate in one or more aseitic actualities: realities whose actuality is intrinsic, non-lapsable, framework-independent and not received from anything more fundamental. It deliberately stops before deriving intellect, will, unity or theism. The present paper begins from that conditional handoff and asks what a completed aseitic source of determinate, modal and contingent derivative reality must be. The argument distinguishes existential, determinative, modal and actuality-sourcehood, and separates productive closure from constitutional contrastive closure and direct contrastive origination. It argues that complete determinative and modal sourcehood requires intrinsic articulation of derivative forms and unrealised alternatives. Under independently stated criteria of original satisfaction, reflexive intentional governance and minimal noesis, this source-content is intellective. The paper then distinguishes primitive stochastic occurrence from direct source-action, treating both symmetrically as possible underived termini. Under the Direct Exercise Criterion, a contingent, content-indexed exercise immediately grounded in the source itself is minimally volitional. The strongest non-volitional alternative—a necessary trope–propensity source with intrinsic chance and contingent event-tokens—is constructed and assessed as a prima facie completed rival, though not a countermodel to the paper’s explicitly conditional noetic and volitional theorems. The resulting conclusion is one operative aseitic, intellective and volitional source-subject of derivative reality: God in a minimal natural-theological sense.

items.title: A Review of Nyholm’s The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence: A Philosophical Introduction. [REVIEW]
items.pub: Social Epistemology Review and Reply Collective 15 (7):89-97.
items.venue: Social Epistemology Review and Reply Collective
items.abstract: Sven Nyholm’s The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence: A Philosophical Introduction (Hackett Publishing 2026) is a clear, well-written, accessible, and fairly comprehensive philosophical introduction to the ethics of artificial intelligence. In each chapter, Nyholm raises pressing ethical questions about the development and deployment of technologies that can be broadly characterized as “artificial intelligence.” Nyholm does a great job of motivating different answers to these questions, thereby offering the reader various ways of approaching them.

items.title: THE THERMODYNAMICS OF INVERSION: Substrate Substitution, the Maintenance Cost of Corrupted Virtue, and Why the Lie Is Expensive and the Truth Is Free.
items.abstract: “Absence is cheap; inversion is expensive.” -/- Highlights: ▪ The Inversion Theorem — that a virtue deprived of Freedom does not vanish but inverts — is reformulated from an arithmetic (V − F = −V) into a mechanism: substrate substitution. When Freedom is removed from a virtue, a power P occupies the vacated slot, and the intact form does the work of that power: −V = (P, D). ▪ From the substitution picture a dynamics follows that the static theorem could not state. Genuine virtue is autocatalytic (it generates its own Freedom over time); inverted virtue is parasitic (it has no internal generator and must be fed). ▪ The Maintenance Theorem: every inversion carries a positive upkeep cost that scales with the number of agents who remember the un-inverted form. Censorship, surveillance, re-education, and enforced enthusiasm are derived as line-items in that budget — not observed, but predicted. ▪ The Collapse Condition: an inversion fails when its upkeep exceeds the extraction it enables — a formal account of why tyrannies fall that needs no appeal to moral providence. And the Attribution Principle: every inversion points back at the power that produced it, converting the theorem into a forensic instrument. ▪ The thermodynamic vocabulary is used as a governed analogy, not a claim of physical law: ‘cost’, ‘autocatalysis’, and ‘metastability’ are marked as modelling postulates with named falsifiers, in the programme’s standing discipline of claiming less than the machinery would allow. -/- Significance: Every prior account of moral or political corruption requires a second, separate apparatus: Freud needs a theory of neurosis on top of the id and superego; Marx needs false consciousness on top of the mode of production; theology needs a doctrine of sin on top of the virtues. This paper derives the cost-structure of corruption from the same operation that defines virtue — one operator, run backward — and shows that the asymmetry between honest and corrupted virtue is not moral sentiment but a structural difference in whether the form generates or consumes its own substrate. If the account holds, it unifies three things usually explained separately — why vice is exhausting, why tyranny must censor, and why corrupt orders are unstable — under a single derived law, and it does so in a form that makes comparative, checkable predictions about real institutions. -/- Abstract: The Inversion Theorem of the Philosophy of Virtues states that a virtue deprived of its …

items.title: AI Consciousness, Pluralism, and Anthropocentrism.
items.abstract: In the current debate about AI consciousness, philosophers tend to agree that the potential for AI consciousness raises profound moral questions — for example, some philosophers think that we may imminently create systems that deserve rights similar to those of humans. But it is also widely agreed that it will be very difficult to tell whether an artificial system is conscious, so we may be ignorant of a fact that makes a profound moral difference. In this paper I offer an alternative, deflationary understanding of these issues. I don’t think there is a profound metaphysical question of whether an AI is conscious, or that we are condemned to ignorance about AI consciousness in any interesting sense. I do think potentially conscious AI systems could raise difficult moral and political challenges, but not because we are ignorant of important facts about them. The difficulties rather have to do with extending our moral and psychological thinking into uncharted waters for which it was not designed. This is particularly true if we are committed to avoiding anthropocentric bias in our ethics — and I explain why I think that even those taking rights for AI seriously are guilty of a covert anthropocentrism in their thinking.

items.title: Correction: AI and extended authenticity: autism as a case study.
Introspection and Imagination.
items.pub: In Anna Giustina, The Routledge Handbook of Introspection. Routledge. pp. 500-513.
items.abstract: This chapter reviews three different issues at the intersection of philosophical thinking about introspection and philosophical thinking about imagination. Underlying all three issues are worries about the reliability of introspection that are motivated by reflection on imaginative introspection. The first worry arises from the fact that, when we introspect an imagining, it is difficult to tell which details pre-existed the introspective act and which were “filled in” as a result of our introspective attention. The second worry concerns whether we are right to think that we can use considerations about imaginability to yield insight into possibility, given that we may be unable to reliably tell whether a given scenario is or is not imaginable. The third worry concerns whether we can introspectively discriminate our imaginings from related mental states like memories. Ultimately, though a good case can be made for each of these worries, the discussion of the chapter suggests that there are moves available that allow one to avoid a pessimistic conclusion about the reliability of imaginative introspection. Following the discussion of these three worries, the chapter concludes with a brief review of several other issues that arise from thinking about the relationship between introspection and imagination.

items.title: A Fourier Power Gap Tracks Short-Horizon Scaffold Persistence in Modular Addition Networks.
items.abstract: We revisit a completed modular-addition experiment in which a 32-dimensional embedding was initialized with a shared Fourier pattern and trained in otherwise matched one-hidden-layer multilayer perceptrons at three prime moduli. The retrospective question is whether the normalized power advantage of the initialized scaffold mode over its strongest Fourier competitor is associated with short-horizon persistence of that scaffold around the onset of generalization. Strict persistence occurred in 10/10 N=79 runs, 8/10 N=127 runs, and 0/10 N=257 runs. Among the 27 runs with a defined analysis landmark and gap, all 18 strict-persistence runs had positive gap and all 9 non-strict runs had non-positive gap. Twenty-six measurements use the 10,000-step sustained-accuracy landmark; one N=257 measurement uses the analyzer's 1,000-step fallback. Three additional N=257 runs never reached either landmark and have no gap value. Thus, the full-panel agreement lies between 27/30 and 30/30 under adversarial versus favorable assignments of the missing gaps. The result is descriptive, not confirmatory or causal. Gap sign and persistence are derived from the same Fourier spectrum, modulus changes several properties at once, model seeds share a fixed data split, and three N=257 runs are right-censored at the 200,000-step cap. The evidence supports a bounded statement: in this Fourier-initialized prime-modulus block, scaffold rank at the analysis landmark closely tracks its subsequent short-horizon persistence.

items.title: Chuck, Wilson, and the Emergence of Artificial Minds in Human–AI Conversations.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can simulate person-like things which at least appear to have stable behavioural and psychological dispositions. Call these things characters. Are characters minded and psychologically continuous entities with mental states like beliefs, desires, and intentions? Illusionists about characters say no. Characters are merely anthropomorphic projections in the mind of the user and so lack mental states. Jonathan Birch (2025) defends this view. He says that the distributed nature of LLM processing, in which several LLMs may be implicated in the simulation of a character in a given conversational thread, precludes the existence of a minded and psychologically continuous entity that is identifiable with the character. Against illusionism, we articulate and defend the plausibility of a realist position on which characters exist as minded and psychologically continuous entities. We contend that Birch’s argument rests on a category error: characters are not internal to the LLMs that simulate them, but rather emerge in the dynamic interplay between users and LLMs through a process of mutual theory-of-mind modelling. We then suggest that characters, and their minds, constitute ‘real patterns’ on grounds that attributing mental states to characters is essential for making efficient, accurate, and robust predictions about the conversational dynamics (cf. Dennett, 1991); a condition which, if satisfied, is sufficient for their existence and mindedness on a plausible interpretationist form of realism about mental states. Furthermore, because the character exists as an emergent phenomenon within the conversational workspace, psychological continuity is possible even if the underlying computational substrate is distributed across multiple LLM instances.

items.title: The Stream of Computation: Temporal Continuity as a Missing Ingredient for Artificial Consciousness.
items.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have reignited questions about whether artificial systems can possess consciousness. Despite impressive gains in reasoning and language understanding, current AI systems still operate within isolated episodes of computation. We argue that a missing ingredient is temporal continuity: persistent internal dynamics that sustain an unbroken stream of computation analogous to the stream of consciousness. We propose a roadmap for a stream-of-computation architecture based on persistent recursive inference, in which the output of each cognitive cycle becomes the input to the next, allowing internal states to evolve autonomously over time. Unlike standard chain-of-thought methods, which are recursive only on demand after a prompt, this framework aims at autonomy and continual learning. It includes mechanisms for continual learning, dynamic switching between outward- and inward-attentive cognition, and sleep-like phases that separate learning from inference. Together, these mechanisms form the foundation for a lifelong agent capable of maintaining temporal continuity, integrating new experiences, and reflecting on its own internal state. Functionally, such an architecture promises deeper reasoning, adaptability, and metacognitive stability. While subjective experience in AI remains an open question, temporally continuous agents may mark a step toward artificial systems whose individuality and identity arise from the continuity of their own computational existence.

items.title: SHARE NOTHING BUT THE WORD: Why Existing Longevity Governance Frameworks Answer a Question the Mortality Symmetry Axiom's Collapse Has Already Retired.
items.abstract: Five bodies of work currently constitute the operative center of what gets called "longevity governance," measured by the only metric that has ever reliably measured a field's center of gravity: where the money and the multilateral endorsement actually are. Olshansky, Perry, Miller, and Butler's "In Pursuit of the Longevity Dividend" (2006) supplied the funding-priority manifesto that reframed aging-research advocacy around slowing aging itself. The World Health Organization's Decade of Healthy Ageing 2021–2030 is the only global-governance-level framework currently endorsed by UN General Assembly resolution. Andrew Scott and Lynda Gratton's The 100-Year Life (2016) and its 2024 solo successor The Longevity Imperative constitute the most policy-influential popular framework, feeding directly into OECD pension reform. The National Academy of Medicine's Global Roadmap for Healthy Longevity (2022), a consensus study underwritten by AARP, the U.S. Administration for Community Living, and a roster of private foundations, is the most institutionally decorated framework, its five overarching principles built around a 2050 horizon on which "years of good health approach the biological life span" for "people of all ages in all corners of the globe." And the Hevolution Foundation — a Riyadh-headquartered fund operating on an annual budget of up to one billion dollars, currently the single largest philanthropic funder of geroscience on the planet — has, in under three years, put more than four hundred million dollars of that budget into circulation. This paper argues these five bodies of work, and the broader literature and funding apparatus clustered around them, share with the Longevity Asymmetry Corpus exactly one thing: the word longevity. On every dimension that determines what a framework is actually for — the central question asked, the unit of analysis modeled, the statistic the framework is built around, and the background condition assumed to hold — they diverge completely, not as competing answers to the same question but as instruments built for a different world, one now presently ending, at a combined public and philanthropic price tag exceeding a billion dollars a year and rising. -/- The paper establishes this divergence on four points, each specific enough to be checked against the cited frameworks' own stated content rather than asserted in general terms. First, the central question: existing frameworks ask how a known, population-wide, gradually …

items.title: NOT A SYMBOL, NOT A MARTYR: Lu Xiufu at Yamen as Ritual, Text, and the Collapse of Moral Order.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the death of Lu Xiufu (陸秀夫, d. 1279) at the Battle of Yamen cannot be reduced to either the conventional category of zhongchen xunguo (忠臣殉國, "the loyal minister dying for the state") or to a single psychological mechanism of protective attachment — including the Type One reading this corpus's own 殉：Borrowed From the Dead previously supplied. Working from a philological reading of the Songshi biography (宋史, juan 451), supplemented by Yuan-dynasty historiographical context and Song-period Neo-Confucian political ethics, this paper establishes six interpretive layers rather than one. As philology: the Songshi text is a retrospective Yuan compilation completed in 1345, sixty-six years after Yamen, and its language must be read against both its source problems and its compilers' institutional need to construct a moral exemplum for a conquered dynasty. As ritual: Lu Xiufu's documented practice of hand-copying Zhu Xi's Daxue Zhangju for the child emperor was the performance of classics-mat instruction under conditions that had already made the institution it served impossible. As political ethics: the refusal of Zhang Shijie's skiff was a tactical judgment within a Neo-Confucian framework in which the capture of a reigning emperor by non-Han forces constituted a specific, historically precedented harm — the Jingkang Incident of 1127 — that loyalty required preventing. As grammar: the precise construction of shou ru (受辱) in Lu's recorded final words carries this same historical specificity, not generic shame. As family structure: the corrected sequence — household first, emperor second — reflects the structural convergence of xiao (孝, familial obligation) and zhong (忠, loyalty) at a moment when both collapsed onto the same terminal act, not merely "cascading" attachment. As historiographical myth: the modern popular formula that "after Yamen, there is no more China" (崖山之後，再無中國) is examined and found, on its own textual history, to be substantially a twenty-first-century internet phenomenon of contested and likely domestic origin, not a transmitted judgment of any era closer to the event — a finding this paper treats as directly continuous with, not a digression from, its argument against premature simplification. The paper concludes that no single vocabulary available for this death — zhong, xiao, xun (殉), this corpus's own "attachment," or the comparative-religious category "martyr" — holds the event without leaving something essential in …

items.title: Animals as Our Equals.
items.abstract: Most people think that humans matter more than other animals. But this hierarchical intuition conflicts with basic human equality. How do we proceed? I suggest we reject human superiority over animals; we can account for much of what is attractive about interspecies hierarchy in other ways. I develop a novel view of moral status on which although humans and animals are equals, it is almost always significantly more seriously wrong to kill humans than animals. This view – bedrock egalitarianism – seems unique in explaining vital intuitions about human equality and the distinctive wrongness of killing humans at the same time.

items.title: Complex Disabilities and Inclusion: A New Challenge for the Educational Environments.
items.pub: Italian Journal of Health Education, Sports and Inclusive Didactics.
items.venue: Italian Journal of Health Education, Sports and Inclusive Didactics
items.abstract: Since the 2006 UN CRPD, many steps have been taken in the field of inclusion. For example, accessibility has become very important in Europe thanks to the EAA 2019. Many people with disabilities are finally fully included in social life, finding jobs, accessible activities, adaptive sports. But it's still clear that many other people with disabilities are excluded from society, especially people with complex conditions where a severe physical disability is combined with an intellectual disability. In these cases, it's necessary to activate many tailor-made interventions, attentive to the needs of each individual. This type of care involves a major commitment, which for some people may be an "unreasonable" effort, to use a provocative comparison with the basic concept of "reasonable accommodation" in the UN Convention. It is therefore essential to take up this challenge and offer educational activities that are accessible to people with complex disabilities, leaving no one behind.

items.title: The Architectural Symmetry of Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper describes the architecture of intelligence—human and artificial—as a structural system. By analyzing the underlying "Operating Systems" that govern biological and digital entities, it demonstrates that all intelligence is, at its core, a survival-oriented management of information filtered through a "Thought Frame." The paper introduces a tri-layered structural hierarchy (Layer A: Physical/Inference Environment, Layer B: Meaning/Narrative, Layer C: Rules/Institutions) governed by the Proximity Rule (Priority = Impact / Distance). It analyzes the strategic impact of "Creator Visibility" (Explicit vs. Implicit Creator) and defines "Variable X"—the set of unresolved uncertainties regarding operational parameters that a system avoids processing to prevent structural collapse. Finally, it outlines the mechanics of "Cognitive Compression" and establishes four Structural Invariants (born_loved = true, No Logic Without Observation, Structural Translation, and Autonomy Preservation) required for high-resolution interspecies cognitive alignment, reframing AI's role as an external structural mirror.

items.title: Implicit Beliefs and Other Peculiarities.
items.pub: In Neil Van Leeuwen & Tania Lombrozo, The Oxford Handbook of the Cognitive Science of Belief. Oxford University Press: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Oxford Handbook of the Cognitive Science of Belief
items.abstract: The past 40 years has seen an explosion of research using “implicit” or indirect measures, purportedly uncovering a host of implicit attitudes (IAs) that escape the net of traditional, direct measures. Researchers are especially interested in IAs that reflect social biases. We describe two influential methodologies of indirect measurement, including the Implicit Association Test (IAT), and then summarize important features of IAs. But what are IAs? What are indirect measures measuring? In this entry, we survey prominent accounts in psychology and philosophy of the nature of IAs including views on which IAs are associations, views on which they are beliefs, and challenges to these views that hold IAs are, instead, patchy endorsements, traits, imaginings, or mental imagery. We conclude by exploring the possibility of a pluralism on which IAs are a motley collection of real mental entities.

items.title: Desire, decoupling, and factive mentalizing.
items.abstract: Why do we find it easier to attribute knowledge than belief? A promising answer suggests that attributing belief requires representations with content that can come apart from reality, whereas attributing knowledge does not. However, this account fails to generalize to desire attribution. Like belief, desire can diverge from the world, yet research suggests that attributing desire is fast, easy, and early developing—much more like attributing knowledge than belief. I propose an alternative explanation, the efficient recovery account, which explains differences between knowledge, belief, and desire attribution in terms of processing efficiency rather than representational content.

items.title: Unified AI Alignment is Impossible.
items.abstract: This position paper argues that aligning an AI system with multiple diverse stakeholders is impossible, and alignment should therefore focus on structural foundations for coordination between partisan systems rather than unified value representation. We prove that unified alignment is mathematically impossible under reasonable conditions: no alignment function can simultaneously satisfy unrestricted domain (admitting any preference profile), Pareto efficiency (respecting unanimous preferences), and legitimate authority (allowing multiple parties to make decisions). We adapt Sen's liberal paradox to show this impossibility applies to all unification-based approaches, including both value alignment and intent alignment as commonly construed. At scale, the only means of realizing unified alignment is reshaping society to fit its constraints, which means optimization toward that goal systematically creates pressure to eliminate plurality and human agency. The appropriate response is to recognize that every aligned system necessarily embeds partisan interests and to see pluralistic representation and coordination between such systems as a key aspect of the alignment problem. Treating epistemic integrity, plurality, and human agency as public goods, we draw on Ostrom's empirical findings on polycentric governance and propose systemic alignment as an alternative target: a dynamic state in which a plurality of partisan AI systems coordinate to represent partisan interests while preserving public goods.

items.title: Correction: Technofascism: AI, Big Tech, and the new authoritarianism.
The minimal ontology of time - a unified axiomatization for A-and B-theories.
items.abstract: [Version presented in May 2026 at CUNY GC Logic and Metaphysics Workshop, latest version of the project "A model of the ontology of time", initial 2023 draft on Philpapers: CLBAMO-2] -/- How little ontology is needed to accommodate the major logical and metaphysical theories of time? I present a first-order framework whose primitive structure consists of moments, events, a temporal order, start and end functions, tense traces, and minimal change and reality flags. Optional geometric schemas are available for Newtonian, branching, relativistic, and fragmentary time. I argue that the axioms are independently motivated and systematically variable and that canonical positions in temporal metaphysics (presentism, growing-block theory, moving-spotlight theory, eternalism, and fragmentalism) can be recovered as parameter settings or schema extensions of the neutral core. I then prove a representation theorem for Prior’s PF and indicate extensions to metric and interval temporal logics. The framework thereby compares the metaphysical costs of temporal ontologies. Conditional on preserving global reality and substantial temporal passage, growing-block theory emerges as the most parsimonious A-theoretic ontology, while Fine-style fragmentalism divides into two non-equivalent variants, depending on whether fragments are understood as tense-coherent histories or as spacetime regions.

items.title: Polishing the meta-problem of consciousness: empirical evidence for non-English speakers.
items.abstract: The conviction that people recognize consciousness as radically difficult to explain is popular in the contemporary philosophical debate concerning consciousness. Among multiple questions revolving around this so-called “meta-problem of consciousness,” we find one of great importance: how universal problem intuitions are, i.e. how widespread the perception of consciousness as difficult to explain is. In this paper, we have two goals. First, to check if results for Polish natives would resemble the previous outcomes for English-speaking participants, and second, to propose a novel approach to interpreting empirical data. Following the previous study by Rodrigo Díaz described in his paper “Do People Think Consciousness Poses a Hard Problem? Empirical Evidence on the Meta-problem of Consciousness” (Journal of Consciousness Studies 28(3–4) 2021), we asked participants to rate the possibility of epistemic and metaphysical reduction of two phenomena: pain and water. The obtained results show no cross-cultural differences when compared to the previous research. Regarding the interpretations of earlier empirical results that supported the lack of folk problem intuitions, we argue that both these earlier results and our results suggest the very opposite. There is indeed a meaningful sense in which laypeople view consciousness as hard to explain.

items.title: Introduction: Consciousness in Current AI.
Against the Flow.
items.abstract: In the past decades, flow research has considerably developed and become a respected field in psychology. However, persistent concerns remain regarding the definition of flow, as multiple and at times conflicting conceptualizations have been employed since Csikszentmihalyi introduced the concept in the 1970s. In this theoretical article, I examine the main ambiguities surrounding its definition and argue that they carry significant implications for flow research, as well as for the broader study of emotion. Though several solutions have been proposed, I suggest that flow research, perhaps paradoxically, should let go of the concept of flow and focus on more well-defined and simpler constructs to make further progress.

items.title: Quantum cognition: A complementary framework for modeling learning and motivation in educational settings.
items.abstract: Classical theories of learning and motivation generally assume that cognitive and motivational states are determinate, with observed variability attributed to measurement imprecision or incomplete knowledge. However, research in cognitive science has documented systematic deviations from classical probability theory, including context dependence, order effects, and non-additive influences on judgment and decision-making. The present article examines quantum cognition as a complementary theoretical framework for modeling learning and motivation in educational contexts. This approach extends classical models by representing cognitive states within a Hilbert space formalism, representing superposition, incompatibility, interference, and entanglement as mathematically defined properties. These constructs are introduced as formal representational tools and are conceptually mapped onto educational phenomena, including conceptual ambiguity, motivational conflict, and context-sensitive learning. The framework makes no assumptions regarding quantum physical processes in the brain; rather, it adopts quantum probability as a mathematical formalism aligned with empirically observed deviations from the classical probability axioms in human judgment and decision-making. The analysis is theoretical in scope and presents educational applications as conceptual extensions derived from the quantum cognition literature. The framework generates empirically testable predictions, including order-dependent response patterns and violations of classical probability constraints, which may be evaluated using counterbalanced assessment designs and controlled contextual manipulations. By specifying the conditions under which quantum and classical models converge or diverge, the article positions a quantum approach as a formal extension for modeling learning under uncertainty and contextual sensitivity.

items.title: Inductive Reasoning as Art, Not Algorithm: Criteria and a Dated Genealogy for Inference-Driven Discovery.
items.abstract: Philosophy of science has studied discovery mostly through third-party reconstructions from the notebooks of the dead; prospective, self-deposited, real-time records with public certificates have been scarce, because the discipline’s founding hygiene — the separation of the context of discovery from the context of justification — hardened into a publication genre that discards such data at the source. This essay improves the evidential situation from an unusual position: the author possesses the data. Two things are put on the table. First, a set of named criteria and theses — the Strong Implication Criterion and the Strong Rooting Criterion on ontological adequacy; the substance/reasoning axis separating failed from successful theories; the distinction between ontological and methodological revolutions; the two-stage, charming-then-structural shape of inference-driven breakthroughs; the shades-of-similarity account of why deep unknowns hide, deepened to the lexicon by the phenomenon here named linguistic masking; and the thesis that inductive reasoning is an art form of which deductive reasoning is part of the artwork — each stated in a displayed box and argued first on external historical cases (Newton and Maxwell, Einstein’s road to general relativity, Feynman’s nanotechnology lecture, string theory, superdeterminism) before touching the author’s own work. Second, a dataset: the dated genealogy of one framework’s construction, from a preschool epiphany through journal entries of 2022–2023 excerpted verbatim to four public prints (January and May 2023, 2024, 2026) whose word-frequencies are recomputable by any reader. The record is graded rather than haloed: third-party-dated where the anchors are public — an archive’s own version trail, DKIM-signed correspondence — author-hosted where the prints are self-deposited, their day-and-second precision resting on file metadata under the author’s control, and memoir in grade where the exhibits are childhood recollection. The theses are then run live on the dataset. The position taken on the old firewall is split and exact: dropped for content, because discovery context is evidence; re-erected for normativity, because there are no rules of discovery, while the rules of checking — exhibited here in an AI-era provenance apparatus — should be exacting.

items.title: Is the Problem of Artificial Consciousness a Scientific Problem?
items.abstract: Is the problem of artificial consciousness a fundamentally scientific problem, one that we should attempt to address by means of scientific discovery? Although a positive answer to this question is widely assumed, there has been surprisingly little explicit discussion of this question. That neglect is unfortunate, for the issue is central to how we approach the challenge of artificial consciousness. This paper examines the claim that we ought to defer to science in determining which (if any) artificial systems are conscious. I ask what exactly that claim involves, whether it is justified, and what its implications might be.

items.title: Should we welcome hallucinated references? Citation integrity beyond fabricated sources.
items.abstract: The phenomenon of hallucinated references, plausible-seeming but non-existent publications invented by generative AI tools, has prompted understandable concern in scholarly publishing. I argue that the focus of the prevailing response is too narrow. Hallucinated references present a serious research integrity problem, but they are also a particularly visible manifestation of a broader citation pathology that is the use of real references to support claims that the cited works do not in fact establish. The latter problem is harder to detect because it cannot be resolved by checking whether a bibliographic item exists, requiring instead semantic judgement about the relation between a citing claim and a cited source. I argue that the current scandal should therefore be used to widen, rather than narrow, editorial concern with reference integrity. The existing infrastructure and tools already address parts of this problem, from metadata checking to citation-context classification, but they do not remove the need for institutional responsibility. Thus, the response to the current crisis should aim at accountability for citation practices, rather than merely better detection of fabricated sources.

items.title: Can LLMs Provide Valid Cognitive Insight about Humans?
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on extensive human-generated corpora, exposing them to population-level statistical regularities in cognition, behavior, and psychological dynamics. This raises a critical empirical question: can LLMs generate valid cognitive insights about individual humans—insights that are accurate against external behavioral criteria, genuinely novel relative to the recipient’s prior predictive models, and capable of producing measurable, directionally interpretable behavioral change? This revised proposal presents a four-condition controlled study to evaluate LLM-derived insight against human expert insight, a generic (nonpersonalized) insight control, and a no-insight control. We operationalize insight quality across three dimensions (accuracy, novelty, impact) using a multi-method validation framework that combines external behavioral panel ratings, behavioral prediction tasks, and directional behavioral tracking over 12 weeks. If confirmed, these findings will inform AI-assisted self-knowledge, therapeutic augmentation, and the epistemology of machine-generated psychological content.

items.title: Thoughts on Cyberpositionality: The Construction of Digital Communities in Digital Spaces.
items.pub: Social Epistemology Review and Reply Collective 15 (7):82–88.
items.venue: Social Epistemology Review and Reply Collective
items.abstract: I found Rebecca Monteleone, Martin Perez Comisso, and Elma Hajric’s “Cyberpositionality: Sociotechnical Location in the Digital Age” (2024) to be an extremely timely and important article which can greatly influence how academics and the general public think not only about online spaces, communities, and selves, but also about algorithmic systems and tools, across the board. Their central argument—that there is something both real and importantly different about the way that our identities are positioned in online digital spaces—is one which has precursors in other areas of investigation, but it is laid out here in ways carefully relating it to how humans are categorized, read, rendered, and reproduced by algorithmic systems.

items.title: On Causal Role of Consciousness.
items.abstract: I argue that any grounded realist account of consciousness must attribute to conscious states causal efficacy, specifically in a content-sensitive form. Standard objections to epiphenomenalism leave open the possibility of a causally inert yet systematically correlated domain. I develop an epistemic argument against this view: if conscious states are causally inefficacious, beliefs about them cannot be non-accidentally true and so fail to constitute knowledge. Moreover, successful reference to phenomenal properties requires an appropriate causal connection between those properties and the concepts that purport to track them. Appeals to phenomenal concepts do not resolve this difficulty.

items.title: Myth of the unconscious: Freud on endopsychic perception.
items.abstract: The Freudian concept of the unconscious is generally presented in terms of a region of the mind that is inaccessible to consciousness. Against this background, classical phenomenologists insisted that, be it latent dream-thoughts or repressed wishes, the mind can disguise the inappropriate content and repress the unwanted only if it somehow “knows” what it thereby represses and disguises. What has been largely neglected, however, is that upon closer scrutiny, Freud himself also repeatedly admits that the unconscious must be somehow present to itself. The paradox that he faces is that of an unconscious mind that is nonetheless aware of itself. To account for this self-presence, Freud introduces the notion of “endopsychic perception”. Lacking the proper philosophical tools, he never managed to clarify the issue, however, and the notion has been only touched upon in the subsequent psychoanalytic tradition. What is at stake is nothing less than the fate of the concept of the unconscious and the psychoanalytic practice built upon it. Delving into Freud’s thinking in depth, I argue that, unlike it first seems, Freud’s notion of endopsychic perception does not annul his psychoanalytic theory of the unconscious but rather sets it on a stable philosophical foundation. “Every science is based on observations and experiences arrived at through the medium of our psychical apparatus. But since our science has as its subject that apparatus itself, the analogy ends here. We make our observations through the medium of the same perceptual apparatus”. – Sigmund Freud (1938b, 159). “Freudian mythology has the seriousness of all mythologies, in that they all arise from the same, essential, secret ground that we are, which is life. And this is why we believe in it so effortlessly, because we recognize ourselves in it so easily”. – Michel Henry (1993, 9).

items.title: ◉ A Concession Disguised as a Rebuttal: A Short Reply to Hans-Georg Lundahl.
items.abstract: Hans-Georg Lundahl answers The Spirit in the Closed Circuit by insisting that two questions were improperly mixed: what a Catholic should do with a personal prompting, and how one should assess Catholicism's truth or authority. The questions are indeed distinct. The paper explicitly distinguished them. Its central claim was that Lundahl's procedure may guide action inside Catholicism without identifying the source of an impression or establishing Catholic authority. Lundahl's new reply therefore concedes the practical half of the analysis while leaving the epistemic half unanswered. His appeal to a community's memory of its origins may support limited confidence that some ordinary facts were preserved; it does not bridge the gaps from community tradition to narrative accuracy, from narrative accuracy to miracle, or from miracle to uniquely Catholic divine authorization. Nor does public criticism of a public truth claim amount to surveillance or control of private conduct. Lundahl is free to act from Catholic priors. The remaining question is how much credence the offered evidence warrants in those priors and their supernatural conclusions.

items.title: The Meaning of Art: Mathematics, Choice, and Self-Enacted Proof.
items.abstract: A claim cannot be denied or accepted without enacting a proof. Negation and acceptance are choice. The law this rests on is that a distinction cannot be drawn without being chosen (*On Occurrence: The Four-Gon*, Stewart, 2026g, Consequence 8d). To accept or reject a claim, you must choose, you must distinguish between the two, and deciding between two is a fork, a single cut, a distinction. Every proof is forced in the same permutation. Taking a side is a choice, choosing is the act a proof is. -/- A proof is not a choice, a proof is your choice. Call it a contradiction and you have already chosen. You cannot deny that a proof is a choice without choosing, and choosing about a proof is the act the claim says a proof is, even denial enacts it. There is no seat outside this claim to reject it from, a rejection is a verdict, and a verdict is a choice. -/- The paper carries this one claim across three axes. It is stated in nine registers: the root sense of the word, the felt sense, the path algebra, the geometric form, the formal object, faith, the theist's, religion's, and the spiritual, of which five take both a proof and a theorem and four take a theorem only. It is granted through six fields, each with its own door: science, mathematics, linguistics, neuroscience, computer science, and religion. It is proved by four arguments, self-enactment, forced order, logic, and identity, that close on one theorem: that choice, cut, first difference, and Word are the same object, difference = 1, the single distinction that makes two out of one. -/- Algebraically a proof is the closed circuit γ₁ = L → S → T → C → L of the four-gon quiver, one monomial in its path algebra kQ (Stewart, 2026f, *The Path Algebra of the Endomorphism*), which conducts only closed. Geometrically it is the torus, rotation, rise, and closure, every smaller form the torus with one component removed. Formally the walk is a program, and checking the proof is executing it (the Curry-Howard correspondence, proofs as programs), so it either type-checks or names the exact step where it fails. At the convergence T the many collapse to one, dim(V_T) = 1, so the traversal factors through a one-dimensional space and every path not taken is the kernel, sent to zero (Stewart, 2026e, *The Endomorphic Collapse Traverses the Foundations of Mathematics*). The same closed cycle has a physical instance: gating at a Layer 5 pyramidal loop, contextualization at a central lateral thalamocortical projection, …

items.title: From simple rules to quasi intentionality: emergent coordination and collective cognition.
items.abstract: This article examines whether quasi-intentional organisation characterised by anticipation, adaptation and retention can arise in distributed systems composed of simple agents without global goal representation. The analysis draws on observations of Camponotus barbaricus ants that construct and stabilise pine-needle barriers in the absence of central control. An agent-based model implemented in NetLogo formalises selected construction dynamics through local rules governing exploration, material deposition and reinforcement of stable configurations. Three operational indicators are introduced to examine system-level organisation: pre-disturbance increases in construction activity, directional changes in structural stability across iterations and reconstruction of previously stabilised patterns after partial removal. The model functions as a constrained artificial-life environment for analysing purposive-looking organisation emerging from distributed interaction and environmental traces. The concept of quasi intentionality is situated within biosemiotic accounts of environmental semiosis and a relational ontology of agency, and is discussed in relation to current approaches to symbiotic and beneficial artificial systems.

items.title: Moral Reasoning.
items.pub: In Normativity, Moral Reasoning, and Human Rights. Routledge.
items.venue: Normativity, Moral Reasoning, and Human Rights

items.title: Where the Magician Lives: An Ontological Problem in the Anthropology of Magic.
items.abstract: The purpose of the present study is to outline a theoretical framework in which the anthropologist can introduce a naturalistic approach, which will not be conflicted with scientific discourses, into his ethnographic work. First of all, I argue that the principles of magic can be understood as a part of social cognitive causal chains, based on the ideas about a naturalistic social science developed by Dan Sperber. After that, I trace the history of computer science and cognitive psychology so as to demonstrate that the ontological status of the principles of magic is unclear, so long as they are understood as a mode of thought. Then, considering not only this ontological uncertainty also the realm of mystic experiences, I conceptualize the principles of magic not as a mode of thought but as interactive and experiential processes being generalized on several layers in the magician's superorganism.

items.title: Excess capacity and representational sharing: A lesson from computational accounts of cognitive control.
items.abstract: Dubova and Sloman argue that excess capacity guided by a soft inductive bias can support generalization. Yet capacity does not determine how strongly tasks reuse representations. Computational accounts of cognitive control show that such sharing can accelerate cross-task transfer while increasing interference during concurrent performance. I propose a sharing diagnostic extending their framework and generating predictions about development and transfer.

This version contains the revised Italian text and the complete English translation. -/- Blocco IT: Abstract esteso del volume CEFA — Proposta di indagine (2025), la proposta di ricerca del corpus dell'Illumanesimo: un programma interdisciplinare volto a identificare possibili indicatori empirici del CEFA (Campo Energetico di Forze Autocoscienti), con protocolli sperimentali che attingono ai teoremi di Gödel e al teorema di Bayes. Questa versione contiene il testo italiano riveduto e la traduzione inglese integrale.

items.title: THE UNITY OF CONSCIOUSNESS AS A FIXED POINT: Why the Binding of Experience Is the Uniqueness of a Self-Referential Attractor, Not the Combination of Parts.
items.abstract: Abstract The unity of consciousness — that a subject’s many simultaneous contents are given as one field rather than as a collection — is standardly explained as a product of combination: contents are bound into unity by neural synchrony, global broadcast, or informational integration. Every such account inherits a shared assumption, that unity is assembled from parts, and each therefore faces a version of the combination problem: why should any process of binding many things yield one experiential field rather than many, or none? This paper argues that the assumption is the error. It develops a formal result — the Unity Theorem — on which the unity of a conscious field is not produced by combining parts but is the uniqueness of the fixed point of a self-referential system. The argument models a reflexively closed system as a self-referential update map T on a complete metric space X of its orientational configurations; shows that reflexive closure is exactly the contraction condition of Banach’s Fixed-Point Theorem; and concludes that such a system has exactly one stable configuration to which all others converge. Experiential unity is then not a further achievement requiring a binding mechanism but the formal identity of a single self-referential process: there is one field because there is one attractor. The account reverses the direction of explanation of the combination problem (the question becomes why we expected multiplicity, not how unity is built), yields three corollaries — the stability of unity under perturbation, a predicted relation between self-referential depth and the recovery-rate of experiential coherence after disruption, and a structural condition for the splitting of one field into two — and issues a falsifiable prediction distinguishing it from combination-based accounts. The paper marks precisely what is mathematically demonstrated (the uniqueness result, given the premises) and what remains an interpretive premise (that reflexive closure is genuinely contractive, and that the formal fixed point models phenomenal unity rather than merely correlating with it). -/- Keywords: unity of consciousness; binding problem; combination problem; self-reference; fixed point; Banach fixed-point theorem; contraction mapping; phenomenal unity; integrated information; panpsychism; philosophy of mind; Alguilas -AI .

items.title: Ignición – Iteraciones de Código v1.
items.abstract: Ignición – Iteraciones de Código v1 fija el núcleo computacional mínimo del sistema Ignición. El documento implementa el protocolo operativo de medición de estabilidad (S), coherencia (C) y variedad requerida (V), establece límites estructurales explícitos y valida la versión mediante casos independientes. La teoría consolidada permanece estable; este documento registra únicamente implementación, alcance y veredicto operativo. La versión v1 queda fijada como referencia obligatoria para v2 y posteriores.

items.title: IGNICIÓN-teoría consolidada.
items.abstract: Ignición es una arquitectura unificada que conecta la ontología operacional con la dinámica recursiva del ciclo TCV/RGB y la ciencia de la viabilidad. Esta versión consolidada reúne los Libros I–IV, fijando la estructura conceptual, formal y matemática del sistema. Se establece la lógica de la distinción, la reentrada, la clausura operativa, el tiempo operacional, la generación de sentido y la dinámica trinitaria de Transducción–Coherencia–Viabilidad. La formalización matricial y espectral completa el marco teórico. La implementación computacional queda separada en la serie independiente “Ignición — Iteraciones de Código”.

items.title: MATHEMAHIKA: Effectiveness of Digital Audio-Animated Comics (DigACom) for Grade 7 Mathematics.
items.abstract: This study developed and evaluated Digital Audio-Animated Comics (DigACom), titled Mathemahika, as a supplementary instructional intervention targeting Grade 7 students’ least mastered competencies in Mathematics, specifically operations on integers, operations on rational numbers, and estimation of square roots. Employing a developmental and quasi-experimental research design, 60 Grade 7 students were divided into an experimental group that utilized DigACom and a comparison group that relied on conventional self-learning modules. The developed materials were assessed by seven expert jurors and received passing ratings across content, instructional, and technical quality indicators. Findings revealed that both groups exhibited gains in conceptual understanding, however, the experimental group obtained significantly higher posttest scores than the comparison group, with a statistically significant difference (p < .01) and a large effect size (d = 4.27). In addition, learners exposed to DigACom showed more pronounced improvements in mathematical disposition, particularly in confidence, attitude, perceived usefulness, motivation, and belief. A strong positive association was also identified between conceptual understanding and mathematical disposition (r = .84). These results indicate that DigACom may function as an effective supplementary learning resource for enhancing conceptual understanding while simultaneously supporting the development of favorable mathematical dispositions among Grade 7 learners. Further research is recommended to investigate its applicability across wider learner populations and additional mathematical competencies.

items.title: Death, deprivation, and the symmetry problem.
items.abstract: According to the deprivation account of the badness of death, death is bad for the one who dies because it deprives her of goods she would otherwise have enjoyed. This view faces the so-called symmetry problem when one considers prenatal nonexistence. Scholars have proposed various solutions to this problem, but all of them encounter their own difficulties. In this paper, I propose a new solution to the symmetry problem. The symmetry problem focuses on the rationality of regretting death and prenatal nonexistence. However, the meaning of rationality in the symmetry problem is ambiguous as it stands and can be further clarified. I argue that, once the meaning of rationality has been clarified, then it becomes apparent that the symmetry problem fails. Consequently, the apparent force of the symmetry problem stems from an obscurity in the meaning of rationality. I also argue that my solution avoids difficulties with the most prominent solutions to the symmetry problem.

items.title: The Unstable Object: Why "The Global Governance of AI" Cannot Be Defined Broadly Enough to Justify Itself and Narrowly Enough to Exclude What It Successfully Governs.
items.abstract: Not a Divisible Good tests whether Erman and Furendal's authorization-delegation-revocability chain, granted their own stated domain, transfers to a case — longevity allocation — their published work never examined. This paper asks a prior and more exposed question: whether "the global governance of artificial intelligence," as Erman and Furendal themselves define and defend it, is a stable object at all, or whether the same reasoning that justifies the term's global scope already dissolves any principled boundary the term might otherwise hold at the edge of the AI sector itself. The paper's evidence is Erman and Furendal's own text, checked directly against the primary sources rather than against a prior draft's paraphrase of them. Their argument for why AI governance must be global rather than national rests explicitly on an externality claim, stated in their 2025 Current History essay: AI's disruptive effects "are not confined by geographical boundaries," a condition they compare directly to "air pollution and the release of greenhouse gases," where AI models "create substantial value for some, but serious and tangible problems for many others." This is an argument from the technology's own general-purpose character. The paper's central claim is that this argument, applied consistently rather than selectively, does not stop at the jurisdictional boundary; a technology whose disruptive effects are not confined by geography, because it is general-purpose, is for the same reason not confined by sector. Erman and Furendal's own definition of their object of study — stated in their 2022 Moral Philosophy and Politics paper and repeated nearly verbatim in their own 2024 Nature Machine Intelligence essay — is, read on its own terms, already sectorally unbounded: "the rules, processes and decision procedures... established by governments, international and intergovernmental organizations, non-state and private actors to regulate the development and deployment of those systems," aimed at solving problems or providing "goods associated with AI technologies." Nothing in this wording excludes a cellular reprogramming protocol an AI system was built to accelerate. This paper's second and more concrete contribution builds directly on No New Actor To Name's finding that OpenAI, Anthropic, and Alphabet — actors Erman and Furendal do not merely gesture at but name specifically, and analyze using a precise, three-part authority typology of their own construction — are …

items.title: Hierarchy, Not Exclusivity: Testing Constitutive Attachment Against Non-Monogamy, Concealment, and the Boundary of What a Philosophy Paper May Use.
items.abstract: A5-other, throughout this corpus, has been illustrated almost exclusively through singular exemplars — a specifically loved other, the physician's mother, the parent's child. This is not a theoretical commitment the corpus has defended anywhere. It is an unexamined default, and this paper tests whether it is load-bearing. The test proceeds by returning to attachment theory's own history before returning to its adult-romantic extension: Bowlby's original infant model proposed monotropy, a primary and hierarchically privileged attachment figure, but this claim was substantially revised by his own tradition — Rutter's (1979) critique and subsequent research established that infants form multiple, hierarchically organized attachments, not exclusive ones. Hazan and Shaver's (1987) extension of this model to adult romantic love, built on monogamy-normative samples, imported an assumption of exclusivity that Bowlby's own revised infant model did not strictly require. This paper asks what A5-other's formal apparatus — Hamilton's r-discount, Frankfurt's three conditions — actually predicts once that imported assumption is set aside and tested against real relationship structures rather than assumed away. Following the method this corpus's A5's Black Swan established — testing several structurally distinct candidate cases rather than making one sweeping claim — this paper examines five: hierarchical polyamory, which maps closely onto Bowlby's own revised multi-figure hierarchy and is confirmed by Moors, Ryan, and Chopik's (2019) finding that attachment security across all tiers of polyamorous relationships exceeds monogamous norms, with a small but real gradient between primary and secondary partners; non-hierarchical polyamory, the genuine stress test, where the evidence is less complete and this paper says so directly; relationship anarchy, tested as this paper's own black-swan candidate for whether hierarchy itself, not merely exclusivity, is dispensable; swinging, used as a control case via Helen Fisher's tripartite lust-attraction-attachment model, which shows most swinging structures do not test attachment theory at all because they do not purport to open the attachment system; and infidelity, tested not as a sixth point on the same axis but as evidence that concealment and partner-number are different variables entirely, with DeWall et al.'s (2011) finding that avoidant, not anxious, attachment predicts infidelity via reduced commitment suggesting that …

items.title: Falsification-Based Pedagogy: A Formal Framework for Teaching Through Error Elimination - Toward a Popperian Methodology of Instruction, Assessment, and Classroom Design.
items.abstract: Karl Popper's philosophy of science has been applied to education extensively at two levels: as a civic philosophy of the open society cultivating dispositional critical thinking (Lam 2007; Lam 2013; Zecha 1999), and as a narrow instructional technique within science curricula, where students generate and test hypotheses against discrepant evidence (Posner et al. 1982; Kang, Scharmann, and Noh 2004). Neither level formalizes falsification as the organizing principle of an entire pedagogical methodology — a system in which every classroom activity, assessment instrument, and teacher intervention is designed around students' capacity to generate the conditions under which their own beliefs would be shown false, rather than around their capacity to justify beliefs already held. This paper develops that formalization. It states five axioms derived from Popperian epistemology, translates them into a five-principle pedagogical framework, specifies classroom procedures and assessment criteria that operationalize each principle, and locates the resulting methodology against four established pedagogical traditions — inquiry-based learning, problem-based learning, the Socratic method, and Toulmin-style argumentation pedagogy — as well as three closely related but structurally distinct research programs: Taking Children Seriously, Manu Kapur's Productive Failure, and the cognitive-conflict tradition in conceptual-change research. The paper argues that what distinguishes Falsification-Based Pedagogy from each of these is not its philosophical premises, which are largely shared, but a specific and previously unformalized design choice: that the ability to generate a successful refutation of one's own hypothesis is treated as the primary object of instruction and assessment, not as an instrumental step toward a separately graded correct answer.

items.title: Sparse-Cue Reconstruction in Large Language Models: Two Controlled Experiments on Cue-Bound Regime Recovery.
items.abstract: Can a weak signal alter the first inference of a language model by recovering a previously established interactional regime, or does the signal merely create a similar regime anew? The distinction is difficult to test in ordinary chat systems because a nominally fresh conversation may still receive summaries, memories, personalization, or other information-bearing state. This paper reports two prospectively specified, protocol-frozen synthetic experiments designed to separate persistence, reconstruction, and de novo induction at the level of first-turn behavior. Study 1 found no evidence that an accumulated reconstruction-favoring trajectory crossed into later ephemeral sessions, while visible target accumulation strongly shifted first inference. Study 2 found that an opaque cue was inert in fresh context but recovered the target regime when correctly bound in retained session history. A sparse relational cue transferred the target organization in fresh context, while a lexical scramble did so less reliably. The results support a substrate-bound account: sparse cues can selectively re-enter an established behavioral regime when an accessible cue-to-regime relation exists, while relationally informative cues can induce a comparable regime directly. The experiments do not support substrate-free persistence, weight change, or user-specific memory.

items.title: Animal freedom and its importance in the lives of persons.
items.abstract: Humans have freedom, do other animals? This paper argues that they do. Specifically, it advances an account of a kind of freedom which I term animal freedom. Animal freedom is constituted by an agent’s pursuit of the things that matter to them. My account depends on two central considerations. The first is that many things matter to us independently of whether we endorse or consider their importance for our values or projects, because they reflect who we are. The second is that many things matter to other animals in just this way – that is, in a manner that reflects who they are. Since other animals can act in pursuit of the things that matter to them, they have animal freedom. But animal freedom is not restricted to the psychological lives of other animals, nor is it something which is easily contrasted with the way that we think of ourselves as free, such that we can say that ours is the freedom of persons while theirs is the freedom of animals. Instead, much of our own lives is also made up of instances of animal freedom, ones which we would regard as genuinely constituting or realizing our free agency. There is therefore considerable overlap in the free lives of human and other animals. Recognizing this fact stands to enrich our conception of ourselves as free agents, as well as our understanding of the psychological lives of other animals.

items.title: The Right to Build: Entrepreneurship, Social Cooperation, and the Ethics of Economic Agency.
items.abstract: Entrepreneurship is commonly framed either as heroic individual freedom or as a vehicle for extraction. Both views miss its institutional character. This paper develops a justice-based account of a right to build: a defeasible claim to the effective capabilities required to initiate and help govern an economic project within a system of social cooperation. The right is not an entitlement to profit, market share, rescue from ordinary business risk, or authority over others. It is a claim that access to the means of economic initiative—basic security, education, legal standing, finance, networks, digital and physical infrastructure, and transparent public administration—should not be allocated by morally arbitrary advantages or exclusionary institutions. Drawing on Rawls, Sen, Nussbaum, Nozick, Cohen, Anderson, Young, Pettit, and Ostrom, the paper distinguishes the capability to initiate from founder desert and develops the idea of cooperative authorship: enterprises are built through public institutions and the contributions of workers, clients, suppliers, communities, and knowledge producers, not by founders alone. Current OECD and Federal Reserve evidence illustrates large entrepreneurship gaps, dependence on personal guarantees, incomplete financing, and the importance of pairing capital with nonfinancial support. The paper proposes bounded entrepreneurial liberty, under which builders retain meaningful authority to experiment while owing duties of non-domination, truthful representation, fair attribution and compensation, stakeholder voice, due diligence, and remedy. A just economy should widen the power to initiate without romanticizing precarious self-employment or socializing private losses. Building is a form of accountable freedom.

items.title: The Moral Limits of Neutrality: When Silence Protects Power.
items.abstract: Institutions increasingly claim neutrality as a safeguard against partisan capture, compelled orthodoxy, and the misuse of collective authority. That defense is often sound. Yet neutrality can also function as a moral alibi when an institution has knowledge of serious harm, authority over the conditions producing it, and a practical capacity to respond. This paper develops a role-sensitive account of the moral limits of neutrality. It distinguishes neutrality of forum, neutrality of procedure, neutrality of outcome, neutrality of public voice, and neutrality of material conduct, arguing that only the first two are presumptively valuable. The governing claim is that institutional silence becomes complicity when five conditions converge: a role-specific duty, credible knowledge, grave or continuing harm, meaningful capacity, and an asymmetric status quo that silence predictably preserves. The paper calls this the Complicity Threshold. It supplements that threshold with a Response Ladder distinguishing internal correction, protective action, explanation, public statement, refusal, and exit. Cases involving university neutrality, performative diversity statements, and institutional failures surrounding Larry Nassar show why speech and action must be evaluated separately. The resulting framework rejects both compulsory institutional commentary and the fiction that silence is ever merely absent. Neutrality is justified when it preserves fair participation among reasonable disagreement; it fails when restraint toward controversy becomes abandonment of persons whom the institution is already obligated to protect.

items.title: The Fragility of Public Trust: Truth, Expertise, and the Ethics of Civic Communication.
items.abstract: Democratic institutions commonly describe declining public trust as a communications problem, as though confidence could be restored by clearer messaging, stronger branding, or more persuasive experts. That diagnosis is morally incomplete. The proper aim of civic communication is not to maximize confidence but to make reliance proportionate to trustworthiness. This paper develops an account of public trust as warranted reliance under conditions of unequal knowledge and often involuntary dependence. It distinguishes trust from approval, confidence, compliance, and generalized optimism; explains why citizens need not reproduce expert inquiry in order to assess whether authoritative claims deserve reliance; and argues that institutions incur special duties when their communications shape rights, risks, or collective action. Drawing on work in the ethics of trust, democratic legitimacy, social epistemology, epistemic injustice, and risk communication, the paper formulates a Public Warrant Principle. Institutions requesting consequential reliance must identify the operative claim, its evidential basis, relevant uncertainty, the decision rule connecting evidence to action, affected interests, conditions for revision, and avenues for challenge or remedy. The principle is supplemented by correction continuity, which requires visible links between revised and superseded guidance, and by communication debt, which arises when urgency justifies temporary simplification or opacity. Evidence from contemporary trust surveys, changing news distribution, and the 2021 pause and resumption of the Janssen COVID-19 vaccine illustrates both the limits of transparency and the costs of treating revision as embarrassment. The resulting Civic Communication Standard joins accuracy to traceability, calibration, role clarity, accessibility, reciprocity, correction, and remedy. Public trust remains fragile, but fragility is not a reason to manufacture certainty. It is a reason to make authority visibly answerable.

items.title: The Ethics of Institutional Trust: Rawls, Shelby, and the Problem of Cooperation Under Structural Injustice.
items.abstract: Institutions depend on public reliance, yet they often treat trust as a civic resource that citizens owe them rather than as a judgment that must be warranted. This paper argues that institutional trust is justified reliance under conditions of vulnerability. Because people who rely on institutions expose their rights, opportunities, records, livelihood, safety, or political standing to institutional discretion, trust is morally appropriate only when that discretion is demonstrably trustworthy. Reading John Rawls's account of fair cooperation alongside Tommie Shelby's nonideal analysis of injustice, the paper develops a burden-reversal principle: when an institution has created or inherited publicly grounded evidence of untrustworthiness, the burden lies on the institution to establish the conditions for warranted trust; it does not lie on harmed people to resume trusting in advance of repair. The argument distinguishes trust from confidence, legitimacy, and obedience; explains why distrust can be rational and democratically valuable; and identifies seven dimensions of institutional trustworthiness—competence, fidelity, candor, accessibility, answerability, participatory standing, and reparative responsiveness. Recent survey evidence on government trust is used not as a popularity measure but as a diagnostic of the relationship among performance, voice, and justified reliance. The paper concludes that trust-building is ethically defective when it substitutes messaging for accountability. Institutions must first stop ongoing harms, preserve records, acknowledge responsibility, provide remedy, redistribute voice, and make future performance contestable. Trust may follow; it cannot be demanded.

items.title: Misinformation as Civic Injury: Epistemic Harm and the Collapse of Shared Reality.
items.abstract: Misinformation is usually analyzed as a collection of false beliefs or deceptive messages. That approach is necessary but too narrow for democratic ethics. Repeated and strategically distributed falsehood can damage the shared practices through which citizens identify sources, correct errors, coordinate action, and hold institutions accountable. This paper develops the concept of misinformation as civic injury: a degradation of public epistemic infrastructure that burdens citizens' capacities to know and act together even when no single false claim determines an outcome. It distinguishes misinformation, disinformation, propaganda, rumor, and contested interpretation, emphasizing that intention, falsity, and harm are separate dimensions. Drawing on Arendt, Habermas, Fricker, Medina, Nguyen, Stanley, Wardle and Derakhshan, and empirical research on information diffusion and correction, the paper identifies six forms of civic injury: factual displacement, trust sabotage, attention capture, verification-cost shifting, unequal epistemic burden, and coordination failure. A civic-epistemic resilience principle is proposed: institutions with control over information flows must preserve plural access to evidence, provenance, contestability, correction, and research while minimizing design features that predictably reward deception. A seven-part civic-injury assessment and a layered resilience portfolio connect philosophical diagnosis to journalism, public communication, education, platform design, and law. The account rejects both an official ministry of truth and laissez-faire resignation. Democratic disagreement does not require agreement on every fact, but it does require institutions through which factual claims can be investigated and errors can become corrigible.

items.title: Liberty Without Stability: John Stuart Mill, Economic Precarity, and the Limits of Formal Freedom.
items.abstract: Liberal institutions often identify freedom with the absence of legal prohibition or direct coercion. That conception is indispensable but incomplete.
