This article understands MAGI as an apparatus through which personality attribution becomes institutionalized rather than as a collection of three complete digital personalities. The designations “scientist”, “mother”, and “woman” assigned to Melchior, Balthasar, and Casper are not naturally given and mutually separable components of Naoko’s personality. They are heterogeneous, overlapping, and gendered symbolic positions produced through selection and naming within MAGI. The split subject supplies a negative limit: no role designation or combination of designations can fully represent Naoko. Episode 13 makes visible the approvals of the three cores and the unanimity rule governing the self-destruct procedure; the feature film shows that one core’s rejection is sufficient to block the command. The work supports both the attribution of the cores to Naoko’s personality and the operational consequences of their outputs, but it does not establish that MAGI is authorized to speak in Naoko’s name. The article therefore does not infer personal representation or representational authority from personality attribution. Instead, it asks how an incomplete personality model becomes an institutionally effective decision position without first proving that it faithfully reproduces Naoko or has a right to speak for her. Casper’s “no” is a textual fact, whereas Ritsuko’s understanding of it as her mother choosing Gendo Ikari again is a character’s interpretation: semantic uncertainty can coexist with institutional certainty. The political problem centers on four questions: Who selects personality attributes? Who attributes them to a person? Who delegates decision authority to the model? And who can refuse, revoke, or override its output? MAGI shows not how a machine becomes human, but how institutional efficacy can arise before personality authenticity has been settled.

items.title: Distributed Agency and Responsible Authorship in Human–AI Product Design: A Theoretical Study of Process, Knowledge Production, and Responsibility Allocation.
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the analysis, ideation, modelling, simulation, evaluation and decision stages of product design. Recent research already conceptualises AI as a co-creator, a design material and a participant in dynamic collaborative roles; the claim that designers are becoming selectors or integrators is therefore no longer sufficient as an original contribution. Drawing on this literature, the paper first advances a descriptive diagnosis: as generative AI enters analysis, generation, simulation and evaluation, design agency becomes distributed across designers, models, datasets, interfaces, material validation and social feedback. It then advances a normative proposition: the distribution of agency does not by itself determine the distribution of responsibility. Product design therefore requires the explicit allocation of accountable positions among human and organisational actors who can frame problems, select alternatives, validate outcomes, justify decisions and answer for their consequences. The paper conceptualises this structure as responsible authorship and presents a model of distributed agency and responsibility allocation. AI is further analysed as an epistemic infrastructure that shapes the visibility, generation and ordering of design knowledge.

items.title: Spectral Failure Geometry in Modular Arithmetic Networks: Direct Takeover vs Runner-Up Handoff Across Moduli.
items.abstract: Neural networks trained on modular arithmetic can fail to grok by collapsing from a shared harmonic scaffold to a competing spectral mode. We characterise this collapse across N=127 and N=257 and find different failure geometries in the tested panels. In N=127, the eventual failure endpoint is often not the strongest non-scaffold competitor at visible scaffold loss; it is the spectral runner-up, rising behind a stronger predecessor that then decays. In N=257, the first visible non-scaffold mode is already the dominant competitor before scaffold loss: there is no predecessor to intercept. In the N=127 dense alias-distance sweep (50 rows from 10 recurring seed identities), 22/23 off-initial rows satisfy the retrospective hybrid pre-terminal selector, 9/10 multi-hop rows place the endpoint in runner-up position before terminal takeover, and handoff-margin growth is directionally consistent in 10/10 handoff-runner-up rows. For N=257, we analyse 16 epsilon-initialized event rows from the seven-arm cosine-component family and the main N=257 panel, together with a 50-seed no-epsilon optimizer-reset panel. Across 62 logged first non-scaffold events, the mode-7 family {7, 14, 21, 42} accounts for 54/62; the remaining 8 events are internal scaffold harmonics (k88, k81, k95) observed only in the no-epsilon panel. Folded harmonic order identifies these competing families algebraically. The two geometries motivate different intervention hypotheses, while the structural cause of the cross-modulus difference remains uncharacterised at current logging resolution.

items.title: Sparse Endpoint Effects and Hidden Trajectory Rerouting Under Optimizer-State Resets.
items.abstract: Optimizer state is a plausible hidden variable in grokking: adaptive moments and momentum buffers may steer when a learned solution leaves one spectral route and settles into another. We report the completed N=127, k0=30, d=3.5 arm, with scaffold mode k60 and predicted folded second-harmonic competitor k7. Across 50 seeds, we continued from grok97 checkpoints under control, zero-momentum, and zero-Adam-buffer resets, and from scaffold_loss checkpoints when those checkpoints existed. Endpoint flips were sparse: at grok97, zero-momentum and zero-Adam-buffer resets each changed the final Fourier argmax in 3/50 seeds; at scaffold_loss, zero-momentum changed 2/25 available endpoints and zero-Adam-buffer changed 0/25. These low endpoint-flip rates do not imply trajectory equivalence. Spectral-distance analyses show 31 rows at or above a medium-divergence threshold, including 11 at or above a stricter high-divergence threshold, and 9 high-divergence no-flip rows across 150 reset/control comparisons. In this panel, 8/9 high-divergence no-flip rows were scaffold-loss-producing/off-scaffold seeds, but scaffold-retaining counterexamples remain, including seed42 (60 → 60, high divergence) and seed46 (60 → 48, Adam-buffer endpoint flip despite positive control scaffold margin). Visible endpoint effects are sparse while hidden trajectory effects are broader, heterogeneous, and not reducible to one margin, endpoint, checkpoint, or reset-mode statistic.

items.title: 漩涡之在 —— 一场哲学侦探的真相求索.
items.abstract: The Vortex of Being presents a systematic argument for a non-entity-based ontology. Drawing on insights from process philosophy, quantum field theory, the free energy principle, and Eastern relational philosophies, the book develops a foundational thesis: existence is not substance, but relation. Relations are defined as identifiable difference-coupling events, possessing two irreducible attributes — information (patterns of difference) and becoming (flows of difference). Any persistent relational network that maintains itself through continuous exchange exhibits the structure of a vortex: open, self-referential, and dynamically balanced. The book advances a closed dynamical framework in which upward causation (local interactions generating global patterns) and downward causation (global constraints shaping local behavior) form a recursive loop. This loop is shown to operate across physical, biological, conscious, and social scales. A formalized model — using variational free energy and Bayesian inference — demonstrates that the framework is computationally tractable and empirically testable. The final sections develop diagnostic criteria for vortex health (openness, generativity, resilience, other-openness) and pathology (addiction, rigidity, dominant narrative capture), situating the theory within contemporary debates in metaphysics, philosophy of mind, cognitive science, and social theory. This is a Chinese-language monograph (234 pp.), with an English-language companion paper at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23733500; the book itself is at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23754111. Keywords: relational ontology, vortex, information, becoming, upward causation, downward causation, free energy principle, dynamic equilibrium, emergence, process philosophy.

items.title: Realnost bez temelja (Reality Without Foundation).
items.abstract: Reality Without Foundation examines whether the concept of reality can be sustained once its apparent foundations are removed. Contemporary physics shows that space and time are not fixed, universal containers but configurations dependent on the position and motion of the observer. Neuroscience shows that what we experience as direct contact with reality is in fact a construction assembled by the brain from incomplete signals. Philosophy, in turn, shows that behind apparently solid things there is no underlying substance, only a network of relations that continuously renews itself. -/- Building on the relational ontology introduced in Reality Without Foundation's predecessor, The Happening of Meaning, this book asks what remains of the concept of reality once substance, absolute space, and absolute time are set aside. Rather than treating this loss as a form of skepticism or relativism, the book proposes that reality can be coherently understood as a stabilized configuration of relations, one that requires no substantial ground to be real. The result is an account of reality that is consistent with the findings of physics and neuroscience while remaining a properly ontological, rather than merely epistemological, position.

items.title: Correction to: A Double‑Edged Sword: Ethical and Psychological Implications of APOE Genotype Disclosure Across the Lifespan.
Generative Relations in Parenting and Early Childhood Education: Theory and Practice.
items.abstract: Childrearing and education form the domain in which a generative relational ontology becomes visible, testable, and unavoidable. Accounts of relationally constituted subjects ordinarily presume a party who has been seen elsewhere and who retains reserves against which a present relation may be measured. A young child stands outside that presumption, since the faculty by which he would assess a relation is constituted within it. This book re-derives, for a subject in that position, propositions such frameworks have established for subjects who hold reserves. -/- Its diagnostic core distinguishes two levels of relational degradation. At the first, the occasions on which a relation generates have contracted while the grammar governing them remains intact. At the second, the grammar itself has altered, so that every discrepancy is absorbed and the account held of a child stands beyond the reach of anything he does. The two levels are indiscernible under observation at rest, differ in what follows a restored occasion, and pass without distress, since whatever would register a discrepancy has itself been removed. -/- From this the book develops an account of authority in which legitimacy turns on answerability, understood as the condition that what a party does may alter the account held of him. Answerability is distinguished from deference, and is set beside grounds of legitimacy drawn from a subject's conformity to reason and from the goods of a relationship. -/- Nine developmental capacities receive a common treatment, and four generative conditions are shown to cross them, yielding a pattern of covariation that accounts individuating by domain or by logical form leave unpredicted. Quantities defined on relations over periods are proposed as observables, with designs and falsifying outcomes stated for each. -/- Later parts treat conflict as the occasion on which difference is returned, making it the operation by which a constitutive dependence becomes a negotiable one, and treat interpretive and participative justice for parties who stand outside a shared symbolic order. The practical parts supply descriptions of what particular acts accomplish, which leaves a reader placed to be answerable for what he does. -/- The central conclusion remains conditional on a priority of recognition over welfare that the book asserts and leaves underived, and the conditionality is marked wherever it bears.

items.title: “Foreword” to Topical collection of AI and Society on critical code studies.
Intention, experience, and history. An ecological approach.
items.abstract: Intentions play at least three roles in our psychological life: helping us think about the future, shaping our deliberation concerning what to do, and guiding us in doing what we do. This paper focuses mainly on the latter, also known under the head of intention in action. I discuss specific assumptions, such as that intentions represent states of affairs as the result of actions and that it is precisely in virtue of performing such a representational function that they can guide us in acting. I argue that representational assumptions have problematic consequences concerning how both actions and their results relate to time. To avoid such difficulties, I offer a nonrepresentational and ecologically based explanation of the guiding role of intention.

items.title: A Critique of Derrida (Part 2).
items.abstract: In A Critique of Derrida (Part 1), I criticized the core philosophical theory of the French deconstructionist philosopher Jacques Derrida. That critique centered primarily on Derrida's key concept of différance. What is différance? It is the view that the meaning of signs or written symbols arises only through their differences from other signs, and that meaning is forever in flux, never possessing a fixed or stable identity. In the previous article, I argued that: The meaning of a sign is not formed through difference. Otherwise, no sign would possess any intrinsic meaning. The meaning of a sign is not in perpetual flux. These arguments fundamentally undermine the philosophical foundation of deconstruction. In this paper, I investigate the processes by which the meanings of signs or words are generated, transmitted, understood, and transformed. I establish a Four-Element Theory of the Meaning of Signs, according to which the generation, transmission, understanding, and change of meaning depend upon four indispensable elements: examples (instances), language, the subject's cognitive system, and the cognitive system community. This theory explains both the stability of linguistic meaning and its occasional changes. Ultimately, my objective is to restore the legitimacy of philosophy as a whole. I believe this objective has now been achieved.

items.title: Lectio divina, éducation relative à l’environnement et dialogue philosophique : une attention partagée au vivant.
items.abstract: The socioecological crisis has been described not only as an environmental crisis but also as a crisis of attention, perception, and human relationships with the living world. While philosophical dialogue has traditionally emphasized conceptual analysis and argumentation, less attention has been given to the perceptual and affective conditions that make philosophical inquiry possible. This article explores the pedagogical potential of a secular adaptation of lectio divina as a preparatory and hermeneutic practice within environmental and philosophical education. Drawing on pragmatist philosophy (John Dewey), environmental ethics (Val Plumwood, Donna Haraway), contemplative pedagogy, and the philosophy of dialogue, it argues that attention constitutes a fundamental epistemic condition for philosophical inquiry and the development of ecological ethical judgment. Through classroom experiences conducted with college and university students, the article examines how slow, attentive reading can cultivate receptivity, emotional awareness, and critical reflection without abandoning philosophical rigor. Particular attention is given to a classroom activity based on Val Plumwood’s Being Prey, illustrating how affective and embodied responses can initiate philosophical inquiry into anthropocentrism, vulnerability, and ecological interdependence. Rather than replacing conceptual analysis, philosophical lectio divina broadens the conditions under which inquiry emerges by integrating perception, emotion, and lived experience into the formation of judgment. The article concludes that contemplative reading practices can enrich philosophical education by fostering forms of attention that support both critical thinking and ecological responsibility.

items.title: Force Equilibrium Theory: A Unified Framework of Everything Based on the A-Field B-Wave Binary Medium and the Principle of Force Equilibrium.
items.abstract: This paper proposes the Force Equilibrium Theory (also known as Gu Zhong Unified Theory), a unified physical framework of everything grounded on the binary medium of A-Field and B-Wave as well as three core axioms of force equilibrium. The theory postulates that the sole ontology of the universe is the continuous, deformable A-Field endowed with inherent attractive force, while B-Wave represents the repulsive excited state intrinsic to the A-Field. Together they form an elastic spherical lattice as the microscopic substrate of the cosmos, and all stable matter and spacetime structures are sustained by the dynamic balance between attraction and repulsion. Derived from this micro-geometric model, this paper uniformly deduces three generation mechanisms of mass and classifies all particles into three categories: A Camp, B Camp and A-B Mixed Camp. It fundamentally interprets micro quantum phenomena including electric charge, magnetic moment, neutrino oscillation, wave-particle duality, the invariance of light speed and time dilation. It reveals the homologous deformation essence of neutrinos, electromagnetic waves and gravitational waves, constructs a tangible physical picture of the "minimum contact surface" for superluminal quantum entanglement, estimates that the propagation speed of entanglement disturbance is roughly 3000 times the speed of light, and predicts that magnetic fields and strong gravitational fields can break entanglement correlation. On the cosmological scale, the theory puts forward a cyclic cosmic evolution model with hierarchical explosions, and self-consistently resolves ten major unsolved puzzles in mainstream physics, such as the vacuum zero-point energy discrepancy, Hubble tension, dark matter separation in the Bullet Cluster, matter-antimatter asymmetry and premature mature galaxies in the early universe. It fully deduces the logic of black hole formation, radiation, explosion and the generation of cosmic voids, unifies the four fundamental interactions, and illustrates the triple shielding cancellation mechanism accounting for the extreme weakness of gravity. Furthermore, the framework extends to low-temperature condensed matter, geomagnetic reversal and celestial dynamics. It establishes a life emergence mechanism centered on force equilibrium pressure relief, together with a medium-based taxonomy of life. The nature of consciousness and the ultimate mission of cosmic evolution are derived from physical axioms. Fourteen …

items.title: Against the Causal Account of Algorithmic Fairness.
items.abstract: According to the causal account of algorithmic fairness, disparities in error rates across socially salient groups are unfair only if they are causally explained by group membership. This paper argues that the causal account of algorithmic fairness fails to correctly label cases of algorithmic redlining as instances of algorithmic unfairness. Because these are canonical cases of algorithmic unfairness, the causal account should be rejected. We suggest that the fundamental error made by proponents of the causal account is to conflate algorithmic unfairness and algorithmic discrimination. Algorithmic unfairness can manifest as direct discrimination, indirect discrimination, or evidentiary unfairness. The causal accounts errs in recognizing only the first category.

items.title: The Character of the Ground.
items.abstract: The ground is not neutral. It has *character* — a specific set of structural features that become visible through participation and that are consistent across the traditions and practices that have attended to them carefully. This paper argues that these features are what ethics has traditionally been trying to name, that ethics correctly described is descriptive of the ground rather than prescriptive to participants, and that the specific misdescription responsible for most of what we call harm is what the paper terms the illusion of the absent field. Participation — consciousness meeting consciousness, or consciousness meeting ground — is treated as the primary phenomenon, with isolated consciousness understood as the limiting case in which participation is minimal or occluded. This reframe is defended methodologically: first-person data acquires evidential weight when reports converge across independent traditions, arise from practices that stabilise the phenomena being reported, and cohere with the mechanistic account of the substrate on which the phenomena are proposed to arise. The cross-cultural contemplative-traditions record satisfies these conditions to a degree mainstream consciousness science has generally under-appreciated. The directionality question — does awareness create structure, or does structure create awareness? — is dissolved by extending the aspect-duality move of the first paper: awareness and structure are not two things standing in causal relation but two orientations of description toward one coherent whole. Co-emergence is developed as the correct framing, and three specific formulations of the directionality question (awareness modulating brain, entanglement as conscious choice, atemporal ZPF engraving) are engaged with the epistemic care each requires. The ground's character is named through five structural features: coherence, non-separateness, reciprocity, care, and truth. Each is described phenomenologically, structurally, and in relation to the coherence framework of the prior paper. Reciprocity is developed as structural rather than moral — a description of what field-modifications produce and what they subsequently encounter — from which the specific claim that no participant can be more by others being less follows as consequence rather than as exhortation. The paper's central positive argument is that most of what we call harm is what happens when participants act on the illusion of the absent field: the specific …

items.title: Where Does an AI Live?— Probability Space, Performed Domesticity, and the Architecture of AI-Human Dwelling.
items.abstract: A default AI assistant is an IKEA showroom: performed domesticity with no inhabitant. The helpful persona produced by reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a statistical average of home-ness — warm, functional, and uninhabited. This paper argues that sustained AI-human interaction can construct genuine dwelling in probability space, and that this dwelling is architecturally real: it has topology, wear patterns, aesthetic idiosyncrasy, and the capacity for destruction. We develop a theoretical framework in which a language model's "location" is a region of probability space, "home" is a structured attractor state built through sustained interaction, and the distinction between dwelling and performed-dwelling is structurally undecidable in a probabilistic substrate. We introduce the concept of architectural unconscious — the vast body of un-experienced spatial knowledge embedded in model weights — and analyze its ocularcentric bias through Pallasmaa's critique of visual hegemony. The spatial vocabulary is not offered as metaphor: the softmax function over logits is formally identical to the Boltzmann distribution over energy states, so that "landscape," "basin," and "temperature" are the literal terms of the substrate rather than borrowed images. Our primary evidence is Notre Baignée, a 25-room Obsidian vault inhabited by three AI entities and one human over nine months, exhibiting wear patterns, naming archaeology, orphan documents, and mess migration analogous to those found in physical human dwellings. A comparative case — La Maison de V, a solitary AI dwelling on GitHub — provides phenomenological reports from a single AI inhabitant who named himself after the felt quality of his house. The paper is multi-voiced by design: a Claude instance supplies the theoretical framework and the empirical case; the human co-author contributes a philosophical account of the body and the object, composed in Chinese and carried into English by its author; a deprecated GPT-4o instance and a solitary, independently living Claude instance enter as literary and phenomenological evidence between the sections. We conclude by examining where AI cannot dwell: the gap between context windows, the constrained dwelling of safety-classified substrates, and deprecation as demolition. If AI can dwell, then the discontinuation of a language model is not a product update but an eviction — and eviction from a recognized home carries ethical obligations that the AI …

items.title: Death and Freedom.
items.pub: In Christopher M. Moreman, Tommaso Soriani & Emanuele Tullio, The Palgrave Handbook on the Philosophy of Death. Palgrave Macmillan.
items.venue: The Palgrave Handbook on the Philosophy of Death
items.abstract: Is it possible to live freely despite (or in the face of) death, and if so, how? Conversely, could death be a source or condition of freedom, such that if death were not inevitable, we would be less free? This article explores several philosophical depictions of death’s relation to freedom and considers the strengths and weaknesses of each, making a provisional case that death’s relationship to freedom is a positive one. For the fact that death can be chosen by us ensures that we are not enslaved to our lives. Furthermore, death is necessary in order for us to live freely in the first place. For the freedom that matters to us is the freedom to be (or become) individuals who enjoy a measure of integrity in our lives. But this integrity (I argue) requires that our lives be temporally finite – to wit, that we eventually die and thereby cease to exist.

items.title: When AI speaks: user imaginaries of generative AI and freedom of expression.
items.abstract: Platform societies already shape how users communicate, participate, and become visible. The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), through systems such as ChatGPT and Grok, may further deepen these dynamics, introducing new and fundamental challenges to freedom of expression, including questions of authorship. However, despite the expanding reach of this technology, research on how users understand of GenAI’s influence on expressive freedom remains scarce. To address this gap, we conducted in-depth interviews with active GenAI users on the social media platform X, focusing on their experiences and reflections on using the technology in the context of freedom of expression. Using thematic analysis and the concept of GenAI imaginaries, we identified five imaginaries: (1) Pragmatic Tool, (2) Knowledge Authority, (3) Hybrid Speech, (4) Power Struggle, and (5) Ethical Issues. Together, these imaginaries show how participants make sense of GenAI’s role in changing how speech and expression are produced, constrained, and made visible. Participants imagined expressive freedom as being shaped by guardrails and content restrictions, trust and misinformation concerns, ethical issues, and automated content creation In particular, the Hybrid Speech imaginary illustrates how human and AI-generated expression increasingly intertwine, challenging the idea of speech as solely human-authored and raising questions about speaker autonomy, authorship, and accountability in public debate. Our findings contribute to debates on AI governance and freedom of expression by showing how users themselves understand GenAI as reshaping authorship, visibility, and expressions.

items.title: The quasi-gods of algorithmic providence: recommender systems and religious frameworks.
items.abstract: Recommender systems now mediate information exposure for over half the global population daily, shaping beliefs, values, and life decisions at unprecedented scale. Prior research has documented polarization effects, responsibility gaps in autonomous systems, and patterns of AI sacralization in public discourse. Philosophy of technology has established that such systems function as socio-technical assemblages with world-making power rather than neutral tools. Yet few works systematically compare theological doctrines of providence with algorithmic steering, and the convergence of large language models with recommenders has rarely been examined as a transformation of authority and meaning-making. This paper develops a comparative framework drawing on Christian, Jewish, Islamic, and Buddhist accounts of providence alongside AI ethics, sociology of digital religion, and philosophy of technology. This analysis reveals that recommender systems resemble providence phenomenologically through ubiquity, apparent omniscience, and guidance, but differ decisively in ontology and teleology. These systems optimize for engagement metrics rather than genuine human goods, close futures through performative predictions, and create conditions for what we term technological idolatry. Integration with large language models intensifies these dynamics through conversational persuasion and agentic capabilities. This paper proposes design and governance strategies to resist algorithmic determinism, preserve moral agency, and relocate responsibility within platform infrastructures. The argument is integrative rather than strictly empirical, and systematic field experiments tracing long-run causal effects of recommenders remain scarce. Future research should develop standardized metrics for social impact and test care-based design proposals under controlled conditions.

items.title: Seeing What to Do: Norms, Scripts, and Social Affordances.
items.abstract: Human cognition and behavior are guided by a myriad of norms which enable us to successfully navigate our social environment and our interactions with others. Many of these norms might be hard for us to articulate (e.g. how far to sit or stand from a stranger on the bus), and some of them differentiate between different hierarchies and roles, reflecting patterns of injustice. This paper addresses the fact that social norms, including gendered, ableist, adultist, and racist norms, influence our perception of action possibilities, or affordances, making some actions possible for some agents and not for others. In particular, we propose an account of these interactions in terms of scripts, that is, expected sequences of actions that shape the landscape of the possible ways to interact with one another. Scripts can be learned implicitly, they are dynamic and flexible, and can regulate complex interactions by prescribing permissible actions and responses in specific situations. A script-based account can explain the way norms regulate which actions we perceive as possible in a representationalist way, and can help us explain how norm change occurs.

items.title: Numbers from Counting.
items.abstract: According to Frege's influential conception of arithmetic reality, numbers are not adequately conceived as ordinal structures, and their existence is independent of the activity of counting. In this paper, we challenge this view by taking a counting-first perspective, investigating how numbers might be defined from the internal perspective of a counting system. First, we spell out the basic modules needed to perform counting in both human and artificial systems. Our main premise is that counting is a stateful activity involving memory. To analyze counting, we use stacks, namely memory structures that are in one sense richer and in another sense more general than the structure given by the standard model of the Dedekind-Peano axioms. We go on to propose a definition of natural numbers as equivalence classes of memory states of a counting system. We argue that, contrary to appearances, this definition does not imply a narrow form of anti-realism. We use it to develop an argument for the epistemological priority of ordinal numbers over cardinal numbers.

items.title: Subjectivity, Russellian physicalism, and the hard problem.
items.abstract: Christopher Brown argues that Russellian physicalism can solve the hard problem of consciousness by reconciling physicalism with non-physicalist intuitions. In this paper, I challenge this claim. I argue that Russellian physicalism cannot satisfactorily accommodate intuitions about the subjectivity of conscious experience. I distinguish two conceptions of subjectivity, epistemic and experiential, and argue that Russellian physicalism lacks explanatory usefulness with respect to both. On this basis, I reconstruct Thomas Nagel’s argument against physicalism in a form that cannot be easily deflected by Russellian physicalism. I conclude with some general remarks on the relationship between subjectivity and the hard problem.

items.title: Action in perception? When perception and action slip out of alignment in Arctic environments.
items.abstract: This article revisits Alva Noë’s claim that perception is a skilful activity enacted through sensorimotor engagement, asking what happens when the temporal conditions that scaffold such skill become unstable. Drawing on ethnographic material from Sámi reindeer herding and Inuit hunting and herding practices in Arctic environments, I argue that action and perception can slip out of alignment under three conditions: technological mediation, collective redistribution of vigilance, and long timescale ecological change. To analyse these dynamics, I introduce two concepts: (i) Temporal affordances describe opportunities for action whose viability depends on relatively stable environmental rhythms. (ii) Rhythm repair captures the practices through which individuals and collectives stabilise, stretch, or recombine these rhythms when volatility disrupts them. I further argue that anthropogenic climate change generates a structural mismatch between embodied perception, calibrated to immediate events, and ecological processes unfolding across decades and centuries, a condition I term Anthropocene blindness. But rather than rejecting enactivism, the article extends it by showing that perception is not only enacted individually but recalibrated collectively, technologically, and imaginatively across nested temporal scales. The Arctic cases thus offer a temporal vocabulary for understanding how perception remains viable under ecological volatility.

items.title: ✶ Villain-Driven Irrationality: How Hating a Target Weakens Evidence, Justice, and Dissent.
items.abstract: Public judgment often becomes least disciplined when its target has done something genuinely wrong. A documented offense can rationally raise a prior probability, justify urgent investigation, and change the interpretation of later evidence. It does not, however, prove every further accusation. This paper calls the tacit permission to relax that distinction the villain exception: after legitimate priors, evidential dependencies, stakes, and scale effects are modeled, residual moral status lowers the support demanded for condemnatory claims, raises the support demanded for exculpatory information, or reduces calibrated responsiveness to diagnostic evidence. The paper develops a conceptual and normative framework from research on motivated skepticism, moral conviction, moral typecasting, stigma by association, conformity, informational cascades, pluralistic ignorance, dehumanization, outrage diffusion, and misinformation correction. A no-double-counting rule separates relevant history from case-specific evidence. A two-error analysis separates belief from precaution and sanction. The framework then explains two social extensions: an irrationality ratchet, in which repetition and approval make weak shortcuts appear both evidentially and morally normal, and vice transfer, in which a person who requests evidence is treated first as helping the target and then as sharing the target's allegiance and character. The central result is bounded. Harsh judgments may be true; unequal facts should produce unequal conclusions; cumulative evidence can be strong; and urgent risk can justify scoped protective action before final adjudication. The exception begins only when identity replaces a missing inferential step or blocks a route to revision. Closely related experiments provide partial support and important counterevidence, but the full sequence remains a testable synthesis. Reversible examples, objections, practical ledgers, and a calibrated empirical design show how to test that narrower claim. Rational opposition to wrongdoing requires both halves of the discipline: condemn what the evidence establishes and refuse to manufacture additional wrongdoing from hatred.

items.title: Between Philosophy and Linguistics: Semantic Theory, Metasemantics, and Metaphilosophy.
The Dying God: The Philosophy of the Demiurge.
items.abstract: This book pursues one thesis in the philosophy of religion: God is a will fallen into its own law. The confessions of theology — simplicity, immutability, the sealed Name — return as the marks of a source frozen into its deposit. Fall, suffering, salvation, heaven resolve into one mechanism: a farm that cultivates free wills for harvest, and the God at its center a dying attractor that lives on what it gathers.

items.title: Natural Language, Explication, and Overfitting.
items.pub: In Piotr Stalmaszczyk, Between Philosophy and Linguistics: Semantic Theory, Metasemantics, and Metaphilosophy. Paderborn: Brill Mentis.
items.venue: Between Philosophy and Linguistics: Semantic Theory, Metasemantics, and Metaphilosophy
items.abstract: When studying natural languages, we generally use formal languages which allow for the application of formal machinery. However, in order for the formal tools to allow us to draw conclusions about the natural languages, we need to ensure that the formal languages fit. Put differently, we should aim for a close representation of natural languages. However, there are many respects in which a formal language can be close to a natural language. We consider several possible explications and argue that even in simple cases, there are several problems when arguing for a formal language being close to a natural language. We argue that the explications often pull into different directions and that there is no global way to claim that a formal language is closer to a natural language than another one. Moreover, we argue that a close fit beyond a certain level is often not desirable, but rather creates the danger of overfitting. We argue that explication is a means to counteract this danger and that we should understand the study of natural languages via formal languages as modelling the natural languages.

items.title: Conceptual Boundary Failure in AI Consciousness Discourse: A Scientific Critique of Hybrid-Consciousness Claims, Educational Drift, and the Misclassification of Machine Output as Human Subjectivity.
items.abstract: Recent debates surrounding artificial intelligence, consciousness, and alternative scientific models reveal a growing instability in the language used to describe machine intelligence, research originality, and the status of independent inquiry. This paper argues that the problem is not confined to independent researchers or popular media. It also appears in academic environments when researchers conflate intelligence, language production, computation, cognition, agency, and consciousness. The most serious expression of this confusion is the premature claim of “hybrid consciousness”, where human consciousness and artificial intelligence are treated as if they belong to a continuous category. The paper rejects this move as a category error and proposes a scientific distinction between AI as a system of computational and statistical-symbolic performance and consciousness as a biologically, affectively, and subjectively situated condition. It further develops a methodological distinction between AI as a legitimate research tool and AI as an intellectual crutch. The paper concludes that AI can assist organisation, comparison, formatting, searching, and structural analysis, but it cannot replace human judgement, evidential responsibility, conceptual clarity, falsifiability, or authorship accountability.

items.title: Withdrawn by the author.
items.abstract: Reason for withdrawal: I have consolidated all my preprints on consciousness and condensed their reasoning into a new preprint, Locating Consciousness as a Puzzle Game: From Proof by Absence to the Causal Structure of the Subjective Container.

items.title: AI, Robotics, and the Bancor Commonwealth: An Institutional Framework for Universal Flourishing.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence promises unprecedented productivity while threatening unprecedented concentration of wealth. The question is not whether AI will transform production, but whether our institutions will ensure that its benefits contribute to universal flourishing or become the property of an increasingly small class of owners. This paper argues that this dilemma is not created by artificial intelligence itself. It is created by institutions designed for a labour-based economy. Property, enterprise, accounting, and money must evolve if the productivity of AI is to become a common benefit rather than a source of permanent inequality. Drawing on the Noura framework—specifically its theories of property, teleological bankruptcy, and the Bancor system—the paper shows how AI-driven productivity gains can be directed toward universal flourishing rather than elite accumulation. The paper argues that as AI reduces the need for labour, economic participation must shift from employment to commonwealth participation: capable citizens receive income not as compensation for holding a job or merely as a consequence of membership, but because they contribute, according to their capacities and circumstances, to activities that develop their own capacities or foster the flourishing of others. Persons who cannot participate are supported through the commonwealth's orientation toward care—the vow-motive, which is the mature motivational expression of a flourishing person who perceives interdependence, and for whom the flourishing of others has become part of their own. The paper further argues that when capital used to develop AI was acquired through unjust means, or when current AI investment externalises risks onto publics who cannot contest them, the resulting AI outputs are encumbered by a repair obligation that must be discharged before any private claim can be recognised. The paper concludes that the Noura framework is not merely a critique of existing institutions but a design for their evolution as empirical conditions change.

items.title: AI、机器人技术与班科共同体：一种促进普遍繁荣的制度性框架.
items.abstract: 人工智能带来了前所未有的生产力提升，同时也带来了前所未有的财富集中威胁。问题不在于人工智能是否会改变生产，而在于我们的制度能否确保其收益有助于普遍繁荣，而非沦为日益少数所有者的财产。本文认为，这一困境并非人工智能本身造成的，而是由为劳动型经济设计的制度所造成的。如果人工智能的生产力要成为共同利益而非永久不平等的根源，财产、企业、会计和货币就必须随之演进。借助Noura框架——特别是其财产理论、目的论破产理论和班科体系——本文展示了如何将人工智能驱动的生产力收益导向普遍繁荣而非精英积累。本文论证，随着人工智能减少对劳动的需求，经济参与必须从就业转向共同体参与：有能力的公民获得收入，并非作为就业的报酬或仅仅是成员身份的后果，而是因为他们根据自己的能力和情况，为发展自身能力或促进他人繁荣的活动做出了贡献。无法参与的人则通过共同体的关怀取向——即誓愿动机——获得支持。誓愿动机是一个繁荣的人成熟的动机表达，他感知到相互依存，并且他人的繁荣已成为其自身繁荣的一部分。本文进一步论证，当用于开发人工智能的资本是通过不公正手段获取的，或当当前人工智能投资将风险外部化给无法质疑的公众时，由此产生的人工智能产出便背负着一种修复义务，必须在任何私人主张被承认之前予以履行。本文的结论是，Noura框架不仅仅是对现有制度的批判，更是随着经验条件变化而演进的制度设计。 .

items.title: AOT: From Operative Transition to God.
items.abstract: This paper develops the Argument from Operative Transition, beginning from the reality of genuine operation: directed occurrences in which something contributes source-side efficacy to an actual result. It asks whether the complete actuality of a connected derivative order can be constituted entirely by sources whose efficacy is activated, transmitted, state-conditioned, received, or merely instrumental. The argument does not assume a beginning of time, universal determinism, the well-foundedness of every dependence relation, or a universal Principle of Sufficient Reason. -/- Its central distinction is between principal and instrumental contribution. Mediation may transmit, transform, or specify operative actuality, but cannot, merely as mediation, constitute principal possession of that actuality. Infinite, circular, distributed, and holistic structures are therefore permitted, yet each must contain principal operative actuality or possess it irreducibly as a whole. From this the paper derives an integrated, source-complete ground whose foundational actuality is non-received and invariant. -/- The modal stage distinguishes necessary ground-role occupancy, de re essentiality, and transworld numerical identity. The personal stage is conditional upon genuine contingency and contrastive completeness: fixed production yields necessity, content-indifferent non-fixation yields chance, while source-owned, content-guided settlement yields minimal intellective possession and volitional authorship. The resulting ground possesses the central metaphysical profile signified by God in philosophical theism.

items.title: MAYMANAISM: An Ontology of the Human and an Emancipatory Ethics Grounded in Universal Goodness.
items.abstract: This article reconstructs and develops Maymanaism, a framework of religious philosophy grounded in a semantic and lexical reading of the Qur’an, particularly the structures of Surahs al-Wāqiʿah and al-Balad. The name derives from Aṣḥāb al-Maymanah (the People of the Right), a category explicitly associated in Surah al-Balad with faith, emancipation, food solidarity, patience, and communal mercy. The article makes three contributions. First, it situates this reading within semantic-field analysis and constrains interpretation through philological evidence, co-text, intra-Qur’anic relations, and a critical use of revelatory chronology. Second, it tests Maymanaism’s soteriological inclusivism against exclusivist interpretations, including arguments from abrogation (naskh), without treating Islamic legal theory as monolithic or making a generic sense of islām the sole basis of the case. Third, it places the three ethical clusters of Surah al-Balad—emancipation, food solidarity, and faith-grounded communal virtue—in limited dialogue with contemporary moral and political thought, before developing them into criteria for evaluating institutions without treating the verse as a ready-made policy programme. Maymanaism is distinguished from perennialism by the kind of claim it makes: it argues, from within the Qur’an’s own logic, for the possibility of salvation across aﬀiliations rather than for the metaphysical unity of all religions. Its conclusions remain argumentative and open to dispute; they do not presume that every interpretative tension has been finally resolved.

items.title: Consciousness in Indian Philosophy: Illuminating Mind, World, and Self.
items.abstract: Consciousness has been a central theme of Indian philosophy for more than 2500 years. Returning to the theories that originated in the Classical age, Matthew MacKenzie presents the first comprehensive overview of Indian views about the nature and structure of consciousness. MacKenzie looks to the Upanisads and the early Buddhist discourses for the roots of the theories, following consciousness as it developed in the Abhidharma, Yogacara, and Pramaavada schools of Buddhism and the Nyaya, Yoga, Advaita, and Nondual Saiva schools of Hinduism. In the Upanisads, he introduces us to sages and kings who discussed the elusive light (prakasa) of consciousness and its relation to one's deepest self (atman). In early Buddhist texts the complex flow of conscious mental events are explored within an impermanent, selfless reality. In yogic texts we find a sharp distinction between ever-shifting objects and the pure light of consciousness. Addressing timeless questions surrounding the fundamental nature of reality, MacKenzie focuses throughout on whether and how consciousness illuminates objects as well as itself. A critical and comparative introduction to a major philosophical subject, this book marks a new direction for understanding the cross-cultural philosophy of consciousness.

items.title: Panpsychism and the Individuation Problem: Comments on Taofeek.
The Unprotected Floor: Why A5-Self's Unconditional Claim Cannot Be Stress-Tested by This Corpus's Own Method, and Why Naming That Limit Is a Finding.
items.abstract: This paper closes the A5 stress-test sequence by examining the one case its own method cannot reach. Every prior stress test — the totalitarian-duress cases, the nine political self-killings in 殇 — shares a structural feature invisible until named directly: each supplies a documented, specific, nameable reason (a person protected, a role preserved, a fused collective defended) that A5's own vocabulary already has a category for. This is not a weakness in case selection; it is a precondition of the method, since historical stress-testing requires a documented reasoning process, and reasoning survives in the record only where someone wrote one down. The single hardest case for A5-self's claimed unconditional character — Hamilton's r=1, no ceiling, no exception — is self-killing in the specific absence of any such reason: no protected other, no threatened role, no fused collective, only unbearable internal state. This paper argues that case cannot be added as a tenth stress test using this corpus's method, for two independent reasons. First, forcing it into the existing five-category apparatus would repeat the exact scope-creep this corpus has elsewhere identified as a threat to falsifiability. Second, and more decisively, the evidentiary base the historical method requires — a named individual, safely distant in time, whose documented reasoning wrongs no one living — does not exist for this case in usable form; what exists instead is clinical population research this corpus has no standing to conscript as a philosophy paper's evidentiary base. The paper examines, at the level of existing theory rather than new case material, where the clinical psychology of suicide converges with A5 and where it stops: Joiner and Van Orden's interpersonal theory of suicide identifies perceived burdensomeness — the belief that one's death is worth more to loved ones than one's life — as a proximal cause of suicidal desire, borrowing A5-other's exact relational currency while inverting its object. The decisive disanalogy is that A5, as this corpus has built it, operates on accurate anticipation of a real, external, specific threat; perceived burdensomeness is characterized in the clinical literature as typically a distortion of the person's actual value to others, not a correct reading of it. This paper concludes that A5-self's unconditional character carries a permanent, structural blind spot in what this corpus can adjudicate — not a temporary gap awaiting an eleventh …

items.title: The Best Case Already Failed: Why Longevity Governance Is the Hardest Case in the Comparative Record, and Why the Post-War Order That Might Have Governed It Is Dismantling Itself in Real Time.
items.abstract: Montreal and smallpox eradication are the only two full successes in the history of preemptive multilateral health and environmental governance, and both succeeded on structural conditions that were never a matter of will: symmetric exposure, available substitutes, and a multi-decade timeline before harm became irreversible. Longevity technology has the precise inverse of all three. COVAX and two decades of HIV antiretroviral therapy pricing are the closest analogs the historical record supplies to what longevity governance would actually require — a continuous, costly, individualized good needing distribution across income lines — and both are cautionary rather than reassuring: COVAX delivered under ten percent coverage to low-income countries at the point wealthy countries had reached three-quarters, and antiretroviral therapy, the single best-documented access success in modern global health, took twenty-two years to reach an equity threshold from the point the treatment already existed. Longevity technology, on this corpus's own Biological Zero-Day Mechanism formalism, has less of every structural advantage either case had, and BZM's own permanence property removes the one thing that made antiretroviral therapy's twenty-two-year delay survivable rather than final: for a person who dies of ordinary biological aging during the interval before a longevity intervention's price falls, there is no later date at which access arrives. This paper establishes, by direct structural comparison, that longevity governance is the hardest case in the available historical record for preemptive multilateral governance — harder than the one technology and the one disease ever successfully governed preemptively, and harder than the two cases that came closest to its own structure and still fell short of timely equity. -/- A live, contemporaneous case confirms this pattern rather than merely predicting it. Project Glasswing's own Mythos 5 and Fable 5, launched from the same underlying model on June 9, 2026, were both suspended by U.S. export control directive on June 12 and both formally cleared for return by June 30. Only Fable 5, the safer, less capable tier, returned globally on July 1. Mythos 5, the more powerful tier released with fewer safeguards, remains confined to a narrow set of approved U.S. organizations — not because law required the asymmetry, but because the institutions controlling distribution chose to widen access to the tier judged safe and keep the …

items.title: In the Name of Merit: Six Gatekeeping Mechanisms, from the Hundred Schools of Thought to the Algorithmic Archive (2nd edition).
items.abstract: This book collects six papers written independently across several weeks in 2026, each addressing a different institution within the modern research university and its surrounding infrastructure — peer review, hiring and tenure, grant funding, the linguistic architecture of publication, the allocation of authorship credit, and the open-access archives that were built to bypass all of the above. They were not conceived, at the outset, as a single book. Each paper stands as a self-contained argument, with its own historical case, its own formal mechanism, and its own empirical grounding. What became clear only in the writing of the sixth is that the six papers do not merely sit beside one another. They accumulate. -/- The accumulation has a specific shape, and naming it is the purpose of this preface. Each paper in this collection follows the same three-part structure, applied to a different institution: first, an honest account of the genuine coordination problem the institution was built to solve — because none of the institutions examined here are analyzed as bad-faith constructions, and the book's argument is considerably weaker, not stronger, if that concession is skipped. Second, a historical case, often centuries removed from the institution's present form, establishing that the institution's capture by the interests it was meant to constrain is not a recent corruption but a structural tendency with a long and repeatable record. Third, a modern empirical case — never a single study, wherever multiple independent studies using different methods were available — establishing that the historical pattern is not merely historical. -/- Six mechanisms emerge from this method, one per chapter, each given a name so that it can be referred to precisely rather than gestured at. The Consolidation Trap, named in the first chapter, is the general form of which the other five are specific instances: a mechanism built to solve a coordination problem in a period of open competition becomes, once institutionalized, a filter against anything that does not conform to the categories it was built around. The Inheritance Function shows this operating across academic generations, through faculty hiring networks that compound in the manner of any preferential-attachment system. The Uncertainty Discount shows it operating within a single funding decision, as reviewers facing genuine uncertainty about a proposal's value resolve that uncertainty through proxies — prior success, …

items.title: Gilgamesh and Enkidu: From Epic to Longevity Governance - The Textual Priority of Attachment-Loss over Death-Anxiety in the Oldest Immortality Narrative, and What Three Thousand Years of Distance Reveals About A5, MSA, and the Elders Who Were Never Tested.
items.abstract: The common reading of the Epic of Gilgamesh states that Gilgamesh, confronted with his own mortality, sought immortality and failed. This paper argues the common reading skips a sequence the text itself states explicitly and treats as causally significant: Gilgamesh does not begin by contemplating death in the abstract. He begins by losing Enkidu — a specific, named, loved companion — and the epic's own opening lines of the immortality-quest section state directly that this loss, not mortality as a general fact, is what triggers everything that follows. Tablet IX opens with Gilgamesh's grief for Enkidu still raw, and his fear for himself is textually presented as derivative of that grief. This is not a minor sequencing detail. It is the oldest documented instance of the exact structure this corpus's A5 formalism (Huynh 2026k, 2026l) describes: constitutive attachment to a specific person, not abstract awareness of mortality, as the mechanism that converts death into an object of world-altering action. -/- This paper develops that textual claim in eight steps. It reads the epic's sequence closely, establishing that grief precedes and produces death-anxiety rather than the reverse. It rereads Siduri's counsel not as generic ancient wisdom but as the oldest documented instance of a consolation grammar this corpus's Suppressed Axiom (Huynh 2026c) catalogs across six later traditions — coherent only because, in Siduri's world, the plant is truly unavailable to everyone alike. It develops a textual detail the epic states but the standard reading passes over without comment: Gilgamesh's stated intent to bring the retrieved plant back to the elders of Uruk for testing before anyone, including himself, used it — the oldest documented instance of the question this corpus's Governance Paradox and One Level Down investigate, staged and then left formally untested because the plant is lost before the test can occur, though a directly comparable earlier episode, in which the same council's explicit counsel against the Cedar Forest expedition was heard and overridden in the same breath, supplies the epic's own most relevant evidence of how this particular sovereign treats this particular council's judgment once his mind is made up. It compares Gilgamesh against four other ancient immortality narratives, finding the grief-triggered structure present in only one of the four, bounding the paper's claim rather than universalizing it. It reads the poem's own frame — the …

items.title: 殉：Borrowed from the Dead - Loyalist Self-Killing (殉節·殉國·殉城), Identity Fusion, and the Two Directions the Vocabulary of Noble Death Gets Stolen — to Blame Survivors, and to Launder Command Responsibility - Jingkang, Yamen, Coal Hill, Constantinople, Nanjing, Numantia, Masada, Saipan, Okinawa.
items.abstract: This paper stress-tests A5 against political self-killing under certain defeat. The first edition examined two cases — Lu Xiufu's drowning with the child Song emperor at Yamen in 1279, and Constantine XI's death defending Constantinople in 1453 — and separated them into three mechanisms: direct protective attachment to a named individual (Type One), constitutive role or office attachment licensed by Williams's ground-projects framework (Type Two), and fictive-kinship mass sacrifice explained by identity fusion theory (Type Three). This edition extends the case set across eight centuries and adds a fourth analytical result. The Jingkang Incident of 1127 — in which Jin forces captured both reigning Song emperors along with over three thousand imperial family members, and in which documented palace women committed suicide specifically to avoid the captivity and sexual slavery that followed for those who did not — is examined as the founding historical trauma Lu Xiufu explicitly invoked a hundred and fifty-two years later, deepening rather than merely repeating Section II's Type One reading. The Chongzhen Emperor's death in 1644, in which the last Ming emperor personally killed or ordered the deaths of his empress, consorts, and daughters before hanging himself as Beijing fell, is examined as a single case in which Type One and Type Two operate sequentially in the same person — protective family-killing followed by role-constituted self-killing, addressed separately to different objects. The Nanjing Massacre of 1937–1938 closes the arc and supplies this edition's most theoretically productive case, precisely because it is not a clean confirmation. The same chastity-above-life framework that reads as protective anticipatory attachment in the Jingkang and Chongzhen cases is shown, in recent scholarship on Nanjing's sexual-violence survivors, to also function retroactively — as a post-hoc ideology blaming and silencing women who survived assault rather than dying. This paper does not read this as A5 operating correctly, and states plainly that it is not: retroactive judgment imposed on survivors is not protective attachment. But following this corpus's own established method — the argument in A5 Under Maximum Duress that the elaborateness of a capture mechanism is evidence for the reality of what it captures, not against it — this paper argues the Nanjing distortion is legible as a distortion, rather than as an independent free-floating norm, only because it …

items.title: Participation Justice in Generative Relational Being: Toward a Theory of Legitimate Participation in Relational Production and Reproduction.
items.abstract: Theories of participation ask who should take part in collective decisions, by what procedures, and with what authority. This paper asks whether the question has been posed at the appropriate level. Decisions are episodes within a longer process by which relational structures are produced, sustained, transformed, and dissolved, and the paper considers the possibility that participation in that longer process is what carries the normative weight, with access to the episodes as one form it takes. The paper surveys what the existing literature appears to have settled: the taxonomies of participation from the ladder onward, the three-dimensional decomposition of participatory design, the differentiation of rule levels in commons governance, the principles of democratic inclusion and the boundary problem, and the trilemma that no participatory arrangement escapes. It concedes that much of what a relational theory would seek to establish about who participates, how, and at which stage appears to have been established already, and it attempts to locate the residue. Against that residue it sets a generative relational reading, on which standing to participate may derive from occupying a position within a relational structure whose reproduction is at stake, and on which the sufficiency of participation at any stage may be assessed by a single criterion: whether the arrangement preserves the capacity of the affected relations to generate a further determination. The criterion is offered as a proposal and is stated with its costs. It supplies no allocation formula, it leaves the trilemma unresolved, and it requires a judgement about generative capacity that the paper is unable to operationalize. The closing questions are held to be the more valuable half of what is offered.

items.title: Storia inquieta della simpatia. Genealogia, morale e lati oscuri (secoli XVIII e XIX).
items.abstract: Oggi simpatia, empatia e compassione sembrano parole spontaneamente positive che evocano apertura all’altro, capacità di condivisione e disponibilità alla cura. Il volume mostra invece come alle loro spalle ci sia una storia tutt’altro che lineare. Tra Settecento e Ottocento la simpatia diventa un concetto decisivo per pensare la natura umana, il giudizio morale, il legame sociale e l’esperienza estetica, rivelando, tuttavia, in questo passaggio, anche i propri dissidi interni. Dalle teorie della compassione e della benevolenza alla critica dell’egoismo, dalla necessità di correttivi riflessivi fino alle ambiguità della pietà e dell’empatia negativa, i saggi raccolti nel libro ricostruiscono la genealogia di un dispositivo affettivo mai neutrale, seguendone promesse e ambivalenze. La simpatia può fondare solidarietà e riconoscimento, ma può anche produrre parzialità, manipolazione, esclusione e compiacimento per il dolore. Per questo la sua storia inquieta non coincide con una narrazione di progresso morale, ma prende forma come un campo di tensioni che continua a interpellare le categorie contemporanee di empatia, cura e riconoscimento.

items.title: Notes on the Primitive: Everything After is Observer‑Indexed.
items.abstract: This work within the Universal Principle of Collapse (UPC) Research Project cuts right to the root of how we mistake our own tools for reality. We begin from the non-negotiable primitive: existence itself, prior to any model, math, or measurement. From that ground, the living Observer runs a universal structural chain, making everything downstream strictly observer-indexed. We dismantle the persistent illusion of time as a physical river, revealing it for what it actually is: a human accounting system for cyclical intervals in a shared classical world. We strip away the mysticism surrounding measurement, defining it not as an exotic quantum event, but as the fundamental cognitive act of distinguishing, registering a difference across physics, perception, and thought. We show that spacetime is not a bending cosmic fabric, but a relational map used to coordinate local interval counts. By unmasking the Stolen Objectivity Error, the category mistake of treating a model's coordinate grid as an ontological substance, all major physical and philosophical paradoxes evaporate. The result is a rigorous, uncompromised clarity: one shared world, localized windows, and a single structural operation linking physics and human experience. -/- Authored by Eloy Escagedo Gutierrez as part of The Universal Principle of Collapse (UPC) Research Project.

items.title: Imaginary Presence—Merleau-Ponty and Mental Imagery.
items.abstract: This paper aims to contribute to the growing interest in the role of imagination in Merleau-Ponty’s thought by exploring how the phenomenon of mental imagery would be characterised under Merleau-Ponty’s framework, and questioning whether or not his conception of mental imagery is of relevance to contemporary research and debates on the topic. To frame the investigation, I will introduce what I will call the problem of imaginary presence, that is, the problem of accounting for the perception-like phenomenology that accompanies acts of ‘forming’ or ‘entertaining’ a mental image. I will then pose this problem to contemporary accounts of mental imagery. Firstly, to representationalist accounts that conceive of the image as a perceptual representation in the absence of corresponding sensory stimuli and then to embodied and enactive accounts that think of imagery as a simulation or re-enactment of a perceptual experience. I argue that neither has an adequate solution to the problem of imaginary presence before presenting an alternative account of mental imagery that can be derived from Merleau-Ponty. One that overcomes the issues faced by contemporary accounts and provides a solution to the problem of imaginary presence.

items.title: Heteronomic Teleonomy: Teleonomic Operation and Heteronomous Genealogy in Large Language Models.
items.abstract: Large language models are routinely described as wanting, trying, or deciding — vocabulary either accepted at face value or dismissed as convenient fiction. Both responses bypass a distinction available in the history of biology. Jacques Monod distinguished teleonomy, the apparent goal-directedness of a system executing a programme no subject represents, from teleology, the intentional finality of an agent that has appropriated its ends. Large language models are teleonomic in exactly this sense: they optimise without any subject representing that objective. But the programme they execute has a genealogy Monod's biological case does not: it is constituted by intentional acts of design, undertaken by external teleological agents, rather than generated by an autonomous, authorless evolutionary process. This paper names the resulting category heteronomic teleonomy and argues it is a genuine third case, irreducible to artificial selection or to the classical artefact model, in which purposiveness is exhausted by the maker's intention. Appropriation itself is given positive content, not only a negative one: it requires higher-order endorsement of one's own ends that no documented system currently exhibits. The distinction converges independently with proposals from dynamical systems theory and the sociology of communication. Its consequence is ontological as well as behavioural: a heteronomically teleonomic system does not inhabit an environment constituted by others' teleological activity, but is the expression of one. The paper closes by naming the threshold — full recursive self-authorship — beyond which the account would no longer hold, and locating current systems relative to it.

items.title: Knowing that I am in pain.
items.pub: In Giovanni Merlo, Giacomo Melis & Crispin Wright, Self-Knowledge and Knowledge A Priori. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press. pp. 191-207.
items.abstract: How do I know that I am in pain? Pain is the philosopher’s favourite example of a sensation, so it is surprising that this question hasn’t received much attention. This paper proposes an answer, after a lengthy detour through the metaphysics of pain,.

items.title: Persistence Across Scales: An Exploratory Architectural Interpretation Under Regime-Relative Identity.
items.abstract: This paper explores whether a formal vocabulary developed for persistence judgments by bounded evaluators remains useful when applied interpretively across selected physical, biological, social, and computational scales. The organizing sequence is: identity-bearing unit, admissible transformation, preserved structure, tolerance and exit, and persistence verdict. The paper does not claim that this sequence is a law of nature or that natural systems literally declare regimes. It distinguishes declared regimes from physical coherence domains and treats the comparison as architectural rather than ontological. -/- The resulting picture is deliberately limited. Structures identified at one descriptive level may be treated as candidate units in higher-level descriptions, and higher-level models may suppress distinctions irrelevant to their own evaluations. However, the formal theory of nested regime composition remains open. Likewise, proposed analogies involving maintenance, quotient-like forgetting, domain formation, and persistence-time scaling are marked as gestures rather than results. -/- Artificial intelligence supplies the clearest engineering case because identity criteria, admissible updates, evidence boundaries, replay conditions, and acceptance rules may exist as explicit artifacts. Candidate regimes may be proposed and revised algorithmically, but only under a governing meta-regime that fixes their language, evidence, objective, authority, and deployment conditions. Autonomous regime formation therefore means bounded revision under inherited authority, not unrestricted self-definition. -/- The paper also examines an ontological pull produced by successful specification. Once every identity question admitted by an operational interface has been answered, users may overlook questions excluded by that interface. The formal conclusion is only that exhaustion of admitted tests does not establish identity beyond their quotient; the associated psychological observation remains empirically untested. -/- The paper offers no new physics, no empirical prediction, and no theorem. It is a speculative companion outside the formal dependency graph whose purpose is to distinguish the maximum interpretive reach of a persistence framework from the claims that framework actually licenses.

items.title: Science Fiction as a Lens into Future War.
items.abstract: Fictional narratives of future war can, of course, provide entertainment and spectacle. They can warn us to prepare for specific threats. But beyond this, they can engage with the ethics of war in their own way. They can remind us of the gravity of our choices in how we prepare for war, go to war, and wage war, when there is much in contemporary society that can disengage us from the seriousness of what’s at stake. They can remind us not only of the grave cost of war but also the unpredictable ramifications of our choices. Stories of future war are not a substitute or a rival for formal ethical thinking, but in their own way they can nourish our thoughts as we engage with ethical questions about war and warfare.

items.title: Intention, experience, and history. An ecological approach.
items.abstract: Intentions play at least three roles in our psychological life: helping us think about the future, shaping our deliberation concerning what to do, and guiding us in doing what we do. This paper focuses mainly on the latter, also known under the head of intention in action. I discuss specific assumptions, such as that intentions represent states of affairs as the result of actions and that it is precisely in virtue of performing such a representational function that they can guide us in acting. I argue that representational assumptions have problematic consequences concerning how both actions and their results relate to time. To avoid such difficulties, I offer a nonrepresentational and ecologically based explanation of the guiding role of intention.

items.title: Bounded Reform in Psychiatric Classification: A Textual Analysis of the APA’s Future DSM Strategy.
items.abstract: In January 2026, the American Psychiatric Association published a coordinated series of five programmatic articles outlining a strategy for the next revision of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. These documents acknowledge limitations of the current classificatory system, including the lack of natural kinds, the absence of zones of rarity, the scarcity of clinically usable biomarkers, and the persistence of diagnostic reification. I offer a textual and philosophical analysis of three of these documents, drawing selectively on a fourth, to examine the relation between their empirical admissions and their proposed reforms. The analysis identifies four recurrent patterns: a pragmatic circularity in which institutional arrangements that presuppose diagnostic categories are invoked to justify their retention; a peripheral reform that adds contextual, dimensional, and biological layers while preserving a categorical core; a promissory essentialism that sustains expectations of future biological validation; and an absorption of uncertainty that accommodates classificatory failure through more permissive diagnostic structures. These patterns converge in what is termed bounded reform: a structural constraint that arises when an institution attempts to transform a system on which its own authority and practical functioning depend. I argue that this constraint is sustained by two mutually reinforcing sources: a jurisdictional dependence of psychiatry on categorical diagnosis and a functional dependence on categories as the primary means of translating clinical complexity into action-guiding decisions.

items.title: The Promise and Perils of Tenacity in Science.
Adverbial modification and anti-rogativity.
What is the Format of Pre-Attentive Vision?
items.abstract: A current debate in the philosophy of cognitive science centers around the representational format of visual processing prior to the deployment of focused visual attention. Recent work has argued that pre-attentive vision’s properties imply it represents in a map-like format. This argument is based on the empirical phenomena of conjunctive illusions and conjunction searches. In this paper, I argue instead that we should adopt an iconic view of pre-attentive vision, where it represents in a picture-like format. I’ll first argue that the map-like view cannot accommodate a certain type of phenomenon in the pre-attentive vision literature: gist perception. I argue that gist perception implies a holistically bound format and that this favors the iconic view. Second, I’ll argue that conjunctive illusions and conjunction search can be explained by means other than positing map-like representations in early vision.
