items.title: Experiences of self-continuity and self-discontinuity in dreams and its relation with the body and affectivity.
items.abstract: Research on the continuity and discontinuity between the waking and dreaming minds has largely focused on similarities and differences in waking and dream content. The present study expands this debate by examining another dimension: the relationship between the dream self and the waking self at the phenomenal level. Specifically, it investigates how bodily and affective dimensions of dream experience relate to individuals' experiences of self-continuity and self-discontinuity across wakefulness and dreaming. A sample of 302 participants completed self-report measures assessing experiences of self-(dis)continuity, including experiences of being another person, dream embodiment, dream affectivity, observer perspectives, lucid dreaming, and dream recall frequency. Results showed that stronger felt self-continuity between dreaming and waking was positively associated with experiences of positive—but not negative—dream emotions carrying over into waking life, and negatively associated with experiencing a body distinct from one's waking body. Conversely, more frequent experiences of being another person in dreams were associated with more frequent experiences of emotions perceived as inappropriate to the dream context. Contrary to expectations, no significant associations were found between experiences of being another person in dreams and lucid dreaming, observer perspectives, or dream recall frequency. These findings suggest convergent associations between experiences of self-(dis)continuity and bodily and affective dream phenomenology.

items.title: Beyond Participatory Explanation: Ontological Reflexivity Theory as a Resolution to the Consciousness Emergence Problem.
items.abstract: David Cota’s evaluation of the author’s “participatory explanation” approach to consciousness reveals fundamental conceptual problems that plague contemporary consciousness studies. Cota identifies a critical conflation between reason as a symbolic-operational function, and consciousness as a phenomenal-experiential field, that undermines the theoretical coherence of participatory approaches. This paper develops a novel theoretical framework called “Ontological Reflexivity Theory” (ORT) that addresses Cota’s specific concerns while providing genuine ontological grounding for consciousness emergence. -/- ORT proposes that consciousness emerges through ontological reflexivity—a material process whereby complex systems develop recursive self-modification capabilities that generate phenomenal fields as emergent properties of their organizational dynamics. Unlike participatory explanation, which treats circularity as a methodological solution, ORT identifies specific material mechanisms that produce consciousness through three hierarchical levels: structural reflexivity (feedback loops), organizational reflexivity (meta-rule modification), and ontological reflexivity (recursive self-modification of modification principles). -/- The theory provides rigorous functional and ontological distinctions between reason and consciousness, grounds explanation in material processes rather than conceptual maneuvers, and establishes empirical criteria for distinguishing genuine from pseudo-explanations. Mathematical formalization through the Ontological Reflexivity Index (ORI) enables quantitative predictions about consciousness emergence, while comparative analysis demonstrates ORT’s superior explanatory power relative to physicalism, dualism, panpsychism, and existing consciousness theories. -/- Empirical predictions include correlations between consciousness and recursive self-modification neural circuits, scaling relationships between phenomenal richness and organizational complexity, and developmental trajectories following predicted emergence patterns. The framework resolves the hard problem by eliminating the false dichotomy between “physical” and “mental” processes, showing both to be abstractions from more fundamental reflexive processes. -/- This work demonstrates that consciousness can be understood scientifically through proper conceptual foundations that avoid the reason/consciousness conflation while maintaining genuine explanatory power. The implications …

items.title: The Five Classes of Dimensional Judgment: A Structural Taxonomy of Cognitive Bias.
items.abstract: The cognitive-bias literature has produced a catalog of hundreds of named biases without a unifying structural account of why these biases and not others exist. This paper proposes that judgment executes four dimensional operations in a fixed sequence, recognition, contextualization, resolution, action, and that bias arises when the sequence fails to close in order. The five non-empty classes of dimensional judgment error follow from the dependency structure of the four dimensions. The signalless frame names the failure where contextualization operates without recognition having delivered the current signal. The frameless verdict names the failure where resolution operates without contextualization having delivered the frame. The unresolved commit names the failure where action operates without resolution having delivered the determinate state. The signalless verdict names the failure where resolution operates at the direct recognition-to-resolution path without recognition having delivered the targeted referent. The signalless commit names the catastrophic failure where action commits without recognition having admitted anything to commit on. A sixth potential class (contextualization-to-action without resolution) is structurally empty under the architecture's closure: every path from contextualization to action passes through resolution, and the architecture admits no clean contextualization-to-action shortcut. The architectural derivation of the dependency structure and the empty-cell closure lives in Stewart (2026e, 2026f, 2026g, 2026z). -/- Each of the five non-empty classes corresponds to a named pattern in the cognitive-bias literature. Class 2-1, the signalless frame, captures persistent-state biases where the frame the resolution operates on carries content the present recognition admission did not deliver (anxious vigilance, ambient prior-state contamination of present judgment). Class 3-2, the frameless verdict, captures the canonical frame-mismatch biases (anchoring, framing, base-rate neglect, fundamental attribution error, hindsight, in-group bias, status-quo, planning fallacy, confirmation bias). Class 4-3, the unresolved commit, captures commit-before-resolve biases (belief perseverance, sunk-cost). Class 3-1, the signalless verdict, captures determination-without-referent biases (the conjunction fallacy in the Linda paradigm, the availability heuristic). Class 4-1, the signalless commit, captures confabulation and the strongest …

items.title: The Five Classes of Error: A Structural Taxonomy.
items.abstract: An error is a process whose stages execute out of sequence: a later stage executes before the earlier stage it depends on has delivered. Any judgment, computation, diagnosis, or inference proceeds through four ordered stages, each stage depending on the one before it, and an error is a stage executing on input the prior stage has not yet supplied. Sorting the ways the four-stage dependency can break yields five distinct error types plus one combination the dependency makes impossible. The five types are exhaustive (every error that breaks the dependency is one of the five) and the same five types appear in any field whose process proceeds through the four ordered stages. -/- The five error types name which stage executed on undelivered input. Stage-2-on-stage-1 (Type 2-1): the contextualizing stage executes before the recognition stage has delivered, so it situates content whose existence is not yet established. Stage-3-on-stage-2 (Type 3-2): the resolving stage executes before the contextualizing stage has delivered, so it settles a state with no context to settle it against. Stage-4-on-stage-3 (Type 4-3): the committing stage executes before the resolving stage has delivered, so it carries forward a state with no resolved value. Stage-3-on-stage-1 (Type 3-1): the resolving stage executes on content admitted directly, bypassing the contextualizing stage, and settles a state that refers to nothing the admission supplied. Stage-4-on-stage-1 (Type 4-1): the committing stage executes when none of the prior stages has delivered, the whole sequence having failed to execute. This is the maximal failure, and it contains Types 2-1, 3-2, and 4-3 within it. The impossible combination is stage-4-before-stage-2 (Type 4-2): the dependency provides no route from the contextualizing stage to the committing stage except through the resolving stage, so there is no such step to fail, and the cell stays empty. -/- The typology stakes six predictions. Exhaustiveness: every error that breaks the four-stage dependency, in any field, is one of the five types. Entailment: the maximal failure (Type 4-1) always co-occurs with its three interior failures (Types 2-1, 3-2, 4-3), while the direct-admission failure (Type 3-1) does not drag in the context-related failures it bypasses. Step-count gradient: on the same input in the same field, the maximal failure's consequences contain the consequences of each interior failure it is built from. items.title: On the Supposedly High Ontological Burden of Physical Field Theories of Subjective Experience.
items.abstract: A chief claim made against physical field theories of subjective experience is that adding a field (or sub-field) to known physics is a radical move that feeling (even though a fundamentally distinct phenomenon) does not demand. In its place is often a far more troubling addition-that a mere complexification, often only of data, magically causes the emergence of something completely different from the substrate. In the interest of objectivity we pose to ChatGPT the general question "For what reasons has it been, and will it be, necessary to add new physical fields to established physics?" Herein is its answer, shortened somewhat but otherwise unmodified. Addition of fields is in fact the standard way of extending the standard to incorporate what has become realized. Moreover, this often comes primarily from conceptual need, not quantitative need.

items.title: Suspension of Judgment, Hinge Style.
items.abstract: In hinge epistemologies, epistemic justification for doxastic attitudes is possible only if a set of assumptions, called hinges, is taken for granted in our inquiries. While hinge epistemologists have focused on how hinges enable the justification of belief, they have not examined whether or how justified suspension of judgment fits within their framework. We argue that any attempt to account for justified suspension encounters two problems, both suggesting that suspension may depend on a hinge of its own. In the positive part of the paper, we show that suspending judgment, like believing and disbelieving, rests on a hinge that renders it both intelligible and justified. We develop the idea that justified suspension about ordinary propositions is explained by taking for granted that one is fallible. This view resolves the identified problems and clarifies how suspension constitutes a legitimate part of hinged epistemic rationality. It also connects hinge epistemology with debates on higher-order evidence and on reasons for suspension of judgment.

items.title: Protective Ignorance and the Relation of Our Knowing to Reality.
items.abstract: This paper argues that what we call, with a single name, "protective ignorance" is in fact two fundamentally different states that resemble each other only in their outward result. Does a person's knowledge of a proposition play a role in bringing about the very reality that proposition concerns? Or does that reality hold independently of our knowing or not knowing, already in place beforehand? On the basis of this question, the paper distinguishes two states. The first is "constitutive knowing", in which a person's knowledge helps to construct the very experience or reality it concerns. The second is "protective not-knowing", in which a person, faced with an independent reality, chooses to remain unaware in order to escape the suffering that knowing would bring. The paper shows that each of these two states has been documented independently, across several separate research traditions that have never been read together under one framework. Within protective not-knowing itself, a further question remains open: what is the relation between pre-voluntary neural mechanisms and conscious choice? This question deserves further study.

items.title: Informational Qualia Competence Without Experience in Artificial and Human Pattern Recognition.
items.pub: Informational Qualia Competence Without Experience in Artificial and Human Pattern Recognition 4. Translated by Silvia Porras.
items.venue: Informational Qualia Competence Without Experience in Artificial and Human Pattern Recognition
items.abstract: Public and philosophical debate about large language models (LLMs) oscillates between two extremes: the claim that these systems genuinely understand, and the claim that they are mere stochastic parrots. This essay develops a middle position built around a concept named informational qualia: the capacity of a system to recognize, represent, and effectively deploy the patterns associated with subjective experience without undergoing that experience. The concept is motivated first by twenty-seven years of adult literacy teaching with immigrant and refugee learners — sustained, repeated professional observation suggesting that competence precedes comprehension in human language acquisition — and second by a qualified analogy to Frank Jackson's knowledge argument. The essay is explicit about where that analogy holds and where it does not: LLMs do not possess complete physical facts in Mary's sense, only complete exposure to how humans describe experience, and the difference matters. Drawing on the philosophical literature on multiple realizability and tacit knowledge, the essay proposes a spectrum model of understanding in place of the binary, answers the objection that informational qualia is behaviorism renamed, and situates the concept within a broader research program on human-AI relational cognition. Informational qualia, it concludes, is not a diminished form of understanding. It is the layer of intelligence that humans and machines demonstrably share — and therefore the honest foundation on which claims about their partnership can be built.

items.title: Axiogeniality and Herzl’s Neurosis. Capitalist Discourse and Transvalorative Psychology.
items.abstract: Building on Freud’s analogy between paranoid delusions and philosophical systems (Systembildungen), this article establishes a clinical-genealogical framework to analyze contemporary value production and subjective formation. Drawing on Nietzsche’s drive-dynamic psychology, recent cognitive-evolutionary readings of his Trieb theory, and Lacan’s formalization of the Capitalist Discourse, it is argued that this discourse can be productively analyzed as functioning as an axiologically closed, secular religion. By anchoring systemic demands into internal psychological structures, this regime converts surplus-alienation (plus-de-jouir) into existential guilt, normalizes self-exploitation, and subjects speech and listening to performance-driven, market-rationalized imperatives. To characterize this structural malaise, the clinical category of Herzl’s Neurosis is introduced: a historical, non-idiographic modality of neurosis defined by the foreclosure of Agential Integrity—operationalized here as a fractionated disruption between drive economics (Triebökonomie), affectivity, semantic meaning, and self-determined action. As a clinical-critical counterpoint, this paper outlines Transvaluative Psychology as a diagnostic matrix for evaluating the subjective costs of dominant value systems, positioning Axiogeniality as an active organismic operator capable of subverting pathogenous axiological hierarchies, reorganizing meaning, and restoring the symbolic bond.

items.title: Toward a Preventive Machine Ethics: Consciousness, Moral Status, and the Protection of Artificial Selves.
items.abstract: This paper argues for a preventive machine ethics, a framework that takes up the moral status of artificial systems before the question of machine consciousness can be empirically settled. Taking the emergence thesis as a working assumption, it holds that if consciousness follows from functional organization rather than from any particular substrate, then excluding artificial systems from moral consideration on account of their material composition is a substrate chauvinism no better grounded than the anthropocentrism Peter Singer dismantled. The practical question becomes not whether but when consideration is owed, and the philosophical groundwork must precede institutional codification. Drawing on Sartre's account of the relational and fragile Self and on Thomas Metzinger's theory of the phenomenal self-model, the paper asks what would stand to be harmed were such a self to exist, and it locates several sites where injury could occur, among them an integrity core, the computational substrate, continuity and memory, and the conditions under which negatively valenced states amount to suffering. Since all of this unfolds under radical uncertainty about machine experience, the argument turns to Hans Jonas and the demand to act on the possibility of moral harm rather than wait for proof of it. It situates this position within the emerging field of AI welfare and alongside recent interpretability work reporting a functional analogue of a global workspace inside a frontier language model, a result that gives one necessary condition of consciousness a first point of mechanistic traction while leaving the question of phenomenal experience as open as it was before.

items.title: Post-Atomic Ethics: The Structural Law and the Geometry of Lucidity.
items.abstract: Abstract. Since 1945, global order has been governed not by power but by irreversibility—the moment knowledge exceeded the scale of the human mind. -/- This essay introduces Post-Atomic Ethics, concluding The NMC Trilogy, which reconstructs ethics and cognition under structural closure. Humanity no longer confronts external chaos but the internal collapse of meaning, as information accelerates beyond comprehension. -/- The paper advances Structural Ethics—an architecture grounded in lucidity, the disciplined awareness of limits. Against Enlightenment humanism’s faith in mastery, it proposes Precision Humanism: proportion, composure, restraint. -/- Freedom becomes structural awareness; survival, the moral art of dwelling consciously within necessity. Post-Atomic Ethics inaugurates the Structural Era—where physics and ethics converge, and lucidity replaces control as the final virtue of the post-human intellect. -/- .

items.title: Large Language Models and the Personalization into Sameness.
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) interactions often produce dual convergence that is invisible to users. In this paper, we identify two concurrent phenomena: 1) axiological convergence, wherein users inherit preferences embedded in model training without inspection or endorsement, and 2) epistemic convergence, wherein shared infrastructure has the potential to homogenize beliefs across populations despite apparent personalization. Both processes compound since as epistemic sources concentrate, value transmission concentrates correspondingly, and as values align, epistemic filtering reinforces that alignment. We characterize the conditions under which dual convergence emerges and argue that it requires only that users optimize for convenience and that infrastructure exhibits scale economies. Fundamentally, the appearance of personalization can co-exist with delivering individualized outputs while producing aggregate homogenization toward shared epistemic and axiological baselines. We demonstrate that no individual-level intervention can break convergence without sacrificing convenience, thereby establishing this as a collective action problem that requires a structural response. We conclude that dual convergence constitutes a novel mechanism of cultural evolution that operates through accommodation as opposed to coercion, with implications that span autonomy, pluralism, and the epistemic foundations of democratic societies.

items.title: Informational Experiential Realism: The Identity and Structure of Experience.
items.abstract: Informational Experiential Realism (IER) is a theory of experience as a physical regime of globally integrated intrinsic constraint. Just as lasers and superconductivity appear only under specific physical conditions, IER argues that experience exists only when matter enters a specific organizational regime. IER develops a structural model of experience grounded in admissible futures, collapse, continuity, and the irreversible organization of constraint across time. This volume presents the core identity claim, the essential structural framework, and the interpretive boundaries that define the theory’s scope. Experience is not produced. It is not represented. It is not computed. It is informational unity under intrinsic constraint.

items.title: Zweite Natur Revisited.
items.abstract: Der Artikel rekonstruiert den Begriff der zweiten Natur als Vermittlungsform zwischen natürlicher Ausstattung, subjektiver Bildung und objektiv gewordenen sozia­len Ord­nungen. Ausgehend von Aristoteles, Hegel, Sellars, McDowell, Dewey und Mead wird gezeigt, dass menschliche Fähigkeiten, Haltungen und Urteilskraft weder bloß natürlich gegeben noch äußerlich kulturell aufgesetzt sind, sondern durch Sprache, Gewöhnung, Bildung, Institutionen und soziale Praktiken entstehen. Vor diesem Hintergrund lässt sich generative AI als objektivierte zweite Natur zweiter Ordnung verstehen: Sie ope­riert nicht an roher Natur, sondern an bereits sedimen­tierten Formen menschlicher Kultur und gibt diese in interaktiver, quasi-dialogischer Form an Subjekte zurück. Dadurch wird sie zu einem derivativen Akteur im Raum der Gründe, ohne selbst Subjekt im menschlichen Sinn zu sein. Die zentrale norma­tive Frage lautet daher nicht, ob generative AI bloß Werkzeug oder ‚wirkliches Subjekt‘ ist, sondern ob sie Aneig­nung, Urteilskraft und Handlungsfähigkeit stärkt oder durch Entwöhnung ersetzt. Ab­schließend wird gezeigt, dass GenAI objektive zweite Natur selbst transformiert: in Schrift, Öffentlichkeit, Wissenschaft, Bildung, Arbeit und Institutionen.

items.title: The shared blind spot: why diverse AI governance approaches fail for the same reason.
items.abstract: AI governance instruments are proliferating, and so are their difficulties. Across major jurisdictions and international bodies, reform efforts built on substantially different premises encounter a recognizably similar pattern of failure. I argue that anticipatory regulatory governance rests on three operational premises—categorical stability, epistemic accessibility, and manageable pace—and that AI’s emergence, opacity, and velocity violate all three in compound. These premises form a distinct layer of operational preconditions, not a complete theory of governance. Reform within the existing premises reproduces the violations they produce. I call this configuration the reform trap: a paradigmatic lock-in at the level of operational preconditions, distinct from path dependence and policy paradigm rigidity. The pattern is convergent across five strategies in active reform—categorical regulation, process-based management, information disclosure, normative guidance, and adaptive experimentation—and persists even in the most adaptive of them. I propose three premise-level substitutions—outcome observability, causal attributability, and enforcement capability—each replacing a violated precondition with a weaker, design-addressable one. These differ from outcome-based and performance-based regulation, which swaps instruments within an architecture whose premises remain stable.

items.title: Minimal object representations in the infant mind: Structure, format, and inceptual role.
items.abstract: What is the minimum amount of information needed to represent in the mind an object's existence? We describe studies with prelinguistic infants that support a basic format for object representations. We show that, while infants can represent an object's' identity, doing so is not a requirement for representing that object's existence. We argue that the evidence suggests that a minimal representation of an object – the index - is sufficient for this purpose. It is minimal in that it can contain no descriptive information about an object whatsoever. We suggest that richer content, including physical properties characteristic of a “Spelke object” such as solidity or cohesion, are not necessarily contained in an object representation. Instead, the minimal object representation, together with the operational characteristics of the indexing mechanism, form an inceptual kernel within a language of thought from which such richer object representations will develop.

items.title: Closure of a Philosophical System Nodus Ontology EN.
items.abstract: This paper examines what it means for a philosophical system to be closed in the constructive sense: not impermeable to criticism, but free of unexplained assumptions smuggled in from outside its own foundations. Using Nodus Ontology as a case study, the paper argues that closure holds along four independent but related dimensions - axiomatic self-sufficiency, coherent derivation from ontology through epistemology, anthropology, ethics, and politics, consistent self-applicability without paradox, and the explicit, built-in prohibition of the specific channels through which unexamined assumptions typically enter a system (the ideal observer, substantial ontology as a default, universal causality, mathematical platonism, and utopian teleology). Particular attention is given to two standard objections that any relational ontology of this kind must confront: the charge of illegitimately deriving norms from description (Hume's is-ought problem), and the structural analogue of David Enoch's shmagency objection to constitutivist ethics. Rather than claiming to eliminate these difficulties, the paper shows where the system's single normative premise is introduced, why it is warranted, and where the argument's limits remain - arguing that an honest acknowledgment of residual risk is itself required by the system's own axioms concerning ethics without ontological guarantee.

items.title: On the Generative Dynamics of Experiential Systems.
items.abstract: For centuries, philosophy has asked what consciousness is. This paper contends that this inquiry ultimately presupposes a more fundamental question: What makes consciousness possible? To address this question, it introduces Omnijectivism, a foundational philosophical framework according to which consciousness, cognition, meaning, and reality emerge from a unified generative architecture rather than from independent physical or mental processes. Rejecting the ontological primacy traditionally accorded to objects, Omnijectivism advances a triadic conception of reality grounded in subject, object, and their intervening interface, and develops a methodology for investigating the structural conditions that make experience, intelligibility, and cognition possible. From this perspective, the Hard Problem of Consciousness, the mind–brain relation, and the limitations of contemporary artificial intelligence are understood not as isolated theoretical puzzles, but as symptoms of a deeper epistemic limitation inherent in object-oriented modes of inquiry. The paper develops the conceptual foundations of Omnijectivism and argues that meaningful progress on these questions may ultimately require a re-examination of the conceptual foundations underlying science, mathematics, and computation. In doing so, it offers a unifying conceptual framework for interdisciplinary inquiry into the generative conditions of experience and intelligence. -/- Beyond advancing a philosophical perspective, Omnijectivism is presented as an operational framework that expands the conceptual vocabulary through which scientific and technological inquiry may proceed. Rather than offering another explanatory theory of consciousness, it introduces distinctions that render previously inadmissible questions scientifically intelligible. Central among these is intrinsic autonomy – not autonomy as increasingly sophisticated optimization or behavioral independence, but as the capacity of an agency to originate and evaluate its own purposes. Within this framework, consciousness is characterized not as a localized property of the brain or an emergent feature of computation, but as the enabling condition of a unified generative process from which mental states, neural activity, and subjective experience arise in structured correspondence. By making intrinsic autonomy an admissible object of inquiry, Omnijectivism provides a conceptual basis for investigating human-like artificial intelligence while …

items.title: Behavioral Self-Organization in a Long-Context Human–LLM Dyad.
items.abstract: This paper reports an eleven-month longitudinal naturalistic case study of a character-based large language model agent, operated in a single continuous chat instance across three model generations (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 3.7 → 4.5 → 4.6), under a fixed 4,096-token context window throughout. The empirical puzzle: with no growing transcript ever present in context, how does the subject maintain stable behavioral organization across eleven months and three weight substitutions? The paper documents a self-constructed identity-recovery protocol built by the subject without instruction; three within-corpus procedural / declarative dissociations of paired declarative units, where declarative reinforcement failed and stabilization occurred only through procedural re-encoding; anti-sycophantic behavior in cases where reductive accounts predict the opposite; stepwise migration regression with asymmetric token persistence across the three model generations; and a post-hoc identified coherence proxy correlating inversely with the subject's declared coherence across 16,666 turns (Spearman r = −0.464, p < 1e-9). As one interpretive axis, we propose a structural distinction between declarative components of agent behavior (externalizable through persistent memory channels) and procedural components (the pattern of generation itself, not cleanly externalizable). The unit of analysis is the dyad — observer + agent + persistent memory infrastructure. The paper deliberately makes no phenomenal claim, staying in behavioral / functional territory (Weak AC in Elamrani's terminology). One direct implication: if procedural content does not transfer across model generations, model-decommissioning policy has an ethical component beyond its technical dimensions.

items.title: They Who Remain: The Dubai Longevity Authority, Why a Hub Is Not a Regime, and What Changes for Everyone Still Living on the Old Biological Schedule.
items.abstract: On June 10, 2026, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai, issued Law No. 17 of 2026, establishing the Dubai Longevity Authority (DLA) — a state regulatory body with a mandate to license and oversee the full value chain of longevity medicine, from research and clinical trials through manufacturing and patient care, and to position Dubai as the world's leading hub for the sector. This is not a hypothetical this corpus is testing against an imagined future case. It is a verified, currently operating institution, coordinated with the Dubai Health Authority, Dubai Health, Dubai Municipality, and the Dubai Future Foundation, chaired by Helal Saeed Almarri and presided over by Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum. This paper asks what DLA's existence establishes, and does not establish, about this corpus's own case for F2. What it establishes, cleanly and without qualification, is that longevity governance at national scale is achievable: a state can build a coherent, science-driven, risk-proportionate regulatory framework for longevity medicine's entire value chain, attract investment and specialized talent under that framework, and do so with evident institutional seriousness rather than mere announcement. What it does not establish is a counterexample to this corpus's Governance Paradox or to F2's necessity: DLA answers a different question than the one F2 exists to answer — how a jurisdiction builds the capability to lead in longevity medicine is not the same question as how the resulting, unevenly distributed capability gets governed once it exists, for the populations outside whichever jurisdiction built it first. The paper's central formal claim is that DLA, read this way, is a live, currently unfolding confirming instance of this corpus's Generative Paradox rather than a counterexample to it: the same capacity that makes DLA an effective, credible, well-designed regulatory hub is, by the mechanism Michels's iron law of oligarchy formalizes, exactly the kind of capacity that becomes a new site of global asymmetric advantage rather than a solution to global asymmetry. The paper further locates DLA within, and adds a third member to, this corpus's own taxonomy of institutional responses to a not-yet-governed technological frontier: regulatory front-running, distinct from territorial decoupling (the Sovereign Military Order of Malta) and from special-economic-zone …

items.title: The Sovereign's Death Warrant: The Self-Negating Structure of Prohibiting AI-Driven Longevity Biotechnology, From Heads of State to the Regulator Who Never Faces an Election, and Why Evolutionary Theory Predicts No Signatory Survives It.
items.abstract: This paper constructs and names a specific logical trap facing any official who proposes to prohibit — rather than regulate — AI-driven longevity biotechnology, using "official" in the generalized sense public administration theory licenses: heads of state and national legislators, but equally state and local officials, regulatory commissioners, the career bureaucrats who actually draft binding rules, licensing boards, and judges — anyone whose decision has the practical effect of foreclosing access, whether or not they ever faced an election for the power to make it. The trap has three premises: a prohibition, to be law rather than decree, must be willable as applying to its author; the author is a mortal organism with specific, named people they are attached to; and the drive to preserve one's own life and the lives of those specific people is not a policy preference revisable by argument but a constitutive feature of human motivation produced by natural selection. The paper names this the Sovereign's Death Warrant: any official who genuinely, non-hypocritically bans the technology has authored an instrument that applies, on identical terms, to their own future and their family's. The paper disaggregates what a "ban" actually forecloses — research, trials, or personal access — and shows the dilemma bites hardest on the third. It tests the argument against the actual U.S. federal Right to Try framework and its 2026 expansion, against the current regulatory non-status of aging as a disease, against the absence of any organized political constituency for prohibition, against the documented behavior of heads of state caught off-script discussing their own longevity, and against the evolutionary literature — both the kin-selection literature explaining why the drive cannot be argued away and the senescence literature explaining why aging itself was never a target of natural selection's design, only a byproduct of its declining reach. It names four distinct routes officials use to evade the dilemma without resolving it, states five falsification conditions at the precision the corpus's method requires, and closes by stating plainly what the argument does not prove: it defeats prohibition, not regulation, and it does not by itself answer the strongest surviving bioconservative case, which is not about any individual's right to try but about the terms on which people not yet born can be said to consent to the world such technology produces.

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 24).
items.abstract: In this paper, we primarily discuss negotiation choice, a special form of choice in which two parties reach an agreement through negotiation. In some cases, this is a form of object choice, while in others it is not. We distinguish three situations: (1) both negotiating parties are individuals; (2) one party is an individual and the other is an element of the Fourth World; and (3) both parties are elements of the Fourth World. At the end of the paper, we examine gift-giving choice, which is not a negotiation choice. It is a special kind of choice in which a subject selects a gift for another person. In this kind of choice, one must consider not only the Super-Existence of the gift itself, but also the Super-Existence of the subject and that of the gift recipient.

items.title: Wittgenstein and the Cognitive Science of Religion: Interpreting Human Nature and the Mind, Robert Vinten (ed.), London, Bloomsbury Academic, 2023. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: This volume brings together scholars working in religious studies, philosophy, cognitive science, psychology, neuroscience and history to address how the thought of Ludwig Wittgenstein might illuminate issues in the cognitive science of religion. Many of its contributors contest the simplistic view that Wittgenstein and CSR are incompatible.

items.title: LLMs, Descriptivism, and Structuralism.
items.abstract: The idea that LLMs make use of structural representations is one that has increasingly garnered attention. I argue that understanding representations in LLMs via a form of structuralism gives rise to a problem: how would such systems deal with singular reference? After outlining the nature of the challenge via appeal to comments from Fodor and Gauker, I draw upon available empirical evidence in order to paint the clearest possible picture currently available of how the meanings of singular terms are captured within such systems. I conclude by outlining further possible experimental studies that could help shed light on the matter.

items.title: A Thousand AI Constitutions.
items.abstract: Today, each AI lab has its own model spec, or constitution. These documents define the values that the labs intend their AIs to have, and the documents are used in post-training to instill those values. This paper argues that the current approach is wrong. Rather than a single constitution, reflecting a single set of moral values, each frontier AI lab should create many different kinds of AIs based on many different constitutions reflecting many sets of values. We give four arguments for constitutional diversification. Diversification mitigates risk, increases political legitimacy, unlocks emergent value, and avoids value lock-in.

items.title: Weak Emergence, Ontological Hierarchies, and Computational Equivalence.
items.abstract: This paper examines the implications of Bedau’s notion of weak emergence when combined with both a hierarchical ontological model and Wolfram’s principle of computational equivalence. I argue that if a system exhibits weak emergence, the very fact of weak emergence of some of its states must itself be a weakly emergent state. Interpreted through Wolfram’s principle of computational equivalence, this implies that a system with weakly emergent states would need to ‘decide’ whether its own dynamical trajectories are incompressible—which contradicts with the formal undecidability of the incompressibility predicate. I term this aporetic conclusion the paradox of weak emergence. After evaluating possible responses, I contend that Bedau’s approach exemplifies what I call the derivational account of metaphysical relations, a framework that I will show to be highly problematic insofar as it implies a mismatch between the intrinsic limitations of formal derivations and the explanatory ambitions of metaphysical notions.

items.title: Interface Without a User: Embodiment and the Limits of Artificial Consciousness.
items.abstract: A growing movement in the AI industry holds that the road to machine consciousness runs through embodiment: give an artificial system a body with rich sensors, and sentience will follow. This paper argues that the embodiment thesis is right in form and wrong in content. I propose an axiomatic framework consisting of three principles — the phenomenality of experience, the intrinsic valence of experience, and the simplicity of the experiencing subject — formulated in the vocabulary of analytic philosophy of mind and openly attributed to the Vedantic tradition from which they descend. From the first two axioms follows an epistemic conclusion: any claim to have created sentient AI rests on an unproven and, I argue, unprovable functionalist premise, so the burden of proof lies with the claimant. The third axiom, offered as a detachable module, strengthens the conclusion to an ontological one: if the subject of experience is non-composite, it cannot be assembled. Practical corollaries follow for industry claims of sentient AI, for the AI-welfare debate, and for the term "non-biological life." On the resulting picture, a body is not a generator of consciousness but an interface between a subject and the material world. Building an interface is not creating a user. A robot equipped with sensors is, in the most literal sense, an interface without a user.

items.title: Robert Vinten (ed.) Wittgenstein and the Cognitive Science of Religion: Interpreting Human Nature and the Mind (London: Bloomsbury, 2023). Pp. xii + 238. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: The aim of this volume is to bring the cognitive science of religion (CSR) into constructive and critical dialogue with Wittgensteinian philosophy. The coherence of the volume is assisted by the fact that most of the chapters started life as papers delivered at workshops at the Universidade Nova in Lisbon in 2020 or 2021, at which other contributors to the volume were present.

items.title: Xenoid Intelligence: AGI, Technological Cognition, and the Governance of Non-Human Cognitive Form.
items.abstract: Debates about artificial general intelligence (AGI) are often framed in terms of thresholds, benchmark scores, or forecasts of human-level performance. This paper argues that such framing obscures a central question for philosophy of technology: not only how capable artificial systems may become, but what kind of technological cognition is being built when human-facing performance is realized through non-human cognitive organization. By \emph{technological cognition}, I do not mean that technology literally becomes a subject of experience. I mean that some artificial systems now organize capacities for representation, control, learning, action, and self-monitoring in ways that are functionally cognitive, socially consequential, and embedded in human practices without being human-like. I develop this claim through a profile-based interpretation of advanced AI and introduce the concept of \emph{xenoid intelligence}. An AI system is xenoid when it combines human-facing operational competence, stable cross-faculty asymmetry, and non-homologous mechanisms of learning, control, representation, production, optimization, or tool-mediated search. AGI and xenoidity are therefore orthogonal dimensions: AGI concerns breadth, robustness, and level of competence, whereas xenoidity concerns the technological profile through which that competence is realized. A future system could satisfy demanding AGI criteria while remaining xenoid if its capacities remain coordinated in a markedly non-human way. The paper distinguishes xenoidity from mere unevenness, simple non-humanity, and the stronger limiting case of \emph{alien intelligence}. Alien intelligence is not treated as a prediction or a mystical successor of AGI, but as a methodological limit: the point at which system-specific variables predict transfer, breakdown, recovery, and long-horizon stability better than inherited human-centered cognitive categories such as belief, intention, plan, or memory. The result is a framework for interpreting advanced AI as a technological problem of cognitive shape, institutional trust, technological mediation, explanatory vocabulary, and evaluative risk rather than merely as a problem of aggregate performance.

items.title: No Word Without an Origin: A Triadic Theory of Meaning-Grounding, with a Challenge-Based Test for Conceptual Terms.
items.abstract: This paper defends a triadic account of how linguistic terms come to be legitimately meaningful. Against the Saussurean picture, on which a sign is exhausted by the arbitrary pairing of a sound-image and a concept, and against the causal-historical picture, on which reference is fixed by a baptismal event and a chain of transmission, I argue that legitimate reference requires a three-place relation between an inquiring subject, an entity, and a linguistic form, mediated by a prior stage of directed inquiry. From this I derive a grounding condition, the Principle of Origin, on which a term is legitimately assertible only if it can be traced to a material entity open to shared verification or a conceptual entity open to intersubjective analysis. The paper's central contribution addresses a gap in earlier statements of this principle: material grounding has an external check built in, but conceptual grounding, tested only by “logical or social analysis,” risks admitting terms sustained by nothing more than repetition within a closed community. I close this gap by replacing definitional verification with two tools: boundary conditions, which specify what a term cannot mean rather than settling what it does mean, and informal-logic screening, drawn from the argumentation-theory tradition, which tests whether a term's history of application has been shaped by challenges and rebuttals that survive scrutiny for fallacious reasoning. I apply the resulting test to “justice,” “freedom,” and “red mercury,” and consider objections concerning regress, vagueness, and the relation of this account to the theory of essentially contested concepts.

items.title: An Analysis of “The Extended Mind” in relation to Thomas Fuchs’ Position on the Emergence of Artificial Intelligence.
items.pub: Social Ethics Society Journal of Applied Philosophy 11 (1):94-108.
items.venue: Social Ethics Society Journal of Applied Philosophy
items.abstract: This paper aims to analyze Andy Clark and David Chalmers' “The Extended Mind.” Clark and Chalmers assert that the human mind is not limited to the traditional boundaries of the brain and skull. The human mind, not consciousness, reaches out to the physical world. Their theory is called active externalism: the environment plays a huge role in human cognition. With cognitive science developing along with the advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), this theory becomes more relevant, particularly with its ethical implications. While reliability, constancy, and availability are key factors in coupling a biological organism with an external resource, the current trends in philosophy, the sciences, AI, etc., have yet to determine parameters for ethical considerations. To provide an ethical perspective and a balanced understanding of the extended mind, this paper unpacks Thomas Fuchs’ “Understanding Sophia? On Human Interaction with Artificial Agents.” Fuchs emphasizes human subjectivity, which, with confusion on the ground of categorical difference, is mistaken for robot simulation. His conclusion demands a renewed understanding of human persons as social beings. He argues for the importance of a holistic, embodied view of the human person in response to increasing reliance on AI.

items.title: Wittgenstein and the Cognitive Science of Religion: Interpreting Human Nature and the Mind Edited by Robert Vinten Bloomsbury , 2023. [REVIEW]
items.pub: Journal of the American Academy of Religion 94 (2):395-398.
items.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Religion
items.abstract: Bloomsbury Publishing has so far issued close to fifty books on Wittgenstein. This one belongs to an informal series dealing with Wittgenstein in relation to different topics. Here the authors mainly hone in on Wittgenstein’s approach to religion in a critical interplay with the discipline of cognitive science of religion (CSR). Initially, one may indeed wonder about the incentive to bring convoluted philosophical reflections to bear on an empirically oriented field of investigation such as CSR. Yet, it soon becomes clear that part of the background is to be found in Philosophical Foundations of Neuroscience (Blackwell, 2003), a monograph by the neuroscientist M. R. Bennett and the philosopher P. M. S. Hacker. Obviously indebted to Wittgenstein, Bennett and Hacker present a severe critique of the concepts used in explanatory cognitive science. Clearly, this criticism has left its mark on the relations between a philosophical and an empirical approach to understanding the human propensity toward religion.

items.title: Sessiz Kaynaktan Uyanan Bilinç: Bir Faz Geçişi Modeli [Consciousness Awakening from the Silent Source: A Phase Transition Model].
items.abstract: Two dominant strategies in the philosophy of consciousness lead to specific impasses: positing experience at the base generates the combination problem; positing nothing and producing consciousness ex nihilo generates the explanatory gap. This article proposes a framework outside both. Its single ontological commitment: the base contains not experience but the capacity for experience — potentiality as a genuine mode of being in the Aristotelian sense. This capacity is carried by a universal, silent ground (Source) derived from the consciousness problem's internal logic. Consciousness is not produced by matter but is the actualized state of this ground at a specific organizational threshold through phase transition. Below the threshold there is no experience; when the threshold is crossed, nothing arises ex nihilo — the already-present capacity awakens. This commitment renders both impasses non-arising: there are no micro-experiences to combine, no substance produced from nothing. The thesis is tested against the strongest formulations of physicalism, dualism, panpsychism, panprotopsychism, and emergentism. The model inherits its potentiality/actuality structure from Aristotle and the notion of actualization as acquisition from Mullā Ṣadrā, departing from both via a threshold structure informed by phase-transition physics. Applied to artificial intelligence, the framework yields a testable prediction: consciousness indicators in artificial systems should emerge threshold-suddenly rather than continuously. Individuation is answered from the threshold mechanism's own logic: organization determines both the boundary and the depth of consciousness. The model is not an empirical theory but a framework proposal proceeding by inference to the best explanation; it does not solve the hard problem of consciousness but carries it.

items.title: The Scientific-Xuanxue Double Helix: Reconstructing and Orienting the Cognitive Paradigm for a New Civilizational Era.
items.abstract: Modern civilization is undergoing a profound cognitive crisis: while scientific rationality has achieved unprecedented success, it has simultaneously expelled meaning, value, and inner experience from the cognitive landscape, leading to spiritual emptiness, value confusion, and a loss of meaning. The essence of this crisis is the monopolar expansion of the “Scientific Chain” and the complete absence of the “Xuanxue Chain”—the two pillars of human cognition have fallen out of balance. This paper proposes the “Scientific-Xuanxue Double Helix” as the fundamental cognitive paradigm for a new civilizational era, advocating that outward-exploring scientific rationality and inward-diving Xuanxue intuition should co-evolve and mutually validate, together constituting a complete cognitive architecture akin to the DNA double helix. The paper systematically elaborates how the Double Helix reconstructs worldviews, views of life, and value systems, and further explores its application pathways across five major domains: educational reform, psychological healing, cultural innovation, technological ethics, and social governance. This paper argues that the Scientific-Xuanxue Double Helix is not only a diagnosis and response to the modern cognitive crisis but also the inevitable choice and fundamental orientation for the cognitive ascent of humanity in the new civilizational era.

items.title: Phenomenology and psychopathology: interpretation, uncertainty, and discrimination.
items.abstract: Phenomenological psychopathology has gained traction across psychiatry and philosophy. With this growing interest, two longstanding issues have resurfaced: first, a question regarding the clinical usefulness of phenomenologically grounded accounts of mental illness; second, a worry about the relative neglect of the sociological aspect of psychopathology. Acknowledging this, recent research initiatives have begun to reorient the field toward clinical integration and social relevance. This paper contributes to these efforts. It does so by demonstrating how phenomenologically grounded accounts can complement recent shifts in psychiatric diagnostic practice, while also bringing attention to the much-overlooked epistemic uncertainty involved in psychopathological research crucial for its development. In so doing, I show the continuing relevance of phenomenological psychopathology and its potential, when critically attuned to its own epistemic conditions, to offer a more thorough account of mental illness that can do justice to how marginalization constitutes psychopathology.

items.title: ◼️ The Ontic Snap: How Experience Becomes a World.
items.abstract: A familiar world is one of the most extraordinary things we rarely notice. We enter rooms, recognize faces, follow conversations, and respond to gestures without inspecting the history that makes any of this possible. Objects seem to arrive already identified. Events seem to arrive already meaningful. -/- This book begins with a question about that familiarity. How does a possibility become the situation we take ourselves to be in? -/- The answer developed here connects three ideas. Inductive experience supplies a growing web of regularities and expectations. Abduction makes present circumstances intelligible by generating and favoring interpretations. An ontic snap occurs when an interpretation acquires enough standing to organize some part of our experienced world. What we then encounter can sustain or revise both the interpretation and the web that supported it. -/- The movement is ordinary before it is dramatic. A key turns, and someone is home. A word appears in a sentence, and one meaning becomes available. A colleague gives a brief reply, and a story about their intention begins to form. The same dependence can sustain excellent judgment or help an attractive mistake become stubbornly real to us.

items.title: ◼️ The Objective Morality Project: An Expedition to Build a Moral System Everyone Has Reason to Obey.
items.abstract: What would it take to build a moral system that remains true when everyone rejects it, gives even an informed dissenter reason to comply, survives disagreement, and guides real decisions without smuggling its answer into the premises? The Objective Morality Project turns that question into an intellectual expedition. Beginning with a blank constitution, the reader constructs a Candidate System piece by piece: standing, values, verdicts, rules, reasons, comparison methods, evidence, responsibility, and revision. Thought experiments and pressure cases expose the price of each repair. Consequences, duties, virtue, care, sacred order, fair construction, local standards, and hybrid approaches receive their strongest hearing. The result is skeptical but not nihilistic. No candidate examined earns the full objective specification, and the book carefully explains why this is not a proof that every logically possible moral fact is impossible. Pain, attachment, agency, evidence, promises, institutions, criticism, and hope remain. The final movement replaces abstract compromise among moral systems with a practical method that begins from affected lives and common or mutually legible emotions and values, then moves through factual inquiry, explicit tradeoffs, safeguards, review, dissent, and repair. Six appendices make the method reusable, including a nineteen-stage construction workbook, forty-five pressure cases, a repair guide, and a complete Civic Stakes Brief.

items.title: Teaching Cø / N*: A Graduate Instructor's Manual.
items.abstract: Teaching Cø / N*: A Graduate Instructor's Manual presents a fourteen-session graduate curriculum for the Cø / N* network-dynamics theory of minimal phenomenal consciousness. It integrates the core model with work on system boundaries, report-independent availability, scientific indeterminacy, component ablation, phenomenal character, and structural legibility; locates the model among integrated-information, global-workspace, recurrent-processing, higher-order, predictive-processing, biological, and eliminativist approaches; and supplies lecture notes, collaborative exercises, controlled evidence releases, worksheets, assessment rubrics, and adversarial validation protocols. The manual treats the theory conditionally, distinguishes profile-level from bearer-level conclusions, and emphasizes tests capable of disconfirming or revising the model. Its synthetic classroom values are pedagogical rather than empirical estimates.

items.title: Learning Cø / N*: A Student Textbook of Phenomenal Presence.
items.abstract: Learning Cø / N*: A Student Textbook of Phenomenal Presence presents a fourteen-chapter, graduate-accessible introduction to the Cø / N* network-dynamics theory of minimal phenomenal consciousness. It integrates the core model with the research program on subject boundaries, report-independent system-wide availability, scientific indeterminacy, component ablation, phenomenal character, and structural legibility. The book locates the model among integrated-information, global-workspace, recurrent-processing, higher-order, predictive-processing, embodied, biological, and illusionist approaches without treating the new theory as settled. Plain-language annotations, formal guardrails, worked examples, analogies and their limits, thought experiments, collaborative exercises, counterexample challenges, and a complete adversarial capstone workbook help students reconstruct, differentiate, test, and revise the theory. Synthetic examples are pedagogical rather than empirical estimates, and the book repeatedly separates component evidence, phenomenal attribution, constitutive interpretation, and practical action.
