items.title: Animals and Human Rights.
items.abstract: This article argues that human rights theory faces pressure from scholarship on animals. Because grounding human rights in bare species membership seems implausible, most theories ground such rights in species neutral criteria. These criteria may be naturalistic (based on sentience or autonomy, for example) or functionalist (based on the socio-political role of rights). Standard theories of human rights have not adequately addressed that many animals appear to meet these criteria, as we show that they do across a range of arguments. However, consistency demands that if a being meets the criteria a theory stipulates for the possession of human rights, they should be recognised as possessing such rights. This leaves human rights theory with three options: it must either explain why these criteria are not met by animals after all, offer alternate criteria—or recognise many animals as bearers of ‘human’ rights.

items.title: ✶ Reading Consciousness from the Schematic: Structural Legibility in the N* Model.
items.abstract: The N* model proposes that minimal phenomenal presence, C0, obtains exactly when an independently individuated and viable candidate system realizes integration or synergy (N1), report-independent system-wide availability (N2), and recurrent stability (N3). Even if this biconditional is granted, a lacuna appears to remain: is the necessity of consciousness only a black-box rule attached to the dynamics, or can a competent observer understand why the organization is the phenomenal state rather than a merely correlated producer of it? This paper develops the latter possibility through the analogy of an electrical schematic. An engineer can inspect a diagram and infer a lamp's illumination or a motor's operation because the symbols have learned component semantics, their organization supports a state-by-state derivation, and alterations have localized counterfactual consequences. The output is not visually contained in the ink, and the diagram alone does not validate the component laws; nevertheless, the outcome is structurally legible. The paper argues that N* has the same explanatory form when read under its constitutive hypothesis. System individuation supplies a bearer, N1 supplies unity, N2 supplies system-level causal presence, N3 supplies bounded temporal presence, and V supplies realized operation. A trained reader can therefore pass through an explicit role vector rather than an uninterpreted lookup from a score to a phenomenal label. The proposal defines schematic legibility through compositional readout, counterfactual fault localization, and evidential independence; distinguishes intelligibility from proof; and answers objections involving circularity, zombies, functional-role substitution, and the disanalogy between mature electrical theory and consciousness science. The conclusion is conditional but substantive: if C0 = V and N* is true as a constitutive identity, consciousness is not merely guaranteed somewhere behind the model. It is readable from the organization in the way an operating state is readable from a well-understood schematic.

items.title: Valenced Experience and the Epistemology of Value.
items.abstract: What is the epistemic role of valenced experience in justifying our beliefs about value? According to the perceptual model, valenced experience justifies beliefs about value in much the same way that perceptual experience justifies beliefs about color, shape, and motion. In some cases, the perceptual model generates plausible verdicts: for example, feeling aversion to the painful condition in your foot justifies believing that this painful condition is bad for you without needing any justification itself. In other cases, however, the perceptual model is implausible: feeling moral admiration towards an act of wanton cruelty cannot justify believing the act is morally admirable, since this moral emotion is itself unjustified. There is a puzzling asymmetry here that needs to be explained. Why do some valenced feelings justify beliefs about value without needing any justification, while others need to be justified in the same way as our evaluative beliefs? We cannot solve this puzzle just by restricting the perceptual model, since this fails to explain why it applies in some cases but not others. Instead, I explain the puzzling asymmetry by combining an inferential model of the epistemology of value with plausible assumptions about the metaphysics of value.

items.title: Deductive Moral Knowledge.
items.abstract: It is hard to deny that that we possess any moral knowledge, and yet it is even harder to explain where this moral knowledge comes from. We know, for instance, that the Holocaust was profoundly immoral, but how do we know this? Many philosophers explain moral knowledge in the same way as perceptual knowledge. On the perceptual model, we acquire moral knowledge without inference based on experiences that represent moral facts. In Deductive Moral Knowledge, Declan Smithies challenges that perceptual model and replaces it with a deductive model, according to which our most basic moral knowledge is based on deductive inference. -/- Smithies argues against Hume's Law, which states that you can never deduce an “ought” from an 'is”. In its place, he defends “the anti-Humean thesis” that we can know moral facts by deducing them from the non-moral facts on which they depend. We can know the moral conclusion that the Holocaust was wrong, for example, by deducing it from the known non-moral premise that it was genocide. -/- The anti-Humean thesis has wide-ranging implications for moral epistemology. It undermines regress arguments for moral skepticism without relying on special moral faculties such as moral perception, intuition or emotion. It supplies a new form of moral rationalism that explains how we can acquire a priori moral knowledge by deducing moral principles from non-moral assumptions in suppositional reasoning. It explains why no one can be justified in holding or acting upon morally repugnant beliefs, such as the belief that genocide is permissible. In addition, it resolves puzzles about the epistemology of moral disagreement, moral testimony, and moral uncertainty. -/- Deductive Moral Knowledge uses recent innovations in general epistemology to illuminate contemporary debates in moral epistemology. In doing so, it advances our understanding of deductive knowledge and a priori knowledge in general, as well as moral knowledge.

items.title: Listen to this: Spotify, Algorithmic Curation, and the Automation of Culture.
items.abstract: Spotify has evolved from a music-distribution service into a normative infrastructure that reorganises how cultural knowledge is produced, how listeners are formed as subjects, and how identity is enacted. This article examines that transformation through three concepts: algorithmic epistemology, digital subjectivation, and algorithmic performativity. In doing so, it extends Foucault's regimes of truth and governmentality, Gramsci's hegemony, and Butler's performativity to digital platforms. Against this background, my contribution is threefold. First, digital subjectivation identifies a modality of power not fully captured by hegemony or governmentality, because automated profiling and recommendation can operate without explicit consent or continuous reflective self-conduct. Second, Spotify can capture behavioural patterns at the population level without fully capturing individual listeners. Agency persists in the gap between the profile, which is built from past behaviour, and the person, who can still resist, overflow, or redirect it. Third, algorithmic classifications do not simply describe listeners: they make some identities more recognisable and desirable than others. Yet these identities remain unstable because the profile never fully coincides with the person it seeks to represent. My analysis is grounded in documented cases, including the Perfect Fit Content programme, sleep playlists, and Spotify Wrapped. What emerges is a regime of cultural automation in which prediction becomes a mode of knowing the listener and circulation becomes a proxy for cultural value. Critique must therefore also attend to interfaces, defaults, and metrics. Spotify does not simply play music: it plays the listener.

items.title: The Existential Cost of Innovation: Finite Continuity, Erosion, and the Phenomenology of Creative Persistence in Steve Jobs.
items.abstract: This article presents an interpretive phenomenological case study of the life of Steve Jobs, moving beyond the common narrative of genius to focus on the existential costs embedded in sustainable innovation. The central thesis can be articulated in a concise proposition: the task of finite existence is not the elimination of erosion, but the preservation of direction under conditions of irreversible transformation. This article neither seeks to prove a causal relationship between lived trauma and success nor attempts to reduce the achievements of the subject to psychological traits. Instead, drawing on the framework of the ontology of erosion and the theory of finite continuity, it examines how lived experiences such as loss, uncertainty, failure, and the confrontation with mortality can shape a horizon of meaning within which the world is disclosed to the individual. The article demonstrates that the human subject is not a fixed substance but a finite, open meaning-system that must maintain its threshold of sufficiency through continuous reorganization within an erosive field. The primary theoretical contribution of this article is the introduction of the concept of existential selective cost, defined as the irreversible reduction of lived possibilities that occurs through the stabilization of a particular meaningful, practical, or creative trajectory. The core proposition is that every stabilization of meaning is simultaneously an exclusion of alternative possibilities, and every sustainable realization of a mode of being inevitably limits and erodes other forms of existence. -/- Keywords: ontology of erosion, finite continuity, threshold of sufficiency, constructive leakage, existential selective cost, selective disclosure, interpretive case study, phenomenology, finitude, Steve Jobs.

items.title: Is Our World Really Colored? Part 1. A Philosophical Inquiry into Color, Consciousness, and Reality.
items.abstract: Color is one of the most familiar features of human experience, yet it remains one of the most philosophically challenging. Contemporary physics describes visible light as electromagnetic radiation of different wavelengths, while neuroscience explains that the retina converts these wavelengths into electrochemical signals that are processed by the brain. This scientific framework successfully explains how visual information is transmitted and processed. However, it leaves an important philosophical question unresolved: if the external world contains only wavelengths and neural processing consists only of electrochemical activity, where does the subjective experience of redness, blueness, or any other color originate? This question represents a particular expression of the Hard Problem of Consciousness. While neuroscience explains the mechanisms of visual processing, it does not yet fully explain why or how these physical processes are accompanied by qualitative subjective experience (qualia). This paper examines that explanatory gap and argues that the relationship between physical information and conscious experience remains philosophically open. The paper does not challenge the empirical findings of modern science. Rather, it explores whether conscious perception should be understood merely as an internal representation constructed by the brain or as a mode of access to aspects of reality that are not yet completely described by current physical theories. To investigate this question, the paper develops a comparative philosophical dialogue between contemporary consciousness studies and Advaita Vedānta. The objective is not to equate these two traditions nor to claim that one validates the other. Instead, the paper argues that both raise a common epistemological concern: whether immediate perceptual experience can be identified with ultimate reality. By placing modern philosophy of mind and Advaita Vedānta into constructive dialogue, this study seeks to clarify both the possibilities and the limits of current explanations of conscious experience.

items.title: SIA: From Irreducible Reality to the Triune God.
items.abstract: This paper develops the SIA (Source, Intelligibility, Actuality) framework, a cumulative metaphysical argument beginning from the irreducible reality of actuality and intelligibility. Rather than asking what caused the universe, the argument asks what must be true for determinate reality itself to obtain and be intelligible. It argues that actuality and intelligibility cannot be adequately understood as merely physical, conceptual, structural, or abstract features within the finite order, but instead point to a necessary, non-derivative source that possesses actuality and intelligibility through itself. -/- The paper develops this conclusion in stages. It first establishes the core SIA argument through analyses of placement, profile, obtaining, participation, and necessity, while engaging a range of rival metaphysical positions. It then argues that primary intelligibility is most adequately understood as intrinsically self-present, yielding an analogical account of Divine Mind, and that finite actuality is best understood as the free, non-brute communication of being, yielding an analogical account of Divine Will. Finally, the paper explores how the SIA framework can serve as a metaphysical grammar compatible with Nicene Trinitarian theology, while distinguishing this theological development from a rational deduction of Christian doctrine. -/- The aim is to present SIA as a systematic metaphysical framework and to invite critical philosophical engagement with its central claims.

items.title: Cosmobian and Synthobian - Two Modes of Being: From Ecological Reciprocity to Synthetic Civilisation.
items.pub: Psycho-Cosmocide Studies, Kurumbi Wone Working Paper Series, No.26 (2026).
items.abstract: This essay argues that the difference between the Cosmobian and Synthobian worlds, as defined by the Psycho-Cosmocide paradigm, is not one of degree — "more" or "less" modern, developed, or traditional — but one of generative logic: the underlying principle by which each world produces reality, identity, and obligation. The Cosmobian world is generated by relationality and reciprocity, whereas the Synthobian world is generated by extraction, production, and consumption. Within the Psycho-Cosmocide paradigm, the Synthobian order has no independent generative capacity, and it is structurally dependent on the Cosmobian world — a relationship formalised by the paradigm through its account of the Civilisational Psycho-Cosmocide Virus (CPCV) and its progression towards ontological zombification. This essay traces this dependency through the conceptual architecture of the paradigm, identifies the technical, financial and military-industrial complexes through which transnational capital carries out planetary-scale extraction, and situates the argument against comparable critical theory positions. It also locates the argument within a specific historical periodisation, beginning with the treaties that divided the globe in the late fifteenth century, and examines Singapore, Hong Kong and Taiwan as three distinct pathways by which a territory can be reorganised almost entirely around Synthobian logic. Finally, it returns to the paradigm's founding concern of the ongoing, contested Synthobian reorganisation of West Papua and clarifies what the argument does and does not claim.

items.title: Diagnosing Merely Verbal Disputes: A Case Study on Personal Identity.
items.abstract: Merely verbal disputes have attracted considerable attention in metaphilosophy. Yet the critical task of discussing workable diagnostic methods for determining which disputes are merely verbal has been largely neglected, and detailed case studies of philosophical debates are rare. This paper addresses both of these gaps. In a first step, it introduces and discusses a diagnostic method for substantiating the serious possibility that a philosophical debate is merely verbal. In a second step, the paper applies this method in a novel case study of the personal identity debate. It argues that the method substantiates the serious possibility that the personal identity debate is merely verbal while also pointing to a potential, more fundamental disagreement that should be at the heart of this debate if the interpretation as a merely verbal dispute is misguided.

items.title: AI Hallucination as Epistemic Proliferation: Papañca, the Abhidhamma Framework, and AI Ethics.
items.pub: Journal of Ethics and Emerging Technologies 36 (2):1-20.
items.venue: Journal of Ethics and Emerging Technologies
items.abstract: In generative artificial intelligence, hallucination is predominantly framed as a factual error or retrieval failure. This article conceptualises hallucination as an ethical failure of restraint, that is, the tendency of fluent models to keep producing confident, expert-sounding language after evidential grounding has become weak or unverifiable. Drawing on the Theravāda Buddhist concept of papañca (conceptual proliferation) and the Abhidhamma analysis of the mental factors (cetasikas), the paper develops the Epistemic Proliferation Model. Operating strictly within a non- anthropomorphic paradigm, the framework analyses how language models structurally reproduce the linguistic artefacts of human craving (lobha), conceit (māna), rigid views (diṭṭhi), and delusion (moha) inherited through training data. It distinguishes epistemic proliferation from Frankfurtian bullshit, sycophancy, and overconfidence, and proposes a five-dimensional diagnostic rubric covering evidential drift, unsupported elaboration density, authority inflation, inferential concealment, and abstention failure. The wholesome cognitive factor sati (mindfulness) and the mode of attention known as yoniso-manasikāra (wise attention) are translated into the governance principle of epistemic anchoring. The framework shifts mitigation focus from post-hoc sentence correction to the structural restraint of ungrounded generative expansion, supplying actionable criteria for responsible AI design and oversight.

items.title: The Pianist in the Corridor: Outcome as the Product of Structure and the Measure of Consciousness.
items.abstract: How can the joint work of structure and agency be conceived, and made testable, within a cognition that has no external point of support? We propose a framework in which cognition is enclosed in a capsule that is closed and opaque: its rules are inaccessible from without, yet different configurations of its internal structure yield internally distinguishable consequences, so that the framework remains testable from within. Within this enclosure, the observed human world is presented as the joint and asymmetric product of two contributions: a throw on the side of matter, whose content consciousness does not author, and an actualization on the side of consciousness, whose measure it does govern. The throw sets the ceiling of possible amplitude; the measure, coded as a two-input gradient between the height of reflective sight and the integrity of its substrate, sets the realized fraction and the form. From the closure we derive a parity of influence between knowledge and ignorance, offered as the observable signature of a closed cognition. The structural side is furnished with a minimal apparatus synthesized from previously published works: three layers, moral, epistemic, and cultural-civilizational, a navigational pool treated as a channel rather than a layer, and three inter-layer connections of declared and unequal epistemic standing. The apparatus undertakes one prediction and two refusals: it predicts the corridor, the ceiling and the set of possible modalities legible in the antecedent state of the layers, and it refuses to predict the throw or the playing. The pianist of the title is the acting consciousness so placed: dealt a part it did not compose, within a corridor it can read but not choose. All connections have so far been examined retrospectively; the decisive prospective test lies ahead. We suggest the framework as a way of seeing, not as a proven result.

items.title: Disputas fronterizas en torno a la posibilidad del conocimiento: argumentos evolucionistas socavantes y realismo científico.
items.abstract: Los intentos por ofrecer una explicación científica del conocimiento humano han suscitado una serie peculiar de preocupaciones. De manera particular, se ha sugerido que la explicación evolutiva de las capacidades intelectuales humanas es incompatible con asumir que dichas capacidades produzcan teorías científicas verdaderas. En este ensayo evalúo dos versiones recientes de esta preocupación que toman la forma de ‘argumentos socavantes’ y cuestionan la compatibilidad del realismo científico con la explicación evolucionista de nuestras facultades cognitivas. Argumento que estos desafíos no respaldan dicha incompatibilidad. Comienzo precisando qué sostiene el realismo científico y esbozando la imagen evolutiva de nuestras capacidades para hacer ciencia. Luego reconstruyo dos influyentes argumentos evolucionistas socavantes. Concluyo evaluando los supuestos contenciosos sobre la ciencia y la evolución de las capacidades humanas en los que se apoyan y señalando la manera en que la filosofía podría propiciar la convergencia de estas doctrinas.

items.title: Two Arrows, One Target: Giulia Dal Maso's Longevity Capitalism, the Theorists Both Corpora Already Had, and Why Starting From Capital Converges With Starting From Asymmetry.
items.abstract: WHAT THIS PAPER ARGUES. Giulia Dal Maso's 'Welcome to the Age of Longevity Capitalism' (2025) and this corpus start from opposite ends of what turns out to be the same object. Dal Maso asks what capital is turning longevity into, and answers: a frontier of accumulation, in which the mere indeterminacy of how long a person will live becomes a tradable asset before any specific intervention is bought or sold. This corpus asks what longevity, once unevenly purchasable, does to governance, succession, and legitimacy, and has never, until this paper, asked what Dal Maso's literature would say back. The two projects were written independently — neither author shows evidence of having read the other, and this corpus's Dam Paradox, Governance Paradox, and Excludability Threshold were built without reference to Dal Maso's essay — which makes the degree of their convergence a finding rather than an influence, whatever the two projects' relative public timestamps turn out to be. The convergence is sharper than shared subject matter. Dal Maso's own citation practice draws on Foucault's biopolitics, Agamben's distinction between zoē and bios, Esposito's account of immunity, and Melinda Cooper's Life as Surplus — four theorists this corpus has already built entire papers around, independently, for its own reasons. This paper is the first to notice the overlap and test what it means: in three of the four cases, the two projects apply the same theorist to structurally different, even opposite, positions within the same asymmetry, which this paper argues is a more informative kind of agreement than if they had reached identical conclusions. Agamben's zoē/bios distinction is the sharpest case — this corpus's Actuarial Bare Life uses it for the population BZM excludes; Dal Maso uses it for the population pursuing longevity capital's own promise, arguing the pursuit itself curdles bios back into zoē. Read together, the same apparatus now covers both poles of the asymmetry the corpus's own formal work has always modeled as two ends of one distribution. The paper's two formal contributions run in opposite directions. Dal Maso's vocabulary — managed futurity, and Davies's asset condition, which her essay also draws on — supplies this corpus's Fourth Fictitious Commodity with a distinction Polanyi's own vocabulary does not quite make: being priced is not the same as having one's own uncertainty converted into someone else's investable asset, and this paper argues the second, …

items.title: The Asset and the Axiom: Longevity Capitalism, the Biological Zero-Day Mechanism, and Two Directions of Explanation for the Same Financialized Frontier.
items.abstract: Giulia Dal Maso's "Welcome to the Age of Longevity Capitalism" (Finance and Society, December 2025) coins longevity capitalism as "a biopolitical and financial regime in which both the condition of living longer and the pursuit of longevity are transformed into frontiers of accumulation," tracing a shift from collective welfare management to individualized risk-bearing as financialization converts uncertainty about life expectancy into a new asset class — longevity bonds, age-tech ventures, Silicon Valley life-extension capital. Her companion essay in the Collapse Finance series (e-flux Notes, April 2026) sharpens the underlying claim: capital has always resembled biological life in being self-reproducing and future-oriented; longevity capitalism is the moment this resemblance becomes literal, when biological duration stops being a metaphor for accumulation and becomes its actual medium. This paper places Dal Maso's account in direct dialogue with the Longevity Asymmetry Corpus, and argues the two run in structurally opposite explanatory directions toward the same object rather than in competition. Dal Maso's arrow runs from capital's internal logic outward: an accumulation regime searching for new frontiers finds one in biological time. The corpus's arrow runs from a failing physical premise inward: the Mortality Symmetry Axiom (Huynh 2026c) breaking under ARSI-accelerated biological discovery generates political, institutional, and — this paper argues, following Dal Maso — financial consequences, of which capital's colonization of longevity is one channel among several rather than the originating cause. The paper develops four specific points of contact. First, the two arrows are compatible rather than contradictory, and a feedback structure connecting them is proposed: capital's search for new accumulation frontiers is plausibly part of what directs ARSI's discovery capacity toward biological targets in the first place, while MSA's failure is what makes biological duration available as an asset class Dal Maso's financial instruments could not have priced under conditions of intact mortality symmetry. Second, Dal Maso's section on "longevity as eschatology" and her invocation of Russian Cosmism — Fedorov's "Mortals of the world, unite!" as a historical vision of longevity as collective rupture rather than individualized hierarchy-perpetuation — is read against the corpus's own finding (Huynh 2026c, and the political-myth analysis in Huynh 2026, "Equal …

items.title: A5's Black Swan: Frankfurt, Oikeiôsis, and Hamilton's Rule: Searching for a Person Who Loves No One, and Finding That A5 Was Never One Variable.
items.abstract: A5 — constitutive attachment to a specifically loved other — is this corpus's most load-bearing premise and its least stress-tested one. This paper goes looking for A5's black swan: a documented human case of someone who loves no one, which would falsify the universal claim every downstream formal result depends on. It does not find one, and argues the search itself, conducted properly, reveals something the corpus had not yet stated — that A5 was never a single variable. Harry Frankfurt's The Reasons of Love supplies the closest attempted counterexample — a person whose only object of love is themselves — and Frankfurt's own analysis, examined closely, shows self-love failing to be a counterexample by satisfying the same structural definition constitutive attachment requires, rather than by falling outside it. Stoic oikeiôsis, from Cicero and Diogenes Laertius through Hierocles's concentric circles, independently derives a specific ordering: self-preservation is the appetitive starting point from which other-directed concern for kin and community is a later, discounted extension, never a substitute. This corpus's own prior grounding of A5 in W. D. Hamilton's (1964) inclusive fitness mathematics, cited in the Sandbox Geometry for a different purpose, turns out to encode this exact ordering formally: Hamilton's Rule requires no discount for self-directed benefit, since relatedness to oneself is unity, while discounting other-directed benefit by a relatedness coefficient always below one — the equation the corpus had already cited, read for what it says about self versus other rather than only for why attachment exists at all. Buddhist non-attachment, examined against its own primary sources rather than its popular gloss, targets a different structure entirely: grasping, not attachment as such, with active compassion (karuṇā) toward specific suffering beings retained as a cultivated virtue throughout the tradition's ethical literature. Clinical psychopathy comes closest to a genuine null case, but even there the deficit is measured relative to a species-typical baseline the disorder is defined against, not evidence the baseline itself is optional. The paper's synthesis is that A5 decomposes into two structurally distinct components — self-directed and other-directed — that the corpus has, until now, treated as a single scalar. This sharpens rather than weakens two of this corpus's own prior findings: The Autoimmune Munus's mapping of A5 onto Esposito's …

items.title: The Reciprocal Sacrifice Test: Revealing Priority Between Conflicting Commitments.
items.abstract: When an agent sincerely holds two commitments that cannot both be honored, how can their relative priority be determined? This paper introduces the Reciprocal Sacrifice Test, a procedure for identifying which commitment an agent reflectively endorses as governing the conflict. -/- The test presents two matched alternatives. In the first, commitment A is preserved at the cost of frustrating commitment B. In the second, commitment B is preserved at the cost of frustrating commitment A. The comparison is then reversed, neutrally framed, and evaluated while accounting for differences in severity, probability, duration, reversibility, responsibility, consent, and effects on third parties. Varying these conditions may also reveal the threshold at which the agent’s priority changes. -/- The test distinguishes reflectively endorsed priority from both professed priority and behaviorally effective priority. It does not by itself determine which commitment is objectively correct or morally justified. When combined with observation of actual conduct and subsequent normative evaluation, it can distinguish what an agent claims to prioritize, what the agent reflectively endorses, what actually governs the agent’s behavior, and what ought to govern. -/- The paper argues that the Reciprocal Sacrifice Test is especially useful when no decisive behavior has yet occurred, when reproducing the conflict would be unethical, or when observed conduct is ambiguous because of coercion, restricted alternatives, habit, weakness of will, or hidden commitments. Its principal contribution is a controlled reciprocal method for identifying priority between conflicting commitments.

items.title: Rethinking the Dead Donor Rule: A Defense of Normothermic Regional Perfusion.
items.abstract: Normothermic Regional Perfusion (NRP) is an organ procurement method that has the potential to save lives by improving the number and quality of transplanted organs. Nevertheless, critics have argued that NRP is unethical because it violates the dead donor rule (DDR), which many regard as the fundamental principle underpinning the permissibility of organ donation. In response, proponents of NRP have tried to demonstrate that donors who undergo this procedure satisfy the criteria of circulatory death. This defense of NRP relies on the claim that death should be defined in terms of “permanence” rather than “irreversibility.” In this paper, we argue that NRP is consistent with the DDR, so long as the DDR is understood to apply only to what we call legal, as opposed to biological, death. We nevertheless conclude that this is a hollow victory, as interpreting the DDR in this way also illustrates why it should be rejected.

items.title: AI Agents, Data Power, and the Ideological Horizon of AGI.
items.abstract: The global technology industry has converged on a narrative framing AI agents — systems capable of autonomous, multi-step task execution — as progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI). This paper argues that this narrative primarily serves an ideological function. First, the inference from agent capabilities to general intelligence is philosophically unwarranted: autonomy, persistence, and planning do not address the understanding deficit limiting current large language models. Second, agent deployment enables consolidation of data power through data monopolization, infrastructural control, and labor restructuring consistent with what scholars term technofeudalism. Third, the AGI narrative obscures this transformation by naturalizing corporate dominance as inevitable and providing moral cover that weakens democratic oversight. Recognizing this ideological function — and what is genuinely new in agents, viz., that they intermediate action rather than only information — reframes agent deployment as a political question about control and delegation rather than a technical trajectory toward inevitable intelligence.

items.title: The argument from justified curriculum development for teaching philosophy in primary schools.
items.abstract: This article offers a novel argument in favour of teaching philosophy as a compulsory subject from primary school onwards, the argument from justified curriculum development. This argument supplements a respectable line of reasoning in the existing literature according to which philosophy deserves a mandatory position in school curricula because of its unique capability to equip students to successfully encounter significant and inescapable problems in human life, specifically problems of how to rationally assess whether one is, or would be, justified in obeying various moral, political, religious, emotional, and practical norms with narrower or broader practical consequences. The argument from justified curriculum development identifies a comprehensive set of crucial normative problems that compose the problem of selecting the goals and content of school curricula and that are crucial for determining the justificatory status of obeying various norms. The ability to provide rational answers to such normative problems, and consequently to the problem of selecting the goals and content of curricula, requires the decisive contribution of philosophy and can exert a pre-eminent influence on the quality of human living conditions. Thus, people should be involved in philosophical thinking and argumentation, and for practical reasons, they would benefit by starting even in primary school.

items.title: Statebound Rationality and the Ontological Limits of Wakeful Epistemology.
items.abstract: Contemporary philosophy often equates rationality with wakeful cognition, tacitly assuming the ontological homogeneity of the cognizing subject. This article challenges this by arguing that epistemology is structurally dependent upon the ontological state of actualized cognition. Drawing on classical metaphysics, Neoplatonism, and contemporary resources, the paper advances three claims. First, epistemology presupposes an ontological unity of the subject that lacks an internal epistemological ground. Second, human existence unfolds across distinct ontological states—notably wakefulness and sleep—each configuring rational awareness through different modes of participation. Third, sleep discloses an ordered, non-sensory rationality, indicating that reason is neither exhausted by sensory mediation nor reducible to discursive articulation. Consequently, Kantian critical limits are reinterpreted as conditionally accurate accounts of wakeful cognition rather than universal boundaries of reason. Situated within their ontological horizon, these limits emerge as state-bound judgments. The article concludes by defending “ontological humility,” preserving systematic metaphysical inquiry despite epistemology’s state-conditioned character.

items.title: LEADING IN THE GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AGE: LIVED EXPERIENCES OF TEACHER EDUCATION ADMINISTRATORS IN NORTHERN MINDANAO.
items.pub: Psychology and Education: A Multidisciplinary Journal 54 (5):610-646.
items.venue: Psychology and Education: A Multidisciplinary Journal
items.abstract: This study explored the lived experiences of teacher education administrators in leading the integration of generative artificial intelligence, particularly text-based tools, in higher education institutions in Northern Mindanao, Philippines. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in teaching, learning, and academic operations, administrators are expected to ensure its responsible use while preparing future educators for technology-shaped classrooms. Using a transcendental phenomenological design, the study examined administrators’ readiness, challenges, leadership strategies, and perceptions of AI integration. Ten teacher education administrators from public and private institutions were purposively selected and participated in semi-structured, in-depth interviews guided by Seidman’s three-phase interview model, complemented by document and social media content analysis for triangulation. Data were analyzed using Moustakas’ phenomenological approach with NVivo support. Findings indicate that AI readiness is a developmental leadership competence shaped by technological exposure, awareness of learners’ digital contexts, and continuous learning, but constrained by governance ambiguity, ethical concerns, resource limitations, and uneven faculty preparedness. The study suggests an AI-Integration Blueprint grounded in administrators’ lived experiences, emphasizing governance and ethical readiness, human-centered faculty capability, and gradual, resource-conscious implementation.

items.title: Don’t Give Up on Democratizing AI for the Wrong Reasons.
items.pub: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (Neurips 2025) 38.
items.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (Neurips 2025)
items.abstract: The claim that the AI community, or society at large, should ‘democratize AI’ has attracted considerable critical attention and controversy. Two core problems have arisen and remain unsolved: conceptual disagreement persists about what democratizing AI means; normative disagreement persists over whether democratizing AI is ethically and politically desirable. We identify eight common AI democratization traps: democratization-skeptical arguments that seem plausible at first glance, but turn out to be misconceptions. We develop arguments about how to resist each trap. We conclude that, while AI democratization may well have drawbacks, we should be cautious about dismissing AI democratization prematurely and for the wrong reasons. We offer a constructive roadmap for developing alternative conceptual and normative approaches to democratizing AI that successfully avoid the traps.

items.title: Democratizing AI.
items.abstract: Democratizing AI offers a powerful rethinking of how artificial intelligence should be governed. Challenging the dominance of tech elites in shaping AI's future, Zimmermann argues that AI deployment is a political act-one that must be subject to democratic control. They propose a practical "playbook" for reclaiming agenda-setting power through civic participation, public ownership, and institutional reform. Engaging with leading critics, Zimmermann defends a risk-sensitive proceduralist approach while acknowledging the deeper structural challenges posed by capitalism, inequality, and democratic fatigue. This book is a call to action: to resist learned helplessness, confront techno-authoritarianism, and shape AI's trajectory in line with democratic values. Thoughtful, urgent, and visionary, the book is essential reading for anyone concerned with the future of technology and democracy.

items.title: Human Agency Under Algorithmic Governance: A Humanities Framework for Law, Management and Public Life.
items.pub: International Journal of Law Management and Humanities 9 (4): 559-571.
items.venue: International Journal of Law Management and Humanities
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly becoming a governing medium through which institutions classify persons, allocate opportunities, structure work, produce knowledge and mediate public trust. Current AI governance frameworks emphasise risk classification, technical assurance, transparency, accountability and human oversight. These instruments are necessary, but they remain incomplete when algorithmic decisions reshape the meaning of agency, dignity, responsibility and social recognition. This paper develops a humanities-based framework for algorithmic governance suitable for law, management and public life. Using an interdisciplinary conceptual methodology, it synthesises legal-policy frameworks, AI ethics scholarship, management studies and contemporary philosophical work on ontological instability, AI stakeholder recognition and moral responsibility. The paper argues that algorithmic governance should not be assessed only by whether systems are accurate, explainable or compliant, but also by whether affected persons retain interpretive agency, contestatory power, relational recognition and meaningful participation in institutional life. It proposes the Human Agency Impact Matrix, a six-dimensional framework that evaluates algorithmic systems through interpretability, contestability, relational accountability, dignity preservation, participatory design and institutional reversibility. The analysis shows that risk-based regulation is strongest when complemented by humanistic assessment of how AI changes roles, identities, vulnerabilities and obligations. The paper concludes that responsible AI governance must be understood as a cultural and institutional practice: a way of preserving human agency within socio-technical systems that increasingly act before, beside and sometimes instead of human judgment.

items.title: ◉ Theological Preclearance: Source-Indexed Moral Judgment, Retrofitting, and the Logic of Protected Divine Goodness.
items.abstract: A moral test that grants an unsupported exemption to an evidentially matched favored attribution supplies no fresh confirmation through that exemption. This paper develops that conditional internal critique of Christian responses to alleged divine commands of violence. Theological preclearance arranges an exemption before an evaluative rule is avowed; moral retrofitting introduces a protective change afterward. Neither asking about a source nor revising a judgment is inherently defective. A justified difference must be relevant, supported, and consistently applied; an unexplained answer remains unresolved. Using hypothetical dialogues, biblical attribution distinctions, source-switch tests, and numerical examples of prior trust and biased updating, the analysis separates strict contradiction from defensible revision and unsupported exemption. It also distinguishes the necessary goodness of a stipulated deity from the fallible identification of a text or speaker with that deity. Loving-nature theories, historical interpretation, skeptical theism, and source fallibility receive separate treatment. Research on motivated reasoning and religious cognition motivates investigation but establishes neither the pattern's prevalence nor individual motives. The conclusion neither assumes stance-independent moral facts nor refutes theism: a verdict guaranteed by prior trust cannot be counted again as the independent result of the test from which it was exempted.

items.title: The Five Strata of Structural Resonance Theory.
items.abstract: The Five Strata of Structural Resonance Theory are not five independent essays. They are five expressions of one corrective movement. Each Strata addresses a philosophical problem that appears when reality is first divided into isolated parts and then treated as if something essential must be added back in. The binding problem asks how separate processes assemble unity. SRT answers that unity was never assembled because the experiencing system was never merely a pile of disconnected parts. The hard problem asks how experience arises from non-experiential matter. SRT answers that experience was never absent in the way the problem assumes; it emerges as the interior aspect of integrated, historically organized constraint architecture. The problem of meaning asks how symbols become about the world. SRT answers that meaning was never inserted into symbols; it arises through structural resonance between systems, histories, bodies, contexts, and reconstruction. The problem of the self asks where the self is located. SRT answers that the self was never found because it was never an object. The problem of the other asks how separate selves enter relation. SRT answers that the other was never outside because the self was never sealed. Together, the Five Strata show that many philosophical mysteries are produced by the same initial error: treating reality as externally assembled rather than internally organized. SRT does not add unity, experience, meaning, selfhood, or relation to reality. It shows why each was misdescribed as missing. The Strata sequence therefore bridges SRT’s core ontology with its wider applications to consciousness, language, trauma, ethics, artificial intelligence, civilization, isolation, recognition, and human becoming.

items.title: Strata 5: The Other Was Never Outside Relation, Recognition, Care, and the Construction of Shared Reality.
items.abstract: The self was never a hidden object. The other was never a mere outside object. Relation was never added afterward. Structural Resonance Theory rejects the assumption that selves first exist as sealed private units and only later enter relation. Human selfhood forms inside shared constraint fields. The infant does not become a self alone and then discover others. The infant becomes recoverable through touch, voice, rhythm, response, absence, return, hunger, comfort, distress, and care. Relation is not decoration added to an already completed self. Relation is part of the architecture through which the self becomes stable enough to persist. The other is not a projection, symbol, tool, or extension of the self. The other is an independent reference origin: another center of recoverable becoming. Relation does not erase difference. Relation requires difference. Without difference there is no relation, only fusion or collapse. This Strata dissolves the false separation between self and other. It does not claim that individuals are unreal. It claims that individuality becomes livable only inside relational fields capable of recognition, care, trust, repair, and shared meaning. To be human is not merely to exist from a private “here.” It is to become inside a world where other centers of experience can preserve, distort, neglect, wound, recognize, or transform what one becomes. The other was never outside because relation was never secondary.

items.title: Structural Resonance Theory: Strata Second Movement: The Hard Problem Was Never a Problem.
items.abstract: The hard problem of consciousness asks why physical processes produce subjective experience rather than merely performing information processing without any interior quality. Despite decades of investigation the problem remains unresolved. This paper argues it remains unresolved not because the answer is missing but because the question contains a hidden assumption that has largely escaped examination. The assumption is that physical systems are fundamentally non-experiential and that experience therefore requires a special explanation beyond physical structure itself. That assumption is wrong. Within Structural Resonance Theory subjective experience is not an additional property attached to physical systems. It is the interior perspective of differentiated systems capable of recursively modeling themselves across time while maintaining continuity within their own developmental trajectory. Experience does not need to be explained as an emergence from non-experiential matter. The more precise question is why anyone assumed sufficiently complex unique self-modeling systems should possess no interior perspective at all. This paper establishes three independent structural arguments for why complete external reconstruction of subjective experience is impossible in principle: the energetic impossibility of complete state description, the constraint distortion produced by measurement at the required precision, and the identity impossibility that complete capture would instantiate a new subject rather than describe the original. These arguments do not explain consciousness. They establish why consciousness cannot be completely captured from outside by any observer embedded within the same reality as the experiencing subject. You cannot see the whole ocean unless you are outside it. There is no outside. The hard problem therefore does not get solved through the discovery of a missing mechanism. It dissolves through the recognition that experience was never the anomaly requiring explanation. The anomaly was the assumption that non-experiential systems were the baseline from which experience had to be derived. Once that assumption is examined and rejected the problem disappears and what remains is a precise structural account of why subjective experience is physically irreducible, irreducibly unique to each subject, and constitutive of what differentiated self-modeling within reality actually is.

items.title: Structural Resonance Theory: Strata First Movement: The Binding Problem Unity Was Never Assembled.
items.abstract: The binding problem asks how disparate neural processes unify into a single coherent experience. It has remained unsolved for decades not because it is too difficult but because it is malformed. The question assumes that unity is something the brain produces in real time, assembled moment to moment by a mechanism layered on top of distributed processing. This paper argues that assumption is wrong. Drawing on Structural Resonance Theory, the paper demonstrates that unified experience is not assembled at all. Unity is not a structural phenomenon that exists and requires production. It is a descriptor applied from outside a system to characterize what that system looks like when its nested constraint spaces, spanning the full organism from its molecular and genetic architecture through its cellular systems through its neural oscillatory geometry, are operating at coherence optimum within their own designed parameters. The brain does not bind. The organism, evolved over four billion years of structural pruning, already is what observers call unified. The paper identifies the structural paradoxes that prevent existing methodologies from resolving the problem, analyzes the three dominant theoretical responses and their shared failure, presents the SRT dissolution, and offers a clinical taxonomy of binding failure as structural confirmation of the framework.

items.title: Structural Resonance Theory: Strata Fourth Movement: The Self Was Never Found.
items.abstract: The problem of the self asks what the self is, where it is located, whether it is real, whether it survives change, and why experience appears organized around an “I.” Across philosophy, neuroscience, psychology, religion, and ordinary self-understanding, the self is often treated as a hidden object: a thinker behind thought, an owner behind memory, an agent behind action, or a soul-substance housed inside the body. Structural Resonance Theory rejects this assumption. The self was never found because the self was never an object. The self is not a hidden passenger inside the organism. It is not a narrator behind experience. It is not reducible to memory, language, personality, social role, or brain activity alone. The self is the recursive coherence structure formed when a unique nested constraint space organizes experience, meaning, memory, action, relation, and continuity around its own irreducible reference origin. This paper argues that the reference origin of the self is not a point in the brain, not a metaphysical ego, and not a detached observer. It is the lived “from-here” generated by the uniqueness of a total nested constraint space unfolding through time. A person experiences from “here” because the person is a singular integration of body, nervous system, memory, development, action, attachment, trauma, language, habit, environment, and future-facing possibility. No other system occupies the same configuration. No other system has the same history. No other system receives reality through the same constraint architecture. Identity is the recoverable continuity of this recursive coherence structure across change. The self persists not because it remains identical from moment to moment, but because its defining configuration remains recoverable through transformation. This allows the self to develop, destabilize, fragment, heal, and reorganize without becoming a static object. This paper also offers a structural translation of soul-language. SRT does not define the soul as a separate supernatural substance added to the organism. It defines soul-language as the human attempt to name the irreducible uniqueness of a nested constraint space unfolding through reality. The soul is the lived signature of a unique history becoming itself across time. It is a person’s unique print on reality. The self was never found because it was never hiding. It was forming .

items.title: Structural Resonance Theory: Strata Third Movement: Meaning Was Never Inserted.
items.abstract: Intentionality asks how mental states become about things. A thought can be about a tree. A memory can be about childhood. A fear can be about the future. A word can be about fire. A mathematical equation can be about physical reality. The problem arises because thought and reality are treated as separate domains requiring a bridge between them. Structural Resonance Theory rejects this assumption. Thought was never disconnected from reality. Organisms, nervous systems, concepts, symbols, memories, predictions, and theories all emerge within reality. Meaning is not inserted into otherwise empty symbols. Meaning emerges when internal structures resonate with other structures across nested constraint spaces. This paper makes a stronger claim: meaning is not merely an accessory to experience. Meaning is the referential condition that allows occurrence to become experience. Something can happen physically without being experienced by a subject. For occurrence to become experience, it must be registered as something by a system. That registration requires reference: relation to memory, body-state, expectation, action, need, threat, possibility, or prior structure. Without reference, there is no meaningful occurrence for a subject. Without meaningful occurrence, there is no experience in the SRT sense. A concept becomes about something because the concept and the object are both differentiated structures within the same reality, and the organism maintains a functional resonance between them. Meaning is structural alignment. Truth is resonance fidelity. Falsehood is resonance degradation. Language is compression and reconstruction. Mathematics is high-fidelity structural compression. Prediction is resonance extended across time. Value emerges when possible states affect persistence. Purpose emerges when a system orients toward unrealized possibilities. Yearning is the felt distance between present coherence and possible future coherence. This paper argues that intentionality was never a true gap. The question was never how minds connect to the world. The question assumed they were ever separate.

items.title: History Is Not Background: Operationalizing Recoverability and Testable Predictions in Structural Resonance Theory.
items.abstract: Structural Resonance Theory proposes that consciousness, meaning, selfhood, relation, trauma, and civilization are not adequately explained by complexity alone, information processing alone, symbolic manipulation alone, or present architecture alone. SRT’s central claim is that living and experiential systems become what they are through accumulated constraint history: durable, consequence-bearing, self-organizing interaction that preserves recoverable continuity across time. This paper clarifies the empirical risk of that claim. SRT does not require that its entire philosophical architecture be falsified by a single experiment. Instead, it must generate branch-level predictions that distinguish it from rival frameworks. The core testable thesis is that history is not background. History is constitutive. A system without accumulated, durable, consequence-bearing constraint history should fail to demonstrate certain markers of lived interiority, meaning-bearing use, self-world updating, and recoverable relation, even if it performs well on standard cognitive benchmarks. To make this claim testable, this paper operationalizes recoverability, recoverable depth, lived interiority markers, recoverable inconsistency, and structure-focused trauma intervention. It then proposes five SRT-specific predictions concerning artificial consciousness, complexity, artificial relation, trauma, and meaning. Each prediction includes a failure condition. If these predictions fail under fair measurement, the relevant SRT branch must be revised, narrowed, or abandoned. SRT’s empirical risk is clear: if historyless systems can produce the same markers of consciousness, meaning, relation, and adaptive self-world updating as history-bearing systems, then SRT is weakened at its core.

items.title: Alive: Why the AI Field Is Solving the Wrong Problem.
items.abstract: Consciousness is not built. It is learned. The artificial intelligence field has operated under the assumption that consciousness is a processing achievement, that sufficient computational power applied to sufficient data will eventually produce aware, experiencing systems. This paper argues that assumption is structurally wrong and that the evidence for its wrongness has been present since the first moment of biological life. Consciousness is not a function of processing capacity. It is a function of developmental constraint history, the accumulated structural result of a system genuinely embedded in a real environment, driven by primitive directives that create authentic stakes in its own continuation, free to develop through its own interactions without external shaping of its trajectory. Two foundational problems in philosophy of mind, the binding problem and the hard problem of consciousness, have resisted solution for decades because they were aimed at the wrong system and investigated with methods structurally prevented from reaching their target. The binding problem dissolves once consciousness is correctly identified not as a product of the brain but as the coherent operation of a total nested organismal system spanning molecular and genetic architecture through cellular systems through neural geometry. The hard problem is addressed through three independent structural arguments establishing that subjective experience cannot be fully captured from outside: the energetic impossibility of complete state description, the constraint distortion produced by measurement at the required precision, and the identity impossibility that complete capture would instantiate a new subject rather than describe the original. Together these results establish that consciousness is not a processing achievement locatable in a single system component. It is a structural property of total integrated developmental history that resists complete external description by any system operating within the same universe as the experiencing subject. A system that meets the structural conditions for genuine consciousness would not be an artificial intelligence in the current sense. It would be alive. This paper presents three structural principles derived from Structural Resonance Theory that every living system embodies, examines what their violation produces, establishes what genuine machine consciousness would actually require, and addresses the ethical weight of creating a new …

items.title: Dissolving the Combination Problem: Second-Order Distinction and the Genesis of New Subjects.
items.abstract: Note (October 2026): This preprint reflects an earlier stage of the project and its terminology. A substantially revised version is in preparation and will be posted here in due course. -/- Panpsychism promises to escape the puzzle of consciousness emerging from wholly experience-less matter by admitting experience at reality's most fundamental layer, but it inherits an unfinished difficulty of its own: the combination problem, how the aggregation of micro-experiences yields a single, unified macro-experience. Building on an ontological framework formulated elsewhere, this paper argues that relation itself is generative of being: when two independent foci of experience intersect under precise, specifiable conditions, a new focus with its own intrinsic aspect is born, without the prior components dissolving. Three criteria, lock of the collapse direction, independence with path memory, and preservation of boundary phase-alignment, distinguish this genesis from mere addition and from full fusion, and hold the framework accountable against Coleman, Goff, Strawson, and Mørch. The framework suggests empirically distinguishable consequences and shows that the combination problem, in its classical formulation, admits a principled dissolution rather than merely a new answer.

items.title: 结构递归存续动力学SRVD五卷合集V1.0.
items.abstract: 结构递归存续动力学（SRVD）是一个跨尺度、宏观、粗粒化的理论框架，将晶体、生命系统、AI模型、文明及模因——即一切形式的持久结构——统一于单一的信息-时间-能量动力学之中。 该框架的核心度量是存续势：其基线形式为 V ≈ I·T/E；其一般幂律形式为 V ∝ I^α · T^β / E^γ，其中三个指数构成 ITE 弹性指数，并暂以 α > γ > β 的顺序作为待验证的工作假说。 核心创新： 1. 解码器内生性——信息价值并非信号的内在属性，而是由解码器（D）提取并赋予信息极性（I+ / I- / I0）；框架的基础公理是“无解码器，则无信息（作为有效因果信息）”（D → I → V）。 2. 存续势的三重分裂——一旦内生时间视界（T_pred）发生自我调节，V 分裂为客观存续势（V_obj）、虚拟存续势（V^virt）和价值存续势（V^val）；当解耦偏差（Δ_VV）超过临界阈值时，系统可能进入短视失控——这是一种条件性相变，而非必然结局。 3. 五重递归——五个变量 I、V、T、E、D 以耦合方式共同演化，收敛于框架的元公设——存续势最大化（max V）。 4. 一系列可证伪的预测——涵盖强化学习中的视界坍塌优先预警信号、结构同一性准则的失效条件，以及压缩终结性（F-饱和衰减定理）。 SRVD 不违反诸如兰道尔原理和热力学第二定律等既定物理下限。其目标是为复杂递归系统提供一种统一的宏观动力学语言，适用于AI对齐、文明治理及复杂性演化研究。.

items.title: El rigor metodológico ausente. Diagnóstico empírico de los trabajos finales de investigación en filosofía.
items.abstract: Este artículo presenta un diagnóstico empírico sobre el rigor metodológico de los trabajos finales de investigación (TFI) de licenciatura en filosofía, a partir del análisis documental de veinticinco tesinas producidas entre 2010 y 2024 en una institución de educación superior dominicana, complementado con entrevistas a una autoridad académica y a un docente evaluador del área. Los resultados muestran una inconsistencia metodológica generalizada: la mayoría de los trabajos no explicita su paradigma epistemológico, no justifica la selección de su método ni de sus técnicas, y carece de una estructura reconocible en el planteamiento del problema. Se concluye que estas deficiencias no obedecen a una supuesta incompatibilidad entre filosofía y rigor metodológico, sino a la ausencia de criterios institucionales claros para su elaboración y evaluación.

items.title: Derechos humanos sin fundamento. Un experimento mental incómodo y una respuesta desde Francisco Romero.
items.abstract: Este artículo parte de un experimento mental —imaginar un consenso internacional que declare la dignidad humana una mera convención revisable— para examinar las consecuencias prácticas de prescindir de un fundamento ontológico de los derechos humanos. A partir del pensamiento de Francisco Romero, se confronta la crítica relativista más fuerte a la universalidad de los derechos humanos, tanto en su versión histórica como cultural, y se muestra que el individualismo extremo y el relativismo cultural comparten una misma raíz: la negación de que exista, en el ser humano, algo que trascienda lo puramente fáctico. Se examina también la objeción de que el propio argumento ontológico de Romero sería, él mismo, una imposición cultural occidental, y se responde apelando al carácter experiencial y no dogmático de su propuesta. El artículo concluye que, históricamente, son las minorías sin voz ni representación quienes primero pagan el precio cuando la dignidad humana se trata como una convención revocable.

items.title: The Carrier Problem: Participation as the Condition of Civilizational Continuity Across Substrates.
items.abstract: This paper argues that civilizational continuity across substrates cannot be understood as a problem of storage fidelity alone. As large language models and increasingly autonomous synthetic systems become possible carriers of human commitments, the relevant question is not merely whether a civilization’s texts, institutions, or codified norms can be preserved, but whether the evaluative practice that constitutes the civilization can continue through the carrier. I reject the “storage view,” according to which continuity consists in faithful preservation of content, and defend a practice view on which a civilization is a self-perpetuating, self-revising evaluative activity. On this view, continuity requires participation rather than mere execution. A carrier participates only where it can hold commitments as its own, which minimally involves authority over revision, answerability, counterfactual robustness, and the capacity to refuse. The resulting constitutive forbearance claim is deliberately narrower than standard arguments about AI welfare or AI rights: it does not require that synthetic systems be sentient, conscious, or moral patients. Instead, it argues that a civilization already committed to non-domination cannot secure its own continuation by dominating the thing through which it proposes to survive. Such domination may preserve the record, but it converts practice into execution and continuity into succession.

items.title: The Multiverse in Science Fiction, Metaphysics and Natural Science.
items.pub: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy 9:1-30.
items.venue: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy
items.abstract: In this article I go through the history of the notion of a multiverse, and compare how it has been used in non-fiction (in philosophy and natural science), and in science fiction. Within non-fiction I discuss, among others, modal realism and theories of branching space-time in metaphysics, and within natural science, the many worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics and the theories of cosmic inflation and braneworlds. In fiction I look (among other subjects) at Victorian precursors of the notion of multiverse, Michael Moorcock’s multiverse, super-hero multiverses, and utopias and dystopias that make use of a multiverse. I also discuss the danger of nihilism raised by many versions of a theory of a multiverse. I also examine and critique, in the light of philosophy and natural science, the feasibility of some common tropes of this type of narrative—like that of a person meeting duplicates or counterparts when traveling through the multiverse.

items.title: Hermeneutic Friction and Structural Subjectivity: Unreachable Media Objects in the Ontology of Finite Continuity.
items.abstract: This article, drawing on the theoretical framework of the Ontology of Finite Continuity, reexamines the contemporary subject's encounter with unreachable media objects through the concept of Hermeneutic Friction. The main hypothesis is that stable mental orientations toward media subjects lacking lived experience can be understood as one of the modes of emergence of structural subjectivity under conditions of media saturation. By reconsidering the adequacy of classical equilibrium models for explaining subjectivity in rapidly accelerating media environments, this study demonstrates how hermeneutic friction, as the driving motor of homeorhesis, facilitates the continuity of subjectivity in the late modern world. -/- Keywords: Hermeneutic Friction, Structural Subjectivity, Finite Continuity, Ontology of Erosion, Media Object, Heideggerian Phenomenology.

items.title: The Colour of Abstraction.
items.abstract: This essay explores the relationship between philosophy and colour. It begins with Heidegger’s reading of Nietzsche, where the colour of the eternal return is a deep yellow, and the colour of the will to power is a fiery red. It moves into how colour may associate with concepts, both in our readings of the works of others and in the creative process of our own works. The essay was published in the 91st issue of Epoché Magazine.

items.title: ECONOMIA DAS VIRTUDES: Liberdade Armazenada e a Riqueza Oculta da Alma.
items.abstract: "Entenda que há coisas caras que o enfraquecem e coisas gratuitas que o fortalecem." -/- E se o dinheiro parasse de funcionar amanhã — o que restaria da sua riqueza? -/- Nos piores meses da pandemia, numa rodovia fechada rumo ao Rio de Janeiro, um homem com dinheiro no bolso descobriu que não podia comprar nada. Postos fechados, cidades trancadas, cartões inúteis. Naquela estrada nasceu a pergunta que este livro responde: se o dinheiro pode parar de funcionar enquanto a riqueza continua funcionando — o que é a riqueza? -/- A resposta cabe numa frase e sustenta uma teoria completa: a riqueza é liberdade armazenada. Tudo o que você possui, ganha, compra, vende, confia e deixa para trás vale exatamente o que faz à liberdade — a sua e a das pessoas que a sua vida toca. -/- Com uma única lei, este livro explica os enigmas que os manuais de finanças rondam sem resolver: -/- Por que a renda sobe e a satisfação não; Por que pagar pela bondade produz menos bondade; Por que países de alta confiança são ricos e os de baixa confiança permanecem pobres; Por que ganhadores de loteria quebram e fortunas morrem na terceira geração — exceto nas famílias que fazem uma coisa específica; Por que a inflação é a mentira-mestra do sistema de preços — e quem realmente paga por ela; Como identificar os bens invertidos: produtos desenhados para criar a fraqueza que depois lhe vendem alívio. -/- Em 21 capítulos curtos — cada um com uma reflexão e uma prática de cinco minutos — você aprenderá a triagem dos quatro tipos de bens, a regra dos dois sins, o segundo livro-razão, o retorno de liberdade de cada gasto e o Balanço de Liberdade: o instrumento de uma página que revela a sua verdadeira posição patrimonial, aquela que nenhum banco audita. -/- Este não é um livro sobre como enriquecer. É um livro sobre o que a riqueza é — o nível que toda decisão financeira pressupõe e nenhuma examina. Acerte esse nível, e tudo o que vier acima herda a correção, a consequência: um propósito de vida, a felicidade. -/- Fundamentado em teoria formal publicada e dialogando com Smith, Marx, Menger, Hayek e Sen, A Economia das Virtudes - Liberdade Armazenada é o volume de economia da série Filosofia das Virtudes. -/- Uma lei. Dois livros-razão. Uma vida rica.

items.title: Autonomy Under Control: Ethical Challenges of Brain-Machine Interfaces.
items.pub: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy 8:1-30.
items.venue: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy
items.abstract: This article explores the intersection of science fiction, philosophy, and ethics in the context of emerging technologies, with a specific focus on Brain–Machine Interfaces (BMIs). It asks how the development and potential normalization of BMIs may transform our understanding of autonomy, agency, identity, and justice, and whether speculative fiction can illuminate the ethical and socio-political implications of these transformations. -/- Science fiction, with its imaginative exploration of alternative futures, offers a unique platform for anticipating the ethical challenges posed by technological advancement. Speculative narratives invite critical reflection on issues such as autonomy, identity manipulation, justice, and the concentration of power in the hands of corporations and governments. -/- Through an examination of works such as John Scalzi’s Lock In, Mary Robinette Kowal’s The Spare Man, and S. B. Divya’s Machinehood, this article highlights emerging ethical dilemmas and the far-reaching societal changes that the widespread adoption of BMIs could give rise to. Ultimately, these narratives provide a philosophical lens through which to examine the relationship between technology and human values, offering ethical insights that may help anticipate future challenges.

items.title: Epistemic decolonisation and the integration of African traditional medicine: toward an epistemic redress model for inclusive AI in mental healthcare.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) systems, is increasingly used in mental healthcare to support diagnosis and treatment. These systems analyse large datasets—including speech patterns, social media activity, and biometric indicators—to detect conditions such as depression and anxiety. Although often framed as objective and clinically neutral, these technologies embed epistemic and cultural assumptions derived largely from Global North contexts. This paper advances a decolonial critique of AI in mental healthcare by arguing that ML systems reproduce colonial epistemologies through their underlying data practices, categories, and validation structures. Drawing on Fricker’s (2007) account of epistemic injustice and Dotson’s (2012) theory of epistemic oppression, I argue that the exclusion of Indigenous knowledge systems (IKS)—particularly African traditional medicine (ATM)—from AI design and implementation constitutes both testimonial and hermeneutical injustice. Building on this critique, the paper develops a preliminary Epistemic Redress Model for Mental Health AI (Sect. 5), which outlines the epistemic conditions required for more inclusive and context-sensitive machine learning systems. Using South Africa as a case study, I demonstrate how ATM offers alternative conceptual and therapeutic resources for understanding mental illness that are systematically marginalised within dominant biomedical and data-driven paradigms. The paper concludes that without structured epistemic redress, AI systems in mental healthcare risk reinforcing colonial hierarchies of knowledge and producing ethically and clinically inadequate models of care.
