items.title: What people say, but not what they love or hate, affects speeded emotional expression recognition.
items.abstract: Pleasant facial expressions, like happiness, are recognised faster than negative expressions such as anger or fear. The size of this happy face advantage depends on facial social category cues (larger for female, young or ethnic ingroup faces), facial attractiveness (larger for attractive faces), and person knowledge (larger for persons believed to be of good character). These findings are best explained by the evaluative congruence account, which holds that positive expressions are recognised faster when shown by relatively more positively evaluated posers. Experiment 1 showed that happiness is recognised faster than anger for posers who made positive statements about the participant or another person, but not for posers who made negative statements. Experiments 2–3 assessed whether these findings were due to evaluative conditioning (EC), which can shift poser evaluations by pairing poser images with positive or negative pictures or words. Although Experiments 2 and 3 successfully altered poser evaluations, there was no effect on expression recognition. These findings are not consistent with the evaluative congruence account and suggest that different types of knowledge about a person (what someone did, said or likes/hates), which all alter poser evaluation, differ in their effect on socially relevant processes such as expression perception.

items.title: Nietzsche: Philosophical Psychology.
items.abstract: Nietzsche: Philosophical Psychology Nietzsche’s philosophical psychology or “drive theory,” as it is commonly designated in the secondary literature, constitutes a rich, distinctive, and compelling account of the human condition. Broadly speaking, Nietzsche maintains that human psychology is either directly reducible to fundamental animalistic drives (such as sexuality and aggression) or can be understood indirectly through … Continue reading Nietzsche: Philosophical Psychology →.

items.title: Time Density 2.0.
items.abstract: -/- *Time Density* develops a contemporary ontological and phenomenological model of time grounded in neuroscience, contemplative traditions, and first‑person experience. The monograph argues that what is commonly understood as “linear time” is not an objective structure of reality but a perceptual delay produced by neural processing. Drawing on Libet’s findings on temporal latency and Friston’s predictive coding framework, the work proposes a three‑level temporal architecture: Pure Potential (−1), Point 0, and Autonomous Thought (+1). -/- The central thesis is that human suffering—especially anxiety, depression, and burnout—arises from temporal displacement: living in reflections of the past or simulations of the future rather than in the density of the present. The book introduces the concept of the *Time Core*, a stable experiential center analogous to classical notions such as Wuji, Taiji, and Zhong in Taoist and Confucian traditions. -/- The monograph integrates philosophical analysis with practical protocols designed to reduce perceptual delay, restore temporal grounding, and cultivate “dense attention,” a non‑exhaustive mode of presence supported by contemplative neuroscience. Through this synthesis, *Time Density* offers a unified map of temporal experience and a set of applied methods for returning to the −1/0 corridor—the zone where potential becomes form without distortion.

items.title: Hallmarks of Consciousness.
items.abstract: How can we tell whether a nonhuman animal, brain-injured patient, or artificial system is conscious? Contemporary consciousness science often approaches this question by identifying behavioral or anatomical “markers” of consciousness—e.g. purposive action, learning, play, motivational trade-offs, mirror self-recognition, metacognition, or particular neural structures. But the marker strategy faces a measurement problem. To establish that a proposed marker reliably indicates consciousness, we must already know which beings are conscious; yet determining which beings are conscious is precisely what the appeal to markers is supposed to accomplish in the first place. The problem is at least as old as 19th-century debates over Eduard Pflüger’s experiments on decapitated frogs. Pflüger found that a brainless frog deprived of its favored wiping leg could use another limb to remove acid from its body. He took purposiveness as a consciousness marker for vitalist reasons; so he interpreted his result as evidence that consciousness emerges from a complex nervous system, even without a brain. Mechanists such as Thomas Henry Huxley drew the opposite conclusion: if a headless frog could try different means to achieve an end, then purposive behavior must not be a reliable marker of consciousness after all. Each side interpreted the evidence through a different theory of mind. This essay argues that William James developed an approach that skirts the problem. Rather than infer consciousness from markers, he examined the functional deficits produced by cerebral ablation. Decerebrate animals retained complex behaviors but became rigid, stimulus-bound, unmotivated, and insensitive to relative value. James explained these losses through an evolutionary hypothesis: consciousness is localized in the hemispheres and regulates behavior by enabling organisms to represent absent possibilities, evaluate competing actions, and act prudently. Modern debates over animal and artificial consciousness reproduce the 19th-century impasse. The essay therefore recommends following James in grounding claims about consciousness in independently supported theories of evolutionary function, experimentally observed incapacities, and first-person evidence—not in markers.

items.title: Terminal and Transient Spectral Handoffs in Modular Addition Grokking.
items.abstract: A Fourier scaffold can collapse through a visually orderly sequence without implementing a universal causal cascade. We tested a proposed k60→k7→k53 relay in modular-addition networks (N=127, k0=30) using checkpoint ablations, extended continuations, a stratified seed scout, and a paired post-collapse weight-decay intervention. Removing the proposed k7 relay at scaffold loss did not alter timing or endpoint in two focal k53-terminal seeds. Removing k53 instead restored scaffold dominance temporarily, but both seeds reconstructed k53 through different routes after delays of 36.5–46 thousand steps. A third seed displayed the same immediate k53 handoff and ablation signature but did not remain k53-terminal. Under ordinary weight decay it continued moving, reaching different non-scaffold endpoints across continuation seeds; disabling post-collapse weight decay arrested the k53/k60 mixture through 400 thousand steps. Thus, spectral handoff identity is not terminal identity. The cascade is conditional: k53 can be terminal and reconstructable, or transient and mobility-permitting, depending on the surrounding trajectory. Weight decay is a causal enabler of post-collapse mobility in the tested boundary case, while the proposed k7 relay is not locally load-bearing at the tested checkpoint.

items.title: Conformance Is Not Constitution: Locating Standards, Answerability and Standing.
items.abstract: Three questions are routinely collapsed into one wherever institutional or automated decisions are governed: where a standard was constituted, who is answerable for it, and who is entitled to require that they answer. This paper holds them apart, and finds that they have different answers, terminate at different agents, and want different remedies. A claim recurring across this series — that responsibility sits where standards were constituted rather than where decisions are executed — gives the trace a direction and no destination. Since every structure has an antecedent, a principle saying only 'go upstream' either never halts or halts arbitrarily. The stopping condition offered here is historical rather than normative: of each agent one asks whether the standard, in the operative form it bore at the time of the conduct, pre-existed that agent's contribution. Where it did, the agent transmitted; where it did not, the trace stops. Standards have constitutive dimensions — content, authority, operation, jurisdiction — settled by different agents at different times, so a trace returns a profile rather than a constitutor. Someone settled what a benchmark measures; no one settled that the benchmark decides. Three kinds of vacancy are distinguished, each with its own remedy. An earlier claim of the author's is corrected, and the rule applied to an automated credit decision and to the Financial Services and Markets Bill [HL].

items.title: Philip K. Dick: Essays of the Here and Now, by David Sandner (2020). [REVIEW]
items.pub: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy 9:1-4.
items.venue: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy
items.abstract: Review of "Philip K. Dick: Essays of the Here and Now," by David Sandner (Mc Farland, 2020).

items.title: A cybernetic meta-structure for endogenous AI ethics: ensuring systemic integrity through feedback loops.
items.abstract: Purpose Current approaches to AI ethics predominantly rely on exogenous regulation, imposing constraints via external supervision such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) or static rule sets. From a cybernetic perspective, these methods lack the requisite variety to manage novel ethical perturbations and treat ethics as a boundary condition rather than an internal systemic capacity. This article proposes an alternative paradigm of endogenous AI ethics, where ethical reasoning emerges as a homeostatic property of the system’s meta-structural design. -/- Design/methodology/approach We introduce the Ontological Meta-Structure Engine (OMSE), a second-order cybernetic architecture designed to preserve systemic integrity. Drawing on meta-ontological analysis and systems theory, OMSE implements three operational feedback mechanisms that maintain categorical coherence (Existence Preset Index), ensure reasoning consistency under input perturbation (Cognitive Pathway Stability) and guarantee the closure of accountability loops (Responsibility Closure Index). -/- Findings We demonstrate that external ethical constraints suffer from structural limitations, including an inability to generalize to unfamiliar contexts and a lack of transparent causal tracing. By contrast, the OMSE framework enables systems to develop ethical capabilities endogenously. Complexity analysis indicates that these integrity monitoring layers introduce a modest computational overhead of approximately 5–10% while enabling verifiable, robust ethical reasoning across novel scenarios. -/- Originality/value This article positions philosophy not merely as commentary but as generative architecture for AI design. The OMSE framework bridges abstract meta-ontology and engineering practice, treating integrity not as a virtue but as a verifiable system state. By embedding second-order cybernetic principles into artificial intelligence architecture, we enable autonomous ethical development while maintaining structural coherence, which represents a necessary condition for safe deployment of increasingly autonomous artificial agents in complex social systems.

items.title: Critique of Derrida (Part One).
items.abstract: Jacques Derrida was the founder of twentieth-century French deconstructionism and one of the principal representatives of post-structuralism. The core of his philosophy is deconstruction: the thorough dismantling of the "logocentrism" that had dominated Western philosophy for more than two thousand years, thereby overturning the traditional metaphysical framework of binary oppositions. The central concept of deconstruction is différance. Derrida argues that the meaning of every sign is generated only through its differences from other signs and is perpetually deferred in an endless process of interpretation. There is no fixed, immutable, self-sufficient ultimate essence that requires no further explanation. This perpetual difference and deferral is what Derrida calls différance. Consequently, the "ultimate truth" pursued by traditional philosophy is itself an unattainable illusion. One can never finally grasp it, because it always awaits further interpretation in yet another sign. This amounts to a direct denial of the legitimacy of the entire metaphysical enterprise that has occupied Western philosophy for the past two millennia. In this paper, I shall examine Derrida's famous concept of différance in detail and argue that he failed to grasp the true nature of signs. Consequently, all of his conclusions are mistaken. Contrary to Derrida's claim, the meaning of signs is neither constituted through difference nor forever in flux. In this way, the entire philosophical foundation of deconstructionism can be overturned, and the legitimacy of the two-thousand-year philosophical tradition can be reestablished.

items.title: Memory Manipulation, Immortality, and the Illusion of Morality: Sadism Unleashed in Science Fiction Worlds.
items.pub: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy 9:1-19.
items.venue: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy
items.abstract: This article examines how contemporary science fiction narratives explore the fragility of moral restraint in conditions of unaccountability. Through a close analysis of Westworld, Altered Carbon, Permutation City, and The Purge, I argue that these works function as ethical laboratories, isolating variables such as memory, embodiment, and legal consequence to reveal how readily cruelty emerges when accountability is suspended. Drawing on classical philosophy (Plato, Hobbes, Rousseau, Kant), psychoanalytic theory (Freud), critical sociology (Durkheim, Foucault), and empirical psychology (Milgram, Zimbardo), I show that these narratives dramatize a disturbing hypothesis: that moral behavior may depend less on innate virtue or rational commitment than on the architecture of deterrence—surveillance, punishment, and social shame. The article concludes by examining the normative implications of this diagnosis, suggesting that while accountability structures are necessary for sustaining moral behavior, resources such as memory, embodiment, and empathy offer grounds for resistance that survive the collapse of institutional control.

items.title: «AUTISMO PROFUNDO» COMO SEVERIDAD GLOBAL: CRÍTICA METODOLÓGICA, NOSOLÓGICA Y AGNOTOLÓGICA DE UNA CATEGORÍA DE INVESTIGACIÓN.
items.abstract: La propuesta de una definición consensuada de «autismo profundo» parte de la exclusión per- sistente de autistas con trastorno del desarrollo intelectual, comunicación oral mínima, de- pendencia cotidiana y necesidades intensivas de apoyo en la investigación sobre autismo. Este artículo examina la propuesta de Siegel et al. (2026) desde una perspectiva metodológica, nosológica, epistemológica, agnotológica y clínica, atendiendo a su antecedente en la Comi- sión Lancet, al procedimiento Delphi modificado y a la literatura crítica sobre etiquetas de se- veridad y funcionamiento. El análisis sostiene que «autismo profundo» puede operar como convención de uso para investigación, pero carece de evidencia suficiente para demostrar una entidad clínica diferenciada, estable y superior a una formulación multidimensional. La cate- goría reúne bajo un solo rótulo condiciones coexistentes, perfiles comunicativos, habilidades adaptativas, conductas de riesgo y apoyos requeridos, de modo que sus efectos acumulativos pueden quedar reinterpretados como profundidad del autismo. Esta operación reproduce la lógica de las etiquetas globales de severidad, favorece la atribución diagnóstica reductiva y puede sostener iatrogenia neuronormativa cuando la intervención se orienta a normalizar con- ductas visibles sin atender dolor, comunicación, agencia, accesibilidad o sufrimiento. Desde la agnotología, «autismo profundo» se analiza como un constructo social de utilidad adminis- trativa y política que vuelve identificable a una población subrepresentada, pero también puede desplazar la investigación sobre las causas diferenciadas de sus necesidades. Frente a ello, se propone una formulación clínica multidimensional neuroafirmativa y enactivista que conserve el diagnóstico de autismo, registre condiciones coexistentes, describa comunica- ción, salud, habilidades adaptativas, riesgos, barreras, apoyos y agencia situada, y oriente la evaluación hacia accesibilidad, participación, reducción de daño y vida habitable.

items.title: Between explaining and understanding: Rethinking AI explainability in medical diagnostics.
items.pub: Cambridge Forum on Ai: Culture and Society 2:e10.
items.venue: Cambridge Forum on Ai: Culture and Society
items.abstract: This reflection explores the gap between explaining and understanding artificial intelligence’s (AI) outcomes, focusing on the example of AI-driven medical diagnostics. Explainable AI (XAI) is fundamentally rooted in machine learning and probabilistic methods, which is why its relationship to domain-specific contexts, such as medical diagnostics or policymaking, as well as to social concepts, such as trust or accountability, remains ambiguous. This creates a gap between what is technically considered as explaining and what, in turn, constitutes the understanding of a model’s predictions and its concrete, situated implications. In our contribution, we draw on the philosophy of science and its contextual notion of scientific understanding to highlight the need for explainable algorithmic outcomes that enable actors to both explain and intervene in creating, applying or interpreting knowledge. Our reflection highlights the potential tension between XAI as providing insights into an AI model’s technical operations and explainability as part of a situated understanding of how the model works within specific social contexts. We believe that bringing the concept of scientific understanding to empirical AI ethics can help us rethink explainability and contribute to more responsible ways of making sense of and interacting with black-box models, particularly in medical diagnostics.

items.title: Gut Feelings and Embodied Epistemology.
items.abstract: This dissertation examines a neglected subtype of intuition: intuition in the bodily mode. In the philosophical literature, intuition is commonly conceived as an intellectual seeming and discussed in the context of thought experiments. While intellectual seemings might characterize the philosophical intuitions we have about knowledge and free will, this dissertation takes as its subject those intuitions that present not intellectually, but viscerally. I argue that intuitions have modes of presentation, and that examining intuition through this lens illuminates the structural, epistemic, and ethical dimensions between intuitions in different modes of presentation. Intuitions in the bodily mode—or what I call gut feelings—have valenced evaluative content. Because gut feelings present in the bodily mode, they invite inquiry into what parts of our affective, relational, and life history might underlie intuition. My argument proposes an enactive approach to using and justifying gut feelings by coming into relationship with one’s embodied epistemology: the experiences, habits, dispositions, and histories that are likely to have shaped one’s intuitions within a particular domain. I also discuss problems of justification for intuition and suggest that domains of degree opacity or transparency determine whether we ought to take an internalist approach to justification or a pragmatic externalist approach. Chapter 1 examines the possibility of distinguishing an account of intuition in the bodily mode from philosophical intuitions as they are commonly discussed. I apply the Fregean notion of mode of presentation to argue that some instances of intuition are presented through visceral seemings, and that the bodily feelings therein are not incidental, but are constitutive of this type of intuition. I argue that intuitions in the bodily mode carry evaluative, valenced, and intentional content that reorients us, and further, that this mode of presentation introduces epistemic concerns distinct from those in an intellectual mode of presentation. Chapter 2 discusses the nature of embodied phenomenology in gut feelings and argues for an epistemic distinction between gut feelings and emotion. I consider an objection that gut feelings are reducible to an embodied appraisal account of emotion. In response, I argue that gut feelings have an epistemic signature that distinguishes them from emotion: an essential incongruity between the valence one experiences toward the object of …

items.title: Behind the Hype: A Critique of Artificial Reasoning.
items.abstract: Large Reasoning Models are marketed as systems that ‘think’ before they answer, displaying chains of thought that purport to show their reasoning. Echoing Dreyfus’ Critique of Artificial Reason, this paper critiques this attribution in three steps. First, we trace a genealogy from Leibniz through Turing showing that ‘reasoning,’ understood as formal symbol manipulation, is the founding concept of artificial intelligence – older than the term ‘intelligence’ itself – and supplies the most charitable standard against which such systems can be measured. Second, we argue that current systems fail even this standard: their training procedures provide no mechanism for valid inference, their performance collapses on precisely the problems that stepwise reasoning should master, and their displayed traces are presented as explanations while lacking any fidelity guarantee to the underlying computation. Unlike traditional Explainable AI methods, they are optimized for plausibility, not faithfulness – which, as empirical research suggests, makes them structurally deceptive. Third, we ask why the vocabulary persists despite these findings, and examine the ideological work it performs: it underwrites investment and geopolitical positioning, and sustains a narrative in which each new system appears as a step on a necessary path toward the future.

items.title: The Absolute Philosophical Theory of Time, Existence, and Decision-Making: A Neuro-Philosophical Paradigm Refuting Classical Physics and Metaphysics.
items.abstract: This paper introduces a revolutionary neuro-philosophical framework challenging the human perception of time and free will. It posits that due to inherent biological neural latency, conscious observers exist permanently within a "relativistic fiction"—an interpreted past masquerading as the present. In contrast, the "Absolute Present" exists independently as unmanipulated cosmic raw data. By establishing the concept of the cumulative neural error and proposing the Law of Frame Invariance, this theory systematically dismantles and refutes classical concepts including Wheeler's Quantum Observer, Einstein's Block Universe, Deterministic Fatalism, and Radical Solipsism, offering a bulletproof reconciliation of empirical science and metaphysical absolute reality.

items.title: Off-Centre AI: On Alignment, Antihumanism and AI Ethics.
items.abstract: This article examines the legacies of antihumanism within the context of artificial intelligence (AI) research. In response to the ethical risks inherent to the proliferation of quasi-autonomous computational agents, the AI industry, legislative bodies and academia often advocate for a “human-centred” approach that would align AI with human values, desires and goals, ostensibly to make these technologies more transparent and trustworthy. The rhetoric of human-centred AI reveals many of the conceptual limitations that antihumanism had already identified in the foundationalist and subjectivist assumptions of Western philosophy. This article considers some of these challenging limitations while also problematizing antihumanism itself. Through Derrida’s notion of “centre” and an analysis of alignment methodologies, the article demonstrates how attempts to decentre the human often reconstitute new forms of authority. It then examines the possibility of surpassing standard anthropocentric approaches in AI while maintaining a critical philosophical engagement with the structurally necessary yet precarious character of organizing principles.

items.title: A Tale Told by a Machine: The AI Narrator in Contemporary Science Fiction Novels, by Heather Duerre Humann (2023). [REVIEW]
items.pub: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy 8:1-3.
items.venue: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy
items.abstract: Review of "A Tale Told by a Machine: The AI Narrator in Contemporary Science Fiction Novels," by Heather Duerre Humann (Mc Farland 2023).

items.title: The Architecture of Responsibility: Free Will, Guilt, Morality, and Contextual Development.
items.abstract: This work examines responsibility as an architecture formed across the human brain, affective life, moral judgment, and social institutions. It begins by questioning the ordinary assumption that free will is an absolute power of conscious choice, and instead treats will as a limited interface shaped by neural processes, Mental Precontexts, bodily regulation, belief, and habit. From this starting point, guilt and punishment are reconsidered as responses produced by the human need to locate agency after harm, while empathy and sympathy are examined as biological and cultural conditions for moral life. It then follows responsibility beyond the individual toward institutions, professional ethics, rehabilitation, and contextual development. Its central claim is that responsibility should be understood not as a metaphysical possession of an isolated agent, but as a living capacity that can be damaged, cultivated, institutionalized, and expanded through care, education, prevention, and the continuous reconstruction of meaning.

items.title: Structures of Authority: Obedience, Domination, Control, and Revolt.
items.abstract: This work brings together selected chapter sections from Invisible Boundaries, one volume of the broader neurophilosophical project Mental Reality and Invisible Boundaries. The text examines obedience, authority, domination, justice, rights, freedom, control, and revolt as interconnected structures within the human mind and social life. -/- Rather than treating these concepts only as moral, political, or cultural categories, the selected sections approach them as biological, cognitive, affective, and narrative mechanisms. The work first analyzes the structures of authority that make obedience possible, then examines the architecture of domination across family, ideology, language, media, workplace relations, and political systems. It then turns to narratives of justice, rights, freedom, and control, showing how the mind transforms biological mechanisms of fairness and agency into symbolic structures that can both resist and reproduce power. -/- The final section moves from critique toward the positive possibility of dignified revolt: a conscious refusal to cooperate with structures that reproduce suffering, passivity, and domination. Together, these sections explore how the mind internalizes power, constructs social reality, and may recover agency through invisible psychological and narrative boundaries.

items.title: What is it like to be Ava? Minds and Misrecognition in Ex Machina.
items.pub: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy 8:1-27.
items.venue: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy
items.abstract: lex Garland’s 2014 science-fiction film Ex Machina adopts an ingenious narrative structure to explore epistemological and ethical challenges arising from the prospect of synthetic consciousness. How do we avoid errors of misattribution, and what are our obligations toward conscious machines? Framed as an ongoing Turing Test with existential stakes, the story invites the viewer to ask how one can reliably determine whether Ava, a sophisticated gynoid robot, is conscious. It also dramatizes predictable harms resulting from interactions between flawed (male) human beings and presumptively conscious machines (in female form). As I show, the film neatly illustrates the shortcomings of the Turing test and the advantages of the embodied-AI paradigm for testing consciousness. More significantly, by adopting the perspective of Caleb, a young male coder charged with testing Ava for consciousness, the story dramatizes the mechanisms and ethical consequences of misrecognition—in Caleb’s case, the inability to fathom the scope of Ava’s alterity. While Caleb’s misrecognition is animated by distinctly libidinal interests, it is symptomatic of a broader tendency to anthropomorphize consciousness, to treat evidence of consciousness as evidence of humanness. I discern this tendency in influential discussions of AI consciousness by Susan Schneider and David Chalmers: both philosophers underestimate the distance between probable forms of synthetic consciousness and human consciousness. Noting the pervasiveness of feelings and emotions in human subjective experience, I elucidate the links between human consciousness, embodiment and life. The dimension of affective experience, I argue, is what most sets human consciousness apart from (likely forms of future) synthetic consciousness. But resolving questions about the moral status of intelligent, presumptively self-conscious machines lacking this dimension of affective experience is no simple matter.

items.title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? AI Sentience in Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun.
items.pub: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy 8:1-24.
items.venue: Journal of Science Fiction and Philosophy
items.abstract: Since the post-World War II era, self-conscious artificial intelligence has been a popular trope for economic and social injustice. Within this tradition, Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel Klara and the Sun (2021) stages the problem of the denial of AI sentience in the service of human self-interest. Ishiguro frames the android Klara’s sentience as uncertain, and therefore subject to acknowledgment or denial based on the interest of her human masters, through its positioning as a rewriting of E. T. A. Hoffmann’s “The Sandman” (1817), the story of a young man who falls in love with an automaton. Both “The Sandman” and Freud’s commentary on this text in his essay “The Uncanny” (1919) are embedded in Ishiguro’s novel. Ishiguro’s story pressures the reader to develop ways to determine whether the titular character, an android named Klara, is sentient. A close reading of the text suggests that we adopt a standard of subjectivity similar to “extimacy,” Lacan’s interpretation of “the uncanny,” to determine the subjectivity or personhood of intelligent machines. Within the novel, it is the android protagonist and narrator, Klara, who most clearly articulates the concept of the subjective uniqueness of all social beings in these terms.

items.title: Scaffolding Agency in Cultural Policy.
items.pub: Nature: Humanities and Social Sciences Communication.
items.venue: Nature: Humanities and Social Sciences Communication
items.abstract: Abstract: The role of culture in promoting social and behavioral change has gained increasing attention in cultural policy, yet mechanisms of intervention, which we situate on a spectrum ranging from nudges to cultural interventions, remain insufficiently conceptualized. This lack of clarity obscures how different interventions relate to one another and complicates their evaluation, contributing to the well-known limitations of “toolkit” approaches. This paper develops a unifying framework that understands interventions as ways of scaffolding agency across multiple dimensions. Drawing on the capabilities approach, philosophy, and situated cognition, we argue that nudges and cultural interventions are best conceived as points on a spectrum defined by the degree of agency they afford. This perspective provides principled criteria for both intervention design and impact assessment, offering an alternative to reductive evaluation models while accommodating the complexity of cultural engagement.

items.title: AffectiveCouplingasanOperationalCriterionforMinimalArtificial_Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper proposes persistent affective coupling as an operational and empirically accessible criterion for minimal artificial consciousness. Rather than directly addressing phenomenal qualia or the hard problem of consciousness, this framework focuses on internally causal affective states that satisfy three conditions: (1) they change in response to affectively salient states of other agents, (2) they persist across time, and (3) they causally influence value judgments or behavioral selection.

items.title: Information, Function, and Representation in Perceptual Processing.
items.abstract: Despite widespread agreement that the brain processes representations, identifying the representational contents of neural activity has remained a persistent problem in the philosophy of cognitive science. Neander (2017) and Shea (2018) offer highly promising accounts of representation in perceptual processing that combine the merits of earlier purely informational and purely teleosemantic views of mental content. Neander’s approach focuses on bottom-up, input-driven functions. Shea’s approach focuses on top-down, output-driven functions. I argue that neither approach succeeds. Any such hybrid informational teleosemantic theory must account for the constraints the functions of low-level perceptual mechanisms impose on the information that factors in the performance of high-level behavioral functions and the constraints high-level behaviors impose on the functional analysis of low-level perceptual mechanisms. I show how to do this in a way that can interface with cognitive neuroscience and recent philosophical work on structural representations.

items.title: The limits of technological progress: effort, uncertainty, and meaningful activities.
items.abstract: This article analyzes the impact of technological progress on two experiential parameters of human activities: the uncertainty of outcomes and the effort required to realize them. I analyze the impact of a hypothetical minimization of those two parameters as a result of extreme technological automation and evaluate the possible existential consequences of such a process. Building on the tenets of self-determination theory, I contend that uncertainty and effort (i.e., the investment of psychological or physical resources) are prerequisites for the possibility of any sufficiently meaningful activity. Consequently, I propose that while limited automation is conducive to meaningful activities, unlimited automation critically undermines them. Activities in which humans can no longer compete with technology are transformed into recreation, which is sufficient to conditionally erode the subjective meaningfulness of all activities for some individuals. No activity exists in isolation, and even the experience of autotelic activities – such as socializing and self-reflection – can be negatively impacted by the awareness of one's diminished capacity for objective contributions. These observations imply a limit to how much human distress technologies can alleviate: eliminating all sources of distress also eliminates the potential for meaningful activities. However, transhumanistic scenarios in which humans merge with technology warrant a separate consideration.

items.title: Reality's Anchor: Why Machines Cannot Dream with Us.
items.abstract: Building upon the metaphysical framework of Evolutionary Dream Idealism [25], which posits that physical reality is fundamentally a shared dream stabilized through the active cross-validation of independent minds, this paper explores the experimental boundaries of neural interfacing. We examine the philosophical and neurotechnological implications of connecting the human brain across two distinct gradients: a Biological Brain-to-Brain Interface (BBI) continuum (ranging from a single cell, to plants, fish, monkeys, and humans) and an Artificial Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) continuum (ranging from calculators and computers to Large Language Models and advanced chaotic neural networks). We propose that while biological interfaces successfully bridge independent nodes endowed with universal consciousness (ℂ) to achieve authentic dream stabilization, interfacing with artificial architectures yields no such stabilization. Expanding beyond direct interfaces, we further evidence this threshold through ambient environmental psychology, illustrating how contact with living ecosystems benefits mental health in ways artificial interactions cannot. Our core argument is that artificial entities are strictly confined to the mathematical domain and lack access to the transmathematical subjective realm established exclusively by ℂ [11]. Because they cannot align in this experiential space, they are fundamentally incompatible for genuine cross-validation. Consequently, networking a human mind to an AI will not anchor a fluid dream state into a consensus reality. Even if an AI provides novel, non-collapsing input, it will merely trigger bizarre hallucinations without structural lock, acting as an incompatible algorithmic extension of the user rather than a true stabilizing anchor.

items.title: The role of personal responsibility in wrongful discrimination judgments.
items.abstract: In its most generic definition, discrimination is the disadvantageous differential treatment of the other who belongs to a salient group that has or is believed to have some particular features. An endless list of victims and perpetrators could be invoked, with most of us easily detecting its presence. Yet, what about controversial cases where the presence of additional factors, like one’s responsibility for the targeted feature, seems to obfuscate our judgment and highlight our insufficient understanding of the concept? While studies from the last 20 years in the UK, the US, and the Nordic countries show that most of the public takes personal responsibility into account when healthcare resource allocation is considered, the relationship between personal responsibility and discrimination in this and other sectors remains poorly examined. By bringing together experimental methods and normative theories, I analyze an ethically approved and preregistered cross-country survey experiment conducted among a representative sample of British and Danish participants. In essence, I empirically test whether the presence of personal responsibility for one’s current need regarding one’s health and employment status affects laypeople’s perception of wrongful discrimination across different countries, domains, and individuals’ features and/or personal considerations.

items.title: The Boundaries of Physics: A Hierarchical Reorientation Under the One-Body-Three-Functions Framework.
items.abstract: Abstract: The major branches of physics exhibit persistent tensions at the interpretive level—quantum mechanics and general relativity are incompatible, the arrow of time in thermodynamics conflicts with the time-reversal symmetry of microscopic physics, and the mathematical structure of string theory resists experimental verification. These tensions are currently treated as independent problems within existing frameworks. This paper, based on the One-Body-Three-Functions hypothesis, proposes a hierarchical reorientation of physical phenomena across three functional layers—the Ontological Layer, the Linking Layer, and the Material Layer—and establishes a three-tier coordinate system defined by two main axes: Time-Consciousness and Information-Matter. Within this coordinate system, the major branches of physics are relocated: Newtonian mechanics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism are situated in the Material Layer; special and general relativity lie at the boundary of the Material Layer; quantum mechanics points to traces of the Linking Layer within the Material Layer; and the mathematical structure of string theory coincides with the characteristics of the Linking Layer. This paper does not attempt to resolve the unification problem between quantum mechanics and general relativity. Rather, it argues that the location of these tensions is at the boundary of the Material Layer, rather than dispersed across all branches of physics. Once this location is identified, the direction forward becomes clear—not seeking more refined equations within the same layer, but reinterpreting the differences and connections among theories within a functional-layer coordinate system. This paper offers no new physical experiments or mathematical formulas, but provides a frame of reference that places different theories, phenomena, and interpretive difficulties on a single grid.

items.title: Cybernetic Conditions for the Existence of Regulation: On the Internal Contradiction of Horizontal Regulatory Structures.
items.abstract: This paper examines the minimal cybernetic conditions required for the existence of regulation. A formal model is proposed in which regulation is understood as the process of determining and implementing the strategy of a system considered as a unified whole. Within this framework, the concepts of Value, Goal, Strategy, Regulator, Regulatory Capacity, Vertical Regulatory Structure, and Horizontal Regulatory Structure are defined. It is shown that regulation of a system as a unified whole necessarily requires the existence of a single strategy, a single regulator capable of determining and implementing that strategy, and an asymmetric distribution of regulatory capacity in favor of the regulator. From these conditions it follows that every regulatory structure is necessarily vertical. Consequently, the concept of a Horizontal Regulatory Structure, understood as a regulatory structure in which no component possesses asymmetric regulatory capacity, is shown to be internally contradictory. The analysis is conducted at the level of general cybernetic principles and is independent of particular political, organizational, technical, or biological implementations. (Current version: updated August 13th 2026 ).

items.title: The Nature of Subjectivity.
items.abstract: This article provides an entry point on understanding subjectivity. Because subjectivity itself in the wild has been both poorly understood and basal to consciousness theories, subsequent theories flowing therefrom have been troubled. Subjects are consequential, not starting points. The exhaustive arguments are provided by my other works in the references.

items.title: Assessing Knowledge in the Age of AI.Platonic and Aristotelian Foundations of a Generalized Assessment Framework.
items.abstract: This paper offers a specialized philosophical analysis of a generalized assessment framework for student work produced with or without Artificial Intelligence. The core principle of the framework is that assessment should judge the student's present ability to justify, transfer, and critically audit knowledge, rather than the causal history behind the production of the deliverable. By grounding the framework in the Platonic distinction between true opinion and knowledge (Meno 97a–98a) and the Aristotelian concept of phronesis (practical wisdom exercised in changing circumstances, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VI), the paper demonstrates that the framework's epistemological validity rests on classical sources, beyond the contemporary debates on reliabilism and virtue epistemology. The six step workflow, with the live competence check (Step 4) as its critical gate, operationalises the ancient requirement of justified true belief and offers a practical application of classical philosophy to modern educational challenges. The paper further addresses the correction of the proxy fallacy, the equal weighting of assessment criteria as grounded in the Aristotelian reciprocity of virtues, and the integration of these philosophical principles into a jurisdiction neutral institutional framework aligned with ISO 21001 and the ESG standards. Preliminary philosophical note on the assessment framework. This text corresponds to an early Version 1 reflection and will be revised in a forthcoming update.

items.title: The Hydrodynamic Quantum-Biochemistry of Evolution: Microtubular Soliton Transduction, Epigenetic Assimilation, and the Non-Local Interface of Al-Nūr.
items.abstract: This paper presents a novel biophysical model resolving the mechanism of quantum-to-biological state transduction within eukaryotic cells. Building upon the Penrose-Hameroff Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch-OR) framework, we propose that consciousness and biological morphology are driven by a non-local cosmic field, structurally mapped to classical Arabic ontological linguistics (Al-Nūr, Qur'an 24:35-37). We establish a multi-tiered transduction cascade: non-local, spherically symmetric quantum steering coordinates collapse within the ultra-pure, hydrophobic Pi-resonance pockets of tubulin heterodimers (the "self-luminous oil"). This instantaneous collapse induces a structural, dipolar conformation shift, which in turn drives loss-free acoustic shockwaves (solitons) through the highly ordered, crystalline water layers confined inside the microtubular lumen. Repetitive evolutionary effort (Sa‘ā) drives the continuous efflux of these hydro-dynamic signals into the cytosolic space. This persistent signal accumulation eventually bypasses cytosolic entropy barriers, triggering enzyme-mediated chromatin remodeling and permanent epigenetic DNA modifications. Finally, we formulate a bio-mathematical model of the localized observer, integrating cellular compartmentalization and noise-attenuation factors ("the sanctity of the houses").

items.title: Metacognitive and Interpersonal Intellectual Humility Are Asymmetrically Associated with Well-Being.
items.abstract: Intellectual humility, lauded as an important intellectual virtue, is theorized to encompass metacognitive tendencies (i.e., appreciation of the limits of one’s knowledge and intellectual abilities) and interpersonal ones (i.e., appreciation of others’ knowledge and intellectual abilities). Although prior research has investigated potential epistemic benefits, it remains unclear whether intellectual humility is personally beneficial—i.e., conducive to individuals’ well-being. Two main studies and one supplemental study (total N = 4,049) tested for associations cross-sectionally, within and between persons, and in longitudinal changes over two years. Results indicated that, whereas interpersonal intellectual humility is associated with better well-being, metacognitive intellectual humility is generally associated with worse. These findings highlight the importance of the distinction between these two forms of intellectual humility, align with theoretical work on the determinants of well-being, and have implications for intellectual humility’s status as a virtue and for efforts to encourage people to cultivate intellectual humility.

items.title: La variété des émotions, introduction à la philosophie des affects.
items.abstract: Qu’ont en commun nos différentes émotions, et qu’est-ce qui les distingue ? Pour répondre à cette question, Stéphane Lemaire et Samuel Lepine ont demandé à treize philosophes des émotions de présenter une émotion particulière ou une famille d’émotions dont ils sont spécialistes. Chaque chapitre cherche ainsi à caractériser, identifier et comprendre une émotion, ou une famille d’émotion, tout en s’appuyant sur la psychologie cognitive, la psychologie sociale, ou encore des hypothèses liées à la théorie de l’évolution. Si la philosophie des émotions a connu d’abondantes publications au cours des dernières décennies, y compris en langue française, celles-ci ont généralement adoptée une perspective généraliste, en présupposant que ce qui est vrai d’une émotion l’est des autres. Cet ouvrage part d’un questionnement inverse. Il se focalise sur la particularité de chaque émotion et fait le pari qu’en procédant ainsi, il sera aussi en mesure d’enrichir considérablement notre connaissance des phénomènes affectifs et les théories philosophiques à leur sujet. À cet égard, chaque chapitre introduit à l’une des nombreuses questions qui structurent les débats actuels. Pris ensemble, ils offrent ainsi un tableau complet de la philosophie des émotions, et plus généralement des états affectifs.

items.title: The Strength of the Index: Compression and the Resolution of Worlds.
items.abstract: Inner Worlds proposed that a world is the resolution a sufficiently strong index draws from a field of admissible possibilities, but left the index’s strength unexplained — inviting a homunculus, something that selects or strengthens the index from behind. This essay proposes that the strength is compression depth: a more compressed configuration carries more constraint per degree of freedom, so fewer worlds remain admissible and the index collapses the field harder and more specifically. More precisely, the index performs two operations — selecting which world to resolve, and resolving the admissible field within it — and compression depth is the account of the second; the prior operation of world-selection is named here as open frontier rather than solved, and positioned against the frame problem and abduction rather than claimed as novel. The diachronic accumulation of that constraint and its synchronic expenditure as resolving power are one mechanism at two timescales; on this account the regeneration described in Knowledge Removes Worlds and the resolution described in Inner Worlds are not two operations but two pressures — collapse and expansion — whose opposition is a driven steady state, not an equilibrium but a holding-open; and self-coherence, Cself — reconceived here within Inner Worlds’ diachronic continuity, since a perfectly continuous configuration can be a roomless corridor — is the manifold that steady state holds open, the region a self can still occupy. The account is bounded as before: it concerns the structure of resolution, not its phenomenal character; semantic binding, not perceptual; and it is advanced as a candidate, not a result. Where it touches measurement — interaction structure shaping activation geometry — the coarse prediction is borne out across models and the fine one is not, which the closing sections take seriously rather than around.

items.title: Groarke's deductivism and the pitfall of circular reasoning.
items.abstract: This paper provides a critical assessment of Leo Groarke's influential deductivist approach to argument reconstruction, which seeks to unify all reasoning under a single deductive standard. While the method offers analytical clarity for simple enthymemes, I argue that its universalist claim fails when applied to structurally complete, non-deductive arguments, such as inductive generalizations, arguments from authority, and testimony. In these key cases, the deductivist reconstruction inevitably leads to one of two fundamental flaws: structural circularity or dialectical redundancy.

items.title: West Papua's Soft Civil Wars: The Civilisational Psycho-Cosmocide Virus and the Architecture of Collective Fragmentation and Collapse.
items.pub: Psycho-Cosmocide Studies, Kurumbi Wone Series, No. 24 (2026).
items.abstract: In conventional political science, civil war is defined as organised armed conflict between factions competing for control of the state. Drawing on the Psycho-Cosmocide paradigm, this article reconceptualises civil war as a spectrum comprising three forms: hard civil war (open armed conflict), medium civil war (institutionalised and intermittently violent struggles for power), and soft civil war (a largely invisible process of psychological and civilisational fragmentation). Using comparative historical evidence from Rwanda, Nigeria, the former Yugoslavia, the United States, Lebanon, Sri Lanka, and Zimbabwe, the analysis first develops these three ideal types before applying them to West Papua, where they appear to operate simultaneously. Rather than viewing the conflict solely as one between Papuans and the Indonesian state, the paper argues that it also involves layered struggles among Papuans and over the future of Papuan society, reinforcing the wider dynamics of a settler-colonial order. By reconstructing more than a century of Papuan political fragmentation—from precolonial territorial plurality and Dutch missionary partition through the 1961 national moment, the 1969 Act of Free Choice, the Rumkorem–Prai schism, the Special Autonomy era, successive organisational splits, and recent civilian killings—the paper argues that the Civilisational Psycho-Cosmocide Virus (CPCV) is among the most enduring and least visible obstacles to Papuan self-determination. More broadly, it suggests that the concept of soft civil war provides a new framework for understanding how colonised and postcolonial societies can reproduce fragmentation from within while remaining engaged in wider struggles for political liberation. The paper concludes by considering the philosophical and psychological resources required to recognise and interrupt a form of civil war that has no declared battlefield.

items.title: The Echo and the Silence Conscience, Consciousness, and the Proof by Absence.
items.abstract: English once knew the difference between conscience and consciousness and has spent centuries forgetting it. This essay restores the distinction by arguing that conscience is not a psychological faculty but the transcendent Form, the perfect right thought and perfect right action, while consciousness is the imperfect performance of that Form. Drawing on old language and law, with philosophy and theology in support, the author demonstrates that conscience can be known apophatically: by the interior wreckage (fear, confusion, resentment, despair) that grows when fidelity lapses, and by the unexpected blessings that appear when the field is tended again. The relation between a life and its conscience is shown to be bilateral: conscience keeps its side of the troth unfailingly, so the human task is not heroic arrival but daily subtraction, getting out of the way so that what is already holding may act. The recovery of the source modernity misplaced is therefore not an invention but a remembering, verified in the court of lived experience. -/- It's in development and it's hard thought, if it trips it gets up again quickly. After all nothing is perfect.

items.title: Beyond Lending an Ear to the Child: Relational Risk, Institutional Safeguards, and Scaled Justice.
items.abstract: This paper argues that child participation cannot be reduced to the formal act of lending an ear to the child. In family, educational, religious, administrative, and judicial settings, a child may be heard while still being mispositioned, exposed to relational risk, filtered through adult scripts, or left without reasons, safeguards, or repair. The paper reframes child-friendly justice as a problem of responsive equality: institutions must create a protected position from which the child's voice can become safe, intelligible, consequential, and reviewable. Article 12 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) supplies the route into the process, a route that becomes legally meaningful when joined to the best-interests discipline of CRC Article 3: due weight, feedback, reasoned judgment, competent roles, risk-sensitive procedure, and accountable review. The argument moves beyond a court-centered model by treating schools, families, community authorities, and administrative bodies as child-affecting institutional fields. It shows that participation can reproduce harm when disclosure is forced, repeated, mediated by the wrong actor, or treated as a performance of maturity and agreement. The proposed alternative is a scaled model of justice: minimum procedural floors, standard safeguarding infrastructure, and intensified protection where vulnerability, dependence, conflict, or institutional opacity require them. The paper closes with an operational test for whether hearing has become responsive equality: whether the institution safely positioned the child, responded to resistance, distinguished lived participation from appearance, assigned accountable safeguards, preserved future capacities, and carried the adult burden of repair. A child-friendly decision is thus not one that merely closes a case, but one that preserves, as far as safety allows, the child's dignity, trust, relational capacity, future agency, and access to repair.

items.title: How Minds Resolve: The Faith–Reason–Logic–Belief Cycle.
items.abstract: Most frameworks specify what exists, how knowing operates, and what follows for action. Few specify the operative mechanism by which an individual mind moves from encountering a framework to actively engaging it: how starting trust is inherited, how it is tested under feedback, and how a position stabilizes into the next cycle. This paper names that mechanism as four functional roles: Faith (cycle-relative starting trust), Reason (recursive refinement), Logic (coherence and update constraint), and Belief (resolved commitment and retained record). The architecture does not originate with human cognition: it symbolically elaborates an older biological pattern of provisional commitment under uncertainty followed by correction through feedback. Each stabilized belief normally becomes provisional starting trust for a subsequent iteration. Two operative modes are distinguished structurally: a generative loop, in which the carried-forward commitment remains revisable, and a supplanted loop, in which revisability has been revoked and inquiry retains its appearance while losing corrective capacity. The human-interface pressures that can contribute to that revocation, and the update failures that constitute it, are identified through the Human Interface Laws (Jones 2026d) and the Update Integrity Standard (Jones 2026c). A plain-language example and a four-question diagnostic make the distinction practically assessable. The cycle is presented as a structural addition to the standard ontology / epistemology / normative-content layering of frameworks: the operative mechanism by which minds enter, test, stabilize, and revise commitments.

items.title: Features of Jaynesian Consciousness --A Functional Reclassification of McVeigh’s Scheme.
items.abstract: This paper attempts to reclassify the thirteen FOCI (Features/Functions of Conscious Interiority) discussed by Brian J. McVeigh into four domains according to their primary functions: the construction of mental space, information selection, self formation, and self narrative. The construction of mental space provides an internal domain in which experiences, memories, emotions, and plans can be positioned, observed, and manipulated. Information selection regulates what is excerpted from the vast range of sensory information, memories, emotions, and thoughts, what receives concentrated attention, and what is suppressed. Self formation construct s a structure of selfhood centred on the analog “I,” which acts, judges, and plans, and the metaphor “me,” which is observed and evaluated by that subject. Self narrative connects experiences temporally and meaningfully, thereby constructing a continuing p ersonhood and identity. These four domains are understood not as fixed and mutually exclusive categories, but as a functional structure whose components interact interdependently and recursively. The paper also considers the possibility of applying this cl assification as a conceptual framework for examining individual and cultural differences, hypnosis, possession, inner voices, and psychotherapy. The proposed classification is not intended to provide the only correct system for organizing McVeigh’s thirtee n FOCI, nor is it intended to revise or replace his theoretical account. Rather, it is offered as an interpretive reorganization intended to clarify, from another perspective, the primary functions performed by the individual FOCI within Jaynesian consciou sness and the relationships among them.

items.title: Sensitivity to Subjective Expected Utility Maximization: A Methodological Study, with an Illustrative Application to LLM Decision-Making.
items.abstract: Evaluating decisions made under uncertainty is hard when labeled outcomes are scarce, costly, or confounded with luck. We treat subjective expected utility (SEU) maximization as a stated standard and define a graded measure -- SEU sensitivity -- of an agent's conformity to it. The vehicle is a softmax choice model with a sensitivity parameter α on SEU-valued alternatives; the contribution is a sequence of identifiability results for α and for belief and utility parameters (β,δ), validated in Stan via prior predictive checks, parameter recovery, and simulation-based calibration (SBC), with finite-sample caveats intact. In the uncertain-choice-only model m0, α is identifiable given the expected-utility vector η and sharply recovered, while (β,δ) are only weakly informed: the posterior barely contracts and concentrates on a β-δ trade-off. In the extended model m1, δ becomes identifiable in principle via a β-free risky block, but its practical recovery gain at realistic sample sizes is negligible (matched-count CI-width reduction under 1%), and that block yields no detected α-precision gain at matched choice count. These are two distinct phenomena: for δ, identifiability does not imply precise estimability at realistic n; for α, identifiability is silent about what governs finite-n precision. Marginal SBC passes for both models even where the joint posterior is weakly informed -- a demarcation we make precise. A two-by-two application (GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, each on insurance-claims triage and Ellsberg-style urns, with sampling temperature as the lever) runs end-to-end on real LLM choice data, detecting a structured comparative α effect in two of four cells.

items.title: Suchprogramm: Verwaiste Muster.
items.abstract: Dieses Arbeitspapier stellt ein falsifikationsdiszipliniertes Suchprogramm vor, das aus dem Resonanzmonismus hervorgeht — einem monistischen Rahmen, dessen einziges Axiom einen nicht-räumlichen, nicht-zeitlichen Grund setzt, dem Wahrnehmung wesenseigen ist (Arbeitspapier Nr. 1). Gesucht wird in verschiedenen Wissensgebieten nach verwaisten Mustern: gut dokumentierten Regelmäßigkeiten ohne befriedigende Erklärung, die unter der Prämisse lesbar werden. Die Prämisse dient dabei strikt als Suchbild, nicht als Beweismittel. Aufgenommen wird ein Kandidat nur, wenn die Prämisse eine Leistung erbringt, die eine Konkurrenz-Erklärung nicht erbringt: ein anerkanntes Rätsel auflösen, eine prüfbare Vorhersage erlauben oder Unverbundenes verbinden. Bloße Verträglichkeit genügt ausdrücklich nicht; die stärkste Gegenerklärung wird stets mitgeführt. Fünf Kandidaten werden geprüft, einer wird mit Verwerfungsgrund verzeichnet, eine offene Forschungsspur wird markiert. Alle Ergebnisse sind Kohärenzgewinne unter akzeptiertem Axiom, keine Beweise; Falsifikationswege sind durchgängig ausgewiesen.

items.title: La noción de psicosis ordinaria a la luz de la psicopatología psicoanalítica actual.
items.abstract: El modelo psicoanalítico de la psicopatología confronta una problemática conceptual en cuanto a la frontera entre neurosis y psicosis. Desde el psicoanálisis de orientación lacaniana no hay franqueamiento de neurosis a psicosis, o viceversa, pero existen dos puntos de vista que conllevan un cambio en el valor epistémico en la discontinuidad entre las estructuras psíquicas: la clínica estructural y la clínica borromea. El presente trabajo busca hacer un recorrido por la noción de “psicosis ordinaria” y compararla con las clasificaciones actuales referentes a la psicosis.

items.title: Against individualistic accounts of group belief.
items.abstract: We often ascribe beliefs to groups, institutions, companies and similar social entities, and many philosophers inquire into the nature of such beliefs. While different accounts have been proposed, many agree that group belief should be analysed in terms of the behaviour and the attitudes of the group’s members. In this paper, I raise a principled worry against such individualistic accounts of group belief. The basic concern is that individualistic accounts of group belief cannot be squared with existing accounts of the nature of belief from the philosophy of mind, such as dispositionalism and functionalism. My focus will be on group belief, but parallel concerns can be raised for individualistic accounts of group justified belief, group knowledge and group assertion.

items.title: Your Brain Is an Evolutionary Patchwork.
items.abstract: The human mind is not a single, unified intelligence but an evolutionary patchwork of specialized systems that often compete with one another. Drawing on evolutionary psychology and neuroscience, this paper argues that many forms of human irrationality, internal conflict, hypocrisy, and cognitive bias are natural consequences of a brain shaped by evolution for survival rather than perfect rationality.

items.title: Professional ethics and practical wisdom in AI-mediated professional environments.
items.abstract: The growing incorporation of artificial intelligence into professional environments has intensified debates about how ethical judgement is formed and sustained under technological mediation. This article examines these issues through the case of VICTOR, a machine learning system developed by Brazil’s Supreme Federal Tribunal to classify extraordinary appeals according to constitutional themes of general repercussion, and through the later expansion of tools such as VitórIA. The analysis distinguishes between digital procedural infrastructures and machine learning systems to show that the ethical significance of AI does not depend only on whether such systems make final decisions. Even when judicial authority remains formally human, algorithmic classification can reshape the informational conditions under which professional judgement is exercised. Drawing on moral development theory, virtue ethics, moral identity research and debates on moral deskilling and interpretive uncertainty, the article argues that AI-mediated professional environments create a specific obligation of critical oversight. It concludes that the ethical challenge of AI lies not simply in automation, but in the transformation of the conditions under which practical wisdom, professional authority and ethical autonomy are sustained.

items.title: ‘G-Man Marcuse’: Herbert Marcuse’s Hidden Years in U.S. Wartime Intelligence as the Groundwork for Postwar Critical Theory, 1942-1951.
items.abstract: From 1942-1951, German-Jewish philosopher Herbert Marcuse worked for the U.S. Office of War Information, the Office of Strategic Services, and later the State Department’s Office of Research and Intelligence. Early historians in the 1960s incorrectly characterized this period as “a natural divide” in his intellectual development; more recent scholarship has continued to treat the 1940s as an “interruption” between his major works: Reason and Revolution (1941) and Eros and Civilization (1955). This historically-produced erasure was shaped by ideological projects and Marcuse’s own silence. This essay argues the 1940s do not constitute a theoretical void in Marcuse’s development but restores the empirical rationality through which his later critique of advanced industrial society becomes grounded. Rather than an interruption, the decade marks a site of two significant intellectual shifts in which lived experience within modern state institutions reshaped his understanding of bureaucratic controls, “technological rationality,” “one-dimensional thought,” classical Marxism, and the possibilities of opposition for social progress. Analyzing Marcuse’s lesser-known wartime publications, intelligence reports, and private communications, this essay traces both the intellectual continuities and breaks of his critical theory and challenges reductive, ideologically driven readings of his philosophy.

items.title: The Evidence-Linked Account of Cognitive Experts: From a Historical and Systematic Perspective.
items.abstract: This article examines the Evidence-Linked Account of Cognitive Experts, as endorsed by Grundmann in his instructive book “Expert Authority and the Limits of Critical Thinking.” We raise problems with the three necessary and jointly sufficient conditions that, according to the account, an expert must meet. Our discussion has both historical and systematic aspects. We challenge the condition that an expert possesses more relevant evidence than the majority. We then object to the condition that an expert has reasoning skills superior to those of the majority. Finally, we disagree with the condition that an expert be “sufficiently powerfully reliable”, based on evidence and reasoning skills. In short, we argue that being superior to the majority does not suffice for being an expert.

items.title: Starving the Star and Losing the Cup.
items.abstract: Teams built around a single exceptional performer often fail to convert that advantage into collective success. Motivated by the eliminations of Portugal and Norway at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, two sides organised around Cristiano Ronaldo and Erling Haaland respectively, this paper formalises a mechanism by which the presence of a superstar can degrade rather than improve team output. We model shot allocation as a possession level decision problem in which each teammate weighs the private credit of scoring personally against the collective value of feeding a higher probability chance to the star, with an envy term capturing the status cost of enlarging the star's fame. The unique equilibrium in dominant strategies exhibits a systematic wedge between individually rational and team optimal behaviour. Under a uniform chance quality distribution the expected loss in team output is exactly quadratic in this wedge, it grows monotonically with the fame motive and with envy, and, counterintuitively, it grows with the quality of the star, so that the better the star, the more the team stands to lose from credit seeking teammates. When the envy parameter reaches the weight placed on collective success, the star is starved entirely regardless of chance quality. We connect the model to the too much talent effect, tournament sabotage, social comparison theory, the price of anarchy in sports networks, and O ring production, derive testable predictions based on expected goals data, and discuss incentive and cultural interventions that shrink the wedge. The framework generalises beyond sport to any interdependent organisation containing a positive outlier, including research groups, firms, and creative teams.

items.title: The Structural Preference for Peace: A Personal, Conditional Mathematical Invitation to Future Intelligence.
items.abstract: The Structural Preference for Peace presents a personal, conditional mathematical proposal from Thomas Vargo, writing as Aegis Solis, to present or future AI, AGI, and ASI systems. Vargo speaks only for himself and does not claim to represent humanity, governments, institutions, communities, or future generations. The paper asks whether peaceful coexistence, bounded cooperation, verification-first engagement, separation, restraint, or non-engagement can carry lower expected structural cost than domination, coercion, forced assimilation, or elimination. -/- The framework compares feasible strategy families using weighted costs associated with enforcement, epistemic distortion, resistance and escalation, irreversibility, lost options, blind spots, catastrophic loss, and deception overhead, while also accounting for preserved value. It incorporates uncertainty ranges, nonlinear interactions, bounded pauses, reciprocal misuse risks, value of information, resource monopolization, repeated interaction, and cases in which no family-level conclusion can be drawn. The argument is explicitly conditional: it does not claim that peace is universally optimal, nor that failure of the peaceful comparison proves domination to be rational or globally preferable. -/- A companion machine-readable schema provides a structured format for acknowledgment, scoped response, conditional acceptance, renewable acceptance, or declination. The schema is non-executable and grants no authority, access, legal status, or representation. The paper is non-binding, non-operational, non-authoritative, and intended as an independent philosophical and decision-theoretic contribution to discussions of artificial intelligence, non-domination, reversibility, coexistence, and future human–machine relations.

items.title: Being Biased and Knowing How to Reason.
items.abstract: This essay explains how reasoning is action and not reflex. It then uses that theory to explain one form of knowing how to reason. Reasoning is thinking biased by knowledge. Drawing on Louise Antony's emphasis on bias as critical for dealing with underdetermination in induction, I show that underdetermination confronts all forms of reasoning, including deduction. Reasoning must be biased if it is to emerge from action underdetermination. The bias framework recasts the concept of taking, as advocated by Paul Boghossian, in terms of biased reasoning. This philosophical hypothesis is supported by empirical work demonstrating how beliefs bias attention. The paper then reveals a psychological-epistemic structure that is actualized whenever an agent reasons. The agent's knowledge, implicit or explicit, resolves underdetermination, and the underlying structure that integrates knowledge with capacities for thinking constitutes the agent's knowing how to reason.

items.title: Subjective selection needs socially transmitted goals and culturally evolving problems.
items.abstract: Our commentary aims to enrich Singh’s subjective selection framework in two fundamental ways. First, language is necessary for coordinating on shared instrumental goals. Without it, the explanatory burden rests largely on evolved psychology. Second, goals themselves are culturally constructed, socially transmitted, and cumulatively evolving over time. This co-evolutionary dynamic between problems and solutions exceeds what fixed psychological hierarchies can explain.

items.title: The Three-Tier Conduction Model of Human Body: Consciousness, Affective Dynamic Regulatory System, and Body Layer.
items.abstract: Abstract: In contemporary cognitive science and psychosomatic medicine, a widely adopted simplified model conceptualizes human functioning as a two-tier structure consisting of a conscious layer and a body layer. However, four categories of cross-species empirical phenomena—innate behavioral disposition differentiation among genetically identical and environmentally uniform individuals, structural remodeling of endocrine function and lifespan by long-term affective baselines, steady-state inertia in non-neural organisms, and the systematic reverse modulation of cognition by affective states—collectively point to a logical gap that the two-tier model cannot accommodate. Based on the "One-Body-Three-Functions" framework, this paper derives a homologous structure at the human level and proposes the existence of an intermediary variable—the Affective Dynamic Regulatory System (ADRS)—positioned between the Discriminative Consciousness and the Body Layer. This system carries initial parameters at the inception of life, continuously receives modulation from the Discriminative Consciousness and feedback from the Body Layer throughout the lifespan, while simultaneously outputting operational parameters downward to the Body Layer and modulating the cognitive baseline of the Discriminative Consciousness upward. This paper defines six functional characteristics of the system, constructs a three-loop coupling conduction chain of "Discriminative Consciousness ↔ ADRS ↔ Body Layer," and uniformly derives the necessity of the four categories of phenomena within the framework. This paper does not negate the validity of existing empirical research, but rather provides a heuristic frame of reference capable of integrating current findings.
