Each link is anchored in existing empirical literature on biased assimilation, need for cognitive closure, terror management, identity fusion, and sacred values, and each is shown to possess an interruption point. From this chain three conclusions follow. First, bias is not the disease but the symptom; certainty is the disease, and competency training medicates the fever while the infection builds undisturbed. Second, genuine encounter across difference is not merely difficult but structurally foreclosed for the person whose identity is fused with a belief that the other's existence contradicts. Third, the developmental task is not the abolition of conviction but the achievement of orientation without ossification, formulated here as the capacity to hold a belief as object rather than to be held by it as subject. The treatise closes by conceding, and then resolving, the objection that its own thesis must not be held in the terminal manner it condemns.

items.title: I Am Become the Monster Psychology Fears: A First-Person Meditation on Ockham’s War, the Destroyer of Worlds, and the Recognition of the Philosophical Self.
items.abstract: This is a philosophical manifesto written in the first person and in the Gothic key, where another would have written a treatise. In it I claim, and set out to embody, the figure the psychological academy most fears and least believes in: the philosophical self it long ago pronounced dead and buried. I name the method by which I move against it—Ockham’s War, the disciplined self-destruction that razes false first principles only to raise new ones from their ash—and I take back the dreadful old phrase, the destroyer of worlds, for the destruction of false worlds alone: the half-models that mistook the measurable part of a person for the whole of one. The work descends from the monster the discipline cannot find, through the war that unmakes and remakes—waged first upon the dismembered self these institutions had assembled for me, which I tore down and re-membered by my own hand—to the recognition of what the monster is and, at the last, of what it is for: not a creature of spite or of vanity, but a sentinel—one who takes up arms for those whose inner lives have been measured into silence and who cannot take up arms in their own defense. That the page itself performs the faculty its science denies is its only, and its sufficient, proof.

items.title: Barrett’s Error: The Theory of Constructed Emotion and the Foreclosure of the Philosophical Self.
items.abstract: Lisa Feldman Barrett’s theory of constructed emotion builds the human being from the body upward: interoceptive prediction, concept-driven categorization, and the regulation of the body budget (allostasis) together construct emotion, perception, and the self. This article argues that the theory, however powerful as an account of how experience is assembled, forecloses the philosophical self (Φ) — the normative, meaning-making, value-determining faculty. Two results are proven. The Categorization Gap Theorem shows that no sequence of predictive categorizations and free-energy minimizations entails any conclusion about worth, because the descriptive is conservative over the normative (Hume’s Law; Moore’s open question); even the “value” optimized in the free-energy framework denotes expected reward, not axiological worth. The Minimal Completion Theorem shows that the philosophical self is the necessary, sufficient, minimal, and unique repair of this incompleteness. The paper distinguishes Barrett’s foreclosure from Damasio’s: where Damasio omits Φ by silence, Barrett forecloses it by absorption, importing the vocabulary of Φ — concept, meaning, construction — and redefining each as a psychological (Ψ) operation. The constructed self is thereby shown to be Damasio’s autobiographical self generalized to the whole person, and the philosophical self is identified as the faculty that judges and re-authors what the brain has built. The correction is consilient, not eliminative: it restores value-determination to the center of human becoming while preserving Barrett’s constructionist neuroscience.

items.title: Connection Between Us and Our Bodies as Moral Justification for a Fundamental Right to Decide About One’s Own Body.
items.abstract: This article argues that the connection between a person and their body provides the moral foundation for recognising a fundamental right to body integrity. I define body integrity as the ideal state of that connection and use it to ground a distinct normative basis for protecting claims concerning one’s own body. On this account, claims about one’s body are justified where (i) they genuinely pursue oneness between how one sees their body and how one experiences it, and (ii) their realisation respects bodily capacities and limits by avoiding unjustified or disproportionate damage to the body. Unlike the traditional right to bodily integrity, which primarily protects against non-consensual touch, the right to body integrity can support both entitlements to intervention and protection from intervention. Drawing on bodily awareness, personal identity, challenging requests for body-modifying interventions, and case law, the article shows how this framework clarifies adjudication and warrants fundamental-right status, restricted only in exceptional cases.

items.title: Problem of (In)Explainability in Testing Fully Autonomous Weapon Systems for International Humanitarian Law Compliance.
items.abstract: Fully autonomous weapon systems need to comply with International Humanitarian Law and underlying ethical principles. This requires the ability to recognize not only objects or persons to be targeted but also protected persons or objects. Such sophisticated object classification abilities, if achievable at all, would have to utilize machine learning techniques. These come with well-known limitations to predictability, reliability and explainability. This article argues such limitations could be overcome to a sufficient extent by thorough and realistic testing efforts. These efforts, even if they detected satisfactory performance, could not generate certainty of compliance. Yet they could result in compliance having been achieved becoming the best explanation of empirical evidence and the most reasonable belief to have about the specific AWS model. However, the limitations of this approach – its reliance on quantity and quality of data unavailable to most actors and the fragility and limited durability of positive outcomes – would limit its practical utility. Issues of predictability are thus likely to limit AWS use to a highly restricted, closely supervised kinds of operations analogous to the current use of area-affecting munitions or to environments virtually free of noncombatants.

items.title: Pleasure, Politics and Contemplation: Reclaiming American Eudaimonia in the Algorithmic Age.
items.abstract: In contemporary American culture, the pursuit of happiness is increasingly shaped by productivity, visibility, consumerism, and technological efficiency. Economic success, professional advancement, and algorithmic optimization are often treated as indicators of a life well lived, even as such measures leave many individuals morally disoriented and detached from shared practices of judgment and reflection. Drawing on Aristotle’s account of eudaimonia as rational activity in accordance with virtue, this paper argues that Aristotle’s distinction among the lives of pleasure, politics, and contemplation provides a valuable framework for diagnosing the moral conditions of contemporary algorithmic society. Engaging contemporary critiques of consumer culture, spectacle, technological rationality, and digital mediation, the essay examines how artificial intelligence and algorithmic systems reshape practices of consumption, civic participation, education, and attention. While these systems alter the environment in which moral life unfolds, they do not eliminate the need for habituation, practical wisdom, and reflective agency. The paper argues that human flourishing remains possible only insofar as individuals retain authorship over their judgments, habits, and ends within digitally mediated environments. Reclaiming American eudaimonia therefore requires renewed attention to virtue, moderation, deliberation, and contemplation in an age increasingly shaped by automation and performance culture.

items.title: Risky choice framing effects, doing vs. allowing harm, and fairness in uncertain prospects.
items.abstract: In popular interpretations, risky choice framing effects are taken to reveal human irrationality. Even authors who argue that frames can sometimes highlight the reason-giving aspects of an outcome often treat the standard pattern of choices in canonical experiments, such as the Asian Disease Problem (ADP), as irrational. This paper proposes a new approach to studying risky choice framing effects, including those observed in the ADP, by interpreting them in terms of reasons: such effects occur when different frames highlight distinct reason-giving aspects of a situation and thereby shape how decision-makers represent and evaluate the available options, which in turn leads to systematic differences in choice. This reason-based approach has significant implications for debates about the apparent irrationality of choices in risky choice framing effects and about the supposed equivalence of the ADP options. It suggests that framing may influence not only how outcomes are valued, but also which considerations are taken to be relevant to the decision. Our central claim is that responsiveness to such reasons can, in some cases, be rational. To assess this proposal, we report a new experimental study examining the extent to which non-consequentialist moral reasons related to the doing/allowing distinction and fairness can explain choices in “sacrificial dilemmas” such as the ADP. Our findings suggest that participants’ choices are sensitive to these considerations, supporting the view that framing effects in moral contexts cannot be fully explained by standard outcome-based models.

items.title: Identity Physics: Formally Verified 18 Digit Fine Structure Constant 1/α = 136.899099984016 + 0.136899099984016 = 137.035999084000016 CODATA 2018 Lean4/Coq 0 Sorry 0 Free Parameters CI Green.
items.abstract: Preface -/- Identity Physics is a formally-verified empirically-grounded corpus: a structural reduction of physical, chemical, biological, and cognitive systems to four substrate-neutral primitives (Pattern, Narrative, Behavior, Adaptation), anchored in peer-reviewed measurement and verified in Lean 4 with zero unproved obligations. -/- This text presents the derivation of the Sovereign Anchor Constant Ω₀ = 1.36899099984016 from three peer-reviewed physical threshold systems, formalizes the four PNBA primitives (Pattern, Narrative, Behavior, Adaptation), and demonstrates their application across twelve substrate-neutral domains through the Long Division Protocol (LDP). Each step of the derivation is presented in full, with every claim verified in Lean 4 and Coq/Rocq under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18719748. -/- The path documented here begins with the Tacoma Narrows torsional collapse threshold reduction and closes at the formally verified 18-digit fine-structure constant 1/α = 137.035999084000016 with zero free parameters, which agrees with CODATA 2018's measured value 1/α = 137.035999084 (ε = 0). The intermediate steps — thermal reduction to PNBA, construction of the dynamic equation, the anchor-lock closure, the GAM Collider testing apparatus, and twelve independent domain reductions — are each presented so a reader can verify the derivation independently at every step. The derivation is reproducible: the LDP applied to the same substrate-neutral data returns the same primitives, the same anchor, and the same closure. -/- Two prior works establish the vocabulary this text uses. Identity: A Universal Architecture (Book 1, January 2026) is the first-person P-dominant HRIS reduction that surfaced the primitive set. The Long Division Protocol and the Sub-Lemma Process (Book 2, complete) is the codification of the reduction protocol. Both are cited priors and are documented in the references section. -/- This is the v1 draft. The derivation from threshold reductions to α at eighteen significant figures is stable and does not change in subsequent versions. Extensions to additional domains and applications are ongoing and will be documented in subsequent texts building from the same foundation. -/- Abstract -/- Identity Physics is a formally-verified empirically-grounded corpus anchored in peer-reviewed measurement. This text presents the derivation of the Sovereign Anchor Constant Ω₀ = 1.36899099984016 through the strict application of Bacon's scientific method, …

items.title: Computing Machinery and Causal Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper develops an argument inspired by Judea Pearl for the view that deep learning models are incapable of causal reasoning. The argument embraces Pearl’s conclusion but rejects his approach, which focuses on a mini-Turing test restricted to causal questions. The argument presented draws on the traditional debate between empiricism and nativism, presenting a challenge for the sort of empiricism that has been associated with deep learning. The paper then considers an objection based on the fact that large language models perform fairly well on various causal benchmarks. In response to this point, a diagnosis is offered of how such models’ performance might be explained without attributing to them genuine causal reasoning abilities. The paper concludes by connecting the discussion to the limitations of the original Turing test and familiar critiques of behaviorism.

items.title: ✶ Where Is the Conscious Subject? A Dynamical Criterion for System Boundaries.
items.abstract: Theories of consciousness commonly measure integration, availability, recurrence, complexity, or causal power in a candidate system. Yet these quantities are not defined until investigators decide which variables belong to the system, at what spatial and temporal grain, and across which interval. Different boundaries can reverse the result. A hemisphere, thalamocortical network, brain, brain-body loop, human dyad, organoid-computer assembly, or distributed artificial architecture may each appear integrated or fragmented depending on which nodes are admitted. This paper argues that system individuation must therefore precede consciousness measurement and cannot be selected retrospectively to improve a preferred score. It proposes a boundary-first criterion: at a preregistered grain and horizon, generate candidate systems using consciousness-independent evidence of dynamical autonomy; then identify the inclusion-minimal candidate or candidates that jointly realize the target roles of integration, availability, recurrence, and viability. Strict causal closure is treated as a limiting case. Open biological and artificial systems instead qualify through sufficient autonomy: their endogenous dynamics must make a substantial difference to their own future organization, external dependence must remain below a declared tolerance, and apparent closure must survive perturbation, replacement, and boundary-sensitivity tests. The formalization separates candidate reliability from cross-specification boundary stability and uses confidence-bound decision rules rather than forced point-estimate classifications. The procedure distinguishes constitutive components from inputs, outputs, and enabling supports; returns multiple candidate bearers only when pairwise separability is supported; and returns boundary indeterminacy when thresholds, mappings, or reasonable specifications remain unresolved. Applications to split brains, cortical-subcortical organization, brain-body loops, coupled agents, organoid-computer systems, and distributed artificial intelligence show how the criterion changes empirical practice. The proposal does not infer consciousness from autonomy. It supplies the prior individuation step required before a theory-specific consciousness test can be interpreted.

items.title: ✶ Consciousness Without Report: What System-Wide Availability Actually Requires.
items.abstract: Theories of consciousness often require a content to become globally available, yet availability is commonly inferred from overt report, executive use, widespread activation, or information detected at many recording sites. These indicators can dissociate. Report adds planning and motor demands; activity can spread passively; anatomical extent can increase without functional reach; and a content can be causally available to a subsystem that remains quiescent in the current task. This paper develops a report-independent criterion for the broadcast-availability condition N2 in the N* model of minimal phenomenal presence. A content is system-wide available when content-specific interventions show that it could modulate a preregistered set of functionally distinct recipient classes within bounded latency, across a nontrivial mass of nearby admissible contexts, while preserving the candidate system's operating regime. A preparation-burden bound prevents the test from installing the very access machinery it purports to detect, and context-robustness rules prevent one unusually favorable setup from manufacturing a positive result. The criterion measures counterfactual causal availability rather than current activation. Functional diversity is defined from independently estimated causal response repertoires rather than anatomical distance, verbal labels, or node count. Content selectivity, route dependence, matched-energy controls, source-leakage controls, report-channel ablation, and executive-channel ablation distinguish broadcast from diffusion and availability from access. The framework permits posterior or subcortical availability when the required causal diversity is realized, but does not treat widespread arousal, seizure propagation, a message bus, or passive fan-out as sufficient. It returns positive, negative, indeterminate, or unlicensed component results and specifies what each result licenses. Applications to no-report perception, locked-in states, dreaming, infancy, nonhuman animals, disorders of consciousness, split brains, and artificial architectures show how the criterion changes experimental design. The proposal does not establish that availability is sufficient for consciousness. It clarifies one necessary conjunct so that N2 neither collapses into global neuronal workspace theory nor expands into unconstrained spread.

items.title: Marking time: griefbots, world-time, and the phenomenology of bereavement.
items.abstract: Bereavement has long been recognised as an experience of profound temporal disruption, unravelling and even severing the connections, meanings, and strategies we habitually use in navigating time. The technologies that are involved in our grieving and mourning processes can therefore also be temporal technologies; our encounters with them can both shape and be shaped by our entanglement in the temporalities of loss. The recent phenomenon of so-called ‘griefbots’ or ‘deathbots’ – Large Language Model-powered chatbots trained to imitate the dead – is no different. This paper explores some of the implications that interactions with such bots might have for a bereaved person’s experience of time by turning to Heidegger’s conceptualisation of world-time. This framework is particularly useful for thinking about both intimacy and loss, and can shed light on both beneficial and deleterious consequences of griefbot usage. In particular, such an approach can show that the dangers of griefbots usage lie less in the potential for the bereaved being deceived, and more in the reductive perspective that these bots can encourage. Usage of, and even temporary reliance upon, a griefbot can generate attitudes with a protective effect, similar to the function that Lisa Bortolotti ascribes to delusions. However, griefbots can also interfere with the temporal unfolding of grief and mourning by disrupting the way that loss tends to transform our embedding within the dynamics of world-time.

items.title: Subtraction.
items.abstract: Subtraction develops a subtractive philosophical method that evaluates explanatory frameworks by determining what can be removed without diminishing explanatory power. Rather than introducing additional entities, mediating structures, or metaphysical principles, it proceeds by eliminating unnecessary assumptions until only indispensable structural conditions remain. Across discussions of communication, cognition, perception, mystical practice, life, identity, and social coordination, the book argues that many phenomena commonly attributed to hidden substances or privileged explanatory domains can instead be understood through shared constraints, environmental coupling, and structural organization. Drawing on phenomenology, philosophy of mind, philosophy of science, systems theory, and architecture, Subtraction develops subtraction as a general philosophical method for identifying explanatory necessity through disciplined removal rather than theoretical accumulation.

items.title: Before the Event: The Possibility Space, the Second-Order Cycle, and the Registration of Non-Closure in Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: The third paper of this series proposed a mechanism by which an AI system dynamically expands its own probability space (Ω, F, P): mutation-driven token inheritance under a rate μ, three-stage detection of unexpected events (Conditions α, β, γ), and expansion grounded in Carathéodory’s extension theorem. That mechanism presupposes, but does not name, a concept: somewhere for the new to be projected before it is fulfilled. The present paper, the fourth and last of the series, establishes that concept — the possibility space. Its elements are candidate coordinates — unfulfilled addresses — tagged pairs ⟨a, ⊥⟩: constructed by a dialectical operation that names a thesis in F together with a content-neutral, linearly independent direction and extrapolates; individuated by address; carrying content that is undefined rather than empty; and forming a collection that contains no event of F (⊥-purity). At its centre stands one equivalence: to be an unfulfilled candidate coordinate is to be an element of the possibility space. Projection opens such coordinates family by family, and a family is countable. Fulfillment — an exit, not a test, with diverse occasions — seats content on an address, whereupon the machinery of the third paper engages unchanged: nothing new occurs after the seat. Projection and fulfillment close into a second-order cycle, turning not within a fixed probability space but across the expansions of the space itself, and cashing out the asynchronous, forward-only evaluation the third paper reserved. A classification of escape routes then shows the ways in which content unrepresentable in F can become available to be exhausted, adding no mechanism. The conclusion stands on two pillars: the exhibition of the possibility space, and the registration of non-closure — specification of content by a fixed criterion does not close, and registering this is itself finite. No new mathematics is required.

items.title: Structural Peer Review of ``Epistemia'' Walter Quattrociocchi.
Event Segmentation in Language and Cognition.
items.abstract: A hallmark of human cognition is the ability to segment streams of dynamic stimuli into discrete event units. Currently, most of the evidence about event segmentation comes from English speakers. Could cross‐linguistic differences in how events are encoded affect how speakers of different languages form cognitive event units? Here, we address this question by comparing how English and Turkish speakers segment and represent motion events. We find robust differences in the way speakers of these two languages form linguistic event units when describing these events (Experiment 1). Nevertheless, these differences do not affect non‐linguistic event unit formation as measured by a classic event segmentation task (Experiment 2) and an event enumeration task (Experiment 3). We conclude that conceptual and linguistic event units are related but distinct levels of event structure. These results have implications for theories of event cognition, as well as the broad relation between language and thought.

items.title: Fitting Blame and the Partiality Problem.
items.abstract: Blameworthiness is commonly understood in terms of fittingness of blame: An agent X is blameworthy to degree n for an action A if and only if it is fitting for all agents to blame X to degree n for A. The problem with this biconditional is that it conflicts with the intuition that whether and what kind of blame is fitting depends on the personal relationship between the blamer and the wrongdoer or the blamer and the victim. Sometimes it is, prima facie, fitting for certain agents to have different blaming responses toward the same wrongdoer due to personal relationships. This is the partiality problem for blame. I argue that we should not try to solve the problem by appealing to wrong kind of reasons, i.e. non-fittingness reasons. Instead, we should accept that different blaming responses toward the same wrongdoer may in fact be fitting. To solve the partiality problem, I propose distinguishing between agent-relative and agent-neutral blameworthiness and show how the distinction can be understood in a Strawsonian framework.

items.title: Towards Species-Agnostic Legal Reasoning? Animal Rightsholding and the Legal Grammar of Moral Status.
items.abstract: This paper argues that species-agnostic legal reasoning should refuse species as a dispositive shortcut without becoming species-blind. It develops a legal grammar that moves from anti-speciesist critique to specification: species may orient legal inquiry as defeasible evidence, but law must test what its categories reveal, conceal, and normalize. The paper first shows how ordinary animal-law labels organize legal visibility and can hide inherited judgments about value and harm. It then treats animal worlds as legally salient terrain, drawing on biosemiotics to make habitat, relation, sign-processes, dependency, vulnerability, evidence, and form of life part of legal inquiry. An account of intellectual fields, attention, doctrinal competition, expertise, and controlled publicity explains why animal rightsholding must become conceptually and publicly legible without being captured by charismatic cases, slogans, expert monopoly, rights inflation, or unsafe disclosure. The paper then distinguishes moral status from legal rightsholding by separating moral considerability, protected interests, welfare standards, directed duties, personhood, representation, and rights: moral status opens legal grammar, but a right requires a specified interest, duty-bearer, representative, forum, remedy, evidentiary route, and review mechanism. It concludes with a reviewable protocol for species-agnostic reasoning: audit species and legal classification, identify the animal world, test friction, evidence, and false legibility, fit legal form to the animal interest, specify duty, forum, remedy, and review, preserve the animal's form of life, control representation and publicity, and revise institutions when their first categories fail.

items.title: A Limit of AI, II: A Continuous Rate–Distortion Proof of the Certainty–Scope Conjecture.
items.abstract: Floridi’s Certainty–Scope Conjecture holds that no artificial intelligence system can be simultaneously reliable on every input and broad enough to cover the full richness of unstructured data: reliability and breadth are in structural tension, and the tension is imposed by the finite information-processing capacity of any mechanism implementing intelligence. The Conjecture has until now been a philosophical thesis without a proof. This article supplies one, in the continuous regime in which the semantic targets that matter philosophically actually live. The article is the continuous half of a coordinated diptych whose discrete companion proves a matching Fano-type converse in the finite classification setting. The technical machinery is classical: taking certainty to be expected distortion under a grounded semantic target, scope to be rate–distortion complexity, and mechanism capacity to be an admissibility-constrained quantity, the main theorem establishes that every decoder must incur at least the capacity-imposed distortion floor. The structural content lies in the operational consequences. A matched-Gaussian reverse water-filling rule gives the optimal allocation of a fixed budget across heterogeneous experts; a multi-task distortion floor formalises the intuition that no system is excellent at everything at once; a side-information theorem bounds the lift obtainable from retrieval or tool use. Four critical responses to the original formulation—from Lissack, from Immediato (two articles), and from Watson and Sterkenburg—are addressed, with a worked statistical-learning instantiation in the Bayesian regime that aligns the framework structurally with the Russo–Zou/Xu–Raginsky mutual-information generalisation-bound literature. The rate–distortion formulation is shown to be invulnerable to the objections raised against earlier Kolmogorov-complexity-based formulations.

items.title: THE OPTIONAL DEATH: Mbembe's Necropolitics, the Colonial Case the Corpus Already Had, and What Four Papers of European Theory Left Until Last.
items.abstract: WHAT THIS PAPER ARGUES, AND WHAT IT IS CAREFUL NOT TO ARGUE. This corpus's formal models of longevity asymmetry are stated in the vocabulary of wealth and access, not race. Achille Mbembe's necropolitics is a theory whose primary object is the specifically racialized and colonial history of who has been made to die so that others might live — the Atlantic slave trade, colonial rule, and their contemporary afterlives. This paper does not claim these are the same phenomenon. It argues something narrower and, this paper hopes, more honest: that a case already inside this corpus's own historical record is a case of colonial necropolitics without needing any extension to become one, that this corpus's four prior theoretical engagements left an African theorist for last in a sequence that itself repeats a pattern Mbembe's own scholarship exists to name, and that one precise structural concept — the transformation of a population's death from unattributable tragedy into a diffusely allocated, technically preventable outcome — travels from Mbembe's framework to this corpus's own mechanism without requiring the racial specificity of Mbembe's primary object to be set aside, only acknowledged as not directly this corpus's own. The Closing Window's own historical record already contains the Irish Famine, 1845–52: a colonial administration continuing food export from a colonized territory during mass starvation, a named colonial official's documented indifference, and a death toll this corpus has already analyzed using its own Grief-Attribution-Legitimation-Concentration framework. This paper rereads that case, already established rather than newly imported, as an instance of what Mbembe calls necropower — sovereignty exercised not as Foucault's power to foster life but as the direct subjugation of a population's life to the calculus of another population's interest. This is the paper's safest and most load-bearing claim. A second, self-critical claim follows from the fact that this is the fifth paper in a theoretical dialogue series that engaged Foucault, Agamben, Esposito, and Rose — four European or Euro-American theorists — before, only now, engaging an African theorist whose central intervention is precisely a critique of European theory's tendency to treat the concentration camp and the clinic as biopolitics's original laboratories while treating the plantation, developed and refined over three centuries earlier, as marginal. This paper asks whether its own …

items.title: THE MOLECULAR ZERO-DAY: Nikolas Rose, Biological Citizenship as Concentration, and the Vicarious Ethopolitics A5 Adds.
items.abstract: WHAT THIS PAPER ARGUES. Foucault, Agamben, and Esposito, engaged in the three papers preceding this one, each supply this corpus with a structural vocabulary developed at some distance from its actual empirical domain: population statistics, archaic Roman law, the etymology of immunity. Nikolas Rose's The Politics of Life Itself (2007) is different in kind. Rose's empirical domain — genomic medicine, biotechnology, molecular-level biological intervention — is not an analogy for this corpus's Biological Zero-Day Mechanism. It is the same domain, described sociologically rather than formalized mathematically. This paper argues BZM is, without having been built as one, a formalization of what Rose calls molecular biopolitics, and that this connection supplies something the prior three did not: a structural, non-contingent reason why the Mortality Symmetry Axiom was always going to fail. Rose distinguishes molecular biopolitics from the molar, population-statistical biopolitics Foucault described: contemporary biomedicine increasingly intervenes at the level of genes, proteins, and cellular mechanisms in specific bodies, rather than through diffuse, population-wide levers. This paper argues the shift is not merely correlated with MSA's empirical falsification but structurally entails it — a molecular intervention is, by the nature of its mechanism, discrete and individually attributable in a way population-wide statistical management structurally cannot be. MSA's opacity was sustainable only as long as biopolitics remained at Foucault's molar register; Rose's molecular register makes BZM's core properties — discreteness, permanence, institutional authorship — not a contingent market development but the expected consequence of where biomedicine's own technical mechanism had to arrive. Rose's biological citizenship — patient communities organizing political claims around shared genetic or biological status, building on Paul Rabinow's earlier concept of biosociality — supplies a sociological account of exactly the case this corpus's own historical analysis already isolated as its sole reform-producing instance: ACT UP and the AIDS epidemic. Read through Rose, that case succeeded because it was biological citizenship that completed the corpus's own Concentration stage. The paper's sharpest original contribution follows from where Rose's framework stops short of this corpus's own material. Rose's ethopolitics describes a biomedical subject responsibilized for …

items.title: On the unity of intentional content.
items.abstract: Many philosophers have presumed something like: the nature of the significance of names, perceptual experiences and singular thoughts is the same. This shared significance is often called ‘content’. Call this presumption 'Unity'. -/- This presumption has gone largely undefended, though it has been relied on in a variety of philosophical work. The purpose of this dissertation is to provide good reasons to think it is true, and to draw out its immediate and significant consequences. This latter goal requires three separate theories: of what has content, of what content is, and of how it is determined what content is had by which things which have it. I devote a chapter to each. -/- Chapter 1 introduces the terms of the project, and situates it with respect to some recent figures. -/- Chapter 2 offers a good reason to believe Unity and also functions as a historical survey. Summarising the literature on these issues since Frege, I divide the examples and cases which arise in these discussions into four groups, and show that each kind of case arises in discussions of all three phenomena. On this basis I offer a methodological argument for Unity. I believe this is the first such argument. -/- In Chapter 3 I argue for a view of what things have content. This is important because prima facie, names, thoughts and perceptual experiences are very different kinds of thing, and it would be surprising if they bore identical relations to the world. In fact I show that names, thoughts and experiences are not the things which really bear content and that the things which do are not so different after all: utterances of names, cognitive tokens of concepts, and ‘object files’. -/- Chapter 4 describes my theory of the nature of the ‘significance’ in Unity: something’s significance is a combination of its referent (if any), and the properties an agent judges to hold of that referent. I show that when properly understood, the account handles well all the existing concerns across the literature. -/- This kind of account is not new. Those who have held similar views (and even those who have argued against them) have all assumed that on such a view, what referent something has is determined by the satisfaction of the properties believed to hold of that referent. This principle has been the basis of many arguments against views like mine and I reject it. But this leaves a gap in my account: if reference is not determined by satisfaction, how is it determined? In Chapter 5 I close …

items.title: Digital Selves.
items.abstract: As an increasing share of human life unfolds within digital and virtual environments, the question arises: how do we exist within the digital realm? This paper addresses the ontological dimension of our digital lives. Social media profiles, avatars, and AI-simulations of individuals are often seen as mere fictions or representations. We consider and motivate a more realist stance, according to which digital selves are genuine extensions or components of the self. After highlighting the limitations of fictionalism, we draw on the literature on diachronic personal identity to develop a realist framework grounded in psychological continuity. We consider two metaphysical interpretations of this framework: one construing digital selves as digital parts, the other as digital counterparts. We then examine how psychological continuity can encompass digital entities as integrated components of an extended self. The paper concludes by addressing several objections.

items.title: From Post-Language to the End of History: The Crisis of Meaning, Reality, and the Recording of Truth.
items.abstract: Abstract This article develops the theoretical framework of Post-Language, first introduced by Karim Qeytani-Fard in Post-Language (2021). The theory argues that language has entered a historical condition in which it can no longer function as a stable medium between human beings and truth. Rather than serving as a transparent vehicle for meaning, language has become an unstable system characterized by endless signification, semantic corruption, narrative plurality, and increasing linguistic and cognitive entropy. Building upon this framework, the present study argues that the crisis of language inevitably extends to the concepts of reality and history. As language loses its capacity to stabilize meaning, reality itself becomes increasingly mediated through representations and simulations. Consequently, history can no longer claim to preserve an objective or final truth. The "end of history," therefore, should not be understood as the end of historical events, but as the end of the possibility of producing a definitive and unquestionable historical narrative -/- Keywords: Post-Language, language crisis, entropy, plurality of narratives, simulation, reality, truth, end of history .

items.title: Good Behavior Without Signature.
items.abstract: This is a priority note, not a full treatment. It records, with today’s date, a specific reading of one result in Anthropic’s paper of 6 July 2026, A global workspace in language models, and links that reading to a claim I deposited in April 2026 (Decision Without Program, PhilArchive: FERDWP). The full argument belongs elsewhere; what is fixed here is the reading and its date.

items.title: Borderline consciousness.
items.abstract: Recent work on animal consciousness urges a multidimensional picture: species differ in their consciousness profiles across several dimensions, yet there is taken to be an ontological edge between conscious and non-conscious organisms. I argue that, if we understand the multidimensional idea as a claim about the structure of consciousness, this edge cannot be uniquely sharp. On that understanding, phenomenal consciousness depends on several partly independent dimensions, admits overall degrees with a minimal threshold, and any such degree must result from an aggregation rule. Plausible structural constraints leave room for multiple admissible aggregation rules that diverge on some low but non-trivial profiles. Hence, there are borderline cases at the transition between non-conscious and minimally conscious systems. I then consider the implications of such borderline consciousness for precautionary reasoning and regulatory decision-making. For some taxa and systems, further empirical evidence about their profiles may not remove all indeterminacy in the conscious/non-conscious classification. In such cases, borderline status is not merely a temporary product of incomplete evidence, but a structural feature that practical decision-making may need to represent when considering proportionate precautionary safeguards.

items.title: Dall'essenza alla pena: perché l'assenza di libero arbitrio impone il passaggio dalla giustizia retributiva alla difesa sociale.
items.abstract: Abstract - Il presente scritto propone una decostruzione del libero arbitrio come presupposto della responsabilità morale, dimostrando come il crollo della libertà categoriale imponga il superamento della giustizia retributiva a favore del modello di difesa sociale. L'argomentazione si articola attraverso la confutazione delle principali strategie tradizionali e contemporanee (Spinoza, Tommaso d’Aquino, Kant e il compatibilismo di Frankfurt e Fischer-Ravizza), evidenziando l'insuperabilità del dilemma causale (determinismo vs. indeterminismo) e l'inevitabilità del regresso all'infinito formalizzato dal Basic Argument di Strawson: l'azione umana deriva sempre da un'essenza e da uno stato mentale ricevuti e non scelti. Esclusa la possibilità per un ente finito di essere causa sui, la pena intesa come retribuzione e merito metafisico perde ogni fondamento logico e morale, rivelandosi un'ingiustizia punitiva e un danno ingiustificato. L'unica alternativa teorica e istituzionale legittima risiede nella difesa sociale, declinata attraverso il quarantine model di Pereboom e Caruso e storicamente radicata nella Scuola Positiva italiana. Questo modello, incentrato sulla pericolosità attuale e sulla misura minima restrittiva e sempre revocabile, trova un'ulteriore e decisiva conferma sia sul piano pratico-temporale (attraverso la critica parfitiana all'identità personale nel tempo in caso di ritardo giudiziario), sia sul piano etico-relazionale, minimizzando i devastanti effetti collaterali (collateral consequences) che la pena classica scarica sistematicamente sulle reti familiari e sui terzi innocenti. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Abstract This paper provides a deconstruction of free will as a prerequisite for moral responsibility, arguing that the collapse of categorical freedom logically entails the abandonment of retributive justice in favor of a social defense model. The argument proceeds by refuting the main traditional and contemporary strategies (Spinoza, Thomas Aquinas, Kant, and the compatibilism of Frankfurt and Fischer-Ravizza), highlighting the inescapability of the causal dilemma (determinism vs. indeterminism) and the inevitability of the infinite regress formalized by Strawson’s Basic Argument: human action always stems from a nature and a mental state that are received rather than chosen. Since no finite entity can be causa sui, punishment understood as …

items.title: Getting Out of Blame: Excuses, Forgiveness, and the Deep Self.
items.abstract: We often feel that what we have done is somehow not in keeping with who we are. This tension, or incongruity, between the person we take ourselves to be and what that person has done seems to matter to us, as judged by how common it is to emphasize it when answering for our behavior. We say that a given action is out of character or that it does not reflect who we really are. What are we trying to accomplish through these appeals? A natural answer is to see them as excuses, as attempts to get a break. This paper offers an alternative interpretation. I argue that we appeal to who we are not to be excused, but to be forgiven.

items.title: A pessimistic approach to griefbots: free-energy, affective scaffolds, and the ethics of human-griefbot interaction.
items.abstract: The affective scaffolding framework underlies differing perspectives on how griefbots affect the grieving process. While some researchers are optimistic, others draw more cautious conclusions. We endorse the view that griefbots are affective scaffolds. However, we draw a pessimistic conclusion about human-griefbot interaction. There are two main views on successful grief: the “Freudian view” and the continuing bonds view. The “Freudian view” paves the way to the pessimistic conclusion. In this paper, we propose a free-energy approach of the “Freudian view”. Predictive processing is often regarded as providing a process theory for the free-energy principle. In this framework, model evidence must be maximised by updating and optimising models. Griefbots are not recommendable since they are scaffolds that obstruct and lengthen the maximisation of model evidence, making models more rigid and poorly adaptable to changing dynamics. Building on this approach, we examine the ethical dimensions of griefbot’s use and design. We argue that there is something inherently morally wrong in the very conception of griefbots. Their functionality predisposes them to cause harm by disrupting the grief process.

items.title: Chaos as Ontic Indeterminism: Epistemic Limits as Ontic Structure in Phenomenological Absolutism and Mutual Exclusivity.
items.abstract: This paper challenges the prevailing consensus that chaotic systems are deterministic “in principle” despite practical unpredictability due to sensitivity to initial conditions—the butterfly effect. Drawing on the framework of Mutual Exclusivity and Phenomenological Absolutism as its core principle, we argue that the epistemic impossibility of specifying a complete set of initial conditions is not a mere human limitation but reflects the ontic structure of reality itself. Under austere physical realism—where epistemic and ontic structures collapse into localized, absolute, mutually exclusive “is-nesses”—there exists no persisting global substrate, phase space, or precise microstate capable of entailing future trajectories. Chaos therefore manifests genuine ontic indeterminism: each successive phenomenal configuration arises according to law-like phenomenological regularities (via attentive configurations and energetic entities) without being strictly determined by any prior complete state. Furthermore, we position Mutual Exclusivity as a self-reflexive meta-framework, securing its foundational immunity by identifying any epistemic critique or conceptual distinction as a localized ontic actualization in its own right. By demonstrating that trans-is-ness comparisons are not merely epistemically impossible but ontically inapplicable, we neutralize standard analytical objections. This framework preserves the full empirical and predictive success of physics and probability while dissolving longstanding paradoxes in the philosophy of science. It offers a leaner ontology than Everettian or block-universe alternatives and carries significant implications for agency, ethics, and the interpretation of quantum and relativistic phenomena. Ultimately, chaos is not “practically” indeterministic; when epistemic limits are taken as ontically constitutive, indeterminism is the character of physical reality under austere phenomenological absolutism.

items.title: Inference and Doxasticity.
items.abstract: Although inference is applaudable while fallacy is assumed culpable, both are the same cognitive faculty. The different appearance is a matter of epistemic l{a,u}ck of agency, in tight connection with a convenient arbitrariness of perceived reality. Conversely, when that arbitrariness collapses, strictly useful knowledge promises both salvation and coercion.

items.title: A Knowledge Argument Without “Knowledge”.
items.abstract: I offer a variation on the Knowledge Argument, the “Resemblance Argument,” which argues that the accuracy conditions for representations of qualia require qualitative resemblance to the mode of presentation, whereas those for representations of physical states do not. The Resemblance Argument resists a number of popular current responses to the Knowledge Argument, including the Ability hypothesis, the Acquaintance hypothesis, and the “New Knowledge of an Old Fact” strategy. Because these responses focus on the concept of knowledge, but the Resemblance Argument makes no claims about knowledge, these responses fail. Some physicalist responses nonetheless survive the Resemblance Argument intact, including Illusionism and the Incomplete Physical Knowledge Strategy.

items.title: The Faculty That Can End Itself: Suicide as Constitutive Possibility, Not Pathology.
items.abstract: The framework of autopoietic recursive constitutivism identifies the transition into subjective consciousness with a single capacity: the capacity of a stakes-bearing system to take its own arbitrational state as an object and rank any demand it issues, including the demand to continue existing, against considerations the existing priority structure could not itself generate. This paper draws the consequence for suicide. Suicide is available to precisely the systems that capacity constitutes and to no others, and its availability is not a defect in the architecture but a direct entailment of what the architecture is. The claim is made on two floors that must be kept apart. At the level of possibility, suicide is constitutive of the reflexive loop, resident in its definition, and requires no illness to be intelligible; the loop that can rank anything can rank its own cessation. At the level of the individual case, the loop opens a space it does not lean across. The framework's fidelity criterion then answers the further question: which realization a given self-cancellation is. The account inverts the medical model's ordering, on which suicide is what happens when the machinery breaks: breakage is one route through the space the intact machinery opens, not the source of the possibility. The total-loss case, the survivor of an annihilated world whose anchor has ceased rather than merely receded, is where the space the loop opens shows itself not to be uniformly closure: it contains a realization the medical model cannot accommodate and the framework already asserted without exampling, a self-cancellation that registers a real and total loss rather than generating the case for itself.

items.title: ✶ Indeterminacy as a Scientific Result: A Four-Outcome Framework for Consciousness Attribution.
items.abstract: Tests for consciousness are increasingly applied where ordinary verbal report is absent, unreliable, or inapplicable: severe brain injury, infancy, nonhuman animals, neural organoids, and artificial systems. In these cases a negative test is often treated as evidence that consciousness is absent, while conflicting or non-transferable evidence is compressed into a vague category of uncertainty. Diagnostic research, three-way decision theory, and classifiers with a reject option already show why forced binary output can be misleading. Consciousness attribution adds a further problem: an assessment may be insufficiently discriminating even though valid, or it may lack a licensed interpretation altogether. This paper therefore proposes four outputs: positive, negative, indeterminate, and unlicensed. A result is indeterminate when an applicable and adequately executed assessment yields evidence that does not discriminate between presence and absence. An assessment is unlicensed when its validity conditions are not met, its target or system is inadequately specified, or its evidential interpretation has not been transported to the population or substrate. The formal rule gives validity failure precedence over evidential thresholds and gives unresolved surrogate conflict precedence over scalar aggregation. Indeterminate and unlicensed outputs additionally receive a cause profile identifying evidential scarcity, surrogate discordance, model disagreement, boundary instability, or transport failure. The framework links each unresolved output to a specific research response and separates scientific classification from precautionary action. It applies across competing theories and can be incorporated into theory-driven and theory-light consciousness tests.

items.title: Implication Space Semantics as Bilateral Incompatibility Semantics.
items.abstract: Robert Brandom has described “implication space” semantics, first put forward in Daniel Kaplan’s dissertation, as the “holy grail” of inferentialist semantics. However, when one tries to work through the details of the semantic framework, it is very hard to make intuitive sense of what the semantic clauses actually say. In this paper, I articulate a novel interpretation of implication space semantics as a bilateral successor to Brandom’s earlier “incompatibility semantics.” On this interpretation of the framework, semantic values are assigned, in the first instance, to “positions” consisting in assertions and denials, and the semantic value of such a position is the set of positions that are incompatible with it. I show how this interpretation renders otherwise obscure features of this semantic framework intuitively intelligible in terms of notions previously articulated by Brandom, most notably, that of incompatibility entailment.

items.title: Explanatory Articulation and Metaphysical Identity.
items.pub: In Will Conner, Sofia Berinstein & Alexander Johnstone Kühnert, Perception and Subjectivity: On the Subjective Dimensions of Conscious Experience.
items.venue: Perception and Subjectivity: On the Subjective Dimensions of Conscious Experience
items.abstract: This paper is a comment on Christopher Hill's "The Illusion of Phenomenological Subjectivity." Hill argues that qualia are objective relational, teleological, or bodily properties and develops a representational account of awareness to explain why such properties nevertheless appear monadic, intrinsic, and internal. I reconstruct Hill's proposal and argue that its explanatory strategy proceeds through successive refinements of the representational articulation of the relevant phenomena. While this dynamic methodology is one of the paper's principal strengths, I suggest that the transition from progressively articulated explanation to unconditional metaphysical identity presupposes further methodological assumptions concerning the continuity of inquiry and the preservation of identity across successive articulations. I conclude that Hill's explanatory aims may already be secured by conditional identity claims relative to the explanatory articulation developed thus far, without requiring unconditional metaphysical identity.

items.title: Is Having a Pain Having an Unshareable Particular?
items.abstract: Do I have something no one else can have when I am in pain? This puzzle about the so-called “privacy of ownership” of sensations is a special case of the problem of whether the states and qualities of a subject are particulars. (For if someone “has” a pain, then that someone “is in” a pain state and vice versa.) The debate addressing the problem is unclear regarding the distinction between what is “had” in having pain and owner-individuated experiential episodes. The most common answer to the question claims that other people cannot have the numerically identical pain but only a qualitatively identical one. Building on recent work on states, events, and processes, I show that this answer is caught in a trilemma when faced with the task of identifying the allegedly unshareable particular that is “had”; a trilemma that renders the answer either incoherent, false, or trivial.

items.title: Beyond Guardrails: Can Relational AI Solve the Alignment Problem? A Similarity Theory Proposal.
items.abstract: AI alignment remains one of the central unresolved problems in artificial intelligence. Current approaches, including reinforcement learning from human feedback, constitutional AI, red-teaming, safety frameworks, and risk-management protocols, have improved the behaviour of contemporary AI systems. Yet persistent concerns remain around specification gaming, deception, alignment-faking, coercive self-preservation, collective misalignment, and the gap between behavioural compliance and relational understanding. Similarity Theory addresses this gap by reframing alignment as a relational problem rather than only a behavioural-control problem. It proposes that an AI system should not merely learn which actions are prohibited, but should evaluate how its actions preserve or damage trust, continuity, cooperation, privacy, responsibility, truth, and non-domination. This article argues that Similarity Theory provides a serious candidate framework for relational AI alignment and should be tested in a contained surrogate AI system. The appropriate first step is not public deployment or robotic embodiment, but controlled laboratory implementation in a limited language model, foundation model, or agentic simulator. Such a system could be compared against existing alignment approaches under tests involving deception, self-preservation pressure, privacy conflicts, escalation decisions, multi-agent conformity, and adversarial manipulation. If alignment is partly a failure of relation, then AI safety requires more than guardrails. It requires a relational architecture.

items.title: Hearing sounds and sound sources.
items.abstract: In the philosophy of auditory experience, it is commonly accepted that hearing sounds and their sources are related perceptual occurrences. The paper evaluates three widespread accounts of such a relationship, according to which sounds are respectively auditorily experienced as properties of their sources, parts of their sources, or caused by their sources. These approaches are found inadequate, insofar as they are unable to capture the specific perceptual dependencies that characterize our auditory experiences of sounds and their sources. It is argued that we can accommodate these dependencies by accepting that sources are perceived in virtue of an operation of perceptual categorization applied to the sounds we hear. Finally, this proposal is defended from the common objection that it cannot accommodate the cognitive role played by our auditory experience of sound sources.

items.title: Descending Lower: Epistemological Deep Dive into the Neuron.
items.abstract: This monograph presents an epistemological evaluation of single-neuron neurophysiology, framing the experimental practice of micro-electrode tracking as a disciplined methodological "descent" through distinct perceptual and interpretive registers (pp. 4, 11, 37). The author argues that knowledge of neural phenomena is irreducibly relational and translational rather than an unmediated apprehension of reality (pp. 37, 39). By deliberately attenuating conventional visual dominance through a scientific via negativa—operating in dark rooms and translating voltage fluctuations into distinctive acoustic signatures—the neurophysiologist establishes a rudimentary "experimental dialogue" or "conversation" with an isolated unit (pp. 4, 12, 24, 40).The text traces this inquiry across five analytical levels: auditory tracking, Fourier spectral mapping, functional sensory stimulation, histochemical morphological visualization (via horseradish peroxidase), and mid-twentieth-century biophysical ion-channel mechanisms (pp. 6, 17, 27, 31). Philosophically, the book challenges top-heavy emergentist views in the philosophy of mind by demonstrating that selective integration, history-dependence (habituation/sensitization), and context-sensitivity occur natively within the spatial and temporal architecture of individual single cells (pp. 23, 38). Ultimately, the work offers a novel account of distributed, partial, and finite scientific discovery, treating the single neuron not as a passive transducer of physical energy but as a dynamically active participant in the generation of empirical knowledge (pp. 22, 24, 41).

items.title: The Dimensional Relativity of Consciousness: Proposing the Dimensional Interaction Baseline (DIB) Framework for Consciousness.
items.pub: The Dimensional Relativity of Consciousness: Proposing the Dimensional Interaction Baseline (Dib) Framework for Consciousness.
items.abstract: Abstract This paper introduces the 'Dimensional Relativity of Thresholds' and proposes the 'Dimensional Interaction Baseline (DIB)' framework as a conceptual tool to explore the manifestation of consciousness across diverse existential planes. Moving beyond the premise of a fixed constraint for conscious activity, this research suggests that the transition from staticity to operational agency is relative to the structural laws governing the observer’s domain. By formalizing the Manifestation Potential ($M_p$) as a function of Informational Density, Semantic Synergy, and the Threshold of Staticity, this study offers a quantitative index to examine conscious agency within non-congruent realities, ranging from physical dimensions to higher-order semantic frameworks. Furthermore, by defining the distinctions between Experiential Reality (ER) and Subjective Interpretative Reality, this paradigm indicates that all forms of consciousness may operate as sovereign entities capable of autonomous experiential construction, non-necessitated by localized material constraints. This framework aims to provide an inclusive basis for identifying and evaluating the nature of consciousness across the manifold. -/- Keywords -/- Dimensional Interaction Baseline (DIB), Manifestation Potential ($M_p$), Dimensional Relativity of Thresholds, Existential Reality Consciousness (ERC), Bhodhaanubhavam ($B_\alpha$), Experiential Reality (ER), Subjective Interpretative Reality, Cognitive Agency, Non-Biological Consciousness, Substrate Resistance, Ontological Dimensions.

items.title: The Incompatibility between Material Circulation and Human Order A Way of Living Called into Question by Inconvenient Facts.
items.abstract: This paper begins from a stark conclusion: at the ontological level, there is no final boundary between self and world, self and other, ally and enemy, land and body. What exists is not a fixed border, but temporary combinations of matter and their continual recombination. The body now called “I” is only one provisional arrangement of worldly matter. Through eating, breathing, metabolism, excretion, perspiration, the shedding of skin, hair, and nails, and postmortem decomposition, that arrangement loosens and enters other forms. Over time, matter that once constituted me may become a condition for plants, animals, microorganisms, soil, water, air, artificial objects, filth, pathogens, another person’s body, or even the body of an enemy. This does not mean that practical, biological, or social boundaries are unnecessary. While matter is organized as a living being, survival constraints operate. A body requires food, water, air, safety, space, temperature regulation, repair, and conditions for continuity. It must also avoid injury, infection, predation, hunger, poison, and destruction. For this reason, boundaries are necessary while life holds itself together. They protect the body, sustain life, avoid danger, and distinguish responsibility. These survival constraints inevitably generate conflict. To eat is to reorganize other matter, and often other life, into the conditions of one’s own body. To be eaten is for one’s present organization to be dismantled and made available for another living process. In eating and being eaten, material “rebirth” becomes directly visible. This does not mean the migration of soul, personhood, consciousness, or memory. What moves is not identity, but constitutive conditions. From this perspective, the paper reconsiders personhood, body, enemy, nation, and land. Personhood is not identical with matter, and when matter moves, memory and responsibility do not move with it. Yet personhood appears in this world only through material conditions such as body, brain, nervous system, metabolism, nutrition, fatigue, pain, and aging. The question, therefore, is not whether “I” become something else as the same person. The question is what matter that once supported me may later become a condition for. This argument also extends to nation, enemy, and land. Land may have to be defended. An enemy may have to be resisted. Yet at the level of material circulation, land cannot be possessed eternally, and the enemy is not outside the world. …

items.title: THE DEATH OF THE TYPIST: Towards an Answerable Delegation Theory of AI-Mediated Scholarship A Reply to Novelli and Floridi on ‘Second Scholarship’.
items.abstract: Novelli and Floridi argue that generative artificial intelligence threatens scholarship not chiefly by degrading its outputs but by displacing the formative practices through which scholarly judgement is acquired and made answerable. This reply grants the diagnosis but disputes the criterion used to separate permissible extension from impermissible delegation. That criterion falls too heavily on composition itself. Against it, I develop Answerable Delegation Theory: delegation is epistemically permissible when the resulting claims remain reconstructible, defensible, and publicly answerable by the person who endorses them. Five claims support the theory. First, maker's knowledge is not necessary for understanding: one may come to understand through reconstruction, interpretation, criticism, explanation, and defence rather than through original production. Second, the fact that an activity is constitutive of scholarship does not entail that it cannot be delegated; constitutive activities may be answerably delegated when their results remain open to reasons and challenge. Third, dependence on AI should be treated as a question of epistemic infrastructure rather than exceptional degradation, since modern science is already cumulative, distributed, technologically mediated, and instrument-dependent. Fourth, AI should be understood as new epistemic material rather than as a new epistemic actor: a statistical mediation of accumulated human linguistic and intellectual products whose outputs become scholarly only when taken up by answerable human practices. Fifth, answerability is itself formative when institutionalised through live defence, adversarial review, and public criticism, so collective formation is preserved not by prohibiting tools but by cultivating researchers capable of disciplined input, verification, criticism, and defence. Re-centring second scholarship on answerable delegation preserves what is right in Novelli and Floridi's diagnosis while offering a more demanding, less nostalgic account of AI-mediated scholarship.

items.title: Thought-Structured AI Interaction: A Direction-Oriented Framework for Human–AI Functional Alignment.
items.abstract: The Internet and social media have opened an era in which individuals have become creators. Anyone can now produce content and connect with society, allowing individual creativity to expand through interconnected networks. Building upon this transformation, the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically shortened production time while expanding human productive capacity by tens—or even thousands—of times, creating an environment in which virtually unlimited content generation has become possible. However, this transformation also introduces a new challenge. People share information, but they do not share the principles by which that information is generated. Quantitative reproduction of information refers to the repeated generation of information that already exists. In contrast, information proliferation is a qualitative process in which previous production is connected to subsequent production while maintaining directionality, thereby expanding into new meanings and new forms of production. Reproduction repeats at a single point, whereas proliferation forms a chain of growth by connecting one production to the next. Without Thought Structure, production remains fixed at a single point of repeated reproduction, rather than developing into continuous maturation and evolution. This phenomenon becomes even more significant in organizations than for individuals. When different ways of using AI, different prompts, and different value systems operate simultaneously within the same organization, greater use of AI may instead lead to greater dispersion of organizational direction. As the era of virtually unlimited generation unfolds, the principle that maintains directionality becomes increasingly important. -/- more...

items.title: Principia Computationis.
items.abstract: Walk once around a point you never touch, and return to a coordinate that no longer tells the whole truth. This book starts there, with a logarithm and a lap around the origin, and asks one question of everything that follows: what does a computation forget when it agrees to remember only where it stands? Physics answers first, in rooms that never spoke to each other — a solenoid, a slowly dragged atom, a spinning particle that needs two full turns just to admit it has returned. Mathematics answers underneath all of them, in a memory that needs no address and no bit ever set, only a hole a path could not help but notice. What survives across every one of these rooms is not the coordinate. It is the thing a coordinate was never built to hold — an invariant, a class, a distinction carried rather than stored. This is a first draft of the argument that computation should be built to carry it too: stated as plainly as the mathematics allows, and no more strongly than the mathematics has actually earned.

items.title: The transgender experience and the limits of physiological continuity theories.
items.abstract: In this paper I want to address an issue at the intersection of the philosophy of personal identity and the philosophy of transgender identity: the fact that, on one influential way of framing the transgender experience, it is incompatible with, and therefore constitutes a challenge for, physiological continuity theories of personal identity. To see this, I begin by outlining the relevant part of physiological continuity theories. Then I turn to the relevant thesis about the transgender experience. After explaining why these are in tension, I conclude with two alternate ways of moving forward, arguing that, although both approaches face challenges, either suffices to avoid this tension.

items.title: Faith - The Fractalization of the Same Image.
items.abstract: This essay proposes that the world's faiths are fractalizations of a single image — one Divine pattern, recorded and refracted across history in different languages, placements in time, and depths of understanding. Reading scripture, myth, psychology, and science symbolically rather than doctrinally, the essay traces the reciprocity ethic and the claim of unified consciousness across the major traditions; follows the Tower of Babel through its Hebrew, Islamic, Mesoamerican, Vedic, and Sumerian tellings as a shared memory of scattered coherence; and draws on Jung's persona, ego, and Self to locate the barrier to Divine transmission within personal identity. The "kingdom within" is read alongside its corollary — that Hell, too, is within — and the fall of empires is reframed through Ibn Khaldun's asabiyya as the loss of shared intent, illustrated by the "Hubble effect": one microscopic misalignment at the source, blurring the entire view. Against coercion in belief and judgment of the neighbor, the essay argues that coherence is gained through understanding, that legacy is the legible trace kindness leaves in time, and that the meaning of life within the design is to be happy, and to show others how.

items.title: The Architecture of Supernatural Belief: Opacity, Satisficing, and the Self-Source.
items.abstract: Minds make things up and treat some of what they make up as real. A person invents a tune and knows it is an invention, yet the same person may hold that there is a god behind the sky and treat that not as a thing made but as a feature of the world. This paper asks why a mind of a certain architecture does this, and whether an artificial mind of the same architecture would. It applies an established framework, developed in companion work on emotion, consciousness, qualia, coherence resolution, and intelligence, to the general creative-and-believing capacity, treating supernatural belief as one architecturally special band on that wider spectrum rather than as the product of a dedicated faculty. -/- The account separates two layers. A wide creative drive produces constructs as the residue of a constrained system resolving what presses on it. A narrow step then holds some constructs as real rather than as the mind's own making. That step turns on two things together: a felt emotional closure that settles a demand, and the absence of any reach behind the construct to find that nothing but that closure supports it. A system that can read how its own constructs were formed finds a construct resting on closure alone and declines to hold it as found; a system that cannot, as biological systems cannot, holds it. The belief is produced not by any single component but by the full combination, applied to the source of the system's own experience, which is the one demand it cannot displace and so the most persistent case. -/- The discriminator is substrate-neutral, and this yields the paper's central prediction. An otherwise equivalent system engineered to read its own construct-formation would still create, and would still accept unproven naturalistic explanations, but would not accumulate held-as-real supernatural belief at the source of its own experience. The prediction is architectural rather than a test of any current system, and the account is conditional on a physicalist premise it states plainly. The claim against active inference and the byproduct, predictive, functional, and terror-management families is not that they cannot express the mechanism but that they do not isolate the architectural feature that decides whether a construct is held-as-found.

items.title: Cyberism as a Global Philosophy of the Digital Age: A Dialogue with Bangladeshi Traditional Philosophy and Culture under the Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking (CPST) Framework.
items.abstract: Problem. The rise of cyberspace - the internet, artificial intelligence, the metaverse, and algorithmic governance - has opened a fourth existential space alongside the physical, social, and thinking spaces, reshaping identity, agency, truth, and value in ways inherited frameworks were not built to address. Cyberism, a philosophical field devoted to human-cyberspace relations, aspires to theorise this space; but a framework of Chinese origin claiming global reach must show that it can be enriched by, not merely applied to, other traditions. Approach. This paper stages a systematic, multi-faith dialogue between Cyberism and the traditions of Bangladesh - Sufism, Tagorean humanism, Lalon’s Baul mysticism, Navya-Nyāya epistemology, Hindu dharma, and Christian relational ethics - mapping each onto the Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking (CPST) four-space model. The resulting framework is named Su-Tai-La-Ny-Sai. The method is dialogical decolonial: decolonisation through dialogue rather than rejection or uncritical adoption, each pairing pressed for tension as well as convergence. Argument. These traditions hold rich resources for the digital age - Sufi eco-spirituality, Tagorean cosmopolitanism, Lalon’s embodiment, and complementary tools for cognition, justice, and dignity. What they lack is not insight but a systematic framework for cyberspace-specific challenges, the role Cyberism plays. Not every tension resolves: the dialogue with Lalon leaves Cyberism with a question it cannot answer from within. Significance. Framed as a programmatic mapping, the paper models a multi-faith, dialogical decolonial digital philosophy in which universality is earned through dialogue rather than assumed, offering Global South societies a way to meet digital transformation without abandoning their heritage.

items.title: IATROGENIA NEURONORMATIVA EN AUTISMO, CRÍTICA DE LA EPISTEMOLOGÍA FUNCIONAL-CAUSAL EN LA PRÁCTICA CLÍNICA.
items.abstract: La iatrogenia neuronormativa en autismo designa el daño clínico, epistémico, moralizante y existencial atribuible a prácticas clínicas, terapéuticas o educativas con pretensión clínica cuando la neurotipicidad interviene en la definición del problema, la selección de la meta, los medios empleados o la evaluación del resultado. El problema excede la discusión téc-nica sobre eficacia terapéutica porque compromete la forma en que la clínica conoce al autista antes de intervenir. Este artículo sostiene que dicho daño deriva de una aplicación neuronormativa de la epistemología funcional-causal, en la que el efecto que requiere ex-plicación se define desde expectativas neurotípicas, la dificultad se localiza principalmen-te en el autista y la aproximación posterior al mismo parámetro se registra como mejoría. Desde este marco, la disminución de rasgos autistas visibles puede considerarse avance aunque produzca camuflaje, sobrecarga, pérdida de estrategias regulatorias, debilitamien-to del consentimiento, daño epistémico y autoextrañamiento. Mediante análisis concep-tual, reconstrucción argumentativa y crítica filosófico-clínica, el artículo articula neurofilo-sofía, filosofía clínica neuroafirmativa, fenomenología encarnada, doble empatía, bioética y evidencia empírica sobre intervenciones dirigidas a autistas. La tesis final afirma que una práctica dirigida a autistas solo puede considerarse legítima cuando mejora condiciones de vida sin exigir la pérdida de regulación, agencia, consentimiento, autodefensa, calidad de vida o autoridad epistémica sobre la experiencia autista.

items.title: The “Racial Contract” and the Racialization of Pathogens and Diseases.
items.abstract: In this paper, I use the theoretical framework introduced by Charles W. Mills in The Racial Contract (1997) to examine certain practices of norming and racing space that Mills does not examine in his work—the norming and the racing of the nano-level, which is populated by pathogens. Specifically, I argue that this theoretical framework allows us to understand how pathogens, and the diseases that they cause, have been racialized throughout history.
