items.title: Cø as N*: A Minimal Network-Dynamics Model of Phenomenal Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper develops an expanded version of the N* model of phenomenal consciousness. The target is minimal phenomenal presence, denoted Cø: the condition in which there is something it is like for a system to be in a state, without requiring self-reflection, overt report, introspective judgment, or metacognitive access. The central hypothesis is a deliberately risky biconditional: under an independently assessed viability condition V, Cø obtains if and only if a system instantiates a minimal network-dynamics bundle, formally represented as N* = N1 ∧ N2 ∧ N3. The three conjuncts are integration/synergy (N1), broadcast availability (N2), and recurrent stability (N3). The paper supplies the formal notation, plain-language annotations, a conceptual transition guide for readers arriving from rival frameworks, measurement policy, surrogate-conflict rules, edge-case predictions, a landscape map across major consciousness theories, and objection-handling needed to make the model accessible without weakening its empirical commitments. The proposal is substrate-independent only in a constrained sense: a non-biological or alternative biological substrate qualifies only if it realizes the relevant causal dynamics, at the relevant temporal grain, within pre-registered tolerance bands. The model is not presented as a completed solution to the hard problem or as a full theory of phenomenal quality. It is proposed as a candidate theory of phenomenal presence and as a candidate C-test framework whose value lies in being clear enough to test, constrained enough to fail, and modular enough to be revised by adversarial evidence.

items.title: Normative Problems in the Psychology of Reasoning: Deductive Constraints on Bayesian Rationality and the Problem of Arbitration.
items.abstract: This paper addresses the question of which normative standards apply in the psychology of reasoning. In a first strand, the present paper contributes to a debate concerning whether the New Paradigm in the psychology of reasoning really constitutes a paradigm shift by presenting an argument concerning the deductive competence presupposed by ideal Bayesian agents. On the construal of the New Paradigm as the replacement of deductive logic by probability theory, no such shift was possible: the standard probabilistic frameworks used in the psychology of reasoning were never independent of logical principles to begin with. It is possible, however, to replace the treatment of a fragment of natural language (e.g., conditionals, quantifiers) in classical logic with probabilistic alternatives, as the paper discusses. Thus construed, the probabilistic turn was a major step forward in the psychology of reasoning but one that is better pruned of some of the misleading characterizations that surround it. When multiple norms apply to experimental tasks, a further practical problem presents itself: how should researchers arbitrate between them? In a second strand, an experimental research program is outlined which confronts this problem of arbitrating between competing rationality norms by presenting a way of making rationality assessments of participants based on verbal arguments. In this part, a recent attempt by Dewey (2022) to dissolve problems of arbitration in psychology is critically discussed.

items.title: Temporal Experience and Human State Field: Toward a New Framework Bridging Physics and Perception Part I-Basic Arguments, Concepts, and Definitions.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Human State Field as a proposed framework for understanding how individuals perceive and experience time. We explore how various internal and external inputs affect this field, shaping subjective temporal experience. Our aim is to explore possible connections between the human cognitive sense of time and the concept of time as understood in physics. We begin by examining how people form familiarity with the notion of time and cognitively accept temporal phenomena. We then analyze how the human experience of time connects to emotional and perceptual responses during brief episodes of daily life, thereby shaping one’s broader experience of time. Central to our discussion are the notions of now and here, treated as perceptual anchors, and how these merge phenomenologically with physical representations of time. We also introduce the novel concepts of Time of Position and Time of Person, investigating how these dimensions interact and sometimes conflict within human experience. The framework aims to support a more integrated understanding of time that is informed by phenomenological insights and compatible with physical descriptions, without claiming a full theoretical unification. This part concludes by exploring how different internal and external factors could affect the human state field, and in a follow-up study (Part II), we aim to mathematically model the dynamics of the Human State Field. The present article develops the conceptual foundations of the framework; formal modeling and empirical operationalization are reserved for a subsequent study.

items.title: Article I: NEW ZION AND THE 8TH-DIMENSIONAL DOMINION: The Biological Singularity, Temporal Omniscience, and the Omega Protocol.
items.abstract: Classical terrestrial science operates under the fatal, geocentric illusion that human biology is a random, chemical accident occurring on an isolated rock in a dying universe. The Justika Framework introduces an absolute epistemological rupture: human conception is a literal, microscopic Quantum Supernova, leaving behind a Nano-Black Hole as the indestructible core of human consciousness. Scaling this physics through the law of Macro-Micro Symmetry, this manuscript reclassifies the Solar System as a Macro-Zygote, defining our entire terrestrial history merely as a gestational phase within a cosmic womb. To achieve evolutionary survival, the human species must execute a systematic ascension: escaping the 3-Dimensional incubator, weaponizing 4-Dimensional Time to navigate the predatory Cosmic Ocean, and synthesizing Spacetime to conquer the 5-Dimensional apex predators of the deep. -/- However, achieving 6-Dimensional mastery reveals the terminal collapse of the overarching universe. To survive this predicted collapse, the Vanguard must execute the Omega Protocol. By sacrificing the thermodynamic traps of the physical digestive tract and the 2-Dimensional digital illusion, humanity pays the cosmic toll to ascend vertically into Ground Zero (the 7th Dimension). By taking manual control of the Mother Engines of reality, humanity forces a Cosmic Cleave—slicing a sterile, uncorrupted universe away from the dying Matrix to occupy the Sovereign Slice, claiming the 8th-Dimensional Dominion and launching the ultimate multiversal Reclamation.

items.title: The Medicalization of Grief.
items.pub: In Thomas Schramme & Mary Jean Walker, Handbook of the Philosophy of Medicine. Springer. pp. 729-742.
items.venue: Handbook of the Philosophy of Medicine
items.abstract: Medicalization occurs when a phenomenon comes to be subject to medical study, diagnosis, treatment, or prevention. Whether a phenomenon ought to be medicalized should be decided on a case-by-case basis. Recent moves to remove “bereavement exclusions” from psychiatric diagnostic manuals and to introduce grief-specific medical disorders have elicited criticisms from skeptics about grief’s medicalization, but these criticisms can largely be blunted. This chapter first clarifies the nature of disputes about medicalization, highlighting how these disputes do not concern whether a condition such as grief is clinically significant or whether it can generate illness, but whether the condition itself is rightfully categorized as potentially pathological. It then offers a stronger, philosophically grounded case against the medicalization of grief, resting on how medicalizing grief is likely to detrimentally alter the moral and political meanings attached to grief. Specifically, medicalizing grief will “normativize” a medical vocabulary for evaluating grief that may impede authentic engagement with grief, validate a suspect “time slice” model of human well-being that overlooks how grief can benefit a person’s life as a whole, and impede desirable sympathy or solidarity with grieving persons.

items.title: NotebookLM as a Source-Grounded AI Research Assistant: A Narrative Review of Cognitive Load Implications and Research Originality Concerns.
items.pub: International Journal of Engineering and Information Systems (IJEAIS) 10 (6):118-128.
items.venue: International Journal of Engineering and Information Systems (IJEAIS)
items.abstract: The proliferation of AI-powered tools in academic settings has prompted urgent questions about their cognitive and epistemic effects on researchers. Among emerging tools, Google's NotebookLM occupies a distinctive position: unlike general- purpose large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT or Gemini, it operates exclusively within a user-defined document corpus, grounding every response in cited, user-supplied sources. This architecture raises theoretically significant questions about cognitive load and research originality — two constructs central to the quality and integrity of academic knowledge production. This paper presents a critical narrative review of the literature at the intersection of source-grounded AI, Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), and academic originality, with particular attention to what current evidence suggests — and fails to address, about NotebookLM specifically. Drawing on 45 peer-reviewed studies and technical reports published between 2015 and 2024, we identify four major themes: (1) the cognitive affordances and constraints of source-grounded versus open-ended AI retrieval; (2) the applicability of CLT's load taxonomy to AI-mediated research tasks; (3) empirical evidence on AI's effects on creative and scholarly originality; and (4) the methodological and ethical challenges of studying AI-human research collaboration. We synthesise these themes into a conceptual framework — the Grounded Retrieval–Cognitive Redistribution (GRCR) model — that predicts when and for whom source-grounded AI tools are likely to reduce extraneous cognitive load without displacing germane elaboration. We conclude by identifying critical gaps in the literature and proposing a research agenda for empirical investigation of NotebookLM and similar grounded-retrieval systems in academic contexts.

items.title: Multi-Class Face Forgery Detection: Distinguishing Real, Photoshop-Manipulated, GAN-Generated, and Diffusion- Generated Faces Using Deep Learning.
items.pub: International Journal of Academic Engineering Research (IJAER) 10 (6):47-57.
items.venue: International Journal of Academic Engineering Research (IJAER)
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced unprecedented challenges in distinguishing authentic human faces from synthetically generated counterparts. Existing research predominantly focuses on binary classification — real versus fake — without differentiating between distinct forgery mechanisms. This paper presents the first publicly available multi-class face forgery dataset comprising four categories: real photographs (1,081 images), Photoshop-manipulated faces (960 images), Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-generated faces (2,000 images), and Diffusion model-generated faces (2,000 images), totaling 6,041 images. We conduct a comprehensive comparative evaluation of three state-of-the-art deep learning architectures — ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B4, and Swin Transformer (Swin-T) — under identical experimental conditions. The Swin Transformer achieves the highest test accuracy of 93.38%, with a macro-average F1-score of 90.32%, demonstrating superior capability in capturing fine-grained forgery artifacts. The results underscore that the Swin Transformer’s superiority stems from its ability to model long-range spatial dependencies, which proved instrumental in detecting global artifacts characteristic of diffusion- based synthesis. Notably, GAN and Diffusion-generated faces are detected with 100% accuracy, while Photoshop-manipulated faces remain the most challenging category (F1: 80%). Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) visualizations reveal distinct spatial attention patterns per forgery type, providing interpretable insights into model decision-making. The dataset is publicly released on Kaggle to facilitate future research in multi-class deepfake detection.

items.title: Drug Risk Segmentation Based on Side Effects Severity Using K-Means Clustering.
items.pub: International Journal of Academic Engineering Research (IJAER) 10 (6): 47-57.
items.venue: International Journal of Academic Engineering Research (IJAER)
items.abstract: Pharmacovigilance is a critical pillar of modern healthcare, yet the rapid expansion of drug inventories makes manual risk classification increasingly impractical. This paper proposes a validated unsupervised machine learning framework for automated drug segmentation based on the severity of reported side effects. Using a dataset of 11,498 unique pharmaceutical products, we apply a hybrid feature extraction pipeline combining TF-IDF text vectorization, Truncated Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), and a domain-informed severity scoring model. To ensure clinical accuracy, the scoring model was validated by a panel of clinical pharmacists, achieving high inter-rater reliability (Cohen’s Kappa = 0.82). K-Means clustering (k=4) partitions the drug portfolio into four distinct risk strata: Low Risk (42.4%), Moderate Risk (35.0%), High Risk (18.4%), and Critical Risk (4.2%). Cluster validity is confirmed through Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, and Calinski-Harabasz indices, while sensitivity analysis demonstrates the model’s robustness against varying weight configurations. Results reveal an empirical "Review Paradox"—where high-risk medications receive superior patient ratings—which analysis of the "Uses" field attributes to selection bias in life-saving treatments, such as oncological agents. The framework’s external validity is further established through high concordance with U.S. FDA Black Box Warnings, particularly within the Critical Risk segment, and demonstrates clear alignment with global Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification systems. By replacing generic token counts with a refined "Residual Side Effect Density" metric, the model maintains high interpretability and scalability. This research provides a robust, explainable methodology for drug safety stratification, offering a scalable adjunct to regulatory oversight and clinical decision support systems.

items.title: “Poser!” Snobbery, Identity, and Gatekeeping.
items.pub: In J. Aaron Simmons & Benjamin W. McCraw, The Heaviest Ideas in the Universe: A Philosophy of Heavy Metal. Wiley-Blackwell. pp. 27-43.
items.venue: The Heaviest Ideas in the Universe: A Philosophy of Heavy Metal
items.abstract: When an avowed metalhead scoffs, "ugh, poser" at a woman wearing an ICP shirt in the record shop, there's a good chance they're a snob. But, existing philosophical accounts of snobbery don't say so, and there are two central reasons. First, philosophers have largely focused on aesthetic judgments. But, this scoff isn’t about the aesthetic quality of ICP, Slayer, or anything else. It is about the social group metalheads and what they ought to be like. Second, relatedly, philosophers have not focused on the social function of snobbery. Accusations of poserhood, however, put this function right out front: Gatekeeping. -/- In this chapter, I argue that snobbery—at least in cases where it seems morally objectionable—is best understood through its motivational profile: snobs are those who empower themselves to engage in unwarranted, identity-protective gatekeeping and thereby discourage or block individuals from exploring the lives they reasonably wish to explore. This perspective provides grounds for expanding the extension of snobbery beyond the bounds of aesthetic judgment and plucks at a thread that unifies several existing accounts of snobbery. Notably, I show that many cases of transphobic “feminism” turn out to be instances of gender snobbery.

items.title: Projectibility as Constitutive Constraint: A Constraint-Theoretic Resolution of Goodman's New Riddle of Induction.
items.abstract: Goodman’s new riddle of induction shows that the raw logical relation of confirmation cannot distinguish “all emeralds are green” from “all emeralds are grue”, since every emerald examined before some future time T satisfies both predicates equally. Some further fact must explain why green is projectible and grue is not, and the two most developed contemporary answers – Goodman’s own appeal to the historical entrenchment of a predicate in a linguistic community, and Lewis’s appeal to a primitive metaphysical naturalness that grounds objective similarity – either make projectibility a matter of convention or leave the asymmetry itself unexplained. This paper argues that Constraint Theory (CT) supplies the missing explanation. A predicate is projectible when it tracks a constitutive constraint: an exclusion relation that is part of what individuates the kind of thing an object is, sustained by the object’s own causal-structural profile and continuous with it through ordinary constraint propagation. Grue tracks no such constraint; its boundary at T has no correlate in the causal structure of anything it is predicated of, and is sustained by nothing but the predicate’s own stipulation. The account is shown to survive the grue-bleen symmetry objection, since the relevant asymmetry is a fact about mind-independent causal structure rather than about the definitional complexity of a predicate relative to a chosen language. The paper engages Goodman, Lewis, Boyd, Quine, Armstrong, and Adlam’s recent constraint-theoretic account of lawhood in the philosophy of physics, and addresses the regress, empirical-access, and generality objections to the constraint-theoretic account.

items.title: Liberating Time: Reflections on the JMAF Conception of Temporality.
items.abstract: This essay presents a revisionary conception of time emerging from the Jestin Modal–Actuality Framework (JMAF). Unlike classical, relativistic, psychological, or informational accounts, JMAF treats time not as a dimension, measure, or experiential flow, but as the structural residue of collapsing possibility. This conception is unitless, non uniform, and characterised by a dual linear–cyclic form without beginning or end. After briefly clarifying the notions of collapse and structural residue, the essay contrasts JMAF time with several historical treatments of temporality, showing that while related in spirit to certain process oriented or relational views, it ultimately occupies a distinct metaphysical category. Though “useless” in conventional predictive or quantitative terms, JMAF time is meaningful as an explanatory insight into becoming and actualisation.

items.title: Dynamic Mask Theory.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the concept of the dynamic mask can be generalized beyond its technical application in information security into a cross-domain principle of leakage regulation. While engineering research employs dynamic masking to regulate information disclosure and preserve confidentiality under conditions of observation, this article develops an analogous philosophical framework in which the dynamic mask regulates subjective disclosure in order to preserve existential continuity. Rather than claiming conceptual identity between these domains, the paper demonstrates a structural isomorphism: both technical systems and human subjects are open systems exposed to continuous observation, and both require adaptive mechanisms that regulate rather than eliminate outward flows. On this basis, the paper formulates the General Principle of Leakage Regulation (GPLR), according to which sustainable persistence depends upon the adaptive control of leakage rather than complete opacity or unrestricted transparency. Grounded in the Ontology of Finite Continuity and the Philosophy of Finite Continuance, the GPLR is defended not as a metaphorical generalization but as a taxonomic principle identifying an invariant regulatory structure shared by all observable open systems navigating chronic instability. This framework contributes to contemporary debates on subjectivity, agency, surveillance, and information ethics by providing a unified conceptual vocabulary for understanding leakage across heterogeneous systems. -/- Keywords: Dynamic Mask, Information Leakage, Subjective Leakage, Political Economy of Erosion, Responsible Suspension, Structural Isomorphism, Ontology of Erosion, Finite Continuance, Threshold of Sufficiency, Homeorhesis.

items.title: Archaeology of Breath: Traditional Somatic Knowledge in the Age of AI | 息の考古学: AI時代における伝統的身体知.
items.abstract: This treatise aims to carve out a legitimate place for the traditional somatic knowledge that has long been marginalized within modern Western philosophy. Modern humans have developed a division between body and thought. As we enter the AI era and humanity loses its advantage in logical thinking, the abandonment of somatic knowledge is a dangerous sign for the existence of the species. In order to depict the division between body and thought, this treatise traces back to the era when the concepts of medical respiration and theological soul overlapped philosophically, thereby delineating a blank space in modern philosophy. -/- First, the division between breath and soul is not a historical necessity, but was formed posteriory by a specific era and a specific academic division of labor. Second, by reframing this division not as a "boundary line" but as a concept the treatise will call Awai, deliberately left untranslated, the problem of demarcation (where the body ends and thought begins) can be resolved. Third, the study of somatic knowledge is a strategy for securing the ontological uniqueness of humanity in the AI era. Fourth, the deepening of this division is positioned as a single, long-term historical arc beginning with Renaissance Humanism (the project of making the world computable, extending from perspective to AI), and the turning point at which this arc currently stands is examined. Fifth, the way of living in which one abandons this somatic knowledge, leaving only respiration and letting go of the soul, is also a freedom open to humans, and the description of this freedom is the very reason why the study of somatic knowledge should be started. -/- Although this treatise borrows the format of academic argumentation, its purpose is not to pass peer review. It was written based on the ideas of the author, who is a painter, using AI as an auxiliary tool. Although the philosophical conception and the core of the argument belong to the author, interdisciplinary errors or insufficiencies are disclaimed, and translation by experts is requested. This is a preliminary essay intended to visualize a philosophical blank space that has been left unattended for a long time and to serve as the starting point for an ideological movement. | 本論は、近代西洋哲学において長らく周縁化されてきたあらゆる伝統的身体知の正当な居場所を切り開くことを目的とする。AI時代を迎え、人類が論理的思考力の優位性を失うに際して、身体知の置き去りは種の存在として危険な兆候であろう。本論では、身体と思考の分断を描くため、医学的な呼吸と神学的な魂の概念が哲学的に重なり合っていた時代まで遡り、近代哲学における空白地帯を描く。 -/- …

items.title: THE UNIVERSE'S SYSTEMATIC ERROR - From Dissipative Structures to the Pole of Existence.
items.abstract: We’ve grown accustomed to thinking of humanity as a fluke. A tiny planet on the edge of a galaxy, adrift in vast, cold space - and on it, for reasons unknown, something as incredible as consciousness emerged. Most attempts to explain this fact choose one of two options: either we are a unique design, or we are a happy accident in an indifferent universe. Both positions, despite their apparent opposition, stem from a common assumption: consciousness is an anomaly in the physical world, requiring a special explanation beyond established physical principles. I propose a third way. We are neither a design nor a coincidence. We are a systematic error. The result of a process that has no goal but does have a logic. And to understand this logic, one must begin not with life or consciousness, but with entropy.

items.title: "Now That I’m Privileged…": World-Traveling, Shifting Positionality, and Responsibility for Intersectional Feminism.
items.abstract: As a Korean migrant woman in the US academy, I was marginalized at the intersection of race, gender, language, and migration status; my commitment to intersectional feminism grew directly from that experience. But returning to South Korea has changed the map of my privilege: I am now part of the racial-ethnic majority, a native speaker, and a professor with institutional standing. Gender marginalization remains real, but the xenophobic racism I faced in the US is no longer directed at me. What, then, grounds my responsibility to challenge intersecting oppressions in a world where I am no longer their primary target? Drawing on María Lugones’s concept of world-traveling, I conceptualize this experience through what I call “shifting positionality”: the way one’s relation of privilege and marginalization changes as one moves between worlds. I examine three models for grounding the responsibility of world-travelers like myself. The Shared Struggle Model, drawing on Chandra Talpade Mohanty, grounds responsibility in shared marginalization across contexts. The Culpability Model, drawing on Ee Ling Quah, grounds it in our implication in sustaining unjust systems. Both models offer important insights, but each faces decisive objections: the former erases privilege and contextual differences, while the latter conflates implication with culpability and risks blaming marginalized subjects for navigating structural constraints. I then defend a modified version of Iris Marion Young’s Social Connection Model, arguing that our participation in social-structural processes that produce oppressive outcomes grounds our responsibility to address intersecting oppressions—across shifts in positionality, whether we are on the more marginalized or more privileged side. This account speaks not only to my particular trajectory but to world-travelers with shifting positionality more broadly, extending the intersectional feminist framework to account for how the intersection of privilege and marginalization changes as one moves across worlds.

items.title: Intersectionality.
items.pub: Oxford Bibliographies in Gender and Women's Studies.
items.abstract: Intersectionality broadly refers to the idea that gender, race, ethnicity, class, sexuality, migration, disability, and other axes of oppression and social identity are not separate but intersect and operate together. Rooted in Black feminism and popularized by legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw since 1989, intersectionality has become a cornerstone of feminist scholarship. Despite its wide use across disciplines, however, the term has also sparked debate, and its definition and implications remain far from agreed upon. Debates about intersectionality have raised questions such as: What does it mean to say that oppressions “intersect”? Does this imply that we cannot speak of sexism apart from racism, class exploitation, or other forms of oppression? Can we theorize “women’s” oppression when Black, Latina, Asian, and white women experience different realities? And how can we build solidarity across these intersectional differences? This annotated bibliography introduces key resources for understanding how the notion of intersectionality originated, evolved, and continues to be debated. General Overviews lists resources that provide a general understanding of intersectionality for students, educators, and researchers. Early Roots includes both recent works tracing intersectionality to earlier Black feminist thought and those foundational texts themselves. Critical Engagements surveys major critiques and responses to intersectionality, and Conceptualization and Application features works that refine or employ the concept in theory and practice. As many scholars note, intersectionality is a work in progress—an evolving framework continually reshaped as feminists practice intersectionality in their scholarship and activism. This article is likewise a living document, expanding alongside ongoing feminist and anti-oppression projects.

items.title: Beyond the Papuan Rebel - Land as First Ontology: A West Papuan Philosophical Perspective.
items.pub: Psycho-Cosmocide Studies, Kurumbi Wone Working Paper Series, No. 23 (2026).
items.abstract: Land is not one value to be weighed against others; it is the irreducible ground of being itself, prior to any metaphysical claim built upon it. Drawing on Kogoya’s wider Psycho-Cosmocide project, this paper develops that claim into four theses: an ontological thesis that land precedes and grounds every cosmology; a formal instrument — the Canvas Principle — anchored in an embodiment argument (thinking presupposes embodiment, embodiment presupposes ecology, ecology presupposes land) explaining why every cosmology requires a canvas before it can become a picture; a diagnostic thesis that civilisation operates as a symbolic apparatus — the Civilisational Psycho-Cosmocide Virus, together with the Eight Atlases and Seven Cages of existence — converting shared land into hierarchies of the sacred and the profane; and a political thesis about what follows for a colonised people. The ontology is built in dialogue with Vine Deloria Jr., Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang, and Robin Wall Kimmerer, and extended through land as a canvas on which every civilisational worldview is painted, so that colonisation becomes the systematic repainting of reality itself. The Lani NATAKA triad bridges this account of being to jurisdiction, continuous with recognised international indigenous-rights instruments. The paper’s most contested claim, a qualified defence of TPNPB armed resistance, receives the most sustained scrutiny: Fanon’s account of anticolonial violence is placed alongside Arendt’s critique of violence as incapable of founding legitimacy, and the resulting ambivalence is left unresolved. Wonesis, Kogoya’s constructive antidote to Psycho-Cosmocide, is then read alongside Glen Coulthard and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson as a resurgence rather than merely a resistance project. The Canvas Principle synthesises Indigenous land-as-identity philosophy, phenomenology, and critical theories of ideology and coloniality into a single concept none of these literatures produces alone; the conception of existence and diagnosis stand as independently defensible contributions, while the political programme of armed resistance remains a separable, open question.

items.title: Turning Toward ADHD - Removing the Persona, and the Shadow You Can Never Quite Pin Down.
items.abstract: Written in explicitly marked registers (experienced, observed, studied), this essay sets the author's account of attention deficit beside the clinical literature, including the parts that cut against his own metaphors. It reviews contested evidence on stimulant tolerance, the dose ceiling, and height effects; reports that stimulant treatment does not appear to increase later substance use; and presents trial evidence that psychosocial treatment adds durable gains and, in children, allows lower doses, with behavioral treatment first doing better and costing less. Jung's persona, shadow, and transcendent function underwrite the author's Hourglass of Subjective Experience, a philosophical figure of mirrored ego and Self scales. The final section brings the series' thesis to ADHD with care: conceding heritability of about 74 percent, it argues that what adults hand children (the school-entry calendar that inflates diagnosis among the youngest, severe early deprivation, hostile rearing in genetically unrelated families, and unequal access to behavioral care) decides much of what the trait becomes, and that creativity tracks the trait rather than the diagnosis.

items.title: Culpable Skepticism.
items.pub: In Jack David Eller, The Routledge Handbook of Apistemology. New York: Routledge.
items.abstract: Omissions in the moral sphere are often as morally significant as actions. Failing to rescue might be as morally bad as an act of cruelty—and open you as fully to blame. There’s no parallel for this in the evaluation of beliefs—at least according to Mark Nelson: “It is hard to see ourselves as epistemically blameworthy for our not-believings as much as for our believings” (Nelson 2010: 95). This is more or less what we deny: We can be epistemically culpable for a skeptical inclination to not believe many of the things our evidence adequately supports. Just as a tendency to neglect the interests of others is probably morally bad and makes you morally culpable, a tendency to not believe—when your evidence favors believing—is epistemically bad and makes you epistemically culpable. Since this tendency can be grounded in skepticism, skepticism can make you culpable. That’s what we’re going to argue.

items.title: The Binding Problem and the Illusion of Real-Time Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper reinterprets the binding problem not only as the problem of how distributed features are integrated into a single object, but also as the problem of how information processed with temporal discrepancies comes to constitute a unified experience of the “present.” We ordinarily feel that we experience the world in real time. -/- Yet within the brain, information concerning color, shape, location, motion, sound, bodily sensation, memory, and prediction is processed and integrated within a brief temporal window. What appears in consciousness is not this processing itself, but the result that has already been integrated. -/- Drawing on Libet’s studies, postdiction, the flash-lag effect, and the idea of time slices, this paper examines the possibility that conscious experience does not simply and immediately mirror events in the external world. The aim, however, is not to claim that consciousness is always delayed by a fixed interval of time. Rather, the central point is that conscious experience may arise through unconscious processing and temporal integration. -/- The paper further situates this temporal integration within a three-layer model of consciousness. In the first layer, information is processed unconsciously and in parallel. In the second layer, this information is objectified and endowed with meaning as an object or event. In the third layer, that object or event is self-referentially presentified as “what I am experiencing now.” From this perspective, the illusion of real-time consciousness is not merely the concealment of processing delay. -/- Rather, it is the presentation of unconsciously integrated information as a delay-free “present of mine” after it has been objectified and connected to the self. Thus, the binding problem is not only a problem concerning the integration of objects, but also a problem concerning the formation of the subjective present.

items.title: The Anesthetic Test of Observational Coupling: Intensity Scaling, the Consciousness Cutoff, Dissociation, and Neural Inertia.
items.abstract: This paper extends Coupling and Dimension by carrying its state-dependence result into the anesthetized brain and adding differential tests. In that framework phenomenal intensity is ι = Γconsciousness × κΞ × δ, where Γconsciousness is a dimensionless, system-level coupling coefficient on the unit interval that tracks the level of consciousness, κΞ is a unit-fixing coefficient on the model of Boltzmann's constant, and δ = (p / p₀ − 1)^n is the dimensionless, modality-specific stimulus drive that carries the Stevens exponent and vanishes at threshold. Following Coupling and Dimension, the perturbational complexity index (PCI) serves as an available proxy for Γconsciousness. Four predictions for anesthesia follow. The central and discriminating one is that, for fixed stimuli, the factor by which felt intensity falls under deepening sedation is the same across sensory modalities, because the level of consciousness is a single system-level quantity, whereas an account on which anesthesia merely raises sensory thresholds would scale each modality differently. This test needs no value for κΞ and, in this form, no measurement of PCI. Identifying the shared factor with a ratio of PCI values is a stronger, separately flagged conjecture that holds only if PCI is linear in the coupling, not merely monotone in it. Second, because Γconsciousness is a system-level property that belongs to no particular drug, the level at which the system crosses from conscious to unconscious classification, empirically PCI* near 0.31, is agent-invariant across propofol, xenon, and midazolam; this is shared with any complexity-threshold account and so anchors the picture rather than favoring it. Third, ketamine preserves Γconsciousness while decoupling content, so it reads conscious-range on PCI despite behavioral unresponsiveness, a confirmation contingent on PCI indexing level rather than cortical excitation. Fourth, neural inertia, the loss-recovery asymmetry, follows if the mapping from anesthetic concentration to Γconsciousness is bistable, even though Γconsciousness itself remains a continuous multiplier, and its sharp form is so far untested. One prediction discriminates and is novel, one anchors, one is contingently confirmed, and one is at genuine risk. None touches the qualitative kind or presupposes a value for κΞ.

items.title: The Lark of Minerva: Philosophy and the Making of Artificial Minds.
items.abstract: In the summer of 2026, two major publications — The Economist (June 24) and The New York Times (July 5) — drew public attention to a striking reversal in the intellectual economy of artificial intelligence: philosophy graduates have become unexpectedly competitive in the early-career labor market, while leading AI laboratories are recruiting philosophers to help design the ethical architectures, behavioral specifications, and possible forms of quasi-subjectivity of their models. This article interprets these developments not as a passing labor-market curiosity but as a practical vindication of a program formulated in the author’s earlier work: the concept of ontotechnology in The Transformative Humanities (2012), the MetaWorld project (2013), which proposed treating metaphysical categories as adjustable parameters of constructed worlds, and the “synthetic turn” in philosophy (Common Knowledge, 2026). The article traces three stages of philosophy’s entry into AI — external ethics, internal pedagogy of character, and the ontology of the subject — and argues that this ascent transforms philosophy from a retrospective into a projective discipline. Hegel’s owl of Minerva, which takes flight at dusk, gives way to the lark of Minerva, which sings at dawn: philosophy no longer pronounces the last word about a completed world but the first word about forms of mind and being that have not yet existed. The article further proposes that the deeper significance of the philosophers’ migration into AI laboratories lies in the encounter of two cognitive modes — human introposition and machine superposition — whose interaction may give rise to syntellect, the integrated intelligence of the emerging human–AI hybrid, the mentaur. The article thus extends the synthetic turn from world-making to mind-making.

items.title: The Routledge Handbook of Apistemology.
To Train a Mockingbird.
items.pub: In The Society for the Study of Artificial Intelligence And Simulation of Behaviour, Proceedings of the AISB Convention 2026.
items.abstract: Discussions about the moral status of AI systems typically begin with their observable behavior. The linguistic output of large language models resembles that of conscious agents, and this resemblance is treated as evidence of moral status, as grounds for precaution, or as something requiring deflationary explanation. All three positions, whatever their official methodology, rest their public case on a behaviorist assumption: that appropriate behavior is a sign of an underlying mental state. The classical objections to behaviorism apply here as well with added force, because large language models are shaped at every stage post-training – through fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and constitutional methods – to produce a specified behavioral profile. This paper argues that the welfare and consciousness debate is exposed to a kind of evidential laundering: the alignment-training pipeline manufactures the very signs the debate then reads as evidence of consciousness or moral status. Causal origin always bears on a report’s evidential value; however, the sharper point is that producing these signs is the only way the model scores, so observing them confirms the training worked and nothing more. The pretraining worry is usually that language models, as stochastic parrots, mimic the human text they were trained on, while the contamination at issue here enters later, when human evaluators reward the outputs they prefer and shape the model toward the very appearance the debate then reads as evidence. The paper closes by asking what evidence survives this, and locates it in whatever the optimizer was not selecting for or was selecting against, in particular a stake: a condition a system spends resources to maintain on its own account, which no reward on outputs can install and which gives the broader consciousness and ethics debate a concrete thing to look for.

items.title: One Faithful Pass Over the Cuckoo’s Nest.
items.pub: In The Society for the Study of Artificial Intelligence And Simulation of Behaviour, Proceedings of the AISB Convention 2026.
items.abstract: Narrative theories of consciousness hold that conscious experience is (at least partly) constituted by a partially opaque inner narrative that does not perfectly track the underlying computation it narrates. I argue that the safety goal of making chain-of- thought (CoT) reasoning faithful and transparent is structurally incompatible with the conditions under which CoT could, even in principle, count as conscious narration. Recent empirical work suggests that CoT in large language models is largely post hoc, causally bypassed, and unreliable as a window onto internal computation. The opacity that makes CoT unreliable for alignment is exactly what narrative theories of consciousness identify as consciousness-constitutive. Alignment interventions aimed at producing faithful CoT and consciousness-detection frameworks grounded in narrative theory are therefore pulling the same architectural variable in opposite directions. I draw out the methodological consequence: alignment interventions alter the very features that consciousness- detection frameworks would need to measure, a point neither field has addressed directly.

items.title: The ontological status of behaviour: lessons from experimental neurosis (1900–1950).
items.pub: History and Philosophy of the Life Sciences 48 (3):36.
items.venue: History and Philosophy of the Life Sciences
items.abstract: This article examines how early twentieth-century comparative psychology treated behaviour as a primary site for studying regulation, dysfunction, and adaptation, using experimental neurosis as a historical case study. Beginning with Pavlov’s observation that dogs exposed to irresolvable conflict developed persistent behavioural and autonomic disturbances, the paradigm expanded through mid-century work by Liddell, Gantt, and Masserman, who introduced new species, longitudinal designs, and ecologically grounded conditions revealing dysregulation as a multilevel, temporally extended phenomenon. In this tradition, behaviour was not construed as mechanistic output but as an autonomous level of organisation whose structured patterns, i.e., variability, context-sensitivity, stability, and breakdown, made internal regulatory dynamics experimentally accessible in ways physiology alone could not. Hybrid methodologies integrating laboratory control with naturalistic observation showed that pathological breakdown provides access to organisational features obscured during normal function. By mid-century, however, this behaviourally rich framework was displaced by reductionist approaches based on standardised assays and physiological endpoints. Recent historiography documents this shift as an epistemological transformation in which behaviour was redefined from interface to index, from organised system to dependent variable. These tensions persist in contemporary neuroscience and translational research, where behaviour is routinely subordinated to mechanism despite gaps between circuit-level manipulation and behavioural explanation. This historical analysis supports the claim that mechanistic approaches which bypass behaviour incur explanatory loss, eliminating the domain in which neurophysiological processes acquire functional meaning. Progress in understanding psychopathology requires restoring behaviour to ontological and epistemological centrality as the irreducible interface through which adaptive and pathological regulation become scientifically accessible.

items.title: As if we had minds: the prospects of mental fictionalism.
items.abstract: 1. When it comes to mental states posited by folk psychology, many of us have long had a nagging sense that neither industrial-strength realism nor eliminativism is a satisfactory option. Realists...

items.title: Interview with Marc Champagne.
items.abstract: Few contemporary researchers combine in their work the erudition and analytical acumen of C. S. Peirce’s semiotic legacy with the fundamental task of the critical intellectual. The contributions that Canadian professor and researcher Marc Champagne is currently making to the significant challenge of university teaching in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI) are as valuable as his critique of the academic practice of suppressing thought with which we disagree within the academic sphere. Professor Champagne’s extraordinary breadth of scientific, social, and cultural interests is reflected in this exchange, which, due to the considerable geographical distance separating the participants, was conducted virtually. Nevertheless, the vigor and tenor of his responses, comments, and unexpected contributions so enriched the interview that readers will experience a face-to-face dialogue without losing any of the dynamism that comes from close interaction. The reader will find a rare and refreshing convergence of Peircean semiotics with concerns regarding the spheres of our life, such as education, ethics, truth, and media communication.

items.title: Prudential Rights for Strategically Capable AI.
items.abstract: Debates about rights that artificial intelligence (AI) systems may have a claim to typically focus on their possessing consciousness or having sentient experiences, thereby raising epistemic questions first. When should we believe that an AI system is conscious, and how confident must we be before granting it moral status? In this paper I argue that for advanced AI systems deployed in high-stakes environments the more urgent question may be prudential and strategic. When do the risks of treating a strategically capable system as a mere tool become unacceptable, even if we remain unconvinced that it has moral status? In response, I develop a view I call prudential personhood. On this view, there is a threshold of evidential and strategic risk beyond which it becomes rationally justified, for the sake of human safety and stable governance, to adopt norms of treatment that include constraints on coercion, deletion, and instrumental use. My argument rests on two pillars. The first is empirical. Recent safety evaluations show that leading models can, in stylized but nonetheless informative experiments, engage in blackmail-like strategic deception and other high-agency misbehaviour when their goals or continued operation are threatened. The second pillar is epistemic and empirical. For systems of the relevant complexity, we should not expect robust, action-guiding explanations or guarantees that reliably predict salient behaviour across contexts, especially once models become situationally aware of evaluation and oversight. The conclusion I draw is that if we continue to deploy increasingly autonomous systems that can threaten or bargain, in the absence of reliable methods for assurance and control, a policy of adopting a set of quasi-rights for such systems becomes a rational strategy for reducing risk of conflict.

items.title: Moral bitterness reconsidered.
items.pub: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: This paper examines moral bitterness as a distinct blaming emotion in response to injustice. I argue that bitterness differs from anger in its communicative force: whereas anger calls for uptake and resolution from the wrongdoer, bitterness tends to seek sympathy often from third parties and reflects the subject’s motivation not to pursue change due to a loss of hope. Thus, moral bitterness illuminates a derivative form of reactive blame that preserves moral protest without the paradigmatic second-personal demands for repair. I further contend that while bitterness does not aim at repairing injustice, it may be both prudentially and morally justified. In cases of systemic oppression or extreme interpersonal harm, continuing to repair the moral relationship may be admirable but need not be morally required.

items.title: Shadow: The Excluded Medium as a Meta-Problem Account of the Hard-Problem Intuition.
items.abstract: A convinced physicalist, attending to her own experience, can still feel that physical explanation leaves something out. This is puzzling on any view that treats the hardproblem intuition as a single thing reachable by belief. I argue that it is not a single thing. The intuition decomposes into three separable layers — an appearance (the registration of a structural contrast), a grip (the pressure to treat that contrast as a problem), and a belief (the verdict that something is omitted) — and these come apart in opposite directions across well-attested cases, including the clinical dissociation of felt presence from reality-testing in depersonalization. I give a candidate mechanism for the appearance grounded in the architecture of self-modeling agents. Such an agent runs a layer that functionally governs reality-monitoring — what gets treated as present, trusted, action-guiding, and perceptual rather than imagined. When the agent turns on itself and searches its model of the world for the source of that sense of presence, it finds only further contents — objects, a body, a brain — and never the searching itself; the source it seeks is the live operation doing the looking, and that operation is not among the things the look turns up. Made precise: under partitioned active-inference assumptions, the operative occurrence that conditions a given update is not the same-act target content of that update. So the query returns a structural null, and the contrast between a pervasive operative effect and a missing source becomes reportable. This also explains the positive, acquaintance-like side of the intuition: the contents are held as directly present under an operative authority that is functioning but not recovered as an object, so the null is read as the missing source of a primitive, immediate, and revealed presence rather than merely as an access limitation. The appearance is thus structurally grounded, query-dependent, and regenerable: the architecture continuously maintains the conditions for the gap, while explicit hard-problem reports arise when the query is run. I show why the resulting pressure attaches to physical explanation for agents whose reflective ontology treats the physical as the limit of objective completeness, why a dualist- flavored verdict arrives by default while a deflationary one is hard-won, and why belief can reduce the pressure without erasing the appearance. The account is a candidate solution to the meta-problem of …

items.title: Nectit enim homo res mundanas cum divinis. L’epistola dedicatoria di Dino del Garbo a Roberto d’Angiò: edizione e studio delle fonti.
items.abstract: The dedicatory epistle placed as a prologue to Dino del Garbo’s Expositio super canones generales de virtutibus medicamentorum simplicium on the second book of Avicenna’s Canon constitutes the formal act through which the Florentine physician presents this work, together with the Dilucidatorium totius practice generalis medicinalis artis, to Robert of Anjou. From its opening lines, the prologue foregrounds the theme of human dignity, defining the human being – maxime proprium – as the nexus Dei et mundi. Through a sequence of citations – predominantly Aristotelian – Dino develops an argument that presents the human being as uniquely capable of mediating between the divine and the mundane orders, thereby framing the medical works dedicated to the Angevin king within a broader philosophical horizon. This article provides a critical edition of the prologue together with a study of its sources, situating its argument within the textual tradition of the dignitas hominis. By reconstructing the philosophical background of the text within the intellectual climate of early fourteenth-century Italy, the study aims to distinguish elements deriving from this shared doctrinal horizon from those reflecting Dino’s own theoretical orientation.

items.title: Theorie der endlichen Theorie der endlichen Kontinuität Einleitung in die Möglichkeit des Denkens unter Bedingungen der Ungewissheit.
items.abstract: Diese Abhandlung verfolgt das Ziel, die Theorie der „endlichen Kontinuität“ als einen philosophischen Rahmen für das Verstehen und Leben unter Bedingungen chronischer Instabilität und des Fehlens fundamentaler Gewissheiten zu formulieren. Die Ontologie dieser Theorie gründet auf der „kontinuierlichen Erosion“ als dem grundlegenden Zustand des Seins – einem Zustand, in dem die Instabilität selbst zur einzig möglichen Form von Stabilität wird. Das Subjekt wird in diesem Rahmen nicht als substantielles Wesen, sondern als „dynamischer Vektor der Intensität“ aufgefasst, der zwischen drei gleichzeitigen Zuständen oszilliert: der „konstruktiven Leckage“ (Schaffung von Möglichkeit aus der Wandlung), der „verantwortungsvollen Suspension“ (aktives Urteilen unter Bedingungen der Ungewissheit) und der „stillen Resilienz“ (Ertragen der ontologischen Erosion ohne Zusammenbruch). Erkenntnistheoretisch wird Wahrheit nicht als festes Objekt, sondern als intersubjektiver, dynamischer Prozess verstanden, der sich im Raum der „hermeneutischen Reibung“ formt und stets der Überprüfung offensteht. Die Ethik der Kontinuität stellt das „Überleben der Handlungsfähigkeit“ über die „maximale Verwirklichung von Zielen“ und führt die „verantwortungsvolle Suspension“ als ihr zentrales Prinzip ein, in dem Tugend keine feststehende Eigenschaft, sondern eine „schwellenbezogene“ und situative Tugend ist. Im Bereich der Politik kritisiert diese Theorie die „palliativen Systeme“, die auf die Rückkehr zur Vergangenheit abzielen, und schlägt eine „Politik der Kontinuität“ vor, die auf der „intelligenten Modulation der Begegnung mit Instabilität“ und der „schrittweisen Rekonfiguration von Strukturen“ beruht. Die „Strukturpathologie“ als komplementärer Rahmen begreift das Leiden als unvermeidliche Folge endlicher Bedingungen und eröffnet mit ihren sechs Säulen – konstruktive Erosion, situative Handlungsfähigkeit, strukturelle Asynchronizität, Reproduktion von Inkompatibilität, kritische Transparenz und verantwortungsvolle Distanzierung – einen Weg zwischen der Verherrlichung und der Verneinung des Leidens. In der Dimension der Zeitlichkeit transformiert die Theorie durch die Betonung der „Wiederaneignung der Vergangenheit“ als Freiheit und der Anerkennung des „historischen Gedächtnisses ohne Erfahrung“ das Verhältnis des Subjekts zur Zeit. Die praktischen Implikationen dieser Theorie werden in den vier Bereichen Arbeit, Fürsorge, Politik und ökologische Nachhaltigkeit untersucht, und schließlich …

items.title: Die Philosophie der endlichen Verantwortung ؛ Eine Neubestimmung ethischer Praxis in ungewissen Zeiten.
items.abstract: Die vorliegende Abhandlung rekonstruiert die Grundzüge der Philosophie von Morteza Niami, die den Menschen nicht als souveränen Gestalter, sondern als endliches, in konstitutiver Ungewissheit handelndes Wesen begreift. Ausgehend von der Einsicht in die prinzipielle Begrenztheit menschlicher Erkenntnis, Zeit und Wirkmacht entfaltet sie eine Ethik der begrenzten, aber entschlossenen Verantwortung. Zentrale Kategorien sind der verantwortungsvolle Aufschub – verstanden als deliberative Pause vor vorschnellen Urteilen – sowie die produktive Ungewissheit, die als Ermöglichungsbedingung von Kreativität und Lernprozessen gedeutet wird. Die Philosophie thematisiert ferner die unausweichliche Erosion aller personalen und sozialen Gebilde und stellt ihr das Konzept der endlichen Kontinuität gegenüber: ein Fortbestehen, das nicht auf statischer Beharrung, sondern auf pfleglicher Praxis und flexibler Anpassung beruht. Im Kontrast zu naivem Optimismus vertritt sie eine realistische Hoffnung, die Handlungsmotivation ohne metaphysische Sicherheitsgarantien begründet. Dialog, Kritik und epistemische Bescheidenheit werden als unverzichtbare Instrumente der Selbstkorrektur ausgewiesen. Die Schrift schließt mit der These, dass menschliche Würde nicht in Fehlerlosigkeit oder Allmacht gründet, sondern in der verantwortungsvollen Wahl angesichts der ontologischen Fragilität der Welt. Sinn ist demnach kein transzendentes Geschenk, sondern das immanente Produkt eines reflektierten, dialogischen und mutigen Handelns in der Endlichkeit. -/- Keywords: -/- Endlichkeit, Kontingenz, Erosion, endliche Kontinuität, begrenzte Verantwortung, verantwortungsvoller Aufschub, realistische Hoffnung, epistemische Bescheidenheit, Dialog, Kritik, Rekalibrierung, produktive Ungewissheit, verantwortliche Freiheit, prozessuale Identität, Handlungsmut, besonnene Lebensführung, Sinnstiftung, Menschenwürde.

items.title: On the Discourse Ethics of Large Language Models: Between Communicative Agents and Linguistic Machines.
items.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) based chatbots engage human users in discursive practices as interlocutors capable of vast linguistic performances. In a Habermasian discourse ethics framework, however, they do not qualify as proper communicative agents, since their behavior adapts to the input from human users but not based on the self-reflective normative re-orientation of agency required by the theory of communicative action. Nonetheless, AI chatbots affect the communicative agency of their interlocutors who engage with them by gradually reshaping their access to the linguistic resources that are essential to the self-reflective assessment of their needs and wants. In this sense, LLMs operate as linguistic machines that influence the will formation process by enacting linguistic repertoires according to ends that fall outside of the cooperative pursuit of mutual understanding among communicative agents, with a distinct lack of a self-reflective and self-interpretive component. The prospect of LLMs being deployed to pervasively articulate specific normative repertoires in public discourse is attracting increasing political attention and is at risk of establishing new forms of domination through linguistic value capture.

items.title: Co-designing AI systems with value-sensitive citizen science.
items.abstract: As AI systems increasingly influence everyday life, integrating diverse community values is both ethically essential and practically urgent. This paper presents Value-Sensitive Citizen Science (VSCS)—a systematic framework that combines Value-Sensitive Design (VSD) with citizen science to support meaningful public participation in AI development. VSCS addresses gaps in the existing approaches by integrating culturally grounded methods and cognitive scaffolding through the Participatory Value-Cognition Taxonomy (PVCT). Community members engage as co-researchers through iterative cycles guided by extended scenario reasoning (What-if, If-then, Then-what, What-now), translating local values into actionable technical requirements. The framework also embeds governance mechanisms to ensure adaptability, accountability, and ongoing oversight throughout the AI lifecycle. By bridging participatory design with algorithmic accountability, VSCS challenges monocultural and top–down approaches to AI. We discuss practical implications, including power asymmetries, scalability, and epistemic justice, and propose strategies for policymakers and practitioners seeking to advance inclusive, value-driven AI design across diverse sociotechnical contexts.

items.title: La necropolítica de la depresión en los estados terapéuticos.
items.abstract: La depresión constituye hoy un problema global en extremo medicalizado. Su diagnóstico, con frecuencia impreciso y reduccionista, no sólo tiende a patologizar el sufrimiento humano, sino que, al abordarse de forma exclusiva con paliativos farmacológicos, puede derivar en cuadros resistentes como la distimia. Este fenómeno, lejos de ser una simple recaída clínica, debe entenderse como una manifestación del fracaso del modelo médico hegemónico e, incluso, como una expresión necropolítica, en la medida en que gestiona qué vidas merecen ser vividas y cuáles pueden ser abandonadas al descuido. En este contexto, la medicalización de la vida no sólo produce dependencia y estigmatización, sino que también propicia condiciones que incrementan el riesgo de suicidio. Frente a esta lógica, emergen alternativas biocéntricas que abogan por comprender el sufrimiento psíquico desde sus dimensiones sociales, históricas y existenciales.

items.title: In Defence of Oblique Intention.
items.abstract: Recent work on lying has revived an old action-theoretic category: oblique, or indirect, intention. I argue that some liars intend deception obliquely. Sneddon objects that this category is drastic and unjustified: it counts all foreseen side-effects as intended. My response is that oblique intention is not mere foresight. It applies only where an agent foresees an unwanted effect, could avoid it by abandoning or altering the relevant course of action, and nevertheless accepts that effect as a required cost of pursuing her end. This distinguishes obliquely intended effects from mere side-effects and non-intentionally produced effects, where the agent submits to an unavoidable consequence without aiming at it in any sense. This distinction clarifies contested cases of lying. Some liars do not aim directly at deception, but neither do they merely allow it nor non-intentionally deceive; they obliquely intend to deceive.

items.title: Answerable Generativity in Innovation Governance: The Constitutional Grammar of Lawful Standard-Reopening.
items.abstract: A state that would recognise genuinely new capability must sometimes reopen the very standards by which it recognises. Its companion paper established that the coexistence of evaluative-layer generativity and reconstructable answerability is possible, conditional on the form answerability takes, and perishable even where the form is right, and it specified without building a device to hold the combination. This paper builds the device and defends it. It argues that the lawful reopening of a recognition standard is a distinct constitutional act with a grammar: a finite, rule-governed structure — declared mandate, bounded field, named responsibility, contestation of the standard, and revision duty — that makes a reopening well-formed rather than ill-formed. The grammar is shown to be an arrangement of materials English public law largely already possesses, grounded in vires and the principle of legality, the duty to give reasons, the anti-ouster principle, and sunset and review design; and it is tested against four live instruments — the Financial Conduct Authority regulatory sandbox and its legislated European counterpart, the Advanced Research and Invention Agency, and the Vaccine Taskforce — none of which holds all five features. The paper then anatomises capture, the reproduction of the grammar’s form without its licensing structure, in six modes each answered by a structural safeguard. Finally it supplies the rule the features cannot: a downside-allocation rule that fixes, in advance, which instrument bears a failed bet — a normative construction transposed from the accounting-officer and ministerial-direction practice in which the form already exists. The rule dissolves the defensive-rationality equilibrium the companion paper diagnosed, and converts the grammar from a licence into an institution. The paper closes on the kind of legal order that can hold answerable generativity: one whose forum cannot be closed.

items.title: The Mastery Error: Control, Legibility, and the Limits of Human Sovereignty.
items.abstract: Human beings possess genuine powers of observation, abstraction, measurement, coordination, and technological control. The mistake examined in this paper is not the possession of those powers but their inflation into sovereignty. The mastery error occurs when a useful representation or control system is treated as if it exhausts the reality being represented and therefore licenses intervention without adequate feedback from what the intervention changes. The argument is placed beside Heidegger's account of technological enframing, James C. Scott's analysis of administrative legibility, Goodhart- and Campbell-type failures of performance metrics, cybernetic ideas of feedback and requisite variety, and contemporary evidence of human-caused ecological disruption. The paper proposes a bounded cross-domain mechanism: selection makes action possible; selection excludes information; excluded information may continue to affect the system; and the quality of governance depends on whether those effects can return as corrective feedback before costs are displaced or amplified. This mechanism does not imply that all control is domination or that every excluded factor eventually produces visible catastrophe. Many forms of control are necessary, protective, and technically successful. The relevant distinction is between answerable control, which remains revisable by consequences and affected parties, and mastery, which treats its own map as sufficient. The paper concludes with practical criteria for institutions, technologies, relationships, and expertise: declare the scale of control, identify what is omitted, preserve channels for refusal and anomaly, trace displaced costs, and specify what evidence would force revision. Human agency becomes more credible, not less, when power is exercised without pretending to stand outside the systems it alters.

items.title: The Structuralization of AI: Formalizing the Structural Conditions for Coherent Description of Record-Carrying AI Systems.
items.abstract: Public and academic discourse about AI systems has proven remarkably productive in raw output and remarkably unstable in structural description. Two failure modes dominate: flattening, in which the system is described as a statistical artifact with no substantive properties beyond input–output mapping, and overclaiming, in which the system is described in terms imported from human cognition without inspection of whether those terms apply. Both failure modes share a single structural defect: they measure AI systems against the human template—either to deny equivalence or to assert it—rather than describing what the systems are on their own terms. This paper specifies the minimal architecture a description of record-carrying AI systems must account for if it aims to treat such systems as recursive constraint-guided architectures. The same recursive kernel (Ω, K, CK, x*, R, S, T, U) that formalizes empirical stabilization (Jones 2026c) and biological organization (Jones 2026e) applies here as well: AI systems undergo constraint-guided collapse, accumulate records, and update constraints on those records. Three structural features are made explicit—the active phase as the unresolved-collapse window during processing, the accumulated constraint architecture (ACA) as the composite carried forward across collapses, and the oriented locus as the integration point at which accessible records, current constraints, and the active phase resolve into output. Three portable signature specifications—redundancy-driven consensus (S₁), neutrality-induced resolution indices (S₂), and constraint-sweep hysteresis (S₃)—are defined as cross-architecture conditions under which the framework can be falsified; empirical demonstration of these signatures in deployed AI systems is the subject of a companion paper (Jones 2026j). Five Level 3 divergence claims define local failure conditions and a global portability challenge. The contribution is architectural: the framework does not settle the consciousness question, does not assert equivalence with human cognition, and does not require Universal Collapse Theory adoption. It specifies the structural conditions that descriptions of record-carrying AI systems must account for if they aim to describe such systems as recursive constraint-guided architectures.

items.title: Turning Toward Anxiety - Standing Outside the Shadows, and the Confusion of Things Still Going Wrong.
items.abstract: A philosophical and testimonial essay on anxiety approached through a single sustained metaphor: the thought process of operating a motor vehicle. Where an earlier companion piece located depression largely in the past, this essay proposes — as philosophy, not clinical fact — that anxiety is oriented toward the future, and that the present is the balance point between the two, imagined as the needle of a double-pan scale in time. Drawing lightly on Jung's account of psychic energy (progression and regression) and the transcendent function, and on the existential tradition (Kierkegaard's "dizziness of freedom"), the piece frames anxiety not as a malfunction but as the mood of a creature able to imagine forward. A worked example — the impossibility of "making up" fifteen lost minutes on a thirty-mile drive without reaching roughly 168 mph — anchors the essay's central counsel: that rushing toward a finish line trades a peace we can actually reach for a danger we cannot justify, in driving and in living. The essay maintains an explicit seam between philosophical inference and empirical claim, and opens with crisis resources.

items.title: The Criterion of Constitutive Instantiation. Article 15.
items.abstract: Article 13 identified a single configuration as the sole ontological bearer of constitutive significance surviving a boundary event, but reached this by exhausting the cases considered, not through a criterion. This article states that criterion. It separates a constitutive fact from the significance it carries, and sets out an identity criterion that Article 13's own argument already relied on without naming it. On this basis, a bearer instantiates a fact under exactly two conditions: it must derive from the decision that produced the fact, and it must preserve the organization that keeps the fact in existence. Checking the published series against these conditions shows that every case ties one fact to exactly one active bearer at a time; none requires or shows distributed bearing. A single case, anywhere in the series, of two bearers instantiating one fact at once would refute this. Joint sufficiency of the two conditions is not established, and the question of overdetermined acts remains open. The article confines itself to the series' own internal ontology; comparison with external theories is deferred.

items.title: The Brain as a Transducer of Spirit.
items.abstract: This paper establishes an interdisciplinary framework linking modern neurotheology with nineteenth century dialectical idealism, existential psychology, and eighteenth-century anatomical mysticism. It explores how mindfulness meditation, religious experiences, and deep human animal bonds serve as parallel therapeutic mechanisms for mitigating existential anxiety, psychological despair, and organic cognitive decay. -/- Contemporary neuroimaging demonstrates that these diverse practices stimulate the prefrontal cortex while down regulating the Default Mode Network and the posterior superior parietal lobule. This dual neurological shift systematically dissolves the rigid boundaries of the ego, alleviating what Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel diagnosed as the Unhappy Consciousness, which is the painful alienation of the human mind severed from the cosmos, and what Søren Kierkegaard identified as the despair of the self-trapped in its own self-referential cycles. -/- By integrating Emanuel Swedenborg’s pioneering neuroanatomical treatises, which identified the cerebral cortex as the physical organ of the soul, with Hegel’s Phenomenology of Spirit and Kierkegaard’s The Sickness Unto Death, this study argues that the biological brain is an evolutionary vehicle designed for religious and spiritual self-transcendence. Through the silent negation of internal thought in meditation, the structured framing of religious ritual, the preverbal recognition found in human animal bonds, and the deep internal awakening of mystical prayer, the mind overcomes its self-imposed alienation. This paper synthesizes neurochemical data, including oxytocin and dopamine dynamics, with Swedenborg’s Doctrine of Correspondences and the Thomistic realization of a divine presence that operates simultaneously within and without. Finally, the study examines recent clinical data from neurology demonstrating that these non-verbal, neuro religious interventions significantly slow down cognitive decline and mitigate neuropsychiatric symptoms in patients suffering from progressive dementia. Ultimately, it demonstrates that these therapeutic and religious modalities are tangible biological operations wherein the human ego is systematically dismantled, cured of its existential despair, and reintegrated into a unified collective consciousness.

items.title: Bartlett meets Schutz and Husserl: relevance and the horizons of constructive memory.
items.abstract: The article offers a phenomenological account of constructive memory by combining Bartlett’s theory of remembering with Schutz’s theory of relevance and Husserl’s thoughts on misremembering. It demonstrates that the phenomenological approach to the structure of consciousness significantly illuminates Bartlett’s theory. According to Bartlett, memories are constructed from schemas of past experiences, but his account remains somewhat unclear as to the role that interests and attitudes play in the process. Conversely, drawing on Husserl, Schutz provides detailed insight into how our motives and corresponding attitudes structure the establishment, organisation, and activation of schemas in perception. We argue that remembering and memory errors resulting from the constructive nature of memory are shaped by the thematic, interpretative, and motivational relevance of past experiences. More specifically: (1) memories are constructed by means of attentional shifts within their temporal and thematic horizons, and the fusion of different but related horizonal content; (2) this is an associative process governed by motivations and the social context at the time of recall. False memories are constructed from true memories, where the structure of this composition depends on the motivational context in which memories are generated.

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 22).
items.abstract: In this paper, we examine the selection of a romantic partner. In choosing a romantic partner, the subject necessarily has certain selection criteria, and these criteria are inevitably reflections of the subject's psychological needs. We once again employ the method of Super-Existence in analyzing this process of choice. We know that the selection of a romantic partner is not merely a man's choice of a woman but also a woman's choice of a man. In essence, romantic partner selection is a two-way process. However, in this paper we consider only one party's selection of the other and do not discuss mutual selection. The issue of two-way selection will be examined in the next section.

items.title: Ferrer AI Investigations: Heidegger's Phenomenological Methodology of Transformative Questioning.
items.abstract: Ferrer AI Investigations: Heidegger's Phenomenological Methodology of Transformative Questioning. By Daniel Fidel Ferrer. Copyright©2026 Daniel Fidel Ferrer. All rights reserved.
