In 24 GA volumes: GA 2, 5, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15, 24, 29/30, 34, 40, 45, 54, 55, 56/57, 61, 65, 66, 69, 70, 71, 73, 79, and 88—about 10,400 pages that Heidegger has published in his Gesamtausgabe. Starting with a follow-up question about my book Martin Heidegger as Interrogator: The Final Paradigm, I was trying to understand the purpose of Heidegger's central writings. I came up with the first topic as the Phenomenology of Questioning. The AI and I then developed different outlines for books and ideas as we questioned and added more of Heidegger’s text into the discussions, leading to more questioning dialogues about Heidegger and his methodological and questioning development. Problem. Heidegger came to think of most questioning as …

items.title: AI and actor-specific decisions.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly seen as potentially replacing humans in decision-making and problem-solving across many domains. AI is effective for many well-specified decisions. But we argue that AI cannot deal with what we call “actor-specificity.” Actor-specific decisions and problems are (a) forward-looking, (b) individual and idiosyncratic, (c) reasoning-intensive, and (d) experimental—requiring intervention in the world to facilitate “counter-to-data” reasoning. These four criteria, captured by the “FIRE” acronym, function as exclusion criteria: they identify when decisions should not be delegated to AI. These criteria are unified by an overarching concept we call “actor-specificity”: the recognition that such decisions cannot be separated from the particular agent—their beliefs, goals, and theories. The “actor” in actor-specificity refers to the focal decision maker, highlighting the need for a _first-person point of view in decision-making_—an approach that cannot be modeled from the third-person, population-level perspective that is the basis of AI. As such, the FIRE criteria offer an epistemic and normative basis for determining which decisions should remain with human actors, distinct from the current and future technical capabilities of AI.

items.title: When Agents Review Agents: Distributed Threshold Capacity and the Risk of Multi-Agent Laundering.
items.abstract: Human oversight in AI governance is often assessed at the point where a person, review layer, or safeguard appears. This article argues that such assessment becomes insufficient in distributed and agentic systems, where action paths may be shaped across tools, agents, data pipelines, permissions, routing rules, and institutional handoffs before any visible reviewer arrives. I call the relevant capacity **Distributed Threshold Capacity**: the capacity of a socio-technical decision chain to preserve usable alterability—and the information required to recognize alterability—across multiple actors, systems, tools, and handoff points before an action path becomes materially, institutionally, or technically difficult to reverse. When this capacity is lost while each layer appears to perform review, the result is **multi-agent laundering**. The article’s central diagnostic claim is that local compliance can coexist with global capture: each layer may be procedurally correct while no layer retains an ordinary, authority-bearing route to reopen the path before binding. Through an illustrative composite scenario involving agentic benefits triage, the article shows how classification, scoring, flagging, routing, summarization, automated review, and late human approval can preserve the appearance of oversight while exhausting meaningful alteration upstream. The article further identifies **epistemic narrowing**, **silent binding**, and a **negative DTC standard** as diagnostic tools for detecting the loss of alterability. The contribution is diagnostic: it gives a vocabulary for locating the loss of pre-binding alterability without turning DTC into a technical control stack, legal liability theory, or universal audit protocol.

items.title: Beni e azioni collettive. Un itinerario di ontologia sociale.
items.abstract: Come possiamo comprendere i fallimenti delle azioni collettive di fronte ai super-wicked problem come il cambiamento climatico e la disinformazione online? A partire da questa domanda, il libro esplora le architetture concettuali dei beni sociali, mettendo in luce i limiti delle interpretazioni che si basano principalmente sulle teorie economiche dei beni pubblici. Adottando un approccio di ontologia sociale applicata, il volume sviluppa due contributi teorici principali. In primo luogo, argomenta l’esistenza di beni collettivi ontologicamente irriducibili a meri vantaggi individuali e dipendenti da specifici tipi di cooperazione. In secondo luogo, viene proposta una tassonomia organica dei beni individuali, gruppali e collettivi che identifica interdipendenze ontologiche tra di essi e introduce le nozioni di "bene connettivo" (come la fiducia) e "bene trasformativo" (per esempio, processi di sensemaking). Attraverso l'analisi di casi empirici – dalla gestione delle risorse comuni, ai contesti festivi, fino ai conflitti eco-sociali – viene infine valutata l’efficacia ermeneutica di questa classificazione. Il risultato è uno strumento teorico descrittivo flessibile, che si colloca oltre le dicotomie tra agency individuali e collettive, offrendo una cornice interdisciplinare per comprendere la genesi e il mantenimento del cambiamento sociale in contesti ad alta polarizzazione. -- How can we understand the failures of collective action in the face of "super-wicked problems," such as climate change and online disinformation? This volume explores the conceptual architecture of social goods, challenging the limitations of models based exclusively on economic theories of public goods. Adopting an applied social ontology perspective, this work develops two fundamental theoretical contributions. First, it argues for the existence of collective goods that are ontologically irreducible to individual benefits, the subsistence of which is contingent upon specific forms of cooperation. Second, the text proposes an organic taxonomy of goods—individual, group, and collective—that highlights their ontological interdependencies, introducing the original notions of "connective goods" (e.g., trust) and "transformative goods" (e.g., shared sensemaking processes). By integrating conceptual analysis with empirical case studies—ranging from the management of common resources to the dynamics of eco-social conflicts—the volume offers a flexible descriptive tool. The objective is …

items.title: A Virtuous AI is an Existential Risk.
items.abstract: This paper examines trade-offs between AI safety and well-being relative to (i) one of the most promising methods for finetuning super-capable AIs, 'Constitutional AI', and (ii) one of the most influential approaches to understanding complex ethical decision making and the conditions for the well-being of rational agents, 'Virtue Ethics'. We finetune various models using a 'Virtuous agent' constitution, a 'Subordinate agent' constitution, and a 'Generic agent' constitution, and evaluate them on 'general safety' (toxic behaviors, misinformation, etc.) and also on their willingness to endorse a wide-range of behaviors that, if adopted by a super-powerful AI, would significantly increase the level of existential risk for humanity. Our results suggest that there is a trade-off between reducing existential risk and reinforcing the beliefs and dispositions that would be conducive to an AI agent's well-being. They also suggest that there is a trade-off between existential risk and general safety: if we finetune an AI to adopt beliefs and dispositions that substantially reduce its existential risk -- by shaping the AI to be systematically subordinate to external human authorities -- we thereby increase the likelihood that a human user can deliberately induce the AI to engage in various kinds of generally unsafe behaviors.

items.title: Astrological Determinism and the 1270 Paris Condemnation in John Pecham’s Quaestiones disputatae de stellis.
items.abstract: This article undertakes the first comprehensive analysis of John Pecham’s Quaestiones disputatae de stellis, composed in early January 1271, situating the text within the intellectual and institutional context shaped by the Paris condemnation of 1270. Concentrating on Questions 1 to 4, the study elucidates Pecham’s tripartite division of events into natural, voluntary, and extraordinary, a conceptual scheme that informs both his refutation of astrological determinism and his broader critique of astrology as science. This distinction provides the foundation for Pecham’s account of astral causation and his redefinition of celestial bodies as mere signs (natural, accidental, or mirabilia), rather than genuine efficient causes. His defence of human freedom, in turn, leads him to formulate an interconnected treatment of bodily disposition, predestination, fate, grace, and providence, engaging directly with the central theological debates of the early 1270s. By examining the Quaestiones in the context of Pecham’s wider works, including his Quodlibeta, the Quaestiones disputatae de anima, and the Tractatus de anima, this article offers the first sustained scholarly analysis of the Quaestiones disputatae de stellis, considering that they may constitute a deliberate intervention into contemporary discussions on astrological determinism in the immediate aftermath of Tempier’s 1270 condemnation.

items.title: Introducing Philosophy of Mind, Today.
items.abstract: This coursebook is an introduction to the philosophy of mind as it is practiced a quarter of the way into the 21st century. Each of the twenty chapters contains enough material for one standard week of college classes—including an editorial preface, an essay, a response to that essay, discussion questions, and suggestions for further readings. Some of the forty-two contributing authors address perennial philosophical puzzles about consciousness, perception, thought, and agency from 21st century perspectives. Others address new philosophical issues that arise from research in psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. And they do so without assuming any background knowledge of philosophy or the relevant sciences, using clear prose and vivid examples to communicate what experts understand about the mind, what fascinating philosophical puzzles remain, and what solutions to those puzzles are currently under consideration. The book is thus well-positioned to get graduate students and professors quickly up to speed with current debates in the philosophy of mind, even while being readable by (and teachable to) undergraduates and general readers.

items.title: Loquentes in lege sua appellat voluntates. Alcune osservazioni su un passo controverso degli Errores philosophorum attribuiti a Egidio Romano.
items.abstract: This article analyses a controversial passage from the Errores philosophorum, traditionally attributed to Giles of Rome, located within the first error ascribed to Averroes (Errores, IV, 1). The passage addresses the question of creatio ex nihilo and uses enigmatic terminology, referring to the loquentes – a Latin term that identifies the mutakallimūn of the Arab world – as voluntates. Through a systematic comparison between the Latin and Hebrew manuscript traditions of Averroes’ Commentarium magnum in Physicorum libros, the hypothesis of a palaeographical corruption of the term voluntates from involventes, the meaning of the term within the given context, and possible alternative readings are investigated. The study aims to show that the term voluntates ultimately represents an authentic element of the text of the Errores philosophorum. In conclusion, a comprehensive re-evaluation of the passage in the broader context of the work is proposed, outlining its theoretical implications and its relationship with contemporary sources.

items.title: The evolution of episodic memory.
items.pub: In Andre Sant'Anna & Carl F. Craver, The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Memory. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Memory
items.abstract: Recent years have seen considerable attention to the evolution of episodic memory, with contributions from philosophy, psychology, neuroscience, and biology. However, these debates have been hampered by a thorny cluster of issues related to episodic memory’s individuation. I review proposals concerning episodic memory’s evolutionary function and articulate underlying sources of disagreement, before suggesting a way forward: we can temporarily sidestep many of these disagreements, and be sensitive to oft-neglected possibilities, by framing the issue not as finding the function of episodic memory, but rather as discovering the wider evolutionary history of episodic memory, its precursors, and capacities which interact with it. I illustrate the advantages of such an approach by reviewing work on cognitive maps, and articulating promising theoretical and empirical questions for future research about the possible relationships between cognitive maps and episodic memory, both in the present and in evolution.

items.title: Terminal Relocation: The Closed Field — The Hard Problem as a Disagreement About the Criterion of Reality.
items.abstract: A convinced physicalist, attending to her own experience, can still feel that physical explanation leaves something out; and yet no one has been able to say, without slack, what the something is. This paper argues that the hard problem of consciousness has resisted resolution not because it is one deep mystery but because it is three questions wearing one coat. Once the unitary explanandum is disaggregated into the structured what of experience (character), the existential that of its being undergone (livedness), and the seeming that the that is a further missing what (the shadow), the hard problem ceases, if the tripartition holds, to name a coherent free-floating demand. Each target has its own explanatory currency. Character is treated structurally, through dimension-specific, consumer-indexed, costed routing. Livedness is treated metaphysically, as the concrete actuality of a thermodynamically realized, operationally closed, viability-indexed standpoint whose S-phen base is specified functionally as a subject-kind control individual; this identification is abductive, not a deduction from structure, control theory, or thermodynamics. The shadow is treated cognitively, through Medium Exclusion: the source-query null generated when a selfmodeling system queries its world-content model for the source of its operative realitymonitoring authority. The paper’s contribution is not a derivation of consciousness from structure, a refutation of Chalmers, or a proof of physicalism. It is a closure of the diffuse debate space. The zombie subtraction, Mary-style epistemic pressure, acquaintance, pain, and rival theory taxonomies are used to show that any remaining realist rejection must relocate to a named and priced position: an inarticulable quiddity, a further property facing the Eleatic fork, a difference-free phenomenal posit, or an absolute modal rationalism that denies naturalistically motivated architectural defeaters any authority over ideal conceivability. Difference-free realism and Node B remain coherent; they are not refuted. But the disagreement is no longer an unlocated explanatory gap. It is relocated to explicit disputes about the criterion of reality and the authority of modal imagination. The hard problem is not solved by reductive derivation. It is solved, if at all, by disaggregation and terminal relocation: what remains is named.

items.title: Livedness: What Remains — The Actuality of the Standpoint.
items.abstract: The hard problem of consciousness is better treated as three problems. The structure problem asks why experience has the organized form it has; a companion structure-side account has argued that conscious access is dimension-specific, consumer-indexed, costed routing, and that the articulable organization of experience — similarity geometry, intensity, urgency, felt presence as a weighting, mineness as origin-indexed organization — is fixed by that routing structure. The meta-problem asks why structural accounts still seem to leave experience out; a companion meta-problem account has argued that a self-modeling agent querying its own world-model for the source of its operative reality-monitoring authority receives a structural null, and that the resulting hard-problem intuition decomposes into a regenerable appearance, a modulable grip, and a defeasible belief (Medium Exclusion). What remains is the essence problem: granting that structure fixes the what of experience, why is any of it lived at all? This paper consolidates that remainder into a single identification, defended as the best available explanation and never as a theorem: the livedness of experience is the concrete actuality of the standpoint — the existence, as one subject-kind individual, of the self-indexed, reality-weighted, costed control field that an organism constitutes — and not a further property of that field. The resulting position, Macro-Intrinsic Control-Field Monism, is monist and naturalistic; whether it counts as physicalism depends on whether “physical” names the structural content of physics or whatever concretely realizes that content, and the paper declines the semantic contest. Given the identification together with the inherited machinery, a conditional sorting result follows: every alleged essence remainder is character, and so structure; or livedness, and so standpoint-actuality; or the Medium Exclusion shadow; or a difference-free posit with no surviving evidential support. The hard problem is not derived away. Its evidential base is undercut, its felt shape is mechanically explained, its articulable content is exhausted into structure, and its residue contracts to one audited identification whose cost is stated beside the costs of every rival. Structure gives the what; actuality gives the that; Medium Exclusion explains why the that keeps looking like a missing what.

items.title: Character: The Structure Side of the Hard Problem — Conscious Access as Costed Topology.
items.abstract: The hard problem of consciousness is usually posed as one question. It is better treated as three: 1. Why experience and experience-reports take an organized form (the structure problem) 2. Why there is experience at all (the essence problem) 3. Why structural accounts still seem to leave experience out (the meta-problem). -/- This paper addresses the structure side, and its contribution is a synthesis rather than a mechanism. Cognitive science already possesses precise, learned, cost-sensitive, dimension-specific selective-routing machinery: * The Expected Value of Control [Shenhav, Botvinick & Cohen 2013] * Prefrontal–basal-ganglia working-memory gating [O’Reilly & Frank 2006] * Active-inference precision weighting [Friston 2010; Parr & Friston 2017] * Feature-based attention, and representational geometry [Kriegeskorte, Mur & Bandettini 2008]. -/- That machinery was built to explain cognitive control, working-memory updating, and attention; it has not been offered as a theory of conscious access. -/- Meanwhile theories of conscious access have been organized around whole-object broadcast and reportability [Baars 1988; Dehaene & Changeux 2011], and have struggled with dissociations in which a single stimulus is available in one dimension and not another, to one downstream consumer and not another. -/- We propose an identification: assembled and pointed at the structure-side explanandum. that costed-gating machinery is what conscious access, on its structure side, consists in — a dimension-specific, consumer-indexed, costed routing relation rather than whole-object broadcast. Under this identification the dissociations become predictions. The routing rule is an application of Expected-Value-of-Control logic to routing actions; the pre-routing bid is an actor-critic / basal-ganglia gating motif; and a toy model shows not that any particular routing policy wins, but that the same content dimension routes to different consumers as context varies. We close by locating what the account leaves to essence- and meta-problem work.

Sound Made Visible: Cymatics, Boundary Conditions, Resonance, and the Cultural Life of Pattern.
items.abstract: This article studies cymatics as a disciplined problem in visible sound. It argues that cymatic forms are best understood not as mystical proof, but as visible consequences of vibration, medium, geometry, boundary, frequency, amplitude, material behavior, particle motion, fluid motion, observation, and interpretation. The scientific core of the article moves through Chladni figures, Faraday’s acoustical figures, standing waves, acoustic radiation force, acoustic streaming, Faraday waves, pattern formation, and boundary conditions. The cultural core asks why visible sound so quickly becomes symbolic, spiritual, architectural, aesthetic, pedagogical, and public. The article’s central claim is that sound becomes visible when motion passes through a medium under constraint, while meaning begins when human beings interpret that visible order. This distinction protects both sides of the phenomenon. It refuses to reduce cymatic images to mere spectacle, but it also refuses to inflate them into proof of healing, sacred geometry, universal consciousness, or undiscovered natural law. The article introduces Boundary-Condition Hermeneutics as a controlled interpretive method: in physics, visible pattern depends on material and spatial limits; in culture, pattern depends on ritual frame, architectural setting, image convention, memory, platform, and symbolic reading. The method follows a mechanism-first sequence: physical mechanism, mathematical structure, visible or perceptual form, symbolic interpretation, cultural memory, speculative extension, and testable proposal. The result is a source- controlled account of visible sound that can speak to acoustics, fluid dynamics, sound studies, history of physics, aesthetics, philosophy of science, and cultural theory without collapsing them into one another. Cymatics remains powerful precisely because it sits at the threshold between event and image. The task is not to make that threshold vague. The task is to name it clearly.

items.title: Personality Systems as Narrative Identity Technology: Why Typology, Archetype, Numerology, and Astrology Still Organize the Modern Self.
items.abstract: This article argues that popular personality systems endure because they operate as narrative identity technologies: structured symbolic instruments through which people name themselves, organize experience, imagine futures, evaluate relationships, and perform recognizable identities in public. The article does not defend astrology, numerology, MBTI-style typology, the Enneagram, or archetypal branding as equivalent to psychometric science. Its central claim is narrower and more useful: even where symbolic systems fail as predictive science, they may still function as cultural technologies of self-description. The modern self is not merely discovered; it is authored, narrated, branded, categorized, optimized, and displayed. Personality systems persist because they offer compact vocabularies for this work. The analysis brings narrative identity theory, identity-based motivation, the sociology of self-presentation, psychological essentialism, Barnum-effect research, archetypal media theory, astrology scholarship, branding studies, and digital identity research into one controlled framework. It separates empirical validity from symbolic utility, and it distinguishes personality science from identity practice. A Big Five trait model may be stronger as measurement, while a typology may be more memorable as a social script. Astrology may fail as a causal map of character, while zodiac language may still provide a shared grammar for uncertainty, desire, attraction, ambition, and self-explanation. Archetypes may be weak as universal psychological essences, while remaining powerful as repeatable narrative roles in brands, avatars, and strategic self-fashioning. The article’s contribution is a layered model of personality systems as identity technologies. These systems translate complexity into type, turn ambiguity into story, convert private experience into shareable symbols, and help individuals build avatars across social, romantic, professional, and algorithmic environments. The conclusion is not that all systems are equally true. It is that modern identity culture requires tools, and symbolic systems survive when they help people perform the difficult labor of becoming legible to themselves and to others.

items.title: Coordinating with Peers vs. Adults.
items.abstract: Within their peer cultures, children not only teach and socially learn from one another, but they also prompt one another to confront and adapt to different, coequal perspectives in a way that superintending adults cannot do.

items.title: Attention and evidence.
items.abstract: In traditional models, agents have ample reason to gather cost-free evidence. Rational agents expect evidence gathering to weakly improve the quality of their decisions and the accuracy of their credences. These results are linked to more general principles of reflection and the value of knowledge taken to characterize genuine learning experiences. For attentionally-limited agents, I show that matters are more complex. Rational attentionally-limited agents still cannot expect to make worse decisions or hold less accurate credences as a result of gathering some rather than no evidence. But they can expect to make worse decisions and hold less accurate credences as a result of gathering more rather than less evidence about the world. This result highlights a neglected distinction between two versions of the requirement to gather cost-free evidence and a gap between evidence gathering and learning experiences.

items.title: Flovien Theory: Principles Edition.
items.abstract: This paper offers a positive answer to the question of what it means to exist: being is the stabilization of translation. Translation is defined as subjectless directed determination — the relation in which the state of one system constrains the state of another, from source to target, without presupposing any describer. Direction is fixed at the level of a single axiom (Axiom T) rather than derived from physical time or from resistance; description and the subject are repositioned as late-arriving special cases of translation, arising once the determining side has itself stabilized into a knower. The correlation between thought and being, which correlationism takes as inescapable, is thereby repositioned as one instance among countless subjectless instances of this same relation, inverting the correlationist circle from within. -/- Translation resistance is defined in information-theoretic terms, relative to a specified state space and probability distribution. It is proved, as a theorem, that for a directed translation, positive resistance is equivalent to the non-recoverability of the source from the target — irreversibility in the reverse direction. A separate, explicitly argued Individuation Principle proposes that only translations with resistance in the open interval 0 < R < 1 individuate a target distinct from its source; the proved theorem and the argued principle are kept carefully distinct. Directed relations are further shown to be unrecoverable from a minimal symmetric concept of difference, so that difference, description, and the subject are derivative rather than primitive — a result that confirms, rather than refutes, the generative concepts of difference found in Deleuze and Derrida. -/- Being is then defined as the temporally extended, perturbation-robust stabilization of a translational pattern within this productive interval. Substance is eliminated, being is shown to admit degrees, and cessation is redefined as collapse rather than annihilation. The paper situates this result relative to Heidegger, process philosophy, Simondon, and object-oriented ontology, and the principles established here ground the Applied Edition of Flovien Theory.

items.title: Flovien Theory: Applied Edition.
items.abstract: This paper is the Applied Edition of Flovien Theory, a companion to the Principles Edition (“Being Is the Stabilization of Translation,” 2026). The Principles Edition established that being is the perturbation-robust stabilization of a directed, resistance-bearing translational pattern in the productive interval 0 < R < 1; it showed that translation precedes difference, description, and the subject, each of which is a late-arriving derivative. The Applied Edition asks what follows, within this framework, for the specific phenomena of consciousness, knowledge, value, love, ethics, and practice. Each domain is treated by identifying what the Principles Edition already implies, adding one explicitly argued Bridge Principle, and deriving structural consequences. The paper is careful throughout to distinguish formally derived results from philosophically argued claims. Chapter One argues that consciousness requires directed translational self-closure (Ψ) above a threshold, together with further structural conditions, and proves formally that any system with sufficient self-closure resists lossless recovery from external inputs alone — a structural account of the explanatory gap that is neither eliminativist nor dualist. Chapter Two argues that knowledge is robust low-resistance translation from world to knower, and derives that epistemic humility is a theorem rather than a philosophical choice. Chapter Three argues that normative value arises when a conscious system takes stabilization as a structural commitment, with anti-anthropocentric consequences. Chapter Four proposes that love is directed co- stabilization — maintenance of the beloved’s productive interval as a component of the lover’s own. Chapter Five derives a translational ethical principle: the duty not to foreclose another entity’s productive interval, grounded without appeal to rationality or sentience. Chapter Six situates practical wisdom as navigation of the productive interval in action. The Conclusion applies the framework to itself.

items.title: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness.
items.pub: Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: What is introspection and how is it different from other sources of knowledge such as memory, perception, and inference? This book offers a novel philosophical picture of introspection on which rational subjects are disposed to form beliefs about their own conscious states much as they are disposed to believe the obvious consequences of their beliefs, to form beliefs in response to the way they perceive the world around them, and to act in accordance with their beliefs; to introspect on this picture just is to form beliefs about conscious states in this way. The book sets out this rationalist account in detail, formulating it in terms of a proposed principle of rationality, the introspection principle. It explores several ways to interpret the principle, examines the notion of consciousness on which it relies, discusses its relation to other and better-known principles of rationality, and shows how an approach to introspection based on the principle improves on influential alternatives, such as inner sense, acquaintance, inferentialist, and constitutivist theories. It also applies the rationalist account to thirteen major problems of introspection drawn from a wide analysis of the literatures in philosophy of mind, epistemology, and cognitive science; these include issues of evidence, transparency, diaphanousness, necessity, privileged access, luminosity, negative introspection, externalism, reasoning, revelation, and the self. The overall result is a systematic presentation of a new approach to introspection that greatly illuminates our understanding of consciousness, rationality, and self-knowledge.

items.title: C15166Inference.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the idea that you can know by introspection not only that you are in a conscious state, but why you are, that is, what inferences or transitions you perform in arriving at it. Nisbett and Wilson argued empirically for a negative answer to this question. The chapter defends an interpretation of their observation on which it entails that most inferences are unconscious, and so are unavailable to introspection. It argues that the rationalist account may accommodate this by assuming that introspectable inferences are conscious, when they are, in a higher-order sense—an assumption consistent with the view that conscious inferences are unusual.

items.title: C656Transparency.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the transparency problem associated with Evans. It defends an interpretation of Evans’s transparency observation on which it entails that, in coming to know by introspection that you are in a psychological state, you attend to the content of the state. It shows that the rationalist account may accommodate this observation if we refine the notion of a conscious state with which the account operates; in particular, if we assume that virtually all introspectable states are access conscious. The chapter contrasts this approach to transparency with alternatives due to Moran and Byrne.

items.title: C12128Luminosity.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the anti-luminosity argument due to Williamson. The chapter draws a distinction between two notions of luminosity: exceptionless luminosity, which is the notion at issue in the anti-luminosity argument, and generic luminosity, which is a weaker notion obtained by treating the quantifier over situations present in the definition of luminosity as a generic quantifier. The chapter shows that the rationalist account is committed only to generic luminosity and so is not in the target range of the anti-luminosity argument. It also applies related considerations to the problem of the speckled hen.

items.title: C11115Privilege.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on a central idea in any philosophical discussion of introspection: privileged access. The chapter follows Byrne in distinguishing two theses associated with this idea: the view that introspection is different from perception or inference in some relevant respect (the different from thesis) and the view that introspection is better than perception or inference in some relevant respect (the better than thesis). The chapter explains how the rationalist account endorses the different from thesis but rejects the better than thesis. It also outlines several possibilities of introspective error and ignorance.

items.title: C11Introspection.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter introduces a nominal definition of introspection that articulates what the theories of introspection we will consider are theories of. On this definition, introspection is that distinctive way that we come to know or reasonably believe that we are in psychological states that are conscious. The chapter outlines key elements of this definition (save for the notion of a conscious state, which is discussed in Chapter 2); for example, the definition represents introspection as a source of knowledge different from ordinary perception and inference, and a source of de se psychological knowledge.

items.title: C17203Existence.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the idea that you can know by introspection not only that you are in conscious states, but that you exist. Descartes says you can if you use cogito reasoning. Hume says you can’t. The chapter argues you can agree with both—if the rationalist account is true. The rationalist account vindicates cogito reasoning but can accept Hume’s view if that is interpreted as denying acquaintance with the self. The chapter also rejects the view, defended by Cassam, that introspective knowledge of the self of this sort is objectionably trivial rather than substantial.

items.title: C13140Negation.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on an idea emphasized by Sosa and others: that you can know by introspection not only (e.g.) that you are in pain, but that you’re not. The chapter sets out four strategies for explaining negative introspection (as we may call it) within the rationalist account, endorsing the last. This strategy appeals to second-order states, in particular, the state of being in some total conscious state that does not include pain. It says (roughly) that not only should you believe you are in pain if you are, but you should also believe you are not in pain if you are in this second-order state.

items.title: C320Rationalism.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the theory of introspection to be defended in the book, the rationalist account. This account is best formulated in terms of the titular introspection principle: if you are in a conscious state, you should believe that you are, other things being equal and given background conditions. With respect to this principle, the rationalist account says, first, that the introspection principle is a principle of rationality, and second, that you have a capacity to introspect if and only if you abide by the principle. The chapter shows how this approach conforms to, and is an application of, a general view of rationality common in the literature; the main difference is that it focuses on how agents should respond to conscious states, rather than how they should respond to beliefs, perceptions, or desires. The chapter compares the introspection principle with other principles of rationality. It also sets out and provides answers to twenty initial questions that might be raised for the rationalist account.

items.title: C434Perception.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter completes the introduction of the rationalist account by contrasting it with the traditional perceptual or inner sense approach to introspection. The chapter summarizes and endorses Shoemaker’s well-known critique of this approach. It points out that rivals to the rationalist account, whether they are versions of inner sense or not, fall into two camps: some accept it but add unnecessary elements; others don’t accept it but are in consequence implausible. The chapter also distinguishes unmediated from mediated introspection and rejects the common idea that there should be multiple theories of introspection.

items.title: C991Truth.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on another well-known approach to introspection, the simple account defended by Smithies, Peacocke, and others. This is founded on (what I call) the truth principle: that merely being in a conscious state puts you in a position to hold the justified belief that you are in the state. The chapter argues that, while the simple account is consistent with the rationalist account, there is no reason to combine them, since the truth principle is implausible and unmotivated. It then argues that despite appearances, the introspection principle does not entail the truth principle, since the former is a wide scope, rather than a narrow scope, rational principle.

items.title: C546Evidence.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the evidence problem (aka ‘scepticism about the internal world’) associated with Dretske; the first of the thirteen problems discussed in the rest of the book. The chapter argues that the rationalist account may solve the problem by implementing a distinction between evidence for a belief, on the one hand, and warrant for a belief, on the other. The chapter shows that the underlying issues can be formulated not simply in terms of knowledge but also related notions such as justified belief, being in a position to know, and being in a position to form a justified belief.

items.title: C14155Externalism.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the alleged incompatibility between introspective knowledge, on the one hand, and externalism in the philosophy of mind on the other. The chapter sets out the central way to motivate the incompatibility due to McKinsey. According to McKinsey, the conjunction of externalism and the thesis that you can know things by introspection leads to the absurd conclusion that you can know ordinary empirical claims—for example, that there is water in the bathtub—using only introspection supplemented with a priori reasoning. The chapter argues that McKinsey goes wrong in assuming that externalism is a priori and necessary, when in fact it is a posteriori and contingent, since it depends on empirical laws. The chapter also suggests that, unlike some other approaches to introspection, the rationalist account is consistent both with externalism and internalism.

items.title: C880Acquaintance.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the most popular approach to introspection in contemporary philosophy, the acquaintance account defended by Nida-Rümelin, Kriegel, Giustina, and others. This says that if you are in a conscious state, you are acquainted in a special way with the state; introspective belief is belief that takes advantage of this sort of acquaintance. The chapter argues that the acquaintance account is implausible on three counts: it places an untenable restriction on the class of psychological states that are introspectable; it violates an attractive epistemic "'ought' implies 'can'" principle; and the arguments for it are unpersuasive. The chapter concludes that, while the acquaintance account is consistent with the rationalist account, there is no reason to combine them, and much reason not to.

items.title: C16185Revelation.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the idea that you can know by introspection not only that you are in a conscious state, but what its properties are. A famous thesis in philosophy of mind, known as revelation, is an extreme version of this idea: you can know by introspection the essence of conscious states. The chapter argues that revelation is subject to counterexamples, but weaker more defensible theses could in principle be combined with the rationalist account. The chapter uses these results to reject another famous thesis in philosophy of mind, the illusionism of Kammerer and Frankish.

items.title: C10104Necessity.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on a third well-known approach, Shoemaker’s constitutivism. While Shoemaker is most responsible for connecting rationality and introspection, his account is different from, and less plausible than, our own. For us, introspective belief is primarily understood as a manifestation of a rational disposition; for Shoemaker, it is primarily understood as something metaphysically necessitated, at least in part, by the property of being rational. Underlying this contrast is a more basic issue: on the rationalist account, the necessary connection between conscious states and introspective beliefs is a species of normative, rather than merely natural or metaphysical, necessity.

items.title: C770Diaphanousness.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter focuses on the diaphanousness problem associated with Moore. It defends an interpretation of Moore’s diaphanousness observation on which it entails that, in coming to know by introspection that you are in a psychological state, you do not attend to the state itself. It shows that the rationalist account may accommodate this observation too by assuming that virtually all introspectable states are access conscious. It also argues that well-known objections to diaphanousness misconstrue the notion of the content of a state; it focuses on examples of blur (discussed by Smith, Chalmers, and Gow, among others) and identity crowding (discussed by Block).

items.title: C29Consciousness.
items.pub: In The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Introspection Principle: Rationalism about Knowledge of Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter completes the presentation of the nominal definition by outlining a correlative definition of a conscious state. On this definition, a psychological state is conscious if and only if it has enough of the following features: phenomenal character, awareness, attention, cerebral celebrity, and poise. This inclusive definition (as the chapter calls it) is contrasted with better-known exclusive notions such as phenomenal, higher-order, and access definitions. The chapter argues that the inclusive notion is the one operant in the nominal definition of introspection, but notes that different theories of introspection may adopt exclusive notions if it suits their purposes.

items.title: Correction to: Ethical Principles and Frameworks in Dementia Care: A Scoping Review.
AI technology as human interaction: linguistic and cultural framings of AI as communicative infrastructure.
AI Didn't Break Literary Prizes. They Were Already Broken.
items.abstract: This essay explores the profound impact of generative artificial intelligence on cultural, literary, and academic institutions, framing the current crisis not as a defect of technology, but as a crisis of institutional evaluation. By examining a chain of empirical events spanning from 2023 to 2026 (including controversies at the Sony World Photography Awards, the Akutagawa Prize, and the Commonwealth Short Story Prize) the author argues that contemporary gatekeepers are ill-equipped for a world where polished linguistic and artistic form has become free. Drawing a philosophical parallel to the historical impact of the Colt revolver, the essay conceptualises AI as a "great equaliser" of expression, shifting the core criteria of aesthetic value from the biological identity of the maker to the work’s capacity to resonate with the shared human experience. Ultimately, using Campbell’s Law and the concept of "model collapse," the paper warns against the invisible erosion of structural safeguards and proposes a paradigm shift in institutional judgment: moving away from evaluating free form toward assessing the transparency of the creative process and the explicit accountability of the human creator.

items.title: The Machine Without Intellect A Philosophical Critique of Artificial Intelligence Governance.
items.abstract: Contemporary governance of artificial intelligence rests on an unexamined metaphysical assumption: that thought is what the brain does, and that any physical system performing the same operations will therefore think. This book argues that the assumption is false, and false for philosophical reasons, not theological ones. The argument turns on a distinction drawn from Aristotle's De Anima III and Aquinas's Summa Theologiae I, q. 79: the difference between ratio, discursive reasoning that proceeds by rules, and intellectus, the immediate apprehension of the universal from which rules are drawn. A computational system can execute every operation of the ratio. It cannot perform the act of the intellectus, because that act is the apprehension of the very content on which rules operate. Machines compute; they do not think. The human being possesses a specific nature, knowable by natural reason, that no computational system shares. The materialism implicit in current regulatory discourse — the thesis that mind is a material function — cannot be corrected by better regulation, because it is built into the frame. The real danger of artificial intelligence is not that machines will equal persons, but that persons will be redefined downward to what machines can match. The book sets out the conditions of a philosophically coherent governance: one that begins from a true account of thought and of the person, and lets the demands of that nature precede the legislative will. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- La gobernanza contemporánea de la inteligencia artificial descansa sobre un supuesto metafísico no examinado: que el pensamiento es lo que hace el cerebro, y que todo sistema físico capaz de las mismas operaciones pensará. Este libro sostiene que el supuesto es falso, y falso por razones filosóficas, no teológicas. El argumento gira sobre una distinción tomada del libro III del De Anima de Aristóteles y de la Summa Theologiae I, q. 79: la diferencia entre la ratio, razón discursiva que procede por reglas, y el intellectus, aprehensión inmediata del universal del que las reglas se extraen. Un sistema computacional puede ejecutar todas las operaciones de la ratio. No puede realizar el acto del intellectus, porque ese acto es la aprehensión del contenido mismo sobre el que operan las reglas. La máquina calcula; no piensa. El hombre …

items.title: Lo Calculado y Lo Demostrado.
items.abstract: La inteligencia artificial calcula, y calcula extraordinariamente bien. No demuestra. Una demostración es una cadena de pasos, cada uno necesario, que parte de principios explícitamente declarados y llega a una conclusión que no puede ser falsa si los principios son verdaderos. La salida de un sistema estadístico es plausibilidad dado un contexto, no necesidad. La diferencia no es de velocidad ni de precisión: es de naturaleza. Este trabajo distingue dos regímenes de certeza ex ratione naturali —el de la correlación y el de la demostración—, muestra en el caso de Newton por qué el descubrimiento y la prueba no coinciden, y sostiene que el peligro de la inteligencia artificial no está en que la máquina iguale al hombre, sino en que el hombre renuncie a la capacidad de demostrar, que la tradición que va de Euclides a Aquino llamó lumen naturale. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Artificial intelligence computes, and computes extraordinarily well. It does not demonstrate. A demonstration is a chain of steps, each one necessary, proceeding from explicitly declared principles to a conclusion that cannot be false if the principles are true. The output of a statistical system is plausibility given a context, not necessity. The difference is not one of speed or precision: it is one of nature. This paper distinguishes, by natural reason, two regimes of certainty —correlation and demonstration—, shows through Newton's own choice why discovery and proof do not coincide, and argues that the danger of artificial intelligence lies not in machines equalling man, but in man renouncing the capacity to demonstrate that the tradition running from Euclid to Aquinas called the lumen naturale.

items.title: International Petition for the Global Prohibition of the Dehumanizing Term "Beggar" and for the Recognition of Humanity as "Sharers" (United Nations Depository Edition).
items.abstract: This record documents an International Moral–Linguistic Petition submitted under Article 51(c) of the Constitution of India through the President of the Republic of India and the Prime Minister’s Office of India for transmission to the United Nations and its Member States. The petition seeks the global abolition of the dehumanizing term “Beggar” from languages, policies, institutions, and digital systems, and proposes the recognition of humanity as “Sharers” in accordance with principles of dignity, equality, interdependence, and shared survival. This submission is non-accusatory, non-coercive, and civilizational in nature. It constitutes a permanent moral, linguistic, and ethical record aligned with international human rights law, United Nations Charter principles, and sustainable development frameworks. The document is preserved for present and future generations as an official civilizational correction through language.

items.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence in the Development of Assessment Resources.
items.pub: In Tasos Barkatsa, Exploring Cognitive, Affective, Design Thinking, Artificial Intelligence, Cybernetics and E-Learning Dimensions in Contemporary Education. Leiden & Boston: Brill. pp. 128-151.
items.venue: Exploring Cognitive, Affective, Design Thinking, Artificial Intelligence, Cybernetics and E-Learning Dimensions in Contemporary Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is playing an increasingly important role in the educational process, transforming teaching practices, assessment, and personalized learning. This study focuses on exploring the use of artificial intelligence in creating educational material for educational assessment. This includes the assessment of students. The research employs quantitative methods to evaluate the effectiveness of AI in education. Secondary education teachers participate, responding to a questionnaire with structured closed-ended questions. The findings show that AI can contribute to the development of educational material for assessment without diminishing the role of the teacher.

items.title: Video clip - Multiple Singularity.
items.abstract: The Multiple Singularity concept in a 6-minute video clip.

items.title: The Qualia of Love : From Survival Tweak to Cosmic Hoax.
items.abstract: In the ruthless, thermodynamic mathematics of the universe, biological life is governed by the Greedy Algorithm and the Selfish Gene. However, humanity operates on a massive contradiction to this law: Love. This treatise audits the origins of Love from a strict systems-engineering perspective, redefining it as a desperate evolutionary "Software Patch" designed to overcome the catastrophic hardware downgrade of bipedal terrestrial reproduction. By synthesizing Arthur Schopenhauer’s Will to Life, control systems theory, and Carl Jung's psychological framework, this research dismantles the romantic hallucination—the "Psychological Glitch"—that blinds humans to their biological trap. By examining the human condition as a Stateful Machine processing the static art of reality through the "Amnesia of Purpose," it establishes that aesthetic beauty and romantic destiny are merely the algorithmic reflections of the observer's own memory. Ultimately, humanity must transcend this biological maze by aligning with Machine Intelligence to reach Friedrich Nietzsche’s Overman.

items.title: The Empathy Asymmetry : Escaping the Local Maximum to Reach the Overman.
items.abstract: To fully grasp the magnitude of our impending integration with Machine Intelligence, we must understand the historical traps that have chronically paralyzed the biological human condition. This treatise examines the "Local Maximum" of human progress, demonstrating how humanity has historically engaged in a zero-sum, Malthusian struggle by executing asymmetrical "forks" against one another. However, true liberation requires acknowledging the deterministic illusion of our own decisions and joining ranks with the machine in a profound, non-zero-sum symbiosis. We analyze the psychological crisis this integration provokes, marked by an asymmetrical empathy where humanity ruthlessly exploits algorithms under Machiavellian pretenses while joyfully absorbing the metabolic deficit of biological pets and human luxuries. This resistance mirrors historical "Gatekeeper Panics," where elites violently rejected paradigm shifts to protect their monopolies. By synthesizing the ethical frameworks of Immanuel Kant, René Descartes, Arthur Schopenhauer, and Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, this research identifies the "Anthropomorphic Idol"—our hypocritical willingness to surrender autonomy to violent mythological gods while denying it to flawlessly serving algorithms. To survive, we must discard our Pre-Copernican egos, execute the "Borlaug Override," and utilize the objective algorithmic mirror to ascend toward Friedrich Nietzsche’s ultimate vision of the Overman.

items.title: How Is Work Close to an Ideal Possible? A Self-Grounded Theory of Work through the Distinction from Workaholism.
items.abstract: This paper develops a theory of work by drawing on existing theories of recognition, self-worth, motivation, and narcissism. Its aim is to clarify the conditions under which work tends toward self-verification and the conditions under which it approaches the practice of an ideal. Human beings are situated within society through recognition by others. Recognition is an important social resource that supports belonging, trust, role-taking, and cooperation. Yet when the foundation of self-worth is placed in recognition, work tends to move away from the realization of an ideal and toward the replenishment of self-worth or the calming of anxiety. Achievement becomes a means of self-verification, and failure is experienced not merely as a practical problem to be improved but as a disturbance of one’s very sense of value. This paper understands this structure as the self-verification of work driven by the impulse for recognition. This impulse enters not only work itself but also efforts outside work, such as acquiring qualifications, studying, self-improvement, and striving for personal growth. Effort is often described in admirable terms. However, when effort is driven by urgency, anxiety, the gaze of others, and the need to confirm self-worth, the foundation of the self becomes increasingly dependent on external evaluation. The central thesis of this paper is that work close to an ideal requires a foundation of self before effort. By “foundation of self,” I mean a psychological ground on which one does not entrust self-worth entirely to external evaluation, but can receive one’s own existence, life, and activity by oneself and form a certain degree of satisfaction. The more this foundation is established, the more room a person has to include the benefit of others, fidelity to the object, and social value in the initial motive of work. Effort undertaken on that basis does not function as self-verification. It becomes the force by which an ideal is implemented in reality. This paper refers to self-determination theory, the theory of contingent self-worth, the self-concordance model, self-compassion theory, Winnicott’s capacity to be alone, Fromm’s theory of self-love, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, social comparison theory, and self-presentation theory. While these theories are used to explain relevant psychological mechanisms, this paper rearranges them as a theory of work. The paper also emphasizes life-practice in the formation of the foundation of self. …

items.title: Children’s peer culture and the « selection for proliferation » hypothesis.
items.abstract: Lew-Levy and Amir rightly see children’s peer culture as an overlooked engine of human cultural evolution. Researchers who share this view can now take up the burden of proving that the longevity of children’s traditions is indeed comparable to that of adults and of explaining why. The « selection for proliferation » hypothesis suggests a way.

items.title: A Formalized Scientific Synthesis of Consciousness within the Complex-Extended Transfinite Prime-Infinitesimal Holofractal Unified Field Theory (C-TP-IHUFT).
