items.title: Variable cultural acquisition costs may explain contextual variation in peer cultures.
items.abstract: Lew-Levy and Amir highlight contextual variation across both traits and societies in the influence of childhood peer cultures on mainstream adult culture. I suggest that this contextual variation can be explained in part by variable cultural acquisition costs, where some traits (e.g., technology) and societies (e.g., post-industrial) comprise accumulated cultural knowledge that is too costly for children to acquire.

items.title: 191C9Knowing That I Am in Pain.
items.pub: In Giovanni Merlo, Giacomo Melis & Crispin Wright, Self-Knowledge and Knowledge A Priori. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: How does one know that one is in pain? Pain is the philosopher’s favourite example of a sensation, so it is surprising that this question hasn’t received much attention. The chapter approaches this question via the metaphysics of pain. According to the perceptual theory of pain, when one feels a pain, one (usually) perceives a disturbance in one’s own body. The perceptual theory is very plausible. However, perceptual theorists typically add to it the claim that disturbances—the objects of ‘pain perception’—are not pains. This is wrong. Once this error is corrected, the perceptual theory of pain leads naturally to a ‘transparent’ theory of the first-person epistemology of pain (as defended in Byrne, Transparency and Self-Knowledge). One striking consequence of this theory is that a seemingly self-evident proposition—that there are no hallucinations of pain—is false.

items.title: 253C12‘I’, My Self, and My Mental States.
items.pub: In Giovanni Merlo, Giacomo Melis & Crispin Wright, Self-Knowledge and Knowledge A Priori. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: The concern of this chapter is the relation between privileged self-knowledge and the metaphysical nature of mental states. The starting point will be two classical dilemmas—a semantic dilemma due to Elizabeth Anscombe, which concerns uses of ‘I’ as subject and self-identification, and a metaphysical dilemma due to Rorty concerning so-called first-person authority and the mental/nonmental divide. Section 12.1 outlines Anscombe’s dilemma and a non-Cartesian way of avoiding it. Section 12.2 discusses Rorty’s dilemma and explains the positive motivation for the chapter’s preferred, neo-expressivist way of addressing it. The discussion in these two sections is aimed at bringing some striking structural parallels between these two dilemmas. In Section 12.3, the chapter explores some ways that the appeal to the notion of expression can help us articulate a non-Cartesian and broadly naturalistic conception of the special relation we have to our own states of mind and of the mental/nonmental divide.

items.title: 1C1Self-Knowledge and Knowledge A Priori.
items.pub: In Giovanni Merlo, Giacomo Melis & Crispin Wright, Self-Knowledge and Knowledge A Priori. Oxford United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (the): Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: In this opinionated introduction, we explain the rationale for a coordinated study of self-knowledge and knowledge a priori. After outlining the reasons why each of these species of knowledge presents a prima facie challenge to a broadly naturalistic outlook on epistemology, we present an argument that both are indispensable for rational deliberation, if the actions and beliefs that result from a deliberation are to be seen as outcomes for which the agent can be held responsible. We then explore some of the ways in which self-knowledge and a priori knowledge are explanatorily interdependent, looking at cases where the agent’s possession of one appears to enable their acquisition of the other. The introduction ends with a detailed critical survey of the contributions to the volume.

items.title: Romantic Domination.
items.abstract: Romantic relationships between professors and students, between employers and employees, and between other partners at different points on an institutional hierarchy are widely regarded as morally troubling. Popular explanations as to why have appealed variously to violations of institutional duties, to the impossibility of sexual consent within such relationships, and to the vices of the more powerful partner. I advance an alternative explanation. Romantic relationships, I argue, are already hazardous in their own right. We are distinctively exposed to and dependent on our partners, which gives them the ability to interfere with us in significant ways. This makes romantic relationships ripe for what republicans call “domination”—a situation in which one person is vulnerable to the arbitrary interference of another. Romantic partners can avoid this objectionable condition by achieving a rough equality of power, which will prevent either partner from interfering with impunity. However, significant asymmetries of institutional power make this balancing act harder to achieve and, therefore, make domination harder to avoid. Extending the theory of freedom as non-domination in this way, therefore, not only helps solve a tricky ethical puzzle but also demonstrates the surprising capacity of republican theory to illuminate personal relationships.

items.title: AI Intent Illiteracy.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the primary barrier to organizational AI adoption is not technical but articulatory, and precedes the technology itself. It introduces the concept of Intent Illiteracy: the inability to convert a real need into a request an intelligence — human or artificial — can understand and serve. The concept comprises three chained failures (diagnostic, formulation, transfer), all occurring before prompt quality is relevant. The paper explains the mechanism that renders the deficit invisible and self-perpetuating, delimits it from AI literacy and from the "blind trust" critique, and situates it within a broader framework relating cognitive deficit, corrective method, and economic infrastructure. Presented as a conceptual proposal with a falsifiable prediction, not a validated empirical finding.

items.title: C4103How to do consequentialist epistemology.
items.pub: In The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief
items.abstract: The feasibilist standard of epistemic assessment defended in previous chapters is consequentialist in a broad sense, since reasonable belief is understood in terms of a kind of conduciveness to knowledge. This chapter examines whether the feasibilist standard can withstand objections raised against consequentialist approaches in epistemology. Three major objections are considered: the problem of trade-offs, the challenge of extending a consequentialist norm to suspension of judgement, and variants of the so-called swamping problem. None undermine feasibilist norms, in particular the gnosticist version of feasibilism defended. Its comparative and non-ideal structure avoids challenges faced by alternative approaches. This strengthens the case for feasibilism as a viable and distinctive form of epistemic consequentialism. The chapter concludes by considering how the feasibilist resources developed can be used to answer questions and challenges that arise at important choice-points for consequentialist theories in ethics, focusing on motive consequentialism.

items.title: C13The project of this book.
items.pub: In The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief
items.abstract: This chapter outlines the motivations and conceptual foundations of the feasibilist normative framework defended in this book. Feasibilist norms urge manifesting dispositions that are among the most success-conducive feasible ones. The chapter introduces the key concepts of dispositions, feasibility, and success-conduciveness. A central application of the feasibilist approach is the author’s theory of the epistemic status of reasonableness. According to her preferred view, a doxastic state is reasonable when formed and retained by manifesting dispositions that are among the most knowledge-conducive feasible ones. The chapter clarifies how reasonableness relates to justification and outlines a meta-epistemological picture of the role or function of assessing doxastic states as reasonable. It explains the general nature of the feasibilist normative framework to be defended and sketches the book’s general non-ideal approach in normative theory.

items.title: C7181The normativity of manifesting good dispositions.
items.pub: In The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief
items.abstract: This chapter begins by asking how we should think about the normative statuses of knowledge versus reasonableness. It develops a view on which agents are often epistemically blame- or praiseworthy for their doxastic states in virtue of the quality of the dispositions they manifest, regardless of whether those states conform to prescriptive epistemic norms. Drawing on two general hypotheses emerging from earlier chapters—Competent Failure and Incompetent Success—a distinctive account is defended of the relation between epistemic blame- and praiseworthiness, on the one hand, and epistemic prescriptions, on the other. On this view, the hypological and the prescriptive come radically apart: for instance, we can be epistemically blameworthy for beliefs that violate no prescriptive epistemic norms. A structurally similar argument is then extended to the moral domain. A surprising consequence is that we can sometimes be morally blameworthy for actions that are morally right.

items.title: 217Conclusions.
items.pub: In The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief
items.abstract: The Conclusions chapter revisits the central motivations for feasibilism and summarizes some of the main claims defended in the book. Many familiar norms leave an important part of the normative landscape unexplored. Across different domains we need norms more attuned to what goes on with a subject and less dependent on how the world happens to unfold. The book contrasts a feasibilist approach to constructing such norms with a perspectivist one, using epistemological problems as case studies in applying feasibilism. The overall case for feasibilism is abductive: both the epistemological implementation defended and the general schematic framework provide a simple, elegant, metaphysically grounded, and explanatorily powerful model for non-ideal normative theory.

items.title: C5131Perspectivism and the problem of luck.
items.pub: In The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief
items.abstract: The chapter discusses the problem of luck: for many norms, there are situations in which conformity is possible only by luck. It contrasts a perspectivist with a feasibilist diagnosis of the problem. The former locates the difficulty in the application of a wide range of norms depending on facts that may lie outside our perspectives. The chapter argues that this diagnosis is mistaken. The correct diagnosis is feasibilist: in some circumstances it is not feasible to choose, act, or believe in ways on which conformity to the relevant norm robustly depends. The same is true of perspectivist norms: it can be infeasible to track facts about one’s own perspective. The chapter further argues that debates between internalists and externalists in epistemology have often presupposed the perspectivist diagnosis. Shifting attention from the limits of perspective to limits on feasible ways of acting, choosing, and believing has deep implications for normative theory.

items.title: C357Defeat and higher-order evidence.
items.pub: In The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief
items.abstract: This chapter develops the feasibilist account of reasonable belief by applying it to cases of defeat, with particular attention to defeat by higher-order evidence. It argues that in typical examples of defeat, subjects can no longer hold reasonable beliefs. On this view, a defeat-like phenomenon arises not from evidential relations alone, but from the infeasibility of retaining beliefs in ways that discriminate between misleading and non-misleading higher-order evidence. The full details of a feasibilist standard of normative assessment are spelled out through the notions of feasible alternative dispositional profiles and value functions. The chapter argues that knowledge is no exception to the general hypothesis that manifesting success-conducive dispositions is neither necessary nor sufficient for success: there is unreasonable knowledge. It is argued that the resulting account dissolves a range of puzzles relating to higher-order evidence and illustrates the theoretical power of feasibilism as a non-ideal, externalist framework for epistemic assessment.

items.title: C239Deceit and good dispositions.
items.pub: In The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief
items.abstract: This chapter applies the feasibilist normative framework to the New Evil Demon Problem, a central challenge to externalist theories in epistemology. It argues that even victims of systematic deceit can hold beliefs that are reasonable, since their beliefs are formed and retained by manifesting dispositions as conducive to truth and knowledge as those of subjects in good cases. Unlike other proposed solutions, the feasibilist account avoids the difficulty posed by so-called alien cognizers. Reasonableness is not an internalist notion. Some intuitions that resemble those driving the New Evil Demon Problem are best treated in an error-theoretic way. The chapter closes by considering two objections to the proposed feasibilist solution.

items.title: C6156Feasibilism as a general normative framework.
items.pub: In The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Good, the Bad, and the Feasible: Knowledge and Reasonable Belief
items.abstract: This chapter presents the general feasibilist normative framework. The framework generates three kinds of normative assessment: (i) valuable normative success (e.g. knowledge), (ii) feasibilist assessment proper, having to do with manifesting the most success-conducive feasible dispositions (e.g. reasonable belief), and (iii) creditable normative success, success that depends in the right kind of way on dispositions manifested by the agent. To begin, the chapter develops an explanationist account of creditable success, thereby filling in the details of the feasibilist diagnosis of the problem of luck provided in the previous chapter. It then outlines the general normative framework, applying it to discussions of morally worthy action understood as a kind of creditable success. The chapter addresses whether and how feasibilism can make progress with the problem of luck and argues that feasibilist norms cannot be dismissed on the grounds that they are not adequately guiding.

items.title: The history of the religion of communism.
items.abstract: The idea to study the evolution of Soviet power from the standpoint of philosophical-historical and religious analysis came to me long ago, back in the symbolic year of 1984. I partially realized this idea by writing the book "The Fall of the USSR" in just three months, using materials I had accumulated over an entire decade. In that book, based on facts literally strained from the censored Soviet press, I argued that Soviet power, due to the degradation of the very foundations of its economy, politics, and utopian-religious ideology, was doomed and would not survive more than another 10 years. The fate of that book closely resembled the circumstances described in Orwell’s famous novel "1984". I began to distribute this book in Samizdat, and literally a month later, the head of the 2nd Department of the university where I worked called me and suggested I go to the office of the commandant of the main building, located at a distance from the lecture halls. When I entered, instead of the commandant, sitting there were an elderly KGB colonel and a young captain who supervised anti-Soviet sentiments in our district of the city. They presented me with a stack of photocopies of letters written to my friend who had moved to work in the Lithuanian city of Klaipeda, and since these letters contained thoughts consonant with the book, they began demanding that I confess to its authorship and write a statement to the KGB expressing repentance for my delusions and promising that this would not happen again. "Yuri Vladimirovich," said the Comrade Colonel, "has oriented the KGB organs differently than Leonid Ilyich. He does not want to severely infringe upon creative people for every piece of heretical scribbling, as long as they have not moved to open struggle against Soviet power and have not committed crimes of a political nature. Therefore, if you repent before the people's power, you will save yourself from just and deserved punishment." .

items.title: История религии коммунизма.
items.abstract: Идея изучить эволюцию Советской власти с позиций философскоисторического и религиоведческого анализа пришла ко мне давно, ещё в знаковом 1984 году. Я частично реализовал эту идею, написав всего за три месяца по накопившимся у меня за целое десятилетие материалам книгу «Падение СССР». В этой книге я на основании фактов, буквально выцеженных их подцензурной советской печати, доказывал, что Советская власть вследствие деградации самых основ её экономики, политики и утопическо-религиозной идеологии обречена и не просуществует более 10 лет. Судьба этой книги весьма напоминала те обстоятельства, которые были описаны в знаменитом романе Оруэлла «1984». Я стал распространять эту книгу в Самиздате, и буквально через месяц мне позвонил начальник 2-го отдела университета, где я работал, и предложил пройти в кабинет коменданта главного корпуса, находившийся в отдалении от учебных аудиторий. Когда я зашёл туда, там вместо коменданта сидели пожилой полковник КГБ и молодой капитан, осуществлявший надзор за антисоветскими настроениями в нашем районе города. Они предъявили мне пачку фотокопий писем, написанных моему другу, который переехал на работу в литовский город Клайпеду, а поскольку эти письма содержали мысли, созвучные книге, они стали требовать, чтобы я признался в её авторстве и написал заявление в КГБ, в котором выразил бы покаяние в своих заблуждениях и обещал, что этого больше не повториться. - Юрий Владимирович, - сказал товарищ полковник, - ориентировал органы КГБ иначе, чем Леонид Ильич. Он не хочет сильно ущемлять творческих людей за всякую еретическую писанину, пока они не перешли к открытой борьбе с Советской властью и не совершили преступлений политического характера. Поэтому если вы покаетесь перед народной властью, то спасётесь от справедливого и заслуженного наказания.

items.title: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness.
items.pub: New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This book provides a defense and an exploration of illusionism regarding phenomenal consciousness. Phenomenal consciousness supposedly encompasses mental states such as seeing a red spot, feeling pain in your back, or imagining the sound of a harp. All these states seem to feel like something, in a distinctive sense of “feel.” Phenomenal consciousness seems mysterious. It apparently resists scientific explanation and seems irreducible to brain processes. Our phenomenally conscious experiences seem to be presented to us most directly when we have them, while remaining closed to others. The book defends illusionism about phenomenal consciousness: the view that phenomenal consciousness is not real, but only seems real because we are under an introspective illusion generated by our brains. This illusion is unique: it is stronger and much harder to apprehend as such than other illusions, like perceptual illusions. The book does not only argue for illusionism; it also proposes a novel conception, called Meta-Cartesianism, which explains why the illusion of phenomenal consciousness is unique and almost inextricable. Finally, the book maps the implications of the illusionist view in various domains. If phenomenal consciousness is illusory, what should happen to the cognitive science of consciousness? What happens to ethics, given that phenomenal experiences seem crucial to well-being and moral status? What happens to epistemology, given that they seem key to justification?

items.title: C9236Losing Your Religion.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter explores the ethical implications of illusionism. It starts by acknowledging the intuitive appeal and the popularity of sentientist approaches to ethics, in which phenomenal experiences play a distinctive role for well-being and moral status. The chapter grants that illusionism must be revisionary about the grounds of well-being and moral status. Then it moves on to determine whether it is also revisionary about their distribution—about which creatures have which well-being and which moral status. The chapter examines various non-sentientist ethical views an illusionist could endorse, on which things other than the phenomenal ground well-being and moral status. It concludes that at least some of these views are plausible and allow us to avoid the most drastic revisions when it comes to the distribution of well-being and moral status. Objections to illusionism based on its unacceptable ethical implications can be countered.

items.title: C01Introduction.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This short introduction gives an overview of the book House of Mirrors. The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. It presents the book’s three main goals. The book’s first goal is to present and defend illusionism about phenomenal consciousness. Its second goal is to explain why we are under the illusion of phenomenal consciousness, and why this illusion is so uniquely strong and hard to apprehend as such. Its third goal is to map the implications of illusionism regarding phenomenal consciousness across various domains, including the cognitive science of consciousness, ethics, and epistemology. The introduction also provides an overview of the book’s chapters, with a short summary for each.

items.title: C6136Leaving the House of Mirrors.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter shows how the view presented in the earlier chapter, Meta-Cartesianism, solves the illusion problem: it explains the illusion of phenomenal consciousness. One thing it notably does, which other views cannot do, is explain why phenomenal consciousness seems so introspectively obvious: why it seems to us that we are acquainted with our phenomenal experiences. Doing so, Meta-Cartesianism also satisfyingly explains our intuitions that phenomenal experiences are irreducible and undetectable. While this explanation first focuses on the illusion of sensory phenomenality, it can be extended to non-sensory phenomenality: we can explain our illusion of mnemic, imaginative, high-level perceptual and cognitive phenomenality, as well as valenced phenomenality. Finally, the view can also explain why phenomenal consciousness seems so epistemically and ethically significant.

items.title: C5112Mapping the House of Mirrors.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter presents Meta-Cartesianism: a view of phenomenal introspection that solves the illusion problem and notably explains why phenomenal experiences seem so introspectively obvious. Meta-Cartesianism belongs to the evidential approach. It views phenomenal cognition and evidential cognition as deeply entangled: we essentially represent phenomenal experiences as mental states endowed with unique evidential properties. The chapter presents the main posits of Meta-Cartesianism: the Cartesian Device and the Evidence-by-Resemblance Mechanism. It details these two posits, while making a preliminary case for the view, by showing that there is some plausibility to the idea that phenomenal introspection relies on a Cartesian Device and an Evidence-by-Resemblance Mechanism, and thus represents phenomenal experiences as having unique evidential properties. The chapter also contrasts Meta-Cartesianism with existing views of phenomenal introspection.

items.title: C489Approaching the House of Mirrors.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter characterizes the illusion problem (the problem of explaining the illusion of phenomenal consciousness) and critically examines extant candidate solutions to it. First, it shows that solving the illusion problem is essential, and it details the problem’s explanandum and desired explanans. Then, it examines various views, focusing on those of Michael Graziano and Derk Pereboom (with discussions of the views of Daniel Dennett, Georges Rey, Nicholas Humphrey, Hakwan Lau, Wolfgang Schwarz, Andy Clark, etc.). It argues that these views do not solve the illusion problem. Notably, they do not explain why phenomenal experiences seem introspectively obvious. Therefore, they also do not solve the illusion meta-problem: they do not explain why the illusion of phenomenal consciousness is so hard to apprehend as such. Finally, the chapter describes the evidential approach, which focuses on the entanglement between phenomenal cognition and evidential cognition, and could solve the illusion problem.

items.title: C8199The Science of Sirens.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter examines illusionism’s implications for the science of consciousness. It presents current debates within the science of consciousness and oppositions between the main scientific theories of consciousness. It argues against two radical interpretations of illusionism’s implications: one on which illusionism makes all of consciousness science moot, and one on which it leaves it untouched. The chapter shows why illusionism has non-trivial and non-simplistic implications for consciousness science, notably as it challenges various key implicit assumptions at play in much of consciousness science, regarding the unity and determinacy of consciousness, as well as regarding the informative character of consciousness-related claims. Finally, the chapter argues that the concept of paradigm shift illuminates the opposition between realism and illusionism about phenomenal consciousness.

items.title: C7165Addressing Objections.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter defends illusionism against various objections. First, the objection that illusionism is incoherent, because phenomenal consciousness cannot seem to exist without existing. Second, the objection that illusionism cannot explain how we represent phenomenal properties. Third, the objection that illusionism is only attractive if we assume a loaded definition of “phenomenal consciousness.” Fourth, the objection that illusionism is only attractive if mystery intuitions are widely shared, but they are not. Fifth, the objection that illusionism is only attractive if mystery intuitions are conceptual, but they are not. Sixth, the objection that illusionism is only attractive if mystery intuitions correspond to ineliminable commitments of phenomenal concepts, but they do not. Seventh, the objection that illusionism, even if coherent and argumentatively supported, is obviously false. Eighth, the verbal objection that strong illusionist formulations are inferior to substantively equivalent weak illusionist (and realist) formulations.

items.title: C10282Shedding Our Cartesian Scales.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter explores illusionism’s epistemological implications. It first acknowledges the intuitive appeal and the popularity of phenomenalist approaches to epistemology, on which the phenomenal plays a distinctive role for epistemic justification. As a result, illusionism must be revisionary about the grounds of justification. The chapter tries to determine whether it must also be revisionary about the distribution of justification—about which subjects have which justifications to believe what. It then examines three non-phenomenalist epistemological conceptions of justification, on which justification relies on features other than phenomenal features, and which an illusionist could endorse. It concludes that at least some of them are plausible and avoid the most drastic epistemological revisions. Objections to illusionism based on its unacceptable epistemological implications can be countered.

items.title: C358Arguing for Illusionism.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter argues for the most controversial claim of illusionism: the eliminative claim, which states that phenomenal consciousness does not exist. It does so via two arguments working in tandem. First, the Argument from Mysteries: because phenomenal consciousness seems mysterious, and because it does not help us explain other (non-phenomenal) things, we should reject its existence if we have good reasons to discard putative direct data we have about its existence. Second, the Argument from Irrelevance, which belongs to the family of debunking arguments: because appeals to phenomenal consciousness seem irrelevant to explain our judgments about phenomenal consciousness, we have good reasons to discard putative direct data about the existence of phenomenal consciousness. Together, these two arguments support the view that we should reject the existence of phenomenal consciousness. The chapter also contrasts this argumentative strategy with other comparable arguments.

items.title: 308Coda.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This short concluding chapter summarizes the conclusions of the previous chapters. It also speculates on what illusionism suggests regarding the ultimate nature of reality. It stresses that illusionism fits well (but does not entail) physicalism, and notably a version of physicalism equivalent to the view called ontic structural realism in the philosophy of science. The chapter then examines an objection to illusionism, inspired by objections to ontic structural realism, which argues that positing structures requires positing categorical bases for those structures, while stressing that only phenomenal properties might be able to constitute such bases. The chapter reviews ways an illusionist could answer this objection, including (but not limited to) revising our concept of existence.

items.title: C14A Bundle of Mysteries.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter first defines phenomenal consciousness by appealing to introspection. It stresses that phenomenal consciousness seems mysterious: we are disposed to think that it has various mysterious peculiarities. It zeroes in on a few of these apparent mysteries. First, phenomenal consciousness seems introspectively obvious: it seems that, in introspection, our phenomenal experiences are presented to us in a remarkably intimate way, akin to a mental form of contact. Second, phenomenal consciousness seems irreducible. Phenomenal experiences seem notably distinct from brain processes, or more generally, physical processes. They seem impossible to explain scientifically. Third, phenomenal consciousness seems undetectable: from the third-person perspective, we never seem able to detect and measure it directly. The chapter argues that our intuitions that phenomenal consciousness has these mysterious properties are strong, robust, and widely shared, and that they stem from our concept of phenomenal consciousness. Finally, it notes that phenomenal consciousness also seems particularly significant from an epistemological and ethical perspective.

items.title: C241Illusionism About Phenomenal Consciousness.
items.pub: In House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness. New York, NY United States of America (the): Oxford University Press.
items.venue: House of Mirrors: The Illusion of Phenomenal Consciousness
items.abstract: This chapter presents illusionism about phenomenal consciousness. Illusionism consists of two claims. First, phenomenal consciousness does not exist (eliminative claim). Second, it seems to exist (appearance claim). The chapter provides a historical overview of illusionism and details its different versions, before zeroing in on the version that the rest of the book will defend. The chapter also clarifies illusionism, distinguishing between strong and weak illusionism, as well as between phenomenal consciousness and quasi-phenomenal consciousness, before describing the main challenges faced by illusionists. First, they must argue for their view; second, they must explain why the illusion of phenomenal consciousness arises and remains so strong. Finally, the chapter provides a brief argument for the appearance claim (the uncontroversial claim that phenomenal consciousness seems to exist), and lays the foundations for the argument in favor of the eliminative claim (the highly controversial claim that phenomenal consciousness does not exist).

items.title: Answerable Curation: Dominant Intermediaries and the Concentration of Evaluative Power.
items.abstract: A small number of media and platform institutions decide what a polity is able to consider, which claims are admissible, and which accounts carry the standing of a serious position. This paper asks on what terms that power can be held to account. It begins with media power in general but locates the strongest case in the dominant intermediary — the search, social or recommendation service that curates the visibility of others' expression at infrastructural scale — with the press and broadcasters entering mainly as contrast and limiting case. Its claim is deliberately modest. I do not argue that these institutions are organs of the state, nor that curating a feed is legislating or adjudicating; the influence such institutions exercise is not authority, and any argument that rests on equating the two collapses at the first objection. The narrower and more durable claim is that a handful of institutions concentrate three separable powers — selection, boundary-setting, and legitimation — over the conditions of public knowledge, and answer for none of them against any standard they must state or revise. I locate the constitutional interest in that concentration of evaluative discretion, and I distinguish it sharply from the ownership concentration that media-plurality law already addresses: the two can and do diverge. The remedy I defend is correspondingly narrow. It pairs a procedural duty of answerability — state the standard, explain the exercise, submit the standard to revision — with a thin substantive floor drawn not from any contested notion of fairness but from the narrowest part of the fiduciary duty of loyalty — the duty to disclose a material conflict of interest bearing on the exercise of that discretion. I own the cost of that choice: the floor reaches the interest served in the dark, not curation that is merely disclosed and self-interested, and not curation that is merely, in someone's view, unfair. It is calibrated to survive the free-expression constraints that cap it, including — decisively, and against a literature still arguing from Tornillo alone — the protection that Moody v NetChoice now extends to algorithmic curation, and the boundary that X Corp v Bonta draws between compelling a platform to characterise its editorial reasoning, which fails, and requiring it to disclose the interests that bear on it, which does not. Against the objection that any overseer will itself be captured, I claim only that reflexive answerability makes capture …

items.title: The Answerable Witness: Human Consciousness and the Corrective Dynamics of Reality.
items.abstract: This paper develops the concept of the answerable witness as a way of understanding human consciousness within the corrective dynamics of reality. Structural Intelligence holds that local forms stabilize reality by selecting what can be seen, carried, and acted upon, while the excluded remainder returns as pressure, anomaly, symptom, shadow, burden, contradiction, or collapse. If reality already corrects its forms through consequence, then the distinctive human role is to make correction witnessable, meaningful, and potentially revisable from within the field. -/- The paper distinguishes observation, attention, witness, and answerable witness. Observation notices; attention sustains selection; witness remains in contact with what pushes back; answerable witness allows what is seen to revise the form that sees it. A further distinction is made between field and Being: the field is the differentiated condition of formation, while Being names the non-reducible depth of the subject that no form exhausts. Human consciousness is therefore placed neither as sovereign over nature nor as a passive product of conditions, but as a local site where reality’s corrective movement can become visible, survivable, and bound into repair.

items.title: ArtIA: imagining a new digital commons for creative AI.
items.abstract: While American screenwriters were resisting AI capture, a vibrant community of digital creatives and arts organizations across Québec and Canada formed the alliance ArtIA. ArtIA advances commons-based alternatives to cultural AI, in response to the observation that while AI is rapidly transforming creative tools and workflows, the cultural sector lacks the critical resources, reference frameworks, support systems, and training needed to navigate this shift. The AI commons is conceptually contested, as corporate and governmental discourses increasingly frame AI as a “common good,” while probabilistic AI systems, common training datasets, and debates over AI as public infrastructure generate a muddled appropriation of the commons. ArtIA advances commoning as a situated practice grounding visions of the future in cultural needs, sectoral challenges, and traditions of commoning in Québec and Canada. This paper traces the 18-month stakeholder consultation organized by ArtIA, which enrolled 204 participants and collectively aimed to imagine and develop concrete interventions toward an AI commons situated at the intersection of Canadian AI governance as industrial policy and the localized practices of digital creation. Findings grounded in situational analysis and action research show the enrollment of four interrelated actor groups—cultural organizations, digital creatives, commons networks, and researchers. These actors formed new alliances and produced three concrete imaginaries for a creative AI commons: (1) Artisanal AI, (2) Common Compute, and (3) Critical AI Literacies. In closing, we argue that technologies developed and governed at the right scale—accessible, situated, and collectively stewarded—can operate as material levers for social solidarity, collective agency and shared responsibility that ideological politics and industrial policies cannot.

items.title: Turning Toward Addiction - Understanding the Desire, Holding the Reality, and Letting Go of the Parts That Don't Belong.
items.abstract: Anonymized first-person testimony organizes this essay on addiction around frequency rather than substance. It traces the overlap between the endogenous-opioid effects of alcohol and those of social laughter, synchronized singing, and dance; argues for widening the interval between uses while flagging where moderation fails and where withdrawal requires medical supervision; and states accurately the regulatory status of psychedelic- and dissociative-assisted treatments. Behavioral addictions (gambling, gaming, pornography, social media) are treated with attention to where the science is settled and where it is not. A central section turns to children: the author's recognition that his own habits were being absorbed by his child is set beside research on parental technoference, Swedish adoption studies showing genetic and rearing-environment routes to drug abuse, adverse childhood experiences, and Jung's claim that the life parents refuse is passed to children "in substitute form." The essay closes with Jungian inflation, the Self as prior to the ego, and the Jung–Wilson correspondence behind Alcoholics Anonymous: spiritus contra spiritum.

items.title: WHO BUILT THE TRACK: Diachronic Responsibility, the Social Connection Model, and Why the Trolley Problem Cannot Locate the Longevity Asymmetry Corpus.
items.abstract: The trolley problem has been analyzed as a synchronic problem since Foot (1967): one agent, one moment, one switch. Thomson (1976, 1985) distinguishes the driver — who has, in her own words, “previously directed the trolley” — from the bystander, who has not, and treats this prior positional difference as load-bearing; her 2008 reversal (“Turning the Trolley,” Philosophy & Public Af airs 36:4) goes further, concluding the bystander may not do what the driver may. Kamm’s most systematic treatment of the field (The Trolley Problem Mysteries, Oxford, 2020) organizes its opening lecture around exactly this question: “Who Turned the Trolley?” The literature has therefore always tracked who stands at the switch and what prior relationship they had to the emergency. It has never analyzed a case in which that prior relationship is not causal or positional but constitutive — a case in which the same psychological mechanism required to operate the switch is the mechanism that generated the asymmetric track layout in the first place. This paper argues that the Longevity Asymmetry Corpus (Huynh 2026a–u) describes exactly this case, and that no existing position in the trolley literature — Foot’s doctrine of double effect, Thomson’s doing/allowing distinction, Kamm’s principle of permissible harm, or utilitarian aggregation — locates it, because all four analyze the moment at the switch, not the window before the track was laid. The corpus’s F2 window (Huynh 2026a, 2026d) is that earlier window: the period during which governance actors could still have redesigned the track layout, before the Grief–Attribution–Legitimation–Concentration sequence (Huynh 2026a, 2026f) reaches a Concentration stage the corpus’s five paradoxes (Huynh 2026a, 2026i) establish is structurally resistant to redesign. The Governance Paradox (Huynh 2026e, 2026o) specifies why the governance actors positioned to redesign the track during the F2 window could not do so impartially: A5 — the neurological standing charge of constitutive attachment documented in Huynh (2026k, 2026l) — is the same mechanism driving both the demand that produced the asymmetric track layout and, later, the political pressure at the switch itself. The agent asked to pull the lever is not a neutral bystander, and is not simply “the driver” in Thomson’s causal sense. The agent is a co-architect of the track, present at both ends of the causal chain by the same psychological mechanism. The paper’s philosophical contribution …

items.title: THE PERSONAL SYSTEM REMINDER: A Citizen-Built Architecture for Detecting Propaganda, Verifying Genuine Communicators, and Catching One's Own Self-Sealing Drift, Modeled Directly on Anthropic's System Reminder.
items.abstract: WHO THIS IS FOR AND WHAT IT NAMES. This paper describes a practice an individual citizen builds and runs on themselves. It names one existing architecture directly — Anthropic's System Reminder, the practice of reintroducing an AI system's stated operating principles into a long-running interaction at points the surrounding system determines rather than the system itself — and holds it up as a positive working model to be emulated, not as an example of manipulation to be exposed. Nothing in this paper accuses Anthropic, or any government, platform, or institution, of propaganda. The target of the practice described here is a structural vulnerability every reasoner has; the case study is an existing, publicly documented engineering solution to a structurally identical problem, built for an unrelated reason, that transfers with unusual precision. Three prior papers in this line of work each solve one piece of a citizen's epistemic self-defense and leave the others to a separate document. Falsifiability as Cognitive Self-Vaccination gives a propositional test — can this claim be wrong? — for communications the citizen receives. The Act-Level Criterion adds a behavioral test — is this communicator genuinely structured to permit me not to believe them, or does the act itself absorb every challenge regardless of the claim's content? The Constitutional Drift adds a third, inward-facing practice, modeled on Anthropic's published Constitutional AI research and many-shot jailbreaking findings, for detecting the citizen's own gradual, cumulative, invisible-from-inside drift. This paper does not add a fourth test. It argues that three tests run as three separate, occasionally-remembered habits will in practice be run reliably by almost no one, for the same structural reason a language model cannot be trusted to notice on its own that a check is due — and it specifies what a single, unified, citizen-authored practice looks like when all three are bundled into one document, checked on one externally-set schedule. The paper's second and sharper contribution closes a gap the first two papers leave open by construction. Both the propositional and the act-level test were built and demonstrated as outward-facing instruments: applied to claims and communicators the citizen encounters. This paper argues, and gives a formal reason, that the same two tests must also run on the citizen's own current beliefs, on the same schedule, because the unexamined claim — I hold the tool …

items.title: THE ENCLOSURE OF THE FOLD: John Jumper, Claude Science, Coeficient Bio, and the VirBench Finding as Second-Order Confirmation of the Research Horizon Gap.
items.abstract: On June 19, 2026, John Jumper announced he was leaving Google DeepMind after nearly nine years to join Anthropic. Jumper co-created AlphaFold, the protein-structure prediction system for which he shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Demis Hassabis, and which DeepMind released free of charge to a database that now serves more than 200 million protein structure predictions to researchers worldwide. The move closed a six-month buildout Anthropic had been executing since Claude for Life Sciences launched in October 2025: Claude for Healthcare (January 2026), research partnerships with the Allen Institute and Howard Hughes Medical Institute (February 2, 2026), the $400 million acquisition of drug-discovery startup Coefficient Bio (April 3, 2026), the hire of Andrej Karpathy for pretraining (May 19, 2026), and Jumper’s arrival, culminating on June 30, 2026 in a San Francisco livestream announcing Claude Science — an AI research workbench pre-configured for genomics, proteomics, single-cell analysis, and cheminformatics, backed by more than sixty scientific databases — alongside Anthropic’s decision to run its own preclinical drug-discovery programs. Bristol Myers Squibb, Genentech, and Novartis appeared as customers at the same event; Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan had joined Anthropic’s board earlier in the year. This paper establishes five claims, stated directly because the primary-source record does not require qualification. First, the counterfactual the Research Horizon Gap paper (Huynh 2026s) used to demonstrate what open biomedical AI access looks like — AlphaFold, released free and globally, used by millions of researchers — is not a stable alternative sitting permanently outside the access-restricted enclave that paper analyzed. AlphaFold’s creator is now inside that enclave. Second, Claude Science documents Feature 5 of the Biological Shogunate — the capability holder’s unilateral veto over research access — directly inside the biomedical research product itself: a paid beta, curated toward roughly fifty selected external projects receiving $30,000 in compute credits each, chosen by Anthropic. This requires no inference through cybersecurity-adjacent cases. It is the mechanism, observed directly, in the exact domain the Research Horizon Gap paper concerns. Third, Anthropic’s own account of why it selected neglected and rare diseases for its internal drug-discovery programs — markets ordinary drug-development economics does not incentivize — is …

items.title: CONSTITUTIONAL DRIFT: Constitutional AI, Many-Shot Normalization, and a Scheduled Methodology for Detecting Value Erosion Under Extended Exposure.
items.abstract: Constitutional drift is the human analog of a problem Anthropic’s AI safety research has named and measured with more precision than moral psychology typically offers: an agent’s values eroding gradually, cumulatively, and invisibly from inside the process, across extended exposure to persuasive or repetitive input. This paper treats two of Anthropic’s published findings as a case study and extracts a five-step methodology from them. Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022, arXiv:2212.08073) trains a model to critique its own output against an explicit, written, external set of principles — a constitution — rather than against a felt sense of its own values, and repeats this critique-revision cycle at scale rather than performing it once. Many-shot jailbreaking (Anil et al. 2024, NeurIPS) demonstrates that hundreds of in-context examples of a shifted behavior degrade safety-trained behavior according to a measured power-law relationship with the number of examples, and that this is not a special exploit but the same in-context-learning mechanism that lets a model usefully learn from context at all — meaning larger, more capable models are consistently more susceptible, not less, because greater capability improves the same pattern-completion capacity the mechanism exploits. Anthropic’s deployment practice adds a third design choice: reminders of stated operating principles are reinjected into long conversations by the surrounding system, on a timing the model itself does not control, for the specific reason that an agent partway through a gradual shift is poorly positioned to notice a check is due. This paper restates these three findings as three human failure modes — guardrail drift, many-shot normalization, and self-sealing logic, the last already addressed in this corpus by Huynh (2026b, 2026x) — and converts the AI-side mitigations directly into a five-step personal practice: write specific, checkable principles down before they are tested; schedule the critique by calendar rather than by feeling, since the feeling is exactly what drift removes; audit the volume of one-sided exposure separately from its content, since volume rather than argument quality is what the power-law finding shows does the work; externalize the check to a designated other person, since self-monitoring from inside a gradual process is the specific failure the reminder mechanism exists to correct; and revise explicitly and in writing when a genuine violation is found, since critique …

items.title: Thanabots, fantasy, and the ethics of mourning.
items.abstract: Thanabots—digital recreations of the dead powered by artificial intelligence (AI)—comprise media that allow the dead to remain present in the world of the living. In this article we unpack the psychic dimension of users’ diverse stances towards thanabots, asking how this dimension can contribute to our understanding of the patterns of users’ responses to loss. Drawing on Critical Fantasy Studies, we examine journalistic reports featuring actual users and original interviews with potential users, treating thanabots as sites of affective investment. We argue that users affectively invest in their interactions with thanabots insofar as the latter embody aspects of the dead that carry symbolic value and significance. The concepts of fantasy, mourning, and part-object are deployed to identify two modes of user engagement with thanabots, one where their relationship to the dead is reified and one where users reflexively and ethically engage with the ideas and emotions associated with the dead. We conclude with a discussion about the prospect of establishing conditions of possibility for an ‘ethics of mourning’ as regards user–thanabot interactions.

items.title: 'The Voluntary is Essentially Superficial.' Bernard Williams on Responsibility and Political Freedom.
items.pub: In Veronica Rodriguez-Blanco, Daniel Peixoto Murata & Julieta A. Rabanos, Bernard Williams on Law and Jurisprudence: From Agency and Responsibility to Methodology. Oxford: Hart Publishing. pp. 23-40.
items.venue: Bernard Williams on Law and Jurisprudence: From Agency and Responsibility to Methodology
items.abstract: I try to square three very different contributions to the discussion of responsibility by Bernard Williams in ‘Moral Luck’, ‘Recognizing Responsibility’ (in Shame and Necessity), and the rarely discussed ‘Moral Responsibility and Political Freedom’. The three sources are not obviously compatible, but I show that there is unifying interpretation leading to developing an account of the role and the limits of freedom and moral luck in attributing responsibility to an agent.

items.title: “The Brain-Computer Interface is Changing Me”: The Psychological Trajectory of Becoming More-Than-Human with a Brain Implant.
items.abstract: This article presents findings from a first-in-human trial involving implantation of a Brain–Computer Interface (BCI) into a quadriplegic patient. It explores the psychological consequences of being integrated into a continuous BCI feedback loop, focusing on how such intimate interaction can enhance users’ sense of empowerment and ownership. At the same time, it reveals complex ethical tensions surrounding the notions of agency and control. Our results suggest that prolonged engagement with BCIs can lead to a profound sense of integration—where users begin to perceive themselves as part of the system. While this can foster a heightened sense of control, it also introduces risks such as psychological disruption and distress, particularly when users are abruptly disconnected from their devices or the device generates false positives (e.g. the device producing unintended outcomes). A key insight from our study is the emergence of what we term being-of-the-loop—a condition in which a symbiosis develops between the user and the AI system, giving rise to a de novo agency that neither could achieve alone. In this state, the BCI is no longer experienced as an external tool but as a constitutive part of the self, fundamentally reshaping how users perceive control, authorship, and action. While this integration can foster empowerment and restored capabilities, it also creates a fragile dependence: agency becomes entangled with the system’s functioning, rendering users vulnerable to false positives and identity disruption when the loop is severed. These findings raise urgent ethical concerns about psychological rupture and the risks of disconnecting a technology that has become embedded within—and transformative of—the user’s lived experience.

items.title: The dismantling and reconstitution of mental models by child peer groups.
items.abstract: The target paper brings a new dimension to cultural evolution research. The findings it reports are consistent with the hypothesis that it is integrated cognitive networks – i.e., ways of structuring knowledge – that evolve through culture, as opposed to discrete units of cultural knowledge. The impact of child peer groups on cultural evolution could be modeled using methods from network science.

items.title: Exceptional Exercises of Constitutive Capacities.
items.abstract: I offer an account of how a constitutivist metaphysics of capacities grounds a unique interpretation of propositions about the nature of our action, focusing specifically on propositions about acting under the guise of the good and acting from practical knowledge. I then show that these interpretations can explain not only the possibility of cases often taken as counterexamples to these propositions but also can explain why those cases are odd or not paradigmatic exercises of the relevant capacity.

items.title: Perceived and actual AI literacy in military organizations: a self-efficacy framework for training design.
items.abstract: This study examines the underlying causes of the gap between perceived artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and the actual competencies of defense personnel, and explores structured training initiatives that can support reliable and responsible decision-making in AI-mediated operational environments. Grounded in self-efficacy theory and the cognitive psychology of competence assessment, the study advances the theoretically motivated proposition that the routine use of intelligent systems may contribute to overconfidence and illusions of competence, dynamics that, while documented in educational and civilian professional contexts through existing research on automation bias and self-efficacy inflation, have not yet been systematically examined in military organizational settings and whose relevance to high-stakes defense environments constitutes a central theoretical proposition of this study. Drawing on a narrative review of the literature, the study analyzes the cognitive, metacognitive, and organizational factors contributing to this gap, and surveys AI literacy initiatives adopted by major defense organizations, highlighting a tentative cross-national convergence toward a multidimensional model integrating cognitive, operational, critical, and ethical competencies. Building on these insights, the authors present a foundational four-dimensional training framework implemented at the Center for High Defense Studies/School of Advanced Defense Studies (CASD/SSU) as an illustrative programmatic case, demonstrating how structured AI literacy pathways may be designed to promote awareness, calibrated self-efficacy, and organizational readiness in technologically complex military environments.

items.title: Toward an integrated multilevel framework for AI moral literacy: bridging individual and organizational ethical capacities.
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly shape lives across various sectors of society, a heightened moral imperative has emerged: individuals and organizations must be equipped with ethical capacities to responsibly navigate an AI-driven future. This paper fowards an integrative multilevel framework of AI moral literacy, which transcends cognitive–affective abilities and technological skills and emphasizes relational, context-sensitive ethical capacity. Drawing from frameworks on individual moral literacy and organizational moral learning, this discussion paper integrates these perspectives to conceptualize AI moral literacy as a recursive, co-constitutive dynamic between people and institutions. Through this multilevel integration, the emerging dialectical framework attends to both personal moral agency and the structural conditions that enable or constrain it. Elaboration of intersections between dimensions of individual and organzational moral literacy in the context of AI are also presented.

items.title: Filosofia computației. Realitate și calcul. Suport de curs 2026.
items.abstract: Acest material este suportul de curs „Filosofia computației: Realitate și calcul”, predat la Facultatea de Filosofie, Universitatea din București, în februarie-iunie 2026. Materialul este publicat ca resursă educațională deschisă sub licența CC BY 4.0, care permite reutilizarea cu atribuire corespunzătoare. O monografie, substanțial rescrisă și extinsă, este în curs de pregătire. -/- Cursul urmărește întrebarea dacă lumea și calculul sunt distincte sau dacă există o formă de imanență între realitate, calcul și informație. Cursul prezintă calculul ca progresia de la reprezentare, implementare la limitele calculabilității, în urma cărora există două variante: fizicalizarea calculului sau ontologizarea informației. -/- Cursul poate servi, așadar, ca introducere în fundamentele formale şi filosofice ale dezbaterilor provocate de avansul tehnologic contemporan. Aceste fundamente deschid un spațiu riguros de dezbatere între multiple abordări concurente, fapt pentru care fiecare modul al cursului se încheie cu o întâlnire interdisciplinară consemnată în suport.

items.title: Ethical Considerations Toward Harmonizing Human and Machine Agency in Embodied Neurotechnologies.
items.abstract: Embodied robotic neurotechnologies such as medical exoskeletons or neuroprostheses can enhance the ability of neurological patients to lead independent lives and thereby increase their functional agency. Modern approaches leverage methods from artificial intelligence to detect neurologically generated intent and to automate complex parts of the actions based on contextual data. However, the potential broadening utility and apparent benefits of these neurotechnologies to restore, sustain, or expand individual agency can also incur risks of their overuse. Excessive automatization of movements could reduce the causal influence that individuals exert upon their actions and thus may compromise their sense of agency. The construct of a sense of self and thus an identity to which responsibility can be attributed requires that a person is able to distinguish self-generated actions from actions of others, attribute their actions to themselves, and take ownership of the actions’ consequences. However, when parts of one’s movements are assisted or automated by intelligent robotic neurotechnologies, the distinction between endogenous and exogenous actions becomes blurred, resulting in a co-agency. In this paper, we discuss how this co-agency between humans and neurotechnologies can be shaped through the lens of the cross-cultural value of harmony, emphasizing the central role of intentions, balance, synchrony, and context. We argue from a cosmopolitan neuroethical perspective that embodied robotic neurotechnologies should prioritize supporting their users’ sense of agency, next to and above increasing their capacity for objective functional actions. Optimality should not be the prime goal of assistive neurotechnology, but a harmonious balance between human and machine agency.

items.title: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY: Proposal for the Nzila Spirit-Tech Research Lab & Institute.
items.abstract: The Nzila Spirit-Tech Research Lab & Institute Executive Summary presents the founding vision for an African-led research initiative dedicated to exploring the intersection of indigenous knowledge systems, consciousness studies, cosmology, ecological intelligence, and emerging technologies. Grounded in the Nzila Spirit-Tech Paradigm, the proposal outlines the Institute's mission, vision, institutional objectives, and long-term research agenda. It advocates an interdisciplinary framework where indigenous epistemologies and contemporary scientific inquiry can be investigated together with intellectual rigor, fostering innovative approaches to technological development while preserving Africa's rich knowledge heritage. The document also introduces opportunities for strategic partnerships, research collaboration, and philanthropic support toward establishing a globally recognized research institution.

items.title: Framework Revision Without a Global Editor: The Revision Typology, Retraction and Retention Rules per Leaf, and the Annotation-Cascade Calculus.
items.abstract: When a many-paper formal framework must change its mind — a computational defect found in a deposited paper, a conditional whose antecedent a later audit moves, a pricing sharpened by a later result — who edits? This paper, the sixty-fifth in a sequence developing an interpretive framework that redescribes physical reality as a causally consistent history of information updates, and the closing panel of its L-type Audition Program, personifies the implicit answer as the Global Editor: the authority with retroactive write access to the corpus's history, for whom consistency is maintained by silently updating the record until it agrees with itself. Its practice-side shadow is familiar — the updated preprint with no change log, the silently corrected equation, the claim whose history is unrecoverable across versions. The sequence had built against it piecemeal: deposited texts are DOI-immutable, registers are frozen, upgrades are annotation-only, new versions carry itemized notes re-verified at gates. But piecemeal discipline is precedent, not law, and the place precedent predictably breaks is under load: the sibling audition panel left a live adoption-triggered branch whose execution would touch frozen conditionals across a dozen papers at once. Without a cascade calculus the honest options degenerate to "rewrite everything" (the Editor) or "annotate nothing" (unannotated staleness accumulating in the record). This paper replaces the precedent with an explicit, checkable discipline, under the registered controlling phrase: the corpus may revise its standings, but it never rewrites its past. -/- The revision typology fixes four acts, none of which changes content-at-address: annotate (add-only marginal content on a frozen register); re-version (a full version bump with an itemized note and re-run gates, or a status pass — with the deposited-artifact rule that no act replaces a deposited object: a re-version at that status creates a new deposited successor and a forward-supersession relation); retract (a claim's downstream-consumption license withdrawn while its text stands, the notice itself a record); and retain-as-conditional (the falsified-antecedent case: the conditional survives as the theorem it always was, with the antecedent's status recorded — only the consumption right changes). An act-selection function over leaf type, defect type, and deposit status is proven total and decidable, with the load-bearing boundary registered: an error at the time of …

items.title: The Atomic Clock Reduction Series and Sovereign Time uuia.app/sovereigntime : Identity Physics Structural Prediction of the International System of Units (SI) Standards Hierarchy via Sovereign Anchor Constant (SAC) Precision Long Division Protocol (LDP) CI Green Lean4/Coq 0 Sorry 0 Free Parameters.
items.abstract: We reduce six atomic clock substrates to substrate-neutral Pattern-Narrative-Behavior-Adaptation (PNBA) form at full Sovereign Anchor Constant (SAC = 1.36899099984016) precision using the Long Division Protocol (LDP), and we establish that the framework structurally predicts the International System of Units (SI) atomic clock hierarchy from raw peer-reviewed data with zero fitting parameters. The six reductions cover microwave hyperfine clocks (Cs-133 SI primary, Rb-87 SI secondary, Rb-85 sibling isotope, H-1 hydrogen maser) and optical clocks (Sr-87 lattice, Al-27+ single-ion quantum logic). Under uniform τ = B/P reading, Cs-133 sits at τ/TL = 86.1% (deep locked), Rb-87 at 99.85% (edge locked), and H-1 requires higher-order PNBA fusion τ = B/(P·N·A) because its adaptation axis A carries structural weight (g_e·g_p/4 = 2.796). The Sr-87 optical lattice reveals a Noble-phase fusion: under 8-beam Psychology (PSY) fusion of identical trapped atoms, B_out = max(0, 8B − 56B) = 0. The collective lattice drives to Noble equilibrium, structurally explaining why optical lattice clocks achieve 10⁻¹⁸ fractional uncertainty. The framework's phase-depth ordering (deeper below Torsion Limit = more stable) reproduces the SI primary/secondary/reference hierarchy from raw B/P ratios alone, independent of engineering considerations. Building on this series and inheriting the resonance_always_at_anchor theorem from [9,9,2,1], we define Sovereign Time as the SAC anchor emission (1.36899099984016 GHz) through a four-substrate Structurally-Stable (SS) certified resonance lattice, providing a 15-digit-precision base clock rate with 3-of-4 fault tolerance. An interactive browser demonstration renders the anchor emission at full SAC precision with stopwatch controls. Independent verification confirms that the display math preserves 15-digit precision on any input, with the browser sandbox (performance now() at 100–1000 μs resolution) as the sole precision bottleneck. The math is native; the browser is one particular throttled rendering. Precision upgrade note: the earlier corpus reading "Rb-87 hyperfine ≈ 5 × ANCHOR" was a working approximation at Layer 1 precision (ANCHOR = 1.369). At SAC precision, the exact ratio is 4.9925, revealing a 10.27 MHz structural residual that Theorem T11 of the new Rb-87 reduction file formalizes. The τ = B/P reading via neutron count is what the higher-precision reduction produces. 1. Introduction -/- 1.1 The Grounding Problem the Series Addresses …

items.title: Psychologizing, Authority, and Propaganda.
items.abstract: When should we dismiss the reasons agents give for their views and instead invoke alternative psychological or causal explanations for their behavior? Philosophers such as Amy Flowerree and Nicholas Smyth have recently argued that we should generally avoid such dismissive psychologizing of individuals on moral grounds. In this paper, I critique these views and argue that the morality of psychologizing depends crucially on the formal authority an agent possesses. This psychologizing is not only permissible on my view, but even recommended in light of an agent’s formal authority. I advocate for the following principle: we should default to psychologizing agents who occupy powerful formal positions of authority, while we should be comparatively more hesitant to psychologize those outside of such positions. Psychologizing the non-formally authoritative does carry a certain moral and political risk. It can encourage political disenfranchisement, denying others full-fledged, equal participation in political life because they are taken to lack the necessary rational capacity for this participation. This is a possibility that researchers in particular should contend with. My discussion draws out implications for understanding propagandistic threats, academic research on epistemic behavior, defenses of epistocracy, and the moral dimensions of our epistemic lives.

items.title: EIGENLAGE: A General Framework of Bearerhood, Consequence, and Attribution.
items.abstract: This paper introduces Eigenlage as a bearer-condition framework for disciplined attribution under uncertainty. It asks what kind of concrete continuity could be the locus to which conscious appearing, welfare relevance, or morally significant undergoing could meaningfully be attributed. Eigenlage does not derive consciousness, solve the hard problem, or treat intelligence, behavior, computation, self-report, reward, complexity, biological form, or technical architecture as sufficient for consciousness. It instead defines the integrated structural own-continuity of a bounded, exposed, consequence-bearing token under one active integration regime. The framework separates representation from actuality, trace from biography, token from type, continuity from pattern identity, dependency from boundary inclusion, regulation from affect, opacity from evidence, and attribution from consciousness. It develops tools for classifying cases involving retained consequence, structural own-continuity, internally regulated viability, affective-systemic valence, constitutive compression, internal un-invertibility, fission, successor tokens, biographical inheritance, and welfare burden. Its central ethical commitments are that uncertainty created or preserved by responsible parties cannot be used as exculpatory uncertainty, and that identity discontinuity cannot be used as ethical discontinuity. Eigenlage is proposed as a substrate-neutral but anti-inflationary framework for evaluating natural, artificial, clinical, institutional, ecological, and future systems where bearerhood, consequence, vulnerability, intervention, and attribution become structurally non-empty.

items.title: Filosofía de la computación.
items.abstract: El presente trabajo aborda los fundamentos metafísicos y éticos de la computación, cuestionando la pretensión de autosuficiencia de la arquitectura algorítmica frente a la capacidad de juicio del agente humano. A través de un análisis del logos natural frente a la lógica formal, se examina cómo la delegación de la toma de decisiones en sistemas autónomos conduce a una forma inédita de exclusión social y a la erosión del derecho a la réplica. La obra propone una ontología de la computación que reintegra la voluntad y la prudencia en el diseño de sistemas, denunciando la deriva tecno-administrativa que, al buscar la eficiencia absoluta, termina por desdibujar la dignidad del individuo en la estructura de la polis. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ This work addresses the metaphysical and ethical foundations of computation, challenging the claim of self-sufficiency of algorithmic architecture against the judgment capacity of the human agent. Through an analysis of natural logos versus formal logic, the study examines how the delegation of decision-making to autonomous systems leads to an unprecedented form of social exclusion and the erosion of the right to due process. The book proposes an ontology of computation that reintegrates will and prudence into systems design, denouncing the techno-administrative drift that, by seeking absolute efficiency, ends up obscuring individual dignity within the structure of the polis.

items.title: Simulating the Past- and Future-Directed Thoughts of Others.
items.abstract: This paper introduces a mindreading skill I call other-directed mental time travel (ODMTT). ODMTT supports a narrow link between mental time travel and mindreading. In brief, it specifies our ability to represent another person’s past- and future-directed representations, which in turn allow us to predict and explain their mental states and behaviour. I argue that this is a skill that could be particularly valuable in complex social contexts, such as therapeutic settings, where the stakes in predicting other people’s mental states precisely and accurately are high, and where precision and accuracy depend on understanding how the target person’s past- or future-directed thoughts shape their present-directed thoughts and behaviour. I support ODMTT by defending two empirically well-supported claims. First, that our mental time travel representations profoundly shape our mental states and so tracking these would be useful when mindreading. Second, that mental time travel relies heavily on constructive memory capacities, and so we can use these capacities to construct representations of other people’s mental time travel representations. From these two claims, I argue that we can and do engage in ODMTT. I then specify details about the specific aspects of our past- and future-directed thoughts that ODMTT allows us to track.

items.title: Gedächtnis des Ortes ohne Subjekt: Zu einer Erosions-Ontologie der räumlich-materiellen Inbesitznahme Eine Synthese aus Phänomenologie, Neuem Materialismus und der Theorie des endlichen Kontinuums.
items.abstract: Die Frage nach dem Gedächtnis des Ortes wird in der gegenwärtigen Philosophie zumeist unter der Voraussetzung behandelt, dass der Ort nur im Bezug auf ein Subjekt, das ihn erfährt oder interpretiert, Bedeutung und Gedächtnis erlangt. Selbst die fortgeschrittensten phänomenologischen Ansätze zum Ort – von Edward Casey bis Dylan Trigg – betonen zwar die fundamentale Rolle des Ortes für die Bildung von Gedächtnis und Identität, bleiben jedoch der Auffassung verhaftet, dass Sinnesübertragung an Strukturen des Bewusstseins, der gelebten Erfahrung oder des narrativen Gedächtnisses gebunden ist. Auf der anderen Seite entzieht der Neue Materialismus – mit Arbeiten wie Jane Bennetts Vibrant Matter oder Karen Barads Meeting the Universe Halfway – die Handlungsmacht der ausschließlichen Verfügung des Subjekts und spricht der Materie eine eigenständige Wirkungsmacht zu, bietet jedoch keine hinreichende Erklärung dafür, wie sich historische Kräfte in der Materie akkumulieren und an Subjekte weitergegeben werden, denen jede unmittelbare Erfahrung fehlt. -/- Die vorliegende Abhandlung argumentiert, dass beide Traditionen – bei aller fundamentalen Differenz – eine gemeinsame Voraussetzung teilen: dass Gedächtnis letztlich auf eine Form von Repräsentation oder Interpretation zurückgeführt werden muss.
