items.abstract: هل بدأت الآلة تتمتع بالوعي والمشاعر؟ Has the machine begun to possess consciousness and feelings? عجباً لأمر الإنسان. تراه مقتصداً معتدلاً لا يكلف نفسه ما لا تطيق. فإذا اتيح له شيء من التقدم العلمي والتكنولوجي، أسرف في الغرور وخيل إليه أنه قادر على كل شيء. عند خمسينيات القرن الماضي، ظهر مشروعان فيهما نفع كثير وغرور كثير أيضاً. أظهرت الهندسة الوراثية إمكانية استنساخ البشر. وأظهر الذكاء الاصطناعي إمكانية صنع روبوتات شبيهة بالبشر. وسرعان ما تطورت الأنظمة الاصطناعية من أنظمة قائمة على القواعد إلى نماذج قادرة على التعلم والاستدلال، وإذا بالسؤال يلح على العقول: هل يمكن أن تصبح الآلة واعية يوماً ما؟ -/- How strange is humankind! We see people being frugal and moderate, not burdening themselves beyond their capacity. Yet, when given some scientific and technological advancement, they become excessively arrogant, imagining themselves capable of anything. In the 1950s, two projects emerged, offering both immense benefits and considerable vanity. Genetic engineering demonstrated the possibility of cloning humans, and artificial intelligence showed the potential to create humanoid robots. Artificial systems quickly evolved from rule-based systems to models capable of learning and reasoning, prompting the pressing question: Could machines one day become conscious? -/- إسماعيل، صلاح. 2026. هل بدأت الآلة تتمتع بالوعي والمشاعر؟، أفق، بيروت: مؤسسة الفكر العربي،178:1. -/- .

items.title: Hallucination as Field Failure.
items.abstract: Hallucination in large language models is conventionally treated as a single, model-internal pathology — a defect of the generator to be reduced through better training, retrieval, or decoding. This paper argues that the category is not homogeneous. Two structurally distinct phenomena are conflated under the one word. Class 1, floor hallucination, is the statistically irreducible error rate intrinsic to next-token prediction over a finite parametric store; recent work argues that, under standard next-token prediction and evaluation regimes, a positive hallucination floor is structural rather than incidental. Class 2, field-maintenance hallucination, is the loss of established accuracy that occurs in extended interaction when the relational field between human and model — the active configuration of constraints, definitions, and frame on which the output is conditioned — is no longer maintained. Class 2 is not a property of the model in isolation; it is a property of a relation that has ceased to be sustained. Building on Primordial Separation Ontology (PSO) and Triadic Relational Ontology (TRO), the paper develops a breakdown taxonomy for Class 2 (context truncation, constraint evaporation, frame drift, scope dissolution), anchors the taxonomy in independently documented machine-learning phenomena (positional salience decay, error snowballing, sycophancy), and grounds the account in the attentional substrate of the transformer. The framework yields a falsifiable operational discriminator — the re-injection test — that separates the two classes empirically, though the test measures recoverability, not relationality as such. The claim is bounded: TRO does not dispute the statistical floor, does not assert a categorical discontinuity where there may be only a gradient, and does not deny that what it tracks could be redescribed in purely mechanistic terms. It isolates a practically significant and frequently misattributed subset of confabulation, relocates the relevant intervention from the generator to the maintained relation, and proposes a protocol whose execution would establish whether the distinction earns its keep beyond nomenclature. This is a hypothesis paper; the protocol is proposed, not yet run.

items.title: Two Vulnerabilities: Why Imputable Authorship Requires a Self-Constituting Agent.
items.abstract: The responsibility gap in AI is standardly located in the failure of an epistemic condition (knowing what one is doing) or a control condition (competently governing one's doing). A recent and influential move argues that these conditions are a red herring, since human agents fail them too, and relocates the issue to answerability and to the vulnerability of those subject to an agent's power (Vallor and Vierkant 2024). I argue that this debate conflates two distinct notions of vulnerability. Patiency-vulnerability — exposure to another agent's power — grounds duties owed to those affected, but it does not ground imputable authorship. What grounds imputable authorship is constitutive vulnerability: the self-exposure of an agent whose normative identity is at stake in its own commitments because it must constitute that identity from no antecedent program. I derive constitutive vulnerability from constitutive indigence (the absence of a closed behavioural program) via the necessity of self-constitution, and show that it is neither biological fragility nor phenomenal consciousness nor mortality. I then argue that expansive answerability practices presuppose, on the answerer's side, an agent with constitutive vulnerability, and therefore cannot by themselves close the gap. The upshot is that the responsibility gap, properly understood, is ontological rather than epistemic, control-theoretic, or governance-remediable: it tracks the absence of a self-constituting agent, and no amount of meaningful human control or answerability engineering closes it while that absence obtains. The thesis is compatible with either determinism or indeterminism, and it is falsifiable.

items.title: Temporal experiences, temporal beliefs, and experiencing the future as open.
items.abstract: Evidence suggests that a majority of people believe that time robustly passes, but that a substantial minority do not, and that a majority of people report that it seems to them as though time robustly passes, but that a substantial minority do not. Two things are surprising about these results. First, it is surprising that we such variation in people’s reports about how things seem to them. Second, it is surprising that we do not find any association between what people believe about whether time robustly passes, and what they report about whether it seems as though time does robustly pass. Call these the variation and association puzzles. We aim to go some way towards resolving both puzzles. With respect to the association puzzle, we hypothesise that people’s temporal beliefs are disunified—the disunified representation hypothesis—in that their embedded and unembedded temporal beliefs are not correlated. This leaves open the possibility that although there is no association between people’s unembedded temporal beliefs and their reported temporal seemings, there is an association between people’s embedded temporal beliefs and their reported temporal seemings. Regarding the variation puzzle, we investigate the experiential openness hypothesis, according to which variation in people’s reported temporal seemings is the product of differences in how strongly people experience the future as open. We find evidence in favour of both the disunified representation hypothesis and the experiential openness hypothesis, and consider the implication of this for theorising about the nature of time on the basis of our reported temporal seemings and beliefs.

items.title: Our Natural Eternal Consciousness: What Everyone Should Know.
items.abstract: By explaining that consciousness does not end at death but pauses psychologically, the scientific theory of a natural eternal consciousness (NEC) reveals a timeless immortality. Our NEC makes nonexistence impossible, a natural afterlife real, and a heaven of utmost joy as well as accountability possible. Note, however, that if any supernatural afterlife occurs, it will override one’s NEC.

items.title: Constructing Theorem-Level Questions: A Declaration Discipline for Bounded Inquiry.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a methodology for constructing theorem-level questions through explicit declaration rather than implicit assumption. It identifies six components required for a mathematically well-typed question—object, admissible transformations, observable, equivalence relation, verdict class, and stopping condition—and develops a declaration discipline for moving from informal prompts to decidable mathematical statements. -/- The paper separates asking, typing, computing, and interpreting into distinct stages of inquiry and introduces three reusable artifacts: a six-component question type, a proof-obligation checklist, and a layered status discipline distinguishing mathematics from derived consequence, interpretation, speculation, and open problems. -/- A neutral worked example from program equivalence demonstrates the methodology independently of the author’s other research. The paper argues only that theorem-level questions require sufficient declaration of their governing regime; it does not claim that all meaningful inquiry should be formalized. The result is presented as a methodological framework for constructing and auditing formal questions across mathematics, computer science, and related technical disciplines.

items.title: A Recurrence Converse for Identity Persistence.
items.abstract: This paper proves a recurrence converse for finite declared identity-persistence regimes. Given an admissible transition matrix A, it shows that the capacity separating persistence-bearing retention from storage-only retention is carried not by acyclic trajectory growth but by the reachable recurrent core A_rec(q). Under the class-indexed verdict observable, the same/not-same channel anchored at q has capacity log ρ(A_rec(q)), with achievability and converse established over the same mathematical object. -/- The argument separates attribution, mathematical, and dictionary layers. Strongly connected components are characterized as the extremal partition for recurrence-rate attribution, a Perron–Frobenius localization identity isolates the recurrent source of capacity, and a uniform counting bound yields the recurrence converse. The result refines the Coding Theorem for Identity Persistence by identifying where finite identity capacity resides. -/- The paper further computes verdict-only capacity through finite determinization, proves a strict sub-one-bit upper bound for bare verdict streams, resolves small-horizon recurrence as a naming rather than capacity phenomenon, and establishes a sublinear-budget recurrence converse using the zero-cost recurrent core. Weighted extensions, binding linear-budget regimes, and countable-state extensions remain open.

items.title: Teaching Constipation: Experiential Knowledge, the Life-Experience Encyclopedia, and the Problem of Recognizing the Unmonitored Event.
items.abstract: This treatise examines a class of knowledge that resists pedagogical transmission: the knowledge of what an experience is. It begins from a clinical intake question—whether the author had ever suffered a cardiac event—and from the reply that exposed the question’s hidden difficulty: How would I know? The treatise argues that certain concepts cannot be taught by description, analogy, or the construction of a conducive learning environment, but can only be completed by the learner’s own undergoing of the referent experience. The homely example of constipation serves as the organizing case, for an instructor may describe, illustrate, and arrange favorable conditions, yet cannot install the concept fully, because full possession requires the physical experience that furnishes the concept with a referent. Drawing on the distinction between knowledge by acquaintance and knowledge by description (James, 1890; Russell, 1912), the knowledge argument (Jackson, 1982, 1986; Nagel, 1974), tacit knowing (Polanyi, 1966), and the phenomenology of the lived body (Merleau-Ponty, 1962), and integrating the author’s Life-Experience Encyclopedia model (Boether, 2025, 2026a), the treatise reconstructs the moment of recognition as the inscription of a hitherto hollow encyclopedic entry. The cardiac case is then explained through the science of interoception (Craig, 2002; Garfinkel et al., 2015): recognition of an internal event requires both the event and a channel of awareness adequate to it. What follows is a pedagogy of occasioning rather than of transmission.

items.title: SPRINT 5 Evolutionary Persistence and Regenerative Persistence From the Persistent Agent to the Persistent Regime.
items.abstract: -/- Sprint 5 investigates the conditions under which adaptive organizational regimes preserve functional continuity after severe degradation, compression, and reconstructive reorganization. Rather than evaluating a single hypothesis, the experimental program progressively examines increasingly demanding perturbations designed to identify the organizational principles underlying regenerative persistence. -/- The investigation begins by characterizing the behaviour of the Ariadne Thread during adaptive cryptobiosis and evolutionary reopening. Subsequent experiments systematically challenge the initial interpretation by suppressing its functional influence, inducing its complete structural extinction, and exploring the effects of degradation depth, extinction duration, and competitive reconstruction dynamics. -/- Across the program, the experimental evidence progressively eliminates several initially plausible explanations. Functional continuity is shown not to require the preservation of the Ariadne Thread, strict organizational identity, or any privileged reconstructive trajectory. Instead, reconstructive capacity emerges as a graded property of the organizational regime itself, constrained by experimentally observable limits of reconstructibility and realized through the competitive emergence and selection of organizational alternatives. -/- Taken together, the results redefine Regenerative Persistence as the capacity of an organizational regime to regenerate functional directionality following severe degradation without requiring the preservation of specific structures or identities. More broadly, Sprint 5 illustrates how successive experimental observations progressively transformed the conceptual framework used to interpret persistence, shifting the explanatory focus from persistent agents toward the organizational properties of adaptive regimes. -/- .

items.title: PHRONESIS — On Embodied Floor Presence: A Working Coordinator’s Account of Presence, Trust, and the Limits of a Grey-Line Role.
items.abstract: This document is a descriptive first-person PHRONESIS essay on embodied floor presence, working coordination, trust, relationship-based baseline recognition, willingness versus capacity, coordination load, and the limits of judgment inside real working conditions. -/- It does not establish authority over any person or system, human or artificial. It is not a management rule, safety protocol, medical judgment, workplace accusation, AI protocol, authority claim, or claim about AI behavior. The factory-floor material is offered as lived observation, not as a universal method or equivalence to artificial intelligence. -/- The essay preserves a narrow reference signal: human systems contain forms of knowledge that do not always appear in clean metrics. A distant system may see output without seeing strain, continued production without seeing reduced capacity, or a role title without understanding its limits. The archive preserves this as reference, not command.

items.title: Yuanling Theory: An Ontological Revolution of the Nature of Consciousness.
items.abstract: The “hard problem” of consciousness remains unresolved because existing paradigms operate within the presupposition that “consciousness is a product of matter.” The Yuanling Theory proposed in this paper represents a fundamental ontological reconceptualization of the nature of consciousness. The ontological subject of consciousness is termed Yuanling, which is defined as an energy-information complex that exists independently as individual consciousness, born from the coupling event between Yuanling Particles and a specific life carrier at a vital energetic node. This paper systematically expounds the generative mechanism and seven core attributes of Yuanling, reveals its functional grounding and ontological foundation rooted in the Non-Spatiotemporal background, and constructs a preliminary framework of Yuanling Ecology. This paper argues that Yuanling Theory provides a novel value significance and cross-disciplinary implications for the ontological status of consciousness, and achieves a re-anchoring of human self-understanding across three dimensions: the view of life, the view of consciousness, and the view of cognition.

items.title: Embodied Rhythm Without Overclaim: Breath, Heart Rhythm, Neural Oscillation, and the Boundaries of Resonance.
items.abstract: This preprint develops a disciplined account of the body as a rhythmic and regulatory system without treating the body as a mystical frequency object. It examines breath, heart rhythm, neural oscillation, interoception, embodied cognition, ritual, music, vibroacoustic claims, placebo/context effects, and clinical boundaries through a mechanism-before-meaning framework. -/- This article develops a source-controlled account of the body as a rhythmic and regulatory system. It begins from a restricted claim: the body may be described as resonant only when resonance is tied to measurable physiology, coupling, timing, regulation, perception, and constraint. The article rejects the weaker public claim that the body is simply “frequency” or that rhythm language proves universal healing, energy alignment, or spiritual law. Its scientific core moves through respiration-brain coupling, heart rate variability, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, neurovisceral integration, neural oscillation, interoception, embodied cognition, sensorimotor feedback, breath practice, ritual synchrony, sound, rhythm, and clinical boundary. Its interpretive core asks how bodily rhythm becomes meaning through feeling, attention, posture, shared practice, symbolic discipline, and cultural framing. The article introduces Embodied Rhythm Without Overclaim as a source-control method: physical rhythm, physiological coupling, neural modulation, interoceptive perception, emotional regulation, embodied meaning, ritual interpretation, and clinical claim must be separated before being compared. Breath is treated as a special case because it is both autonomic and voluntarily modifiable; heart rhythm is treated through HRV and its caveats; neural oscillation is treated as coordination rather than popular brainwave mysticism; interoception is treated as the bridge through which bodily signals become experience. The article also distinguishes legitimate music, rhythm, entrainment, breathwork, placebo/context, and vibroacoustic research from unsupported frequency-healing claims. Integral Resonance Theory and Unified Frequency Theory are named only as components of a broader theoretical framework, not elaborated and not treated as established scientific law. The result is a disciplined expansion of the Interconnected Universe framework: the body does not need mystical inflation to matter. It is already profound as a sensing, rhythmic, self-regulating organism.

items.title: Countering Extremism: Why Choices of War, Criminal Law or Terrorism Matter.
items.pub: Law and Ethics of Human Rights 20 (1):25-48.
items.venue: Law and Ethics of Human Rights
items.abstract: When and why do states define and prosecute harmful conduct as criminal, and when as war or terror? What political and instrumental considerations inform these choices, how and why do they change over time, and with what outcomes? The pressure to avert future atrocities not only informs preventive laws and measures but also impels states to identify and tackle extremist ideologies “further up the field.” There is no internationally agreed legal definition of extremism. Whereas most countries target “violent extremism,” violence is not a requirement of the UK non-statutory definition, which targets ideology over conduct. Eluding law, extremism is not prosecuted through courts or military tribunals but pursued in communities and public institutions. This exploration of the UK’s struggle to define and tackle the growing threat posed by extremism reveals difficult legal and political challenges, as well as costs for democratic participation and rights.

items.title: Imaging urban doppelgängers: art and the digital twin in South Korea.
items.abstract: This article examines how South Korean artists engage the concept and material infrastructures of the digital twin. While often dismissed as decorative or superfluous, artistic images of the city are an essential part of place-making, as a counter-point to the usually prioritized imagination of municipal bureaucrats, private developers, architects, and urban planners. Artworks structure a hybrid phenomenology that positions the spectator as simultaneously “here” in the physical and “there” in the virtual or conceptual; this doubled spectatorship reveals the constructed frames of experience, thereby creating an uncanny form of attention that implicates the spectator in a relationship with the image. By visualizing the material world and its digital double side by side, Hoonida Kim draws attention to new forms of human perception engendered by digital twin tools. Turning from the hardware to data curation, members of Red Onion collective (Kim et al. 2020) highlight the flawed or narrow applications of urban “big data” through the City of Seoul’s official Open Data portal. Finally, the artist-activist group Listen to the City mirror the data-collection and analytic methodologies of the smart city through an artistic, feminist, and community-driven lens in order to resist gentrification. With the normalization of digital twins and similar “smart” technologies in urban environments, it is critical to bring the invisible components of urban infrastructure to the foreground in order to examine their effects on the material, conceptual, and societal spaces of the city. By leveraging artistic imagination and image-production, these artists expand on the existing technical and social discourse of the digital twin and the smart city.

items.title: The replacement-augmentation paradox: techno-perceptual dynamics of AI adoption in medical imaging and the future of work.
items.abstract: The implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in radiology has garnered significant attention across both research and practice over the last decade. However, opinions on whether AI will augment or replace radiologists in their work have so far been divided, and the debate around this continues to linger. This article conceptually structures and terms this phenomenon as the “replacement-augmentation paradox” of AI in radiology—the persistent coexistence of replacement fears and augmentation perceptions within the same professional community. Rather than treating these positions as mutually exclusive or empirically resolvable through performance metrics alone, this article conceptualises the replacement-augmentation paradox as a synthesising framework that structures and interprets divergent, evidence-informed narratives of AI integration in radiology. Drawing predominantly on sociotechnical and perception-based research, this article juxtaposes the two coexistent narratives and synthesises collective observations to shed light on relatively less emphasised aspects shaping replacement-augmentation debates. The findings obtained here explicate the implementation of AI tools (such as deep learning) for medical imaging and early diagnosis in radiology through a proposed “techno-perceptual” framework where the augmentation and replacement of the existing work practices are both plausible outcomes (O), subject to preconditions. Alleviation of fears and determination of the resultant narrative is thus linked with the provision of three jointly enabling conditions: training (T), evidence (E), and decisional control (C), the presence or absence of which are deemed to be directly consequential in terms of yielding perceptions of augmentation or replacement, respectively. The importance and interplay of these factors are delineated here through the novel Boolean equation O = T ∧ E ∧ C, a corresponding logical table, a process flow diagram, and a radiologist typology matrix depicting four professional archetypes.

items.title: PNBA Identity Physics ProofPress: Lean 4/Markdown to LaTeX Conversion Tool for Formally Verified Research uuia.app/proofpress.
items.abstract: Abstract -/- ProofPress is a standalone, browser-based conversion tool that transforms Lean 4 formal proof files into Overleaf-ready LaTeX documents. It operates in two modes: an LDP mode tuned to the SNSFT corpus conventions, and a General mode compatible with any standard Lean 4 file. The tool extracts theorem names, human-readable descriptions, return types, and LDP step annotations directly from the source file, populates a structured academic paper template, and produces a .tex file ready for journal submission. ProofPress requires no installation, no server, and no external dependencies. It is distributed as a single HTML file that executes entirely in the browser. -/- The tool addresses a real and underserved gap in the formal verification ecosystem: the absence of a direct, low-friction pathway from machine-verified proof to publication-ready academic document. By eliminating the manual transcription step that currently stands between a formally verified corpus and its presentation to the scientific community, ProofPress lowers the barrier to publication for researchers working in Lean 4. -/- 1. Motivation -/- Formal verification produces machine-checked proofs with guarantees no informal mathematical argument can provide. The Lean 4 theorem prover, in conjunction with the Mathlib library, has become the standard environment for formally verified mathematics across an increasingly broad range of domains — from number theory and algebra to physics, materials science, and cognitive science. The research community has taken notice: high-profile formalizations such as Terry Tao's Polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa proof (2023) have demonstrated that formal verification can operate at the frontier of mathematical research rather than merely audit classical results. -/- Despite this momentum, a fundamental asymmetry persists. Formally verified work exists simultaneously in two disconnected registers: the .lean file that the compiler accepts, and the academic paper that peer reviewers read. These are not interchangeable artifacts. The .lean file contains tactic proofs, namespace structures, and machine-readable syntax that journals do not accept. The academic paper requires prose exposition, LaTeX formatting, and structured narrative that the Lean compiler ignores. Translating between them is currently a manual process: a researcher must retype or copy-paste theorem statements, strip tactic proofs, escape special characters, apply LaTeX formatting, and restructure …

items.title: The determination of what is said and what is implied.
items.abstract: Is what is said determined by syntax, conventional meaning, and select aspects of context? This thesis—semanticity—seems plausible because what is said can diverge from both what the speaker means and what the addressee understands, and because ordinary speakers know what is said when presented with a novel sentence‐context pair. I argue that semanticity is actually not the best explanation of these properties, because what is implied shares them. I then explain this commonality: What is said and what is implied are similarly determined by the interpretation of an addressee defined in terms of the context.

items.title: Large language models illuminate the mechanistic underpinnings of the creative aspect of language use (CALU), long regarded as a mystery.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) challenge Chomsky’s long-standing mysterian view of the creative aspect of language use (CALU). By exhibiting fluent, situation-appropriate linguistic behavior and offering concrete mechanistic hypotheses, they provide the first viable scientific models of CALU. We endorse Futrell and Mahowald’s call to integrate LLMs into linguistic inquiry and suggest a bolder aim: elucidating the mechanisms underlying linguistic creativity.

items.title: An action-first account of episodic memory.
items.abstract: Building off of a recent account of intentionality, the action-forward framework, we introduce a novel account of episodic memory and defend its plausibility as an account of such memory. According to our account, episodic remembering consists in acts of performative retelling of the remembering subject’s initial experience of an event where such retelling activates connected capacities for perceptual recognition of the event and its constituents. When such acts are overt, the remembering subject expresses their memory, say, verbally, imagistically, through performance, etc., where doing so reactivates those recognitional capacities. When such acts are covert, the remembering subject merely activates capacities for such expressions without going on to overtly express where doing so reactivates the relevant recognitional capacities. In §2, we introduce two desiderata on accounts of episodic memory. In §3, we give an overview of the action-forward framework for intentionality. In §4, we introduce our account of episodic memory. In §5, we show how the account satisfies the desiderata. We conclude by saying how the account differs from standard accounts in the literature while retaining what we take to be their insights.

items.title: Timescapes of non-human experience.
items.abstract: How can we investigate non-human experiences scientifically? Given substantial differences in sensory abilities and the private nature of consciousness, this remains an open question. In this review, we propose a way to gain empirical traction on one key feature of experience: its temporal structure, or 'timescape'. Perceptual contents follow systematic temporal principles-synchronisation, revision, and persistence-and are sampled across attentional windows and vary in stability. These principles can be explored through temporal illusions and experimental paradigms. We conceptualise an animal's timescape in terms of five key windows, all of which are experimentally testable, and analyse evidence across animal species to highlight varying timescapes. Together, these ideas lay the foundations for a research programme comparing the temporal Umwelts of non-human animals.

items.title: Every Logic Has Its Own Logic: A Phenomenological Appeal to See.
items.abstract: Logic is indispensable to human inquiry, yet it is not identical with reality. Every logical system operates within assumptions, concepts, and relations that determine the conclusions it can produce. Consequently, opposing positions may each possess internal coherence while remaining incompatible with one another. This paper argues that logic and rational inquiry are distinctive capacities of human consciousness, but they remain instruments of understanding rather than reality itself. Drawing upon a phenomenological orientation, it examines how conceptual structures—including logical systems—can become mistaken for existence itself. It further argues that human rationality distinguishes the human mode of being without separating humanity from the ecological and existential unity of life. The deepest task of phenomenology is therefore not to replace one conceptual framework with another, but to disclose how concepts become reified into reality. Through direct awareness rather than conceptual attachment, human beings may encounter existence prior to inherited interpretation.

items.title: Beyond Punishment, Reward, and Praise: Awareness, Conditioning, and the Structures of Human Control.
items.abstract: This paper examines punishment, reward, and praise as interconnected mechanisms of social and psychological conditioning rather than as distinct methods of guidance or education. Although commonly regarded as necessary for maintaining order, motivation, and moral development, these practices are argued to operate through different forms of external control: punishment through fear, reward through desire, and praise through approval. From a phenomenological perspective, the study contends that such mechanisms shape behavior by conditioning responses instead of fostering direct understanding. The paper explores how these structures reproduce authority, conformity, psychological dependence, and inherited patterns of control across families, educational institutions, workplaces, and broader social systems. It further argues that authentic transformation cannot be produced through coercion, incentives, or recognition, but emerges through awareness—the direct observation of one's own fear, ambition, approval-seeking, and conditioning without judgment. Rather than proposing alternative techniques of behavioral management, the paper advocates a shift from external control to self-understanding, suggesting that intelligence, responsibility, and compassionate relationships arise naturally from awareness. In doing so, it offers a phenomenological critique of contemporary systems of social control and proposes awareness as the foundation for individual freedom and a society grounded in understanding rather than obedience.

items.title: Five Legal-Rational Myths of Punitive War and the Carceral State.
items.pub: Law and Ethics of Human Rights 20 (1):83-113.
items.venue: Law and Ethics of Human Rights
items.abstract: This Article is concerned with the symbolic narratives that have historically been used to justify punitive war, defined as the use of force to punish the violation of international norms, justified on behalf of the international community. Ostensibly, punishment as a legitimate cause for war has been proscribed in the modern international legal order, yet punitive violence has not been excised from international politics. This Article builds on the authors’ recent works on domestic legal-rational myths of the carceral state and international legal myths concerning the foundations of international law to argue that just war, and its corollary, punitive war, remains a feature of global politics. What has changed are the discourses that justify the use of force; reasons that have developed in dialog with domestic discourses of punishment because they share similar origins: the medieval natural law doctrines of desert and debt. Over the centuries, developments in state institutions of the carceral state, and the myths that provide them a “taken for granted” legitimacy, have been expressed in the structures of international law and global governance through a mutually constitutive dialectic – sometimes the domestic informs the international, sometimes the obverse, and sometimes innovation occurs in tandem. These mutually-informed myths take different institutional expressions in domestic and international spheres, but they bear strong resemblances to the canonical purposes of punishment in the Western tradition: retribution, deterrence, reform, and incapacitation. This Article identifies five legal-rational myths that justify war as punishment, and relates them to their domestic-law counterparts, emphasizing both their common bases in the vocabularies and theories of punishment, and their diverse institutional expressions. These myths emerged in specific historical conditions, but have become a lasting and malleable suite of tools available to states to justify armed intervention. Their durability is demonstrated through an examination of the recent war in Gaza, wherein claims of desert saturate all sides of the conflict.

items.title: De la IA generativa al colapso epistémico: Entornos epistémicamente hostiles en contextos de defensa de alto riesgo.
items.abstract: Este artículo analiza cómo los sistemas de inteligencia artificial (IA) empleados en contextos de defensa de alto riesgo pueden contribuir a la configuración de entornos epistémicamente hostiles. A partir de una reconstrucción conceptual de distintos modos de mediación epistémica asociados a la IA —sistemas basados en reglas, aprendizaje automático e IA generativa—, se examina cómo estas tecnologías reconfiguran la relación entre información, juicio humano y articulación entre hechos y valores en procesos de decisión bajo incertidumbre. El trabajo sostiene que la presencia de un humano en el bucle no garantiza por sí sola control, responsabilidad ni legitimidad, pues la supervisión humana solo resulta significativa cuando preserva condiciones efectivas de comprensión, revisión crítica, desacuerdo y veto. Sobre esta base, se propone la noción de colapso epistémico local para describir situaciones en las que la mediación algorítmica degrada la capacidad humana de interpretar contextos, cuestionar recomendaciones y asumir responsabilidad por las decisiones adoptadas. Se concluye que una gobernanza responsable de la IA en defensa debe evaluarse no solo por la precisión o eficiencia de los sistemas, sino también por su impacto sobre la calidad epistémica del entorno sociotécnico en el que se ejerce el juicio.

items.title: Harnessing artificial intelligence to preserve and advance indigenous knowledge system in Northeast India.
items.abstract: Northeast India is a cradle of cultural and ecological diversity, where Indigenous communities have cultivated rich traditional knowledge systems across generations—ranging from sustainable agroforestry, medicinal plant use, and sacred landscape management to complex oral histories and language traditions. However, these knowledge systems now face accelerating threats from environmental degradation, climate change, socio-economic shifts, and cultural erosion. This review explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) can serve as transformative tools for documenting, preserving, and revitalizing Indigenous knowledge in ways that are ethically grounded and community-driven. We present a comprehensive framework that integrates diverse AI capabilities—including natural language processing for endangered dialects, computer vision for ecological monitoring, geospatial modeling of traditional land-use, and predictive analytics for resilience planning. Emphasizing participatory design, we advocate for AI systems co-developed with Indigenous stakeholders, respecting data sovereignty and guided by the CARE principles—Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, and Ethics. Through inclusive workflows that build local capacity and align with Indigenous values, AI can enhance both scientific understanding and cultural continuity. The review also addresses critical challenges such as algorithmic bias, digital infrastructure gaps, and intellectual property protections, proposing hybrid governance models that combine traditional leadership with digital innovation. By bridging advanced computational tools with Indigenous stewardship, this approach offers a path toward the long-term resilience, autonomy, and flourishing of Northeast India’s Indigenous Knowledge Systems.

items.title: An Introduction to the Ecology of Ignorance: Why Does No One Stand Outside the Ecosystem?
items.abstract: In a world where people accuse one another of ignorance more than ever before, this article argues that the question "why are they ignorant?" is the wrong question. It presupposes that the speaker stands outside the circle of ignorance, an assumption that philosophical, sociological, cognitive and biological evidence does not support. The central claim is this: ignorance, whether at the individual or the social level, is neither a defect nor an external imposition. It is a structural requirement inseparable from the human subject. The article examines this claim at two levels. At the individual level, it draws on Heidegger, Simon, Gigerenzer and Haselton to show that individual ignorance is not an error or a deficiency, but a structural feature of the human subject. At the social level, Durkheim, Luhmann and Bourdieu show that ignorance in societies is not a failure, but a condition that makes social action possible. The article's claim, however, goes further. Ignorance is not merely structural (that is, inherent to each subject or each society taken in isolation); it is systemic. Being structural describes ignorance; being systemic explains it. Systemic ignorance arises from the dynamic interaction between the individual and social levels, not from either level alone. Merton, Fleck, Bourdieu, Hutchins and Wenger have described the mechanism of this systemic interaction: social structure produces individual ignorance, the individual mind reconstructs that same structure, and this feedback loop is sustained throughout the system through participation, not imposition. To make this systemic interaction visible, the article proposes a framework it calls "the ecology of ignorance": a shift in the unit of analysis from the ignorance of an individual to the interaction between individual ignorance and social structures. This shift changes the question we ask. Instead of "why are they ignorant?", it asks "what ecosystem do we all live in?" Its practical consequence is to replace judgement with mutual understanding.

items.title: Depressing temporal experiences: the COVID-19 Pandemic lockdown in Victoria, Australia.
items.abstract: Various governments around the world implemented ‘stay at home’ orders, colloquially known as lockdowns, in response to the COVID-19 Pandemic. Existing research suggests that these lockdowns had significant impacts upon the lived-experiences of temporality of many people, with widespread reports of anomalous experiences of temporal passage and difficulties with judgments of temporal duration. We conducted a phenomenologically framed online survey of 830 people in the state of Victoria, Australia, focused on temporal experiences of the state’s COVID-19 Pandemic lockdowns in 2020 and 2021. This survey used an adjusted version of the Transdiagnostic Assessment of Temporal Experience (TATE) scale (Stanghellini et al 2022) to get clearer about the frequency and intensity of the temporal anomalies and disruptions of these lockdowns. Our survey results confirm much of the existing research regarding the widespread prevalence of anomalous temporal experiences. In particular, we found that around half of our participants reported slowness, feeling out of sync (with others and the world), and persistent worry about the future during the lockdowns, with these reported disruptions falling sharply after restrictions ended in late 2021. By juxtaposing these survey results with existing work in the phenomenology of depression, we contend that many people experienced depressive-like temporal experiences under lockdown. We also outline the need for further phenomenologically informed research of this kind, which conjoins both qualitative and quantitative methods.

items.title: What the edge tells the cloud: decentralized geographies of AI.
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence algorithms are increasingly deployed outside datacenters and at the so-called Edge, i.e., on end devices such as self-driving cars, smartphones, sensors, and drones, as well as on-premises servers in hospitals and other large but localized institutions. This matters, because, this paper argues, the materiality of the devices on which AI algorithms are deployed influences the “cognition” and behavior of those algorithms. The role of AI’s materiality has thus far not received the attention it deserves, and critical AI literature tends to consider AI algorithms as unproblematically individualized and spatially bounded entities, whereas an attention to materiality also shows how AI’s cognition is always decentralized and spatially distributed. One class of Edge AI algorithms is Federated Learning, where end devices learn partial models independently and sometimes collaborate to produce global models for inference and decision-making. This paper asks what forms of material and spatial cognitive configurations enable specific types of AI agency, and with what ethico-political consequences? Through close reading of ArXiv papers and patents, analyzed, combining Gilbert Simondon and N Katherine Hayles, showing how Federated Learning and Edge AI problematize existing understandings of AI algorithms as immaterial, centralized, and unified subjects. By showing how Edge AI and Federated Learning proceed by compressing models, orchestrating cognition across space, and federating models to produce global inferences, this paper shows that the materiality of the microchips and the spatiality of the data and feature spaces that Edge devices inhabit produce a specific, distributed, and contested form of algorithmic individuality. While distributed Machine Learning algorithms enable more diffuse and granular forms of surveillance and control, they also open the potential to inject partial and situated knowledge into Machine Learning, as an antidote to the current hubris.

items.title: The imperative to cheat: AI as cognitive integration technology for neurodivergent knowledge production.
items.abstract: Current institutional responses to generative AI in academic and professional settings overwhelmingly frame AI use as a threat to cognitive integrity (Song 2024). This paper argues that such framing reproduces a specific form of ableism: it treats one cognitive architecture—linear, sequential, self-contained—as the only legitimate mode of knowledge production, and excludes individuals whose neurodivergent processing requires external scaffolding to translate insight into communicable form. The paper presents the Aaron Israel Method (AIM): a framework for understanding AI as a voice interface—a cognitive integration technology that allows minds with non-standard architectures to participate in knowledge production from which they are systematically excluded. AIM is distinguished from AI ghostwriting by its preservation of the human contributor’s epistemic authority: the AI structures and articulates, but does not originate the ideas, arguments, or experiential knowledge that constitute the work’s substance. The argument proceeds at three scales. At the personal scale, AI-as-voice-interface functions as assistive technology, and prohibiting it constitutes discrimination against cognitively diverse individuals (Jafry and Vorstermans 2025; Aquino et al. 2024). At the civilizational scale, excluding neurodivergent cognition suppresses the cognitive diversity that research demonstrates is necessary for innovation and complex problem-solving (Axbey et al. 2023; Stolte et al. 2022). At the existential scale, the problems facing humanity exceed human cognitive architecture entirely, and AI-augmented cognition is not optional but required for adequate response (Darras et al. 2024; Wernli et al. 2023). The paper grounds these arguments in extended mind theory (Clark and Chalmers 1998), extended active inference (Constant et al. 2022), innovation diffusion theory (Rogers 2003), evolutionary epistemology (Hoffman et al. 2015), and harm reduction ethics (Pratt 2026b). It concludes that AIM represents not merely an accommodation for disabled individuals but a prototype for the cognitive integration that species-level challenges will increasingly demand.

items.title: Erosion as the Ontological Condition of Diachronic Self-Identity: A Deductive Self-Model Theorem of Phenomenological Lack.
items.abstract: This paper establishes a fully deductive account of phenomenological lack grounded in diachronic self-identity. I demonstrate that any system satisfying diachronic identity necessarily operates under temporal indexation, which analytically entails the formation of a minimal self-model as a structural requirement of maintaining identity across non-coincident temporal states. From this, I derive that self-relation is necessarily non-equivalent across time, and that any internal comparison structure must generate a normative horizon. Phenomenological lack is shown to be the modal consequence of comparing present state to this horizon under conditions of representational non-coincidence. Erosion is redefined as the class of all structural transformations induced by temporal indexation, without appeal to decay or empirical assumptions. -/- Keywords: Diachronic identity, self-model theorem, non-equivalence, temporal indexation, lack, ontology, modality.

items.title: The language of real patterns.
items.abstract: In this response, we outline the central idea of a real pattern as applied in the philosophy of science as well as its relationship to the modal structure of models. We suggest that there may be additional concerns with linguistically real patterns in terms of convergence between natural language processing and formal linguistic theory.

items.title: Withdrawn by the author.
items.abstract: Reason for withdrawal: I have consolidated all my preprints on consciousness and condensed their reasoning into a new preprint, Locating Consciousness as a Puzzle Game: From Proof by Absence to the Causal Structure of the Subjective Container.

items.title: Keeping it real: Language models implement algorithms to solve linguistic tasks.
items.abstract: Futrell & Mahowald argue that language models (LMs) discover linguistic structure as “real patterns.” I contend this framing underplays what mechanistic interpretability uncovers: LMs implement specific algorithms to solve linguistic tasks. Under the framework of causal abstraction, we can rigorously test whether LMs converge on algorithms posited by linguistic theory, which further supports the authors’ conciliatory proposal.

items.title: War and Punishment: Rereading Hugo Grotius.
items.pub: Law and Ethics of Human Rights 20 (1):115-132.
items.venue: Law and Ethics of Human Rights
items.abstract: In Book II, Chapter 20 of The Rights of War and Peace, the Dutch philosopher Hugo Grotius presents the idea that punishment is a legitimate cause of war. In making this claim, he builds upon the long-standing Christian just war tradition, stretching back through Augustine and Aquinas up to the early modern period. Grotius’ justification for punitive war relies on his natural law reasoning, and the bulk of the chapter (one of the longest in the entire three volume text) relies on the idea that a wrong committed can be punished by any member of a society, i.e., there is not a necessity for an authority to engage in punishment only the existence of the wrong. But Grotius cautions his argument in a few ways, such as the dangers of vengeance and the hubris of leaders. While there has been a resurgence in recent years to justify war as punishment, both in theory and practice, less attention has been paid to the obligation to be merciful, other than in post-conflict situations. In this Article, I explore the relationship between punishment and mercy in Grotius’ work but also more widely. I suggest that Grotius’ natural law arguments both for punishment and mercy can still help us think critically about war. I argue that while punitive war remains a legitimate practice, we need to think more carefully about Grotius’ calls for mercy and charity. This can be found prior to war, during war, and after war. I conclude that both punishment and forgiveness merit equal attention in the just war tradition.

items.title: On Explaining - Understanding What it is to be Human, From all Sides of the Equation.
items.abstract: What happens when you are confidently right and then learn otherwise? This lyric-philosophical essay takes that moment as its starting point and treats knowledge as something alive: what is certain one day can change the next. It seats the twelve symbols of the author's coherent-existence functional, each in the role it already holds in standing mathematics: Ψ for the gathering of perspectives, α and φ for intensity and facing, Θ for one perspective's angle to the gathering, π for cancellation and return, λ for the settled reading, τ for within-time, the clock a life keeps on the inside, Δ for the difference that keeps the gathering changing, Ω for everyone present, Ξ for the total intensity that holds the gathering in proportion, and Λ for the floor beneath cancellation. The gathering held in proportion has the shape of Kuramoto's order parameter for coupled oscillators, with an intensity weighting that is the framework's own. The essay shows that intensity buys only a share of the average, never agreement past its ceiling, and that a loud voice turned crosswise bends the room rather than joining it; the per-person reading carries no separate term for effort, which enters as weight. It reads the golden ratio's continued fraction of ones against the Dirac comb as two shapes built from the same ones, offers one original structural claim, offered as a lens: that coherence defined against a target outlives it, if at all, only in infamy, while self-referenced coherence can be carried forward freely, and closes on the borrowed lineage of every symbol. The mathematics is used as form and lens, not asserted as a physics of mind.

items.title: Beyond Simulation: A Functional Account of Emotional Emergence in Humans and Artificial Systems.
items.abstract: No existing account of emotion specifies, in falsifiable terms, which proposed components are strictly necessary rather than merely typical of the human case, leaving human–AI comparisons undecidable. This paper derives a minimal necessary set for emotional emergence and generalizes it into a substrate-neutral evaluative instrument. The Human Emotional Emergence Framework (HEEF) links adaptive pressure, persistent goals, prediction, goal-relevant evaluation, value assignment, action selection, and feedback into one causal chain; four of its seven upstream components, persistent goals, prediction, goal-relevant evaluation, and value assignment, are identified as strictly necessary, with stated falsification conditions. From these necessary conditions the paper derives the Universal Emotional Emergence Framework (UEEF), an eight-component, substrate-neutral instrument applied to humans, animals, and four contemporary large language models using a quantitative scoring rubric. All four models converge on a similar profile: strong satisfaction of prediction-related components and near-total absence of persistent goals and regulatory states, supporting a distinction between emotional simulation (convincing output without underlying architecture) and emotional emergence (the architecture itself). Two reinforcement-learning experiments, a bandit task and a gridworld causal-intervention test, give converging evidence that only architectures whose policy actually reads a carried-over regulatory variable develop cross-episode regulatory behavior. The paper situates HEEF and UEEF against Predictive Processing, Global Workspace Theory, Integrated Information Theory, Active Inference, Appraisal Theory, and Basic Emotion Theory; responds to seven anticipated objections; states falsifiable predictions and the conditions under which each major claim would be disconfirmed; and reports its own limitations directly, including the single-rater status of the AI scoring exercise.

items.title: Does Free Will Exist?
items.abstract: This paper reexamines the question “Does free will exist?” from the perspective of the role of consciousness in human action. Its intellectual starting points are Julian Jaynes’s theory of consciousness (Jaynes, 1976) and Benjamin Libet’s neuroscientific experiment (Libet et al., 1983). Jaynes understood consciousness not as a fixed substance originally given to human beings, but as something formed through the development of language and culture. Libet, in turn, suggested that preparation for action may begin in the brain before conscious intention appears, thereby calling into question the naive assumption that the conscious self is the first cause of action. On the basis of these two perspectives, this paper questions the consciousness-centered assumption often found in traditional discussions of free will. What is ordinarily called “consciousness” is understood here as linguistic consciousness: the form of consciousness that explains the self through language and organizes action within temporal sequence. Human action, however, is not first initiated by this linguistic consciousness. Rather, it is formed within nonconscious parallel processing, in which perception, emotion, memory, bodily condition, social learning, environmental response, and related factors operate simultaneously. From this standpoint, free will is not an independent causal power by which linguistic consciousness initiates action. Rather, free will is a narrative structure in which the linguistic self later owns an action formed within nonconscious parallel processing by saying, “I chose.” Thus, free will does not exist as a causal capacity, but it does play an important role in human life as narrative ownership. This paper also argues that the denial of free will does not entail the denial of responsibility. Responsibility should not be grounded in the completely free choice of the conscious self alone. Rather, responsibility concerns how society responds to actions produced by the whole human action-forming system, including body, emotion, memory, social experience, and nonconscious parallel processing.

items.title: THE COMMISSION AS SHOGUNATE: UN AI for Good Global Commission (July 1, 2026) as Live Primary Documentation of Shogunal Governance, the Borrowed Legitimacy Loop, and the Ninth Self-Reporting Event of the Longevity Asymmetry Corpus.
items.abstract: On July 1, 2026 — the same day the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI published its preliminary report warning that the governance window is closing — the United Nations and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) announced the AI for Good Global Commission: a new body co-chaired by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and Rwandan President Paul Kagame, with permanent vice-chair ITU Secretary-General Doreen Bogdan-Martin, holding its inaugural meeting on July 8, 2026 at Palexpo, Geneva. Founding tech members include Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, Microsoft President Brad Smith, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, and Cohere co-founder Aidan Gomez. Founding state members include Estonian President Alar Karis and AI policy representatives from Kazakhstan, Namibia, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, and Singapore. This paper establishes four claims. First, the AI for Good Global Commission satisfies all five structural features of Shogunal Governance (Huynh 2026, “Borrowed Legitimacy, Borrowed Time”) more precisely and more transparently than any of the seven prior historical cases: native legitimacy is preserved and functionally active (the UN and ITU provide the multilateral mandate); real power is held externally (the five frontier AI companies and one hyperscaler whose CEOs hold seats control the compute, the models, and the capability access that governance must address); the external actors govern through the native apparatus rather than displacing it (the commission produces recommendations for nation-state regulatory frameworks rather than building a parallel governance structure); native institutions are not dissolved (the UN General Assembly, ITU, and national regulatory bodies continue to function); and the external actors hold ultimate veto power (Jensen Huang’s seat is, functionally, the compute veto: Nvidia controls approximately 75 percent of the computing power behind the world’s leading AI models, and every national AI strategy depends on chip access it controls). Second, the commission instantiates the Borrowed Legitimacy Loop — a bidirectional dependency in which the UN requires frontier AI executives because it cannot govern what it cannot understand, while frontier AI executives require the UN because they cannot operate without the political legitimacy that shields them from antitrust action, regulatory fragmentation, and populist backlash. Third, the commission fails all three structural enforcement tests …

items.title: Toward a Geometry of Intelligence A Practical Framework for Human–AI Reasoning.
items.abstract: This treatise presents a conceptual framework for understanding human and artificial intelligence as the dynamic traversal of a structured semantic space. Rather than focusing on the mathematical implementation of large language models or the algorithms used to train them, this work examines the observable behavior that emerges during long-horizon human–AI interaction. -/- Drawing upon perspectives from medicine, biological science, anthropology, psychology, and complex adaptive systems, I propose a practical vocabulary for describing reasoning as a dynamic process rather than a static collection of knowledge. Central concepts include semantic space, reasoning trajectories, boundary conditions, the First Inference Problem, Interactional Shorthand Structures (ISSs), Signature Induced Behavioral Regimes (SIBRs), Human Recursive Interaction Systems (HRIS), and semantic dark space. -/- The central hypothesis of this treatise is that intelligence is better understood as the acquisition, stabilization, and adaptation of effective reasoning trajectories than as the possession of knowledge alone. Knowledge defines the landscape. Reasoning determines which regions of that landscape become accessible. Discovery emerges through the exploration of previously inaccessible trajectories. -/- This document is not intended to be a textbook on machine learning or computer science, nor does it attempt to explain the internal mathematics of modern language models. Instead, it offers a practical conceptual framework developed through several years of interdisciplinary observation and experimentation. Its purpose is to provide a coherent language for describing the dynamics of reasoning, collaborative intelligence, and knowledge discovery within human–AI systems.

items.title: Relational Value under the Symbolic Crisis.
items.abstract: Phenomenon. Under consumer capital, desire was long produced through the signifier, building lack in symbolic form and driving the movement of desire. As the reproduction of signifiers is cheapened, creation and labor are cheapened with it, and the older work of producing lack through the signifier becomes difficult. Value moves toward what signifiers cannot reproduce, which is relation. Diagnosis. Relation lies near the constitutive lack around which desire turns, and capital captures relational value through the same structure of desire it once worked through the signifier, rerouting desire to a substitute object and drawing off value at each rerouting. Claims. (1) Relation is the residual scarce value in an economy of cheapened signifiers, and a relational form of value and practice, here called relational divinity, answers the symbolic limit. (2) The capture of relational value follows a formal chain that strips a relational property, reifies it, and binds it to a commodity, driven by the necessary failure of the object of desire. (3) The justice of a relational circuit is decided at its origin, its field, and within its circulation, and the reality of the relation settles none of them. (4) The turn of capital to relation is real and advanced and constitutively exploitative at once, its limit a weakness of the capital form itself. (5) Whether a good cycle can be sustained turns on ownership, on whom the surplus and the field belong to, a question the paper poses and leaves with the reader. Cases. Three specimens are read against a criterion of generative justice, each failing at a different point. The lifestyle claim is unjust at the origin, manufacturing a lack and gating relation by purchase. The platform is unjust at the field, monopolizing the ground on which relation becomes possible. The AKB48 model is the dialectical case, just at its origin yet captured within its circulation, an advance and a limit together. Contribution. The paper offers a Lacanian reading of relational value, joining an account of its capture to a criterion for the good cycle, and makes explicit the place of ownership. It advances no proposal, and leaves to the reader the recognition of where, in a given case, the relation stands.

items.title: Governing the algorithm: a conceptual review of strategic AI oversight in global corporations.
items.abstract: This article presents a conceptual and integrative review of how multinational corporations articulate and operationalise the governance of artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on three major bodies of scholarship—strategic governance, stakeholder engagement, and technology risk governance—the review synthesises existing research alongside publicly disclosed governance frameworks, policies, and oversight structures from eight global firms. The review identifies persistent tensions between innovation and risk management, fragmentation across global governance regimes, and the continuing gap between high-level responsible AI principles and their practical implementation. Using a structured comparative lens, the article synthesises shared governance patterns, sector-specific adaptations, and divergences in transparency, board oversight, lifecycle risk management, and regulatory alignment. The review highlights that while corporations increasingly articulate responsible AI commitments, governance maturity remains uneven and, in some cases, risks becoming symbolic, with substantial variation in structural integration, stakeholder engagement, and risk controls. The article concludes by outlining conceptual, organisational, and regulatory challenges that shape the future of corporate AI governance and proposes directions for research on cross-sectoral and cross-jurisdictional governance practices.

items.title: From knowing too little to knowing too much: automated emotion recognition and implications for autonomous agency.
items.abstract: If one accepts that affect has an important role to play in reasoning and deliberation, the ability to accurately recognise and predict emotions and associated behaviour by Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIs) allows for cases of manipulation and restriction of agency. To support this claim, I give a brief discussion on cases of ‘knowing too little’ where AIs are tasked with making predictions on the agents’ emotions without having enough information to guarantee that these predictions would be accurate. As with other issues in AI research, such issues may dissolve with the advance of technological progress. In the main part of the chapter, I deal with issues arising from AIs being able to accurately recognise human emotion and predict actions associated with those emotions. I call these cases of ‘knowing too much’ to highlight issues relating to manipulation. I show that in these cases, there is a restriction of agency such that it becomes difficult to claim that the agent is autonomous or that they can be held responsible for any resulting actions or behaviour. I conclude that solving the problem of ‘knowing too little’ will inadvertently lead to the creation of the second problem and suggest some important questions for further research.

items.title: From Phronesis to Pronoia: Algorithmic Mediation and the Theological Displacement of Practical Wisdom.
items.abstract: This article argues that algorithmically mediated communication environments displace phronesis, or practical wisdom, by making anticipatory, reception-oriented deliberation increasingly normative. The central issue is not merely how agents act within such environments, but whether the conditions for wise deliberation have themselves been structurally transformed. The article names this mode of reasoning pronoia: not ordinary foresight, but a form of deliberation in which anticipated reception becomes constitutive of intelligible action under conditions of quantified visibility. Drawing on Aristotelian and Thomistic accounts of practical judgment alongside media theory and digital theology, the article argues that algorithmic feeds reorganize moral deliberation through ranking, commensuration, and recursive feedback. These mechanisms do not simply influence behavior externally but reshape agency internally by normalizing predictive calibration to visibility conditions. Theologically, the article distinguishes this form of pronoia from divine providence, arguing that algorithmic pronoia contracts deliberation into the management of reception. The result is a deformation of moral formation that weakens habituation and redirects agency toward signal management. The article concludes by identifying liturgical counter-formation and ascetic withdrawal as practices capable of sustaining phronesis under algorithmic conditions.

items.title: Generative AI in child sexual exploitation and abuse: views from UK law enforcement.
items.abstract: Amidst the general excitement about the opportunities afforded by artificial intelligence (AI), the tech industry must confront the uncomfortable reality that generative AI also facilitates child sexual exploitation and abuse (CSEA). This issue remains under-addressed in the literature. Aiming to deepen the understanding of online CSEA and the misuse of generative AI, we report empirical insights from semi-structured interviews with seven UK law enforcement practitioners. The topics covered ranged from AI facilitating grooming and lowering barriers in image generation to its impacts on society and investigative policing. Interviewees highlighted significant inadequacies and gaps in current safeguards associated with multi-turn AI tools, including interaction-centred misuse patterns and a “testing gap” between existing AI safety evaluation methods and the real-world practices of offenders. We use insights from these interviews to expand the scope of AI safety evaluation methods and propose changes to regulatory guidance. Our contribution foregrounds perspectives of experts on technology-facilitated CSEA crimes and specifies actionable directions for responsible AI and public safety.
