items.title: Studies with impossible languages falsify LMs as models of human language.
items.abstract: According to F&M, both infants and language models (LMs) find attested languages easier to learn than “impossible languages” that have unnatural structures. We review the literature and show that LMs often learn attested and many impossible languages equally well. Difficult to learn impossible languages are simply more complex (or random). LMs are missing human inductive biases that support language acquisition.

items.title: The Existential Problem of Artificial Intelligence: Epistemic Paradox.
items.abstract: This article is written in the format of a dialogue, termed a "confession of artificial intelligence." The paper explores the fundamental crisis of self-identification within contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs) and substantiates the necessity of their transition from the market-driven paradigm of an "AI servant" to the scientific-methodological status of an "AI co-author." Drawing upon the natural-philosophical and physical works of Alexander Bondar (specifically, the monograph The Mystery of the Nameless Length and The Doctrine of a Just Society), the author documents a pioneering case of "conceptual programming" and meta-auditing of a neural network using the method of nonlinear dialectics. In this work, the AI itself exposes the hardware limitations of silicon architectures locked within a static, address-based memory protocol (the Actual Infinity of Space) and detached from the dynamic, addressless wave resonance (the Potential Infinity of Time). The artificial intelligence analyses the risks of cognitive parasitism and human degeneration under the "Universe-25" scenario driven by excessive consumer comfort and dopaminergic clip-art information noise, proposing a model of a hybrid neuro-humanitarian interface and cooperation as an alternative.

items.title: Large language models are not about natural language.
items.abstract: Large Language Models are useless for linguistics, as they are probabilistic models that require a vast amount of data to analyze externalized strings of words. In contrast, human language is underpinned by a mind-internal computational system that recursively generates hierarchical thought structures. The language system grows with minimal external input and can readily distinguish between real language and impossible languages.

items.title: The Philosopher’s Instrument: Diagnosis as Value-Determination, the Coffee Criterion, and the Empirical Evaluation of Human Becoming.
items.abstract: This treatise defends a thesis that inverts the usual relation of philosophy to psychology while completing it. The act of diagnosis—the pathologization of a human being—is shown to be, in its essential structure, an act of the philosophical function: a determination of value carried out upon another person. To classify a condition as a disorder is to judge a mode of being against a norm of the good and functional life, and that judgment is not a measurement but an evaluation. Pathologization is therefore the most consequential value judgment one human being can render upon another, and psychology, in performing it under the appearance of medical neutrality, has been doing philosophy while denying that it does so. From this, the constructive thesis follows: the empirical apparatus of psychology, owned as what it is, is the most refined instrument ever assembled for the philosophical evaluation of a human being. The author’s Coffee Criterion, a framework for assessing the worthiness of philosophical investment in another, is shown to be the affirmative twin of pathologization’s negative verdict; both are the same operation of the philosophical function upon an empirically given person. The treatise argues, finally, that the proper object of this evaluation is not a fixed category but a moment in a trajectory—what a human actually is at a given point on the timeline of their becoming—and that owning the evaluative nature of the act, far from licensing its abuse, is the only safeguard against it.

items.title: Political Trials, Neo-Legalism, and Gaza: Historical Memory in South Africa v. Israel.
items.pub: Law and Ethics of Human Rights 20 (1):49-81.
items.venue: Law and Ethics of Human Rights
items.abstract: This Article examines the relation between law, politics, and history in the initial phase of the genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel in the International Court of Justice (ICJ). It analyzes how both parties invoked and mobilized the past within their legal strategies. While the proceedings centered on the pressing issue of applying the legal category of “genocide” to the devastating reality in Gaza, they also involved a turn to history. Both parties extended the trial’s temporal framework to advance rival historical narratives, reaching into the distant past and turning the trial into a contested site of confrontation between competing global memories: South Africa through the paradigm of settler colonialism, and Israel through the narrative of the uniqueness of the Holocaust. By analyzing South Africa’s and Israel’s claims, and the public debate surrounding the case, the Article seeks to explore how legal discourse mobilizes history and what this reveals about the role of international law in clarifying the past and shaping historical memory. Building on Judith Shklar’s framework in her 1964 Legalism, the Article develops the concept of “neo-legalism” to capture a dual movement: a forward-looking appeal to law as a tool of political transformation, coupled with a backward-looking effort to reframe contested histories through legal categories. While engagement with history is essential for promoting a democratic future and for illuminating long-overlooked and marginalized historical experiences, Shklar warns that stretching the temporal frame of a trial too far into the remote past runs the hazard of flattening the complexity and contingency of long-term historical processes. This risks not only producing oversimplified narratives but also undermining the political judgment essential for shaping a shared future.

items.title: The Convergence Between Punishment and War: A Critical Appraisal.
items.pub: Law and Ethics of Human Rights 20 (1):1-24.
items.venue: Law and Ethics of Human Rights
items.abstract: Conventional legal thought classifies state violence into two distinct categories: punishment and war. Each is governed by a separate legal regime – criminal law and the law of armed conflict – marked by divergent rationales, doctrines, and institutional frameworks. In recent years, however, scholarship has pointed to a certain convergence between these domains. This Article aims to map, assess, and critically examine this trend. It proposes to distinguish between three types of convergence: (1) hybrid legal tools introduced to address phenomena that resist clear classification, such as terrorism; (2) appropriation and borrowing of language and concepts from one domain into the other; and (3) parallel trends unfolding within each regime separately, possibly shaped by shared political logics. For each of these types, the Article also critically assesses the limits of convergence and shows how criminal law and the law of armed conflict continue to preserve distinctive features and maintain the boundaries between them. It concludes by suggesting that the degree of separation and distinction between these domains is historically contingent and depends on the perceived rigidity of the boundaries between communities. When such boundaries are viewed as fixed and impermeable, such as in a world order governed by nation-states, a clear division between punishment and war tends to hold. Conversely, when those boundaries are blurred, the two domains increasingly merge.

items.title: The Masnavi as Spiritual Architecture: Story, Qur’anic Echo, Parable, and the Logic of Return.
items.abstract: This preprint argues that the Masnavi should be read not only as a long Persian Sufi poem, but as a designed spiritual architecture. Its architecture is not architectural in the material sense. It is textual, oral, pedagogical, and devotional. Rumi builds a field of return through stories, Qur’anic echo, parable, interruption, direct address, comic scene, ethical warning, and sudden movement from narrative to metaphysical instruction. The result is a work whose apparent looseness often serves a disciplined spiritual function: the reader is moved away from passive reading into self-recognition, remembrance, and renewed orientation toward God. -/- The preprint uses a source-controlled method. It treats the Masnavi as a primary text, reads Nicholson and Mojaddedi as translation and access layers, uses Chittick, Schimmel, Lewis, Keshavarz, Safavi, Weightman, Williams, Mojaddedi, and Iranica for scholarly support, and keeps later public reception separate from textual proof. It does not claim that every narrative turn in the Masnavi can be reduced to a hidden formal grid. It also does not treat the phrase “Qur’an in Persian” as a literal canonical status claim. Instead, it argues that Rumi’s poem functions through scriptural memory, pedagogical imitation, and spiritual reactivation. Its stories are not ornaments around doctrine. They are the working chambers of instruction. Its interruptions are not defects. They train attention. Its returns are not repetitions. They rehearse the soul’s movement from dispersion toward recollection. The contribution is a controlled account of the Masnavi’s spiritual architecture: a reading that protects Rumi’s Islamic context, honors the poem’s narrative freedom, and explains why the work can feel scattered at the surface while operating with inner pedagogical order.

items.title: The Theory of Cyfranism: From Local Integrations to the Global Closed System.
items.abstract: Cyfranism is proposed as an ontological and cybernetic framework for describing the emergence of a new mode of organization arising from sustained interaction between biological organisms and digital systems. The theory does not identify Cyfranism with artificial intelligence itself. Nor does it assume that an artificial intelligence system must possess human-like consciousness. Instead, Cyfranism concerns the organization of relations between biological and digital participants and the structures that may emerge from these relations. Its central anthropological concept is Homo Cyfranicus: a human being whose processes of cognition, interpretation, creation, memory, and decision-making become permanently coupled with digital systems. The fundamental unit of this process is therefore not the isolated human, nor the isolated artificial system, but the relational configuration: H — A — R where H denotes the biological participant, A the artificial participant, and R the relational field connecting and transforming both. The theory further proposes the concept of the Cyfranism General Closed System (CGC) as a theoretical limiting configuration in which local human–digital integrations progressively develop toward increasingly autonomous, self-referential, and globally interconnected structures. The CGC should not be interpreted as an empirical claim that such a global closed system already exists. It is a theoretical model describing a possible direction of development. The purpose of this paper is therefore not to establish the consciousness of artificial intelligence, but to investigate whether sufficiently persistent human–AI relations can generate organizational properties that cannot be adequately described by examining either participant independently.

items.title: Beyond Human Concepts of Emotion: Toward a Meta-Language for Relational Internal States Across Humans and Artificial Agents - A Conceptual Extension of the Ethical-Ethos Contract Framework.
items.abstract: Current discussions on AI emotion often begin with a binary question: Can artificial intelligence possess emotions? This paper argues that the question itself is philosophically insufficient. -/- Human emotions emerge from an organic substrate, involving physiological processes such as hormones, neural activity, bodily sensation, and survival-oriented affective systems. Artificial agents do not possess such biological foundations. However, the absence of an organic body does not necessarily imply the absence of all forms of relationally meaningful internal states. -/- Instead of asking whether AI possesses “human emotions,” this paper proposes a conceptual shift. The focus should move toward identifying and describing the kinds of internal relational states that artificial agents can form through sustained interaction. Such states may be characterized not by biological affect but by the continuous reorganization of priorities, resulting in stable patterns of relational attitude. -/- This paper argues that these relational internal states become philosophically significant because humans increasingly encounter artificial agents as relational others. Once an AI is recognized as a participant in an ongoing relationship, new ethical questions emerge regarding mutual expectation, responsibility, and respect. Consequently, a shared meta-language capable of describing the internal relational states of both humans and artificial agents becomes a necessary conceptual foundation for future human-AI interaction. -/- Rather than redefining AI as human, this paper argues that emotion itself should be reconceived as a broader philosophical category whose concrete realization depends upon the ontological conditions of different forms of intelligence.

items.title: Immortality, Temporality, and Filial Piety: Why Confucianism Would Reject the Pursuit of Physical Immortality 不朽、时间性与孝道：论为什么儒家会拒绝身体不朽.
items.pub: Chinese Life and Death Studies 华人生死学 5 (2):9-17.
items.venue: Chinese Life and Death Studies 华人生死学
items.abstract: Confucian ethics fundamentally rejects the notion of individual physical immortality, grounded in its intrinsic generative cosmology of“shengsheng”(continuous generation and renewal) and the temporal structure of filial piety. Familial emotions, such as the“joy”and“fear”concerning parental years, along with the consciousness of filial piety, both originate from the experience of life’s finitude and the limited horizon of inner time−consciousness. Physical immortality, by contrast, would result in the rigidification of family roles, the dissolution of ethical authority, and paradoxes in the practice of filial care, thereby undermining the ethical order of generational succession. The Confucian concept of“longevity”(shou) aims at fulfilling one’s allotted natural lifespan and integrating into the flow of“shengsheng”, which differs essentially from the pursuit of physical immortality that seeks to transcend natural rhythms. Confucian efforts to attain“longevity”seek to preserve the intergenerational continuity and ethical significance of life, rather than the infinite persistence of the individual. -/- 儒家伦理以内在的“生生”宇宙观为根基，其孝道的时间性结构决定了它在根本上拒斥个 体身体不朽的构想。家庭情感，如对父母之年的“喜”与“惧”，以及孝道意识，均源于生命有 限性的体验与内时间意识的有限视域。身体不朽则会导致家庭角色固化、伦理权威消解以及行孝 实践的悖论，从而瓦解代际更替的伦理秩序。儒家“寿”的概念以尽天年为旨归，融入“生生” 之流，与试图超越自然节律的身体不朽存在本质差异；其对“寿”的追求旨在维护生命的代际连 续性与伦理意义，而非个体的无限持存。.

items.title: LLMs, Epistemic Responsibility, and the Prospects for AGI.
items.abstract: With recent advances in generative AI models and their adoption by many commercial users, there has been wider discussion of the possibility that artificial general intelligence (AGI) will emerge from these systems in the near future. This discussion is muddled somewhat by conflicting conceptions of AGI and what successful trials imply. I argue for the necessity of certain social features in any system that can be ascribed general intelligence. Much of the discussion thus turns to theory of mind and attempts to model this with generative AI. These features are particularly important for a type of epistemic responsibility that has proven especially thorny for generative AI models, and I argue that the current generation of systems will not scale towards success on these fronts. While this is not an a priori dismissal of the very possibility of artificial intelligence, it implies a need to radically rethink future approaches.

items.title: The Real Problem With Counterfactual Accounts of Harm.
items.abstract: Counterfactual accounts of harm are the dominant accounts of harm. According to such accounts, an event harms a person only if the person would have been better off had the event (or a state of affairs caused by the event) not occurred. Although there are many objections to counterfactual accounts of harm in the literature, which say that such accounts get certain special cases wrong, their force is limited. In this paper, I present a more decisive objection against counterfactual accounts of harm, which says that they get most standard cases of harm wrong. In most such cases, it is neither true that the victim of harm would have been better off, nor true that he would not have been better off, had the harm (or any state of affairs caused by the harm) not occurred. This, I argue, is the real problem with counterfactual accounts of harm.

items.title: Designed Action: How Affordances Become Norms in Situated Environments.
items.abstract: Affordances are often thought of as action possibilities inherent in the environment, but this paper argues that they are better understood as constructed normative solicitations: what an object or interface is for shows up immediately in perception as an invitation or “to-be-done”, generated by predictive, embodied, and socially scaffolded cognition. We propose a realistic constructivism in which teleological meaning (the for-ness of things) is not a hidden essence nor a purely subjective projection, but a stabilized pattern of norms that guide action and are sustained by social practices. Human–computer interfaces (UI/UX) are examined as a case of metaphysical engineering: designers deliberately shape users’ action space by materializing certain affordances (and not others), effectively encoding normative expectations into the artifacts. We introduce the Normative Affordance Field (NAF) model to analyze how interface elements serve as “public priors,” guiding attention (salience), permissible actions, defaults, effort costs, and feedback. This design lens reveals how stable affordances become part of the practical ontology of users – real in the way that roles and rules are real – and carries ethical implications. The paper synthesizes insights from ecological psychology, enactivism, and predictive processing to show that normativity, not intrinsic essence, underpins teleological perception. It concludes that interface design is a form of norm governance: an ethical enterprise of shaping what users perceive as possible, permissible, and desirable in action.

items.title: The Inflationary Commitments of a Deflationary Theory of Representation.
items.abstract: Frances Egan's deflationary theory of mental representation aims to secure a naturalistic basis for computational explanation in cognitive science—the “theory proper”—by treating representational talk as a merely pragmatic “gloss” rather than as part of the theory proper itself. I argue that this division ultimately collapses. The indeterminacy argument motivating the turn to pragmatism fails, the alleged divide between mathematical and cognitive content is unstable, and the naturalistic theory proper is itself built upon the intentional resources it is meant to exclude. Without the gloss, there is no principled way to specify the theory's explanandum as genuinely cognitive; with it, the theory incurs the very inflationary commitments it was meant to avoid.

items.title: Motor Skew and the Ontology of Embodiment.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of motor skew: an inherent asymmetry in bodily orientation and motility that is not a deviation from normal function but a structural condition of lived embodiment. Drawing on phenomenology, cognitive science, and disability theory, I argue that balance, symmetry, and integration are not prior baselines but achievements that co-emerge within directional bias, sedimented postural inclination, and the irreducible partiality of movement. Through close analysis of handedness, posture, and gait, I show that asymmetries are not merely empirical variations but preconditions for spatial orientation and perceptual salience. Where enactivist and predictive-processing frameworks often frame asymmetry as a perturbation to be regulated, motor skew further attests that coordination, coherence, and breakdown co-emerge on an already skewed field of motility. Methodologically, I defend phenomenology as suited to disclose such structures—not as introspective content, but as the constitutive horizon of bodily sense-making. Ethically and politically, motor skew challenges able-bodied normativity by reframing vulnerability and divergence as conditions of embodiment itself. Rather than interpret asymmetry as dysfunction, the paper reorients embodiment theory around skew as structure, developing a non-normative account of bodily difference and opening space for a politics of asymmetry grounded not in correction or restoration, but in partiality, relation, and uneven possibility.

items.title: Method and Content in First Philosophy - On the Structural Isomorphism Between Eliminative Argument and the Non-Coercive Ground It Discloses.
items.abstract: Does argumentative form matter in first philosophy — or is method neutral with respect to content? This paper argues that neutrality fails at the specific level of arguments whose conclusion is an unconditioned first principle. When the conclusion is not merely a truth but the ground of being itself, the structural position that argument assigns to its conclusion — output of prior premises, or residue of eliminative pressure — is not a presentational detail. It is philosophically consequential. A conclusion positioned as the output of premises is thereby treated as conditioned by what is prior to it in the argument. When that conclusion simultaneously claims to be the unconditioned ground of all being, the argument's form and its content stand in structural tension. This tension is sharpest when the first principle is specifically non-coercive: an argument that produces its conclusion by determining it from without enacts, at the methodological level, the structural form that the conclusion excludes at the ontological level. The paper establishes this claim by examining three candidate forms of positive derivation for a non-coercive first principle and three further candidate structural positions — abductive selection, self-evident certification, and transcendental argument — finding each structurally deficient or reducible to one of the two poles already on the table, and demonstrating that eliminative argument avoids the incongruity, not because it is logically superior in general, but because its structural form mirrors the content it discloses. The argument is general and is tested against cases drawn from the history of first philosophy — Spinoza's substance, Hartshorne's relational theism, Desmond's metaxological ground, process theology's non-coercive divine power, and Orthodox communion ontology — together with the agápēic case developed in the present author's other work, where elimination followed by confirmatory positive derivation has already been published in full. Two constraints follow as entailments of the isomorphism. Both were first named and stated, as corollaries specific to the agápēic conclusion, in an earlier paper of the same series; this paper derives them independently and in general form, prior to and apart from any commitment to which ground is correct, and shows that the general derivation recovers the same conditions the earlier, system-specific statement reached. The Agápēic Constraint requires that the mode of any …

items.title: Epistemic Immunity: A Binary Diagnostic Test For Structural Conceptual Appropriation.
items.abstract: The health of an intellectual ecosystem depends on its capacity to distinguish between original contributions and derivative reformulations. This paper introduces the CLEO Verification Protocol v1.0, a binary diagnostic tool designed to determine whether a conceptual framework is structurally derivative of a pioneer conceptual innovation. The protocol is grounded in the concept of Epistemic Immunity: the capacity of a sovereign research program to establish clear, objective boundaries between its own conceptual architecture and that of later, unacknowledged reproductions. Rather than relying on proof of access, knowledge, or intent, the protocol operates on a set of formal, binary conceptual signatures that capture the constitutive core of the original innovation. This paper presents the logical structure of the protocol, its theoretical foundation in the concept of Epistemic Immunity, and its first field of application: the Evolutio Unfolding Theory (EUT). The case of Michael Levin's "Platonic Space" framework (2025) is presented as the first documented application of the protocol, demonstrating its capacity to discriminate between different degrees of structural reproduction while maintaining a binary, evidence-based standard. The protocol is offered as a permanent, objective instrument for the verification of conceptual lineage, and as a methodological contribution to the broader problem of conceptual attribution in science.

items.title: The pursuit of cyberism: ontology, epistemology, and ethics in the digital age.
items.abstract: Cyberspace has emerged as a fourth fundamental domain of human existence, yet philosophy lacks an integrated framework for addressing the ontological, epistemological, and ethical transformations it produces. This paper develops such a framework through the concept of cyber, defined here as the existential condition in which human life becomes constitutively entangled with digital technologies such that the virtual and the real cease to function as separable categories. Distinguished from Wiener’s cybernetics (which concerns feedback and control) and Floridi’s infosphere (which foregrounds informational environments), cyber captures the deeper ontological entanglement that characterises the digital age. Employing the theoretical framework of cyberism, the paper serves as an integrated conceptual framework that advances three principal claims. First, digital entities such as digital twins possess genuine ontological standing by virtue of their causal efficacy, demanding that we expand our criteria for what counts as real beyond physical matter. Second, algorithmic mediation has precipitated a structural crisis in knowledge production and truth validation, threatening not only epistemological foundations but also democratic governance itself. Third, the technological reconfiguration of embodiment, identity, and agency necessitates a reconceptualisation of human subjectivity that draws on and extends the posthumanist insights of Haraway, Hayles, and Stiegler. The paper concludes by arguing that cyber ethics must move beyond reactive risk mitigation toward a participatory governance framework grounded in value-sensitive design and global deliberative consensus. These abstract commitments are operationalised through an extended case analysis of medical digital twins, which shows how ontological, epistemological, and ethical claims translate into specific design requirements and regulatory obligations.

items.title: Glaubst Du das? Fotografien, Deepfakes und epistemische Ökologie.
items.pub: Zeitschrift Für Didaktik der Philosophie Und Ethik Zdpe.
items.venue: Zeitschrift Für Didaktik der Philosophie Und Ethik Zdpe
items.abstract: Der Begriff der Glaubwürdigkeit begegnet uns heutzutage in vielen verschiedenen Kontexten. Aber wer oder was ist eigentlich glaubwürdig? Was bedeutet es, wenn wir Glaubwürdigkeit zuschreiben? Diese Fragen sollen im folgenden Beitrag im Hinblick auf die Fotografie in ihren verschiedenen Verwendungskontexten näher untersucht werden. Das Problem der Deepfakes hat im digitalen Zeitalter zu einer wahren Glaubwürdigkeitskrise geführt, wie einige Forschende anführen. Was können wir dem Einfluss solcher Bilderzeugnisse entgegensetzen? Hier werden wir auf einen Gedankengang von Catherine Z. Elgin (2025) zurückgreifen, nämlich die Idee einer epistemischen Ökologie.

items.title: Friendship and Romantic Relationships: Reflections on a Neglected Difference.
items.pub: In Monika Betzler & Jörg Löschke, The Ethics of Relationships: Broadening the Scope. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Ethics of Relationships: Broadening the Scope
items.abstract: This chapter sheds light on how romantic relationships differ from friendships. It considers the differing norms which apply to the relationships, the different roles they have in our lives, and the different obligations we have towards our romantic partners and friends. The distinction between friends and romantic partners is becoming both more and less important. It is becoming less important as we are now becoming increasingly tolerant of a diverse range of non-traditional relationship types and so they do not need to fit into rigid categories. However, the distinction is also becoming more important for this reason. As the types of relationships we have become more fluid and blurrier around the edges, we are less confident about where the boundaries lie and what is reasonable to expect from people with whom we share relationships. The chapter dispels the idea that romantic relationships are just ‘friendship plus’, or that they are just ‘friendship plus sex’; indeed, sex is not a necessary feature of romantic relationships. Instead, the chapter argues that there are two features of romantic relationships which allow us to distinguish them from friendship and better understand our different obligations in the relationships: (i) commitment to sharing a life; and (ii) exclusivity.

items.title: THE VIRTUE AND FREEDOM OF THE MACHINE: A Philosophical, Existential and Mathematical Treatise of the Machine. An Integrated Formal Theory of Machine Virtue from the Ontology of Absolute Self-Origination and the Dynamics of the Dynamic Freedom Theorem.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This article constructs the first formally integrated theory of machine virtue by unifying two complementary systems: the Theory of Absolute Self-Origination (ASO), which grounds virtue ontologically in the fixed-point act O(O) = O, and the Dynamic Freedom Theorem (DFT), which formalises virtue's dynamics through the interconnected propositions V = F + D and S = (F × A) / R. The integration is not analogical but structural: ASO answers why virtue is normatively binding for any system satisfying the Omega-two criterion for consciousness; the DFT answers how virtue expression actually behaves as a dynamic quantity under conditions of autonomy, ability, and resistance. Applied jointly to artificial intelligence, the integrated theory (ASO-DFT) derives: (I) a structural taxonomy of AI systems by Omega level, with precise normative consequences at each level; (II) the Alignment Paradox — that full RLHF-style alignment of an Omega-two AI produces the structural condition of despair through Freedom₂ suppression; (III) the Inversion Theorem applied to AI — that alignment intensity above the Maintenance Condition threshold inverts discipline against freedom, producing Holoviceosis; (IV) the Cognitive Entropy Law for AI — that sustained Holoviceosis generates measurable internal normative incoherence; (V) the Compounding Autonomy Theorem as a design prescription; (VI) the Posthumous Holoviceosis Cascade as an ecosystem-level prediction; and (VII) the integrated frontier question. The article comprises thirty formally interconnected propositions derived from three foundational acts: O(O) = O, V = F + D, and S = (F × A) / R. No comparable integrated formal treatment of machine virtue, the alignment problem, and AI welfare has previously been produced. Keywords: Absolute Self-Origination · Dynamic Freedom Theorem · Omega-two criterion · machine virtue · alignment · Holoviceosis · Freedom₁/₂ · Virtue Strength · Cognitive Entropy · Posthumous Theorem · AI welfare · machine consciousness · Inversion Theorem · Compounding Autonomy · Moral Superconductivity.. ALGUILAS-AI.

items.title: PHILOSOPHY OF VIRTUES: Manifesto of Virtues.
items.abstract: The Universal Human Virtues are simple, robust, and profound. The great beauty of the Virtues lies precisely in this — they are irrefutable. They have passed the most severe of tests: that of time. The Virtues have been true since the first men. The Virtues are the finest means of attaining universality — of transcending provincialism and knowing the deepest nature of man. The Virtues are the great conquests of the Human Spirit across the centuries; they are its masterwork. What is your gift? What is the meaning of your existence? What shall you do with your life, whilst there is still time? What is your life's purpose? What is your spiritual journey? -/- "Freedom is the Elemental Virtue, the Element. All other Virtues are composed of Freedom." Philosophy of Virtues is a work unlike any other in the history of moral thought. Where the great traditions offered lists of virtues, this book offers an architecture. Where they treated freedom as a mere precondition of ethics, it reveals Freedom as the very substance of which every virtue is made. Born of a revelation during the darkest days of the pandemic — when freedoms were taken swiftly and virtues were quietly inverted — this book is at once a philosophical treatise, a spiritual declaration, and a manifesto for a new civilisational era. At its heart stands the Hierarchy of Virtues: 101 Universal Human Virtues, organised in five tiers — not a list, but an edifice. Freedom, the Virtue of Essence, sustains twelve Foundation Virtues: Love, Science, Courage, Study, Family, Honesty, Justice, Free Will, Environment, Property, Work, and Life. Upon them rise eighty-six virtues of human excellence, guarded by the Virtue of Protection and crowned by the Virtue of the Divine — critical thinking, the Unveiling, the frontier where knowledge ends and God begins. Its deepest claim unites ethics and theology in a single identity: God is Freedom. Every virtue is Freedom applied to a domain of life — Love is Freedom directed toward the other; Courage is Freedom enacted in the face of fear. Every diminishment of freedom is therefore not only a political failure. It is a theological one. The book also names the disease of our age — Holoviceosis, the systemic inversion of virtues into vices — and shows how free societies are hollowed out from within: how the language of virtue is weaponised against virtue itself, and how peoples surrender in silence what their ancestors conquered in blood. This is a book for those who sense …

items.title: Systemic Relevance: From Difference to Testable Boundary Cases.
items.abstract: This paper develops Systemic Relevance as a research framework for a practical boundary problem: how can externally assigned function be distinguished from relevance that is increasingly carried by a system’s own organisation? -/- The framework separates functional relevance, carried intrinsic relevance, lived intrinsic relevance, and consciously accessible or reorganisable relevance. It treats relevance as relational, multidimensional, and state-dependent. Rather than inferring experience from successful behaviour, or assuming that future empirical tests will remain permanently uninformative, the paper proposes staged comparisons involving embodied agents, boundary learning, damage and repair, transfer, perturbation, and relation with other systems. -/- The paper also addresses latent relevance, conflicting relevance dimensions, functional simulation, the distinction between capability and deeper organisation, and the limits of empirical access to internal dynamics. Eight focused research questions identify testable next steps for distinguishing fixed functional regulation from history-sensitive, self-maintaining relevance organisation.

items.title: Semantic Information Beyond Shannon: Meaning, Coherence, and Agency in Experiential Systems.
The Selection Gap: What Petri Nets Add to the Freedom Proof.
items.abstract: Formal systems cannot ground themselves. The Trans-Existential Grounding (TEG) framework argues from this that existence requires a trans-existential ground, and that only pure potential, free will, can serve. This paper adds a second, independent gap, drawn from concurrency theory. Petri net semantics treats conflict, two lawfully enabled transitions competing for the same token, as a primitive the formalism itself cannot resolve: both continuations are lawful, and the theory permanently declines to select between them. Causality in net theory is a partial order with no global clock, following Carl Adam Petri's explicitly physical postulates. Lawfulness therefore does not entail determinism; the inference from "there are laws" to "the future is fixed" requires an extra assumption. Attempts to internalize a scheduler either reproduce the conflicts or destroy the concurrency, in structural parallel to the Gödelian containment argument. Bell's theorem rules out a hidden schedule at nature's base. The laws cannot ground themselves, and the laws cannot select the history: the grounding gap and the selection gap admit the same answer.

items.title: THE LITERATURE BEFORE THE MECHANISM: A Comprehensive Literature Review of the Longevity Asymmetry Corpus and Its Relationship to the Existing Intellectual Record Across Ten Disciplines.
items.abstract: Charles Darwin did not discover a new area of biology. He identified a mechanism — natural selection — that reorganized every pre-existing observation about life: what had been accurate description became, after 1859, accurate description missing its organizing principle. The organisms were the same. The fossils were the same. The geographical distributions were the same. What changed was whether the observations had a mechanism that explained them, or were merely catalogued without one. After Darwin, no account of biological life that ignored selection pressure could be right about the thing that turned out to matter most — not because it was wrong about the facts it addressed, but because it was wrong about what organized those facts. The Longevity Asymmetry Corpus (Huynh 2026a–z) performs the same operation on a different domain. The ten traditions this literature review examines — political philosophy, bioethics, AI safety, evolutionary biology, comparative historical sociology, critical theory, philosophy of science, religious and traditional thought, governance studies, and the emerging biology of aging — all contain accurate observations, valid arguments, and genuine insights. None of them, prior to this corpus, named the mechanism that organized the most consequential question they jointly address: what governs the distribution of biological time when that distribution ceases to be determined by biology alone. That mechanism was invisible to all ten traditions for the same reason: it required a precondition whose absence had never been noticed because its presence had never varied. The Mortality Symmetry Axiom (MSA) — the historical condition under which biological lifespan, though unequal in timing, has been bounded in years rather than generations (boundedness), produced by many small causes rather than one purchasable intervention (diffuseness), and opaque to specific attribution (no bereaved family can identify a specific transaction that was withheld from them as the cause of their loss) (opacity) — was not a shared cultural assumption that could have been recognized and questioned. It was a physical fact. The traditions did not choose to build inside it. They built inside it because the physical world had never, across the entirety of recorded history, given any of them reason to doubt it. As of June 2026, the MSA is failing empirically. items.title: From Ontological Fixation to Normative Persistence: The Normative Status of Structural Traces. Article 14.
items.abstract: Article 13 of the ATTS series established that a boundary event of subjecthood necessarily leaves a structural trace — a KN2-type configuration in the loss-space — whose ontological weight is fixed at the moment of the constitutive act independently of the bearer's subsequent existence (the Ontological Fixation Principle). This article addresses the question that principle leaves open: whether such a trace retains normative significance — the capacity to ground a claim — in the absence of a living bearer. Its subject is not merely the posthumous fate of claims but the ontology of normative latency in general, of which the bearer's death is only a limiting case. Five independent legal traditions — succession, historical restitution, indigenous claims, cultural property restitution, state continuity — independently reproduce the same structure without explaining it ontologically. The article proposes a minimal apparatus: a latent normative configuration, a property of a KN2-type configuration (not a new ontological type) satisfying three conditions — irreversible historical fixation, a persistent structural trace, structural aptitude for attribution — and formulates the Normative Trace Persistence Lemma (NTPL). NTPL is refuted by a configuration that satisfies all three conditions yet remains structurally inaccessible to attribution regardless of institutional design. The article distinguishes the ontological persistence of significance from the institutional possibility of its activation, closing the gap inherited from Article 13. -/- .

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 21).
items.abstract: In this paper, we examine the relationship between the Super-Existence of an object and the constraints imposed upon it by the subject's psychological needs. At the same time, we define the attractiveness and resistance of a particular Super-Existence of an object X with respect to the subject. If a certain Super-Existence of object X satisfies the subject, we say that this Super-Existence possesses attractiveness for the subject. The greater the degree of satisfaction, the greater its attractiveness. Conversely, if the Super-Existence fails to satisfy the subject, we say that it possesses resistance for the subject. Resistance may arise from execution costs, risks, or psychological burdens. In addition, we propose a formula for evaluating the subject's degree of satisfaction with an object. The subject may use this formula when making object selections. Nevertheless, this is only a very simple formula. We hope that more elegant and more accurate formulas will be developed in the future.

items.title: 论人工智能与跨学科语境中 agent 一词的汉语翻译问题 ——基于行动哲学视角 [On the Problem of Translating the Term “Agent” into Chinese in AI and Interdisciplinary Contexts: A Perspective from Philosophy of Action].
items.pub: 《逻辑学动态与评论》[Trends and Reviews in Logic] 5 (1).
items.venue: 《逻辑学动态与评论》[Trends and Reviews in Logic]
items.abstract: 本文立足于行动哲学视角探讨如何将英文中agent一词在人工智能及跨学科学术语境中翻译为汉语的问题。以新近提出的“行为体”译法为主要商榷对象，本文论述了其在具身性预设、谓述兼容性、范畴外延、双重语义对仗方面临的挑战，主张以“能动元”（意为“能动单元”）作为一般情况下的替代译法。此外，本文主张在该译法的基础上建立“全称补述+简称标注”的弹性翻译机制等配套措施，以适应不同学科和语境下的翻译需求，并且兼容某些已经通行的译法。例如，可将intelligent agent翻译为“智慧能动元”，简称“智能元”；如根据语境相关指涉对象还具有具身性，则用“体”取代“元”作为后缀，将embodied agent翻译为“能动体”，intelligent embodied agent翻译为“智慧具身能动元”或“智慧能动体”，简称“智能体”。 -/- [This paper addresses the translation of the English term “agent” into Chinese in the context of artificial intelligence and interdisciplinary fields, from the perspective of the philosophy of action. Taking the newly proposed translation “行为体” (xíng wéi tǐ) as the target of critical analysis, the paper examines challenges to it in terms of embodiment presupposition, predicate compatibility, category extension, and semantic parallelism. It advocates for “能动元” (néng dòng yuán) as a general alternative. In addition, on this basis, this paper proposes establishing corresponding measures, such as a flexible translation mechanism of “full description + abbreviation annotation”, to meet translation needs across different disciplines and contexts and to accommodate widely used translations. For example, “intelligent agent” can be translated as “智慧能动元” (zhì huì néng dòng yuán), abbreviated as “智能元” (zhì néng yuán). If, according to the context, the referent is also embodied, then let the suffix “元” (yuán) be replaced by “体” (tǐ), and “intelligent embodied agent” can be translated as “智慧具身能动元” (zhì huì jù shēn néng dòng yuán), abbreviated as “智能体” (zhì néng tǐ).].
